This is a narrative review article published in the journal Clocks & Sleep (September 6, 2023) by Ahmed S. BaHammam (King Saud University, Saudi Arabia) and Abdulrouf Pirzada (North Cumbria Integrated Care NHS, UK). The review examines the interplay between meal timing, circadian rhythms, clock genes, circadian hormones (cortisol and melatonin), and metabolic function. Key findings include:

- **Core thesis**: Synchronizing mealtimes with the body's natural circadian rhythms promotes metabolic health and prevents metabolic disorders. Consuming meals later in the day is associated with elevated prevalence of metabolic disorders, while early time-restricted eating (early breakfast and earlier dinner) improves blood glucose levels and substrate oxidation.

- **Circadian system**: The central biological clock is located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus, with peripheral clocks in all cells. Clocks rely on external signals (zeitgebers) for synchronization, primarily light for the SCN and food intake/glucocorticoids for peripheral clocks. Circadian misalignment is linked to impaired glucose tolerance, reduced insulin sensitivity, NAFLD, elevated proinflammatory cytokines, increased blood pressure, and decreased energy expenditure.

- **Clock genes**: BMAL1 and CLOCK stimulate transcription of Cry and Per genes in a feedback loop. Feeding rapidly impacts clock gene expression in animals; early breakfast activates the CLOCK:BMAL1 complex, improving insulin sensitivity, β-cell responsiveness, GLUT-4 activity, muscle glucose uptake, and post-meal incretin secretion (GLP-1, GLP-2, GIP).

- **Historical meal timing**: In the Middle Ages, the main meal was at midday (no electricity for evening cooking). Ancient Traditional Chinese Medicine (2,500+ years) recommends carbohydrate-rich meals between 0700-1100 with smaller meals later. Medieval England: dinner around noon-1pm, supper 4-6pm. Industrial Revolution shifted dinners later. NHANES data shows average dinner time at 6:24 p.m. and last eating episode at 8:18 p.m.; post-dinner snacks provide ~45% of total calorie consumption. Breakfast and lunch times shifted later over 40 years (1971-2010) while dinner timing stayed stable.

- **Hormonal patterns**: Ghrelin peaks at 8:00 a.m.; adiponectin peaks around 11:00 a.m. (activates AMPK, enhances fatty acid oxidation, improves insulin sensitivity). Lower evening adiponectin favors fat accumulation and lipogenesis. Cortisol peaks in the morning (~7-8 a.m.) and aligns with dawn.

- **Energy expenditure**: Resting energy expenditure is lowest during the resting phase; respiratory quotient highest in early active phase. Thermic effect of food (diet-induced thermogenesis) is lower in the evening than morning. A randomized crossover study comparing early eating (8am-6pm) vs. late eating (1pm-11pm) in overweight/obese adults found late eating led to higher hunger, reduced energy expenditure, decreased serum leptin, and increased ghrelin-leptin ratio, with adipose tissue gene expression changes favoring lipid storage and adipogenesis.

- **Animal studies**: Wistar rat experiments showed chocolate consumed at breakfast (active phase) facilitated SCN re-entrainment in jet lag models and reduced weight gain, while chocolate at dinner hindered re-synchronization and increased body weight.

- **Search methods**: PubMed and Google Scholar searched with 40+ keywords; 1598 papers identified, 139 met inclusion criteria (original human/animal studies and systematic reviews published up to May 31, 2023).

- **Caveat**: A consensus statement from the American Heart Association noted that while epidemiological evidence indicates potential adverse effects of late-day meals on cardiometabolic risk, clinical intervention studies are scant and insufficient for definitive conclusions.
args.key_excerpts: "Achieving synchronization between the central and peripheral body clocks is essential for ensuring optimal metabolic function."

# Does the time of day you eat matter?

[Healthy Eating for Kids](https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/wellness-and-prevention/healthy-eating-for-kids-and-teens)[Kids' and Teens' Health](https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/wellness-and-prevention/kids-and-teens-health)[Food and Nutrition](https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/wellness-and-prevention/food-and-nutrition)

#### What is Chrononutrition?

[Watch on YouTube - ![Image 2](https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/-/media/youtube-video-thumbnails/healthy-bytes-what-is-chrononutrition/chrononutrition-maxresdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sir4Q_XlC8E&ab_channel=JohnsHopkinsMedicine)

[](https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/wellness-and-prevention/does-the-time-of-day-you-eat-matter)
## What is Chrononutrition?

Chrononutrition is the timing of your food intake in relation to your circadian clock. The circadian clock system is a function of the body that controls all your biological activities. This includes when your awake and sleeping times, your metabolism and energy level, your body temperature, and when you feel hungry. This is all driven by something called your**circadian rhythm.**

## What controls your circadian rhythm?

Your circadian rhythm is normally controlled from inside your body by your genes and hormones, however there is something called _zeitgebers_. These are cues from outside your body that influence your circadian rhythm. Zeitgebers are cues given by the environment that reset the circadian rhythm. Zeitgeber sounds a little like a light saber! And just as a light saber carries power for the Jedi, so are zeitgebers when it comes to your circadian rhythm. Examples of the key zeitgebers in humans are environmental cues like sunlight, exercise, and eating.

## What happens when your circadian rhythm is disrupted?

Some research tells us that disrupting when you're feeding versus fasting or sleeping and waking will change your circadian rhythm.This alters how the body processes nutrients from the diet such as calories from sugars and fat. When the circadian clock gets off schedule, a person may use fewer calories. Eating meals at the wrong time can lead to weight gain, even if energy intake is not increased.Historically, people would eat during daylight hours and sleep during night time hours, however in our present day, this may not always be true. Our lifestyle and dietary patterns have also changed with more meals eaten outside the home or family setting and more irregular eating patterns, including breakfast skipping and late-night eating. Irregularity in meals (such as eating at inconsistent times, skipping meals), the frequency of meals (the number of meals), and timing (when you eat) all influence your circadian clock and metabolism.

## Take Home Messages:

*   Eat a healthy breakfast in the morning.
*   An earlier dinner is best and make this the last food intake of the day.
*   Stay away from late-night eating.
*   Remember that your body operates on a 24-hour clock but food is best consumed starting in the morning to the early evening hours which are 5:00-7:00 PM for optimal health!

args.summary: This is a Johns Hopkins Medicine health article titled "Does the time of day you eat matter?" that explores the concept of chrononutrition — the timing of food intake in relation to the body's circadian clock. The circadian clock system controls all biological activities including sleep/wake cycles, metabolism, energy level, body temperature, and hunger, all driven by the circadian rhythm. The article explains that circadian rhythm is controlled internally by genes and hormones, but is also influenced by external cues called "zeitgebers" (environmental cues like sunlight, exercise, and eating that reset the circadian rhythm). Research indicates that disrupting feeding/fasting or sleeping/waking patterns changes the circadian rhythm and alters how the body processes nutrients like calories from sugars and fat. When the circadian clock gets off schedule, a person may use fewer calories, and eating meals at the wrong time can lead to weight gain even without increased energy intake. Modern lifestyle changes—including irregular eating patterns, breakfast skipping, and late-night eating—negatively influence the circadian clock and metabolism. The article's key take-home messages recommend eating a healthy breakfast, having an earlier dinner as the last food intake of the day, avoiding late-night eating, and consuming food between morning and early evening hours (5:00–7:00 PM) for optimal health. The page also promotes the Healthy Weight Initiative at Johns Hopkins All Children's Hospital in St. Petersburg, Florida, which offers a multi-level approach to pediatric obesity including the Healthy Steps clinic.
args.key_excerpts: "Chrononutrition is the timing of your food intake in relation to your circadian clock."

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: How To Travel the World Without Jet lag ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2829880

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article titled "How To Travel the World Without Jet Lag" by Charmane I. Eastman and Helen J. Burgess from the Biological Rhythms Research Laboratory at Rush University Medical Center, published in Sleep Med Clin (2009 Jun 1;4(2):241, doi: 10.1016/j.jsmc.2009.02.006, PMID: 20204161, PMCID: PMC2829880). The article provides evidence-based guidance on minimizing or avoiding jet lag through circadian rhythm manipulation using bright light and melatonin.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Jet lag symptoms include difficulty sleeping, daytime sleepiness, impaired performance, fatigue, irritability, disorientation, depressed mood, and GI disturbance. In 2007, over 31 million US residents flew overseas (12M to Europe, 7M to Asia). Frequent jet travel has long-term health risks including cognitive deficits, temporal lobe atrophy, menstrual cycle disturbances, increased cardiovascular disease and type II diabetes risk, and higher cancer risk in flight attendants. Chronic jet lag in mice accelerates tumor development.
- Jet lag results from misalignment between the endogenous circadian clock (SCN) and the destination time zone. Flying east requires phase advance; flying west requires phase delay. Since the human circadian clock's free-running period (tau) is slightly longer than 24h, phase delays occur faster than phase advances (92 min/day delay vs 57 min/day advance after real flights; up to 144 min/day delay vs 93 min/day advance with bright light in lab studies).
- Antidromic (wrong-direction) re-entrainment is common after eastward travel crossing 8+ time zones. In one study, 7 of 8 subjects flying 11 time zones east re-entrained by phase delaying instead of advancing.
- The light phase response curve (PRC) shows bright light phase advances when applied late in sleep/after Tmin (temperature minimum) and phase delays when applied early in sleep/before Tmin. Melatonin pills (3mg) produce max phase advances when taken ~5h before DLMO (dim light melatonin onset), or 7.5h before sleep onset, or 12h before Tmin; 0.5mg dose best taken ~2h before DLMO, 4.5h before sleep, or 9h before Tmin. Both light (3,500 lux from light boxes) and melatonin produce roughly equivalent phase advances. Melatonin in the US is a dietary supplement, not FDA-approved for jet lag.
- PRCs have "dead zones" (times of reduced sensitivity). The melatonin dead zone corresponds to times when endogenous melatonin is being secreted.
- Recommended jet travel plan for flying west: use bright light box 2h before bed for 2 nights before flight, delay sleep 1-2.5h/day, avoid bright light after waking, phase delay ~1-2h/day, keep sleep aligned with clock to avoid jet lag.
- Recommended plan for flying east: pre-flight phase advancing by taking 0.5mg melatonin 4.5h before sleep onset, going to bed 1h earlier daily, and getting morning bright light. After landing, continue bright light in morning and melatonin in afternoon, advancing sleep 1h/day (not more—2h/day advance shows no additional benefit and causes misalignment). Alternatively, especially for night owls, phase delay before flying east even across 6-7 time zones.
- Drugs (caffeine, hypnotics, large melatonin doses) only mask symptoms of jet lag; they do not fix the underlying circadian misalignment, which can take a week or more to resolve.
- Even 1-2 days of preflight shifting helps reduce subsequent jet lag. Light boxes with larger illuminated areas are recommended; cool white fluorescent boxes produce same phase shifts as blue-enriched boxes. Outdoor sunlight (10,000-100,000 lux) is more intense than light boxes (3,500 lux) and generally more effective.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Jet travel across multiple time zones produces jet lag, which includes difficulty initiating or maintaining nighttime sleep, daytime sleepiness, decreased alertness, loss of concentration, impaired performance, fatigue, irritability, disorientation, depressed mood and gastrointestinal disturbance."
</key_excerpts>



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


--- SOURCE 2: Frontiers | Interventions to Minimize Jet Lag After Westward and Eastward Flight ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2019.00927/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed opinion article published in Frontiers in Physiology (31 July 2019, Vol. 10) by Gregory D. Roach and Charli Sargent of the Appleton Institute for Behavioural Science, Central Queensland University, Adelaide, Australia. The manuscript provides evidence-based recommendations for minimizing jet lag after westward and eastward transmeridian flights, with specific application to athletes traveling to the Tokyo 2020 Olympic Games.

Key content points:

1. **Travel fatigue vs. jet lag**: Travel fatigue refers to symptoms during/immediately after long flights (fatigue, disorientation, headache) caused by sleep loss, dehydration, hypoxia, and cabin discomfort. Jet lag refers to symptoms occurring days after flights across 3+ time zones (headache, irritability, daytime sleepiness, difficulty sleeping, poor performance, gastrointestinal issues) caused by desynchrony between the circadian system and local time cues.

2. **Circadian system basics**: The central circadian pacemaker is located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus with a period of ~24.2 hours. Sunlight is the most powerful zeitgeber (time-giver). Melatonin onset occurs ~2 h before habitual bedtime, CBTmin (daily minimum core body temperature) occurs ~7 h after melatonin onset, and CBTmax occurs ~12 h after CBTmin.

3. **Direction of travel matters**: Westward flight requires a phase delay (shifting backward/later); eastward flight requires a phase advance (shifting forward/earlier). The experience of jet lag differs markedly by direction.

4. **Phase response curves (PRCs)**: Light exposure in the ~12 h prior to CBTmin causes phase delays; ~12 h after CBTmin causes phase advances. Larger shifts occur with longer, brighter, and bluer light. Melatonin in late afternoon/early evening (a few hours before endogenous melatonin onset) causes phase advances; morning ingestion causes phase delays. A 3.0 mg dose produces more reliable phase shifts than 0.5 mg, though similar magnitude. Exercise has phase-shifting properties, but its PRC was established under moderate light conditions, so a light-independent PRC remains to be established.

5. **Sunlight guidance**: Indiscriminate sunlight exposure generally aids adaptation after westward travel but can be counterproductive after eastward travel (e.g., after 8 h east from LA to London, sunlight provides contradictory delay and advance signals).

6. **Adaptation schedules**: The manuscript provides detailed schedules (Figures 4 and 5) for using light exposure/avoidance and 3.0 mg melatonin ingestion to adapt to time zone shifts of 3, 6, 9, and 12 h east/west. Examples for Tokyo travel include: 3 h west (e.g., Wellington to Tokyo): partial adaptation day 1, complete day 4; 6 h west (Anchorage to Tokyo): partial day 2, complete day 6; 9 h west (Minneapolis to Tokyo): partial day 3, complete day 7; 3 h east (Dhaka to Tokyo): partial day 1, complete day 4; 6 h east (Doha to Tokyo): partial day 3, complete day 6; 9 h east (London to Tokyo): partial day 5, complete day 8; 12 h (Buenos Aires to Tokyo): delay schedule partial day 6/complete day 10, advance schedule partial day 7/complete day 10.

7. **Key assumptions**: Schedules assume a normal sleep period of 23:00–07:00 (CBTmin ~04:00), main sleep at same local time as normal time zone, and arrival at 13:00 local time.

8. **Pre-travel/during-travel adaptation**: To delay prior to westward travel (3–4 days before), gradually move bedtime later (30–60 min/day), maximize evening light, minimize morning light, take 3.0 mg melatonin 1 h after rising. To advance prior to eastward travel, gradually move bedtime earlier, minimize evening light, maximize morning light, take 3.0 mg melatonin 6.5 h before bed.

9. **Evidence base**: Phase response curves form the primary basis. Computer simulations support light schedule efficacy. Laboratory trials show light and melatonin independently shift the circadian system, and their effects are additive when combined. A meta-analysis of 10 field studies (Herxheimer & Petrie, 2002) shows melatonin interventions are effective at shifting the body clock and reducing jet lag. Field evidence for light-based interventions is equivocal, and combined light/melatonin interventions have not yet been tested in field settings.

10. **Practical notes**: Light exposure during daytime should be outdoor sunlight without sunglasses; after sunset, use bright indoor light, light box, or light-emitting glasses. Light avoidance involves staying inside with lights off/dim (naps limited to 1 h); wrap-around sunglasses if daytime outdoor avoidance is unavoidable. Athletes should ensure melatonin is not a prohibited substance and is from a reputable supplier.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The circadian system cannot immediately entrain to the timing of zeitgebers in a new time zone, so after long-haul flights to the west or east, the circadian system is initially aligned with the timing of zeitgebers at the point of departure rather than zeitgebers at the new location. A period of desynchrony follows while the circadian system is entrained to the timing of zeitgebers in the new time zone—and it is this period of desynchrony that gives rise to the symptoms of jet lag."

"Light exposure, per se, does not cause the circadian system to align with the new time zone. Rather, light exposure shifts the timing of the body clock either backward (delay) or forward (advance), as required after westward and eastward travel, respectively."

"Exogenous melatonin is both a chronobiotic and an hypnotic, i.e., it can shift the timing of the circadian system, but it can also make it easier to fall asleep and/or stay asleep."

"To delay the circadian system in the 3–4 days prior to westward travel, gradually move bedtime and get-up time later (i.e., 30–60 min per day), maximize evening light exposure, minimize morning light exposure, and take 3.0 mg of melatonin 1 h after rising from bed. To advance the circadian system in the 3–4 days prior to eastward travel, gradually move bedtime and get-up time earlier (i.e., 30–60 min per day), minimize evening light exposure, maximize morning light exposure, and take 3.0 mg of melatonin 6.5 h before bed."

"A meta-analysis of 10 field studies examining the efficacy of melatonin-based interventions indicates that they are effective at shifting the body clock and at reducing subjective ratings of jet lag (Herxheimer and Petrie, 2002). To date, the efficacy of combined light/melatonin interventions has not been assessed in field-based settings, so this is a critical next step for the advancement of knowledge in this field."
</key_excerpts>



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


--- SOURCE 3: Advancing Circadian Rhythms Before Eastward Flight: A Strategy to Prevent or Reduce Jet Lag ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1249488

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article from the journal Sleep (published Jan 1, 2005; PMCID: PMC1249488; PMID: 15700719) by Charmane I. Eastman and colleagues from Rush University Medical Center (Chicago, IL) and Brown University. The study tested a strategy to prevent or reduce jet lag from eastward flight by phase-advancing circadian rhythms before travel.

STUDY OBJECTIVE: To develop a practical pre-eastward flight treatment that advances circadian rhythms as much as possible without misaligning them with sleep.

DESIGN & METHODS: A between-subjects design compared two groups of young healthy adults (26 total: 11 men, 15 women; ages 22-36). One group had their sleep schedule advanced 1 hour per day, the other 2 hours per day, over 3 treatment days. Both groups received intermittent morning bright light (four 0.5-hour pulses of ~5000 lux separated by 0.5 hours of dim light <60 lux, totaling 3.5 hours daily) using light boxes. Circadian phase was measured via dim light melatonin onset (DLMO) from saliva samples taken before and after treatment. Subjects completed sleep logs, symptom questionnaires (Stanford Sleepiness Scale and Columbia Jet Lag Scale), and wore wrist actigraphy monitors.

KEY RESULTS: 
- The 2-hours-per-day group showed a slightly larger phase advance than the 1-hour-per-day group (medians of 1.9 vs 1.4 hours; means of 1.8 vs 1.5 hours), but this difference was NOT statistically significant.
- By treatment day 3, circadian rhythms became misaligned relative to sleep in the 2-hour group, and subjects had difficulty falling asleep (increased sleep-onset latency and reduced sleep efficiency), while the 1-hour group did not experience this misalignment.
- The 2-hours-per-day group did slightly better on symptom questionnaires, but in general sleep disturbance and other side effects were small in both groups.
- On treatment day 3, the bright light started about 1 hour after the temperature minimum (Tmin) for the 1-hour group but about 1 hour BEFORE the Tmin for the 2-hour group—light before the Tmin can phase-delay rather than advance.

CONCLUSIONS: A gradually advancing sleep schedule combined with intermittent morning bright light can effectively advance circadian rhythms before eastward flight and theoretically prevent or reduce jet lag. Given the morning light treatment used, advancing sleep 2 hours per day is NOT better than 1 hour per day because it is too fast for the circadian rhythm advance, causing misalignment. The article provides a diagram (Figure 6) showing a practical preflight schedule: advancing wake time 1 hour per day with 2-3 hours of intermittent morning bright light, starting about a week before travel (for a Pacific-to-Europe flight), so the traveler arrives already phase-shifted to the destination time zone.

BACKGROUND CONTEXT: Jet lag results from temporary misalignment between the endogenous circadian clock and the destination's sleep/wake schedule. Reentrainment is slower after eastward flight because the human free-running period (tau) is slightly longer than 24 hours, making phase advances harder than phase delays (delays proceed about 3x faster than advances). Early estimates from flights are ~92 min/day for delays (westward) vs ~57 min/day for advances (eastward). Eastward travelers risk "antidromic reentrainment" (shifting the wrong direction) depending on light exposure timing after landing. Preflight phase advancing reduces this risk and can reduce time needed for reentrainment after landing.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the first of two articles authored by an American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) Task Force reviewing the scientific literature on the evaluation and treatment of circadian rhythm sleep disorders (CRSDs) using evidence-based medicine methodology. Published in SLEEP journal (2007;30(11):1460-1483), this first part reviews general principles of circadian biology underlying clinical evaluation and treatment, then reports evidence on shift work disorder (SWD) and jet lag disorder (JLD). The second part will cover advanced sleep phase disorder (ASPD), delayed sleep phase disorder (DSPD), free-running disorder (FRD), and irregular sleep-wake rhythm (ISWR).

Key findings:
- Six CRSDs are recognized in the ICSD-2: delayed sleep phase type, advanced sleep phase type, irregular sleep-wake phase type, free-running type, jet lag type, and shift work type.

- Circadian science principles: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) generates circadian rhythms; intrinsic period is slightly longer than 24 hours; entrainment depends on light-dark cycle (zeitgebers). Novel melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cell photoreceptors are most sensitive to blue light. Light intensity >1000 lux generally needed to treat CRSDs, though lower intensities can work under special circumstances. Light exposure in morning resets pacemaker earlier; evening light resets later. Melatonin PRC is ~180 degrees out of phase with light PRC; melatonin threshold for chronobiological effect is ~50 pg/mL.
- Methodology: MEDLINE searched through October 2006 using 13 search terms (2,084 total citations); studies graded using Oxford System for Evidence-Based Medicine; PICO evidence tables constructed; inclusion required at least 8 subjects (except for rare ASPD and FRD cases where single case reports were accepted).

URL: https://healthcare.utah.edu/healthfeed/2025/05/jet-lagged-get-your-sleep-schedule-back-track-after-travel

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from University of Utah Health explains how to recover from jet lag and get your sleep schedule back on track after travel. Jet lag occurs when traveling across three or more time zones (especially west to east) and disrupts the body's circadian rhythm. It is technically a temporary sleep disorder that usually resolves within a few days. Symptoms include extreme fatigue, insomnia, irritability, nausea, headache, and difficulty concentrating.

According to Kelly Baron, PhD, a clinical psychologist specializing in behavioral sleep medicine at University of Utah Health, the circadian rhythm cannot be reset like a watch, and the more time zones crossed, the longer it takes to catch up. The general rule is about one day of adjustment per time zone crossed. Traveling west is easier than traveling east because the internal clock is slightly longer than 24 hours, making it easier to stay up later than to wake up earlier.

The article provides specific strategies for before, during, and after travel:
- **Before:** Gradually shift sleep schedule 30 minutes earlier per day (if traveling east) or 30 minutes later (if traveling west), working up to 1-2 hours. A melatonin supplement can help.
- **During:** Sleep on the plane if it will be morning at your destination; stay hydrated but avoid caffeine and alcohol; move around during waking hours.
- **After:** Follow local time for eating and sleeping, get natural sunlight exposure during the day (keep curtains open, dim lights and avoid screens before bedtime), limit naps to 30 minutes maximum, and resume a consistent daily routine.

Baron encourages patients that disrupted sleep from travel is normal and typically resolves within a few days, recommending daytime sunlight and activity. The article also links to related sleep resources at University of Utah Health and related articles on daylight saving time, difficulty falling asleep, septoplasty and snoring, bedroom temperature, and baby sleep safety.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"One of the factors that controls our sleep is our circadian rhythm, and it can't just be reset like you would a watch," says Kelly Baron, PhD, a clinical psychologist who specializes in behavioral sleep medicine at University of Utah Health. "When you change time zones, you experience a misalignment between your light/dark cycle. The more time zones you cross, the longer it takes you to catch up."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a blog post by Robin Esrock, a bestselling author, speaker, and TV host who has traveled to over 120 countries, published on his website robinesrock.com on January 9, 2026. The article, titled "How to Nap When You Have Jet-Lag," provides practical advice on managing jet lag through strategic napping and other techniques, drawn from the author's personal experience (he wrote it while dealing with jet lag after returning from Brazil).

Key tips include:
- **A nap is not sleeping**: It should be a strategic, controlled intervention with boundaries and an exit plan, not a full rest period.
- **The magic window is 20–40 minutes**: 20 minutes is safe, 30 is ideal, 40 is risky; anything longer causes a "Nap Hangover."
- **Timing matters**: Nap between 1pm and 3pm local time; napping after 4pm is dangerous.
- **Stay semi-dressed** and nap on top of the bed to stay in "day mode."
- **Keep some light in** — don't nap in total darkness, as it's a sleep cue that confuses your circadian rhythm.
- **Caffeine trick**: Drink coffee right before the nap; caffeine kicks in 20–30 minutes later, right as you wake.
- **Walk it out**: Sometimes the best remedy is no nap at all — go outside, get light in your eyes, and eat something healthy.
- **The goal is bedtime, not comfort**: Every decision should funnel you toward a normal local bedtime.
- **Melatonin**: Use sparingly in low doses (1–3mg max) at target bedtime, not for napping.

The post also includes nine key facts about jet lag: (1) jet lag is about light, not lack of sleep; (2) flying east is harder than west due to the body's slightly longer-than-24-hour circadian cycle; (3) jet lag measurably slows reaction time like mild intoxication; (4) it affects digestion via the gut's own circadian clock; (5) morning light advances the clock (good for eastbound travel) while evening light delays it (good for westbound); (6) short naps help while long naps delay recovery; (7) melatonin timing matters more than dosage; (8) athletes and pilots show performance drops for days after travel; (9) jet lag increases injury risk and accident rates.

The webpage also includes site navigation, a sidebar with blog archive listings dating back to 2012, an extensive category list, and a newsletter subscription prompt. Copyright belongs to Esrock World Media 2005-2026.

- Natural adjustment without intervention is ~1 time zone per day (eastward ~1 hour/day, westward ~1.5 hours/day)

EASTWARD PROTOCOL (e.g., US→Europe/Asia):
- Pre-flight (3-5 days before, optional for 5+ zones): go to bed 30-60 min earlier nightly, take 0.5-1mg melatonin 1 hour earlier, which reduces jet lag severity by 30-40% and cuts adjustment time 1-2 days

TROUBLESHOOTING: Can't sleep at bedtime = take melatonin earlier, increase dose, ensure darkness. Waking at 3-4 AM = do NOT take middle-of-night melatonin (delays adjustment); get bright light at real wake time. Severe fatigue >5 days = consult healthcare provider.

--- SOURCE 4: Coffee naps might be the weirdest—and smartest—way to recharge | National Geographic ---
URL: https://www.nationalgeographic.com/health/article/caffeine-nap-explained

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This National Geographic article (published September 10, 2025, by Leah Worthington) explores the science behind "caffeine naps"—drinking coffee immediately before a short nap (about 20-30 minutes)—and whether this combination offers greater cognitive benefits than either strategy alone.

The article explains the biological mechanism: adenosine, a neuromodulator that builds up in the brain as cells burn energy, binds to receptors (A1, A2A, A2B, A3) and slows neural activity, causing sleepiness. Caffeine acts as an adenosine antagonist, blocking these receptors and keeping nerve cells firing, which creates alertness. This "yin-yang relationship" means caffeine consumption leads the body to generate more receptors over time, causing tolerance and dependence.

Key research findings discussed include:
- Caffeine takes roughly 20-30 minutes to take effect, which conveniently matches the duration of an ideal short nap (napping longer than 30-60 minutes leads to deep sleep and lingering "sleep inertia" or brain fog).
- A 1997 study observed improved driving ability among participants who combined caffeine with a short nap; a 2001 study described caffeine's benefits in reducing post-nap sleepiness.
- A 2020 pilot study by Professor Siobhan Banks (University of South Australia) found that 200 mg of caffeine immediately before a 30-minute rest reduced fatigue and boosted cognitive performance.

Experts quoted include endocrinologist Scott Rivkees (Brown University), sleep researcher Seiji Nishino (Stanford), Siobhan Banks, and Nora D. Volkow (director of the National Institute on Drug Abuse). The article notes limitations: most studies involved healthy volunteers in their 20s and 30s, results may not apply to middle-aged/older adults or those with sleep disorders, and individual sensitivity to caffeine and napping varies. Experts caution that caffeine naps are not a substitute for proper sleep. Banks recommends at-home experimentation starting with smaller doses.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"When activated, [the receptors] slow nerve transmission and release of neurotransmitters," says Scott Rivkees, a pediatric endocrinologist and professor at Brown's School of Public Health.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: How to Beat Jet Lag and Get Better Sleep While Traveling – Lifestyle Medicine ---
URL: https://lifestylemedicine.stanford.edu/sleep-traveling-jet-lag

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Stanford Lifestyle Medicine article (published October 21, 2025, by Sharon Brock, MS, MEd) provides expert advice from sleep physician Dr. Cheri D. Mah, MD, MS, co-head of the Stanford Lifestyle Medicine Restorative Sleep pillar, on how to beat jet lag and improve sleep while traveling.

**Key strategies by phase:**

**Before the flight:** It takes approximately one day per time zone for the inner clock to shift. Travelers should proactively adjust their sleep schedule days before departure — going to bed and waking up one hour earlier per day if traveling eastward, and the opposite (one hour later) if traveling westward. It's also essential to avoid starting the trip sleep-deprived.

**During the flight:** Create a dark, quiet, cool, and comfortable environment using eye masks and earplugs. Stay hydrated with water while avoiding alcohol, caffeine, and sugary beverages. Avoid high-action or horror movies; choose relaxing entertainment instead. Adjust sleeping and eating times to the destination's time zone during the flight and bring snacks in case meals are missed while asleep.

**After the flight:** For eastward travel, get sun exposure and drink caffeine in the morning, avoid light in the evening, and consider taking melatonin 30–60 minutes before the new bedtime for the first couple of days. If experiencing an energy lull, take a 20–30 minute power nap, exercise, or use caffeine (at least 10 hours before the new bedtime).

**First Night Effect:** Research shows the left side of the brain stays more alert in new environments as a protective mechanism. To counteract this, Dr. Mah recommends returning to the same hotel/hotel chain, or bringing familiar items from home (eye mask, lavender spray, photos) to cue the brain that it's time for sleep.

**Travel Sleep Kit packing list:** Eye mask, earplugs or noise-cancelling headphones, travel pillow (with pillowcases from home), melatonin, curtain clips, light-blocking stickers, and a journal/pen for pre-bed to-do lists. Optional items include a white noise machine, air filter, and humidifier (30–50% relative humidity is ideal for sleep).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Most people just jump on an airplane and then try to adjust their body clock after they arrive, which is not really a plan," says Dr. Mah. "Instead, we can be more proactive in our thinking about sleep when we travel and strategically make adjustments."

--- SOURCE 6: Grasp ---
URL: https://paths.grasp.study/modules/09ba6598-0dc1-4c08-bf1b-f47c2dbca21a/lessons/24b47902-a9cf-4304-bb41-79aaf31778d3

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the fifth lesson in the "Foundations of Sleep Science" module, focused on the **Two-Process Model of Sleep Regulation**, a cornerstone framework in modern sleep science first proposed by Swiss sleep researcher Alexander Borbély. The model explains that alertness or sleepiness at any moment results from the interaction between two forces: **Process S** (homeostatic sleep drive), which builds pressure to sleep like an hourglass through the accumulation of adenosine from the moment of waking, and **Process C** (circadian rhythm), which not only promotes sleep at night but generates a strong alerting signal during the day to counteract rising sleep pressure.

Key concepts covered include:
- **The daily push-and-pull**: The brain actively works to keep a person awake during the day by using Process C to fight against ever-increasing Process S.
- **The "wake maintenance zone"**: Process C reaches its peak strength in the early evening to counteract very high sleep pressure, explaining the "second wind" phenomenon where people feel alert a few hours before bedtime despite feeling tired in the late afternoon.
- **The "sleep gate"**: Sleep onset requires two steps: (1) high sleep pressure (Process S) built up from being awake, and (2) withdrawal of the alerting signal (Process C) as the biological night begins (signaled by darkness and melatonin release from the SCN). This withdrawal allows unopposed sleep pressure to take over, causing a rapid transition into sleep.
- **Graphical model**: Process C is a smooth, wave-like circadian rhythm; Process S rises during wakefulness and falls during sleep. Sleep is most likely when the distance between S and C is minimal and C is descending.
- **Sleep deprivation**: When a person stays awake through the night, Process S continues to build far beyond its normal peak while Process C continues its 24-hour cycle, creating an enormous gap representing overwhelming biological pressure to sleep—the scientific representation of "sleep debt."

A practical example (2 PM vs. 7 PM nap) illustrates the model: at 2 PM, a natural dip in Process C makes napping easier despite only moderate sleep pressure; by 7 PM, high sleep pressure is counteracted by Process C's near-daily peak in the "wake maintenance zone," making sleep difficult.

The lesson includes two resources: a YouTube video ('The 2-Process Model of Sleep' from The BioClock Studio) and a reading from The Better Sleep Clinic on circadian rhythm. The next lesson will cover **zeitgebers** ("time-givers")—environmental cues that entrain the circadian rhythm, focusing primarily on light but also touching on temperature and meal timing.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The Two-Process Model, first proposed by Swiss sleep researcher Alexander Borbély, posits that your level of alertness or sleepiness at any given moment is the result of the interaction between your homeostatic sleep pressure (Process S) and your circadian alerting signal (Process C)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: Sleep homeostasis and the circadian clock: Do the circadian pacemaker and the sleep homeostat influence each other’s functioning?☆ ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6584681

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article by Tom Deboer (Leiden University Medical Center, The Netherlands) published in Neurobiology of Sleep and Circadian Rhythms (2018; PMC6584681) examining whether the circadian clock and the sleep homeostat directly influence each other's functioning. The paper reviews evidence from behavioral and EEG-determined sleep studies, electrophysiology, gene knockout mouse models, and mathematical modeling.

Key findings:
- Sleep is regulated by two processes: a homeostatic process (process S) and a circadian process (process C), as formalized in the two-process model by Borbely (1982) and Daan et al. (1984).
- The master circadian pacemaker is located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus, which generates rhythms via transcription-translational feedback loops involving 5-7 core clock genes.
- Sleep homeostasis is demonstrated through EEG slow-wave activity (SWA) in NREM sleep, which increases with prior waking duration, decreases over sleep, and is elevated after sleep deprivation. Slow-wave energy (SWE) lost during sleep deprivation is virtually fully recovered.
- The evidence for direct influence of the circadian clock on sleep homeostatic mechanisms is sparse and limited. Clock gene knockout studies (Cry1/Cry2 double knockouts, Clock mutants, Bmal1, Npas2) show altered sleep homeostasis, and human PER3 polymorphisms affect EEG/behavioral sleep homeostasis markers without affecting circadian parameters, suggesting clock genes play roles in sleep homeostasis outside the SCN.
- The strongest evidence that sleep homeostatic mechanisms influence circadian clock functioning comes from sleep deprivation experiments showing attenuated phase shifts of circadian rhythms to light pulses when sleep homeostatic pressure is high—suggesting the circadian clock is less susceptible to light when sleep pressure is high.
- A strong central clock induces deep sleep, which strengthens clock function; weakening one impairs the other.
- Practical implications: shift work and jet lag adaptation may be improved by introducing nap schedules to reduce sleep pressure, thereby increasing clock susceptibility to light.
- Core body temperature and melatonin release (circadian markers) do not change with sleep pressure, but longer sleep deprivations including a second night are needed to confirm whether this holds.

The review concludes that the two processes act independently on downstream physiology but that there is more evidence for sleep homeostatic mechanisms influencing circadian clock functioning than vice versa.
</summary>

The data suggest that the circadian clock is less susceptible to light when sleep pressure is high."

--- SOURCE 9: Sleep Drive and Your Body Clock ---
URL: https://www.sleepfoundation.org/circadian-rhythm/sleep-drive-and-your-body-clock

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Sleep Drive and Your Body Clock

This article from the Sleep Foundation, written by Eric Suni and medically reviewed by Dr. Anis Rehman, MD, explains how two body systems regulate sleep drive (the body's need for sleep): sleep/wake homeostasis and the circadian rhythm.

**Key Concepts:**
- **Sleep/Wake Homeostasis**: Balances the need for sleep ("sleep drive" or "sleep pressure") with the need for wakefulness. Sleep drive increases the longer one is awake, and diminishes during sleep. If it worked alone, alertness would decline steadily throughout the day, but it doesn't due to the circadian rhythm.
- **Circadian Rhythm**: Approximates homeostasis in coordination with environmental cues like sunlight. Alertness dips and rises throughout each 24-hour period. On average, people feel most tired just after midnight and during an "afternoon slump" after lunchtime. Artificial light exposure outside daytime hours can disrupt the circadian rhythm and sleep drive.
- **The Suprachiasmatic Nucleus (SCN)**: A group of cells in the hypothalamus that controls the circadian biological clock. When the eyes perceive light, the retinas send signals to the SCN, which triggers hormone production. In the morning, sunlight causes body temperature to rise and cortisol to be released (increasing alertness). In the evening, melatonin levels rise and body temperature lowers, promoting sleep. Evening exposure to light (especially blue light from electronic devices) suppresses melatonin and makes it harder to fall asleep.

**Age-Related Changes in Sleep Drive:**
- **Infancy**: Newborns require up to 18 hours of sleep in multiple short periods. They develop a circadian rhythm around 4-6 months of age.
- **Adolescence**: Up to 16% of teenagers experience sleep phase delay, with melatonin levels rising later in the evening. This makes it hard to fall asleep before 11:00 p.m., which conflicts with early school start times and prevents teens from getting the recommended 8-10 hours of sleep per night.
- **Senior years**: The internal sleep clock loses consistency with aging. Older adults tend to become tired earlier in the evening and wake earlier in the morning, resulting in less overall sleep and increased risk of cognitive decline. Those with Alzheimer's, dementia, or neurodegenerative diseases experience even more severe changes.

**Disruptions to Sleep Drive:**
- Daylight Saving Time changes, jet lag, and shift work can throw off circadian rhythm, causing insomnia, daytime sleepiness, and difficulty focusing.
- Shift work disorder can cause insomnia, excessive daytime sleepiness, mood problems, and increased risk of on-the-job accidents or injury. Shift workers may also experience hormonal imbalances related to cortisol, testosterone, and melatonin.

**Recommendations:** While changing circadian rhythm is difficult, sleep drive can be adjusted by following regular sleep and wake times, allowing 7 or more hours of sleep nightly, adjusting meal times and caffeine intake, and using bright light therapy (for night shift workers). If sleep issues persist after lifestyle changes, consult a doctor.

The article includes 9 cited references from PubMed sources on topics including light's effect on circadian physiology, sleep phase delay in youth, circadian rhythms and neurodegenerative diseases, and shift work-related injuries.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Sleep drive, or the need for sleep, increases the longer you are awake. Aging, hormone imbalances, and disruptions to your circadian rhythm can increase your sleep drive."
</key_excerpts>

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: Interventions to Minimize Jet Lag After Westward and ... ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2019.00927/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed opinion article published in Frontiers in Physiology (July 31, 2019, Volume 10, DOI: 10.3389/fphys.2019.00927) by Gregory D. Roach and Charli Sargent of the Appleton Institute for Behavioural Science, Central Queensland University, Adelaide, Australia. The paper provides practical recommendations for minimizing jet lag after transmeridian flight, specifically aimed at athletes traveling to the Tokyo 2020 Olympic Games, though applicable to all travelers.

**Key Concepts:**
- Distinguishes between travel fatigue (symptoms during/immediately after flight: fatigue, disorientation, headache, caused by sleep loss, dehydration, hypoxia, discomfort of aircraft cabins) and jet lag (symptoms in days after flight across 3+ time zones: headache, irritability, daytime sleepiness, poor sleep, poor mental/physical performance, GI dysfunction, caused by mismatch between the circadian system aligned to departure time zone and desired sleep/wake timing at destination).
- Human circadian rhythms (~24h) are generated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus with a period of ~24.2h, entrained by zeitgebers; sunlight is the most powerful zeitgeber.

**Phase Response Curves (PRCs):**
- Light: Exposure in ~12h prior to CBTmin causes phase delay; ~12h after CBTmin causes phase advance; largest shifts in the 3–6h either side of CBTmin. Larger shifts with longer duration, higher intensity, and shorter (blue) wavelengths.
- Melatonin: Late afternoon/early evening ingestion causes phase advance; morning ingestion causes phase delay. A 3.0mg (pharmacological) dose produces more reliable phase shifts than 0.5mg (physiological) dose, though similar in size.
- Exercise: 1h moderate-intensity bout shifts circadian system (delay ~9h before CBTmin, advance ~9h after), but PRC established under 50 lux light so effects independent of light not yet confirmed.
- Light and melatonin effects are additive (especially for advances); light and exercise are not additive, so exercise excluded from guides.

**Direction of Travel:**
- Westward flight: circadian system runs ahead of local time; must delay (shift later). Example: London to Los Angeles (8h west), CBTmin at 20:00 in LA initially; person feels sleepy in evening, difficulty staying asleep.
- Eastward flight: circadian system runs behind local time; must advance (shift earlier). Example: LA to London (8h east), CBTmin at midday; sleepy late morning/early afternoon, difficulty falling asleep at night.
- Indiscriminate sunlight exposure helps adaptation after westward travel but can be counterproductive after eastward travel (provides contradictory signals). After eastward travel, avoid sunlight before midday and maximize exposure 3–6h after midday.

**Adaptation Schedules (based on assumed sleep 23:00–07:00, CBTmin ~04:00, arrival at 13:00 local):**
Westward:
- 3h west (e.g., Wellington NZ to Tokyo): delay 3h; partial adaptation day 1, complete day 4
- 6h west (e.g., Anchorage to Tokyo): delay 6h; partial day 2, complete day 6
- 9h west (e.g., Minneapolis to Tokyo): delay 9h; partial day 3, complete day 7
- 12h west (e.g., Buenos Aires to Tokyo): partial day 6, complete day 10 (using delay, which is favored given ~24.2h natural period)
Eastward:
- 3h east (e.g., Dhaka to Tokyo): advance 3h; partial day 1, complete day 4
- 6h east (e.g., Doha to Tokyo): advance 6h; partial day 3, complete day 6
- 9h east (e.g., London to Tokyo): advance 9h; partial day 5, complete day 8
- 12h east: advance schedule partial day 7, complete day 10

**Practical Implementation Notes:**
- Light exposure during daytime: be outside in sunlight without sunglasses; after sunset: bright indoor light, light box, or light-emitting glasses.
- Light avoidance: inside with lights off/dim; naps limited to 1h; wrap-around sunglasses with minimal light transmission if outside unavoidable.
- Complete adaptation = CBTmin occurs at same time as pre-travel (04:00); partial adaptation = CBTmin occurs during night-time sleep (practical goal, greatly reduces jet lag symptoms).
- If athletes use melatonin, ensure it's not a prohibited substance under relevant drug code and sourced from reputable supplier.

**Evidence of Efficacy:**
- Computer simulations with validated mathematical models support light schedule effectiveness; laboratory trials show light and melatonin independently shift circadian timing and are additive in combination.
- Field studies on light-based jet lag interventions are equivocal; meta-analysis of 10 field studies shows melatonin-based interventions effective at shifting body clock and reducing jet lag (Herxheimer and Petrie, 2002). Combined light/melatonin efficacy in field settings not yet assessed—identified as critical next step.

**Pre-shifting (Before/During Travel):**
- Advantages: reduces adaptation time, less pronounced jet lag. Disadvantages: may interfere with sleep, be socially disruptive, complicate estimating CBTmin timing upon arrival.
- To delay (westward) 3–4 days before: move bedtime/get-up later (30–60 min/day), maximize evening light, minimize morning light, take 3.0mg melatonin 1h after rising.
- To advance (eastward) 3–4 days before: move bedtime/get-up earlier, minimize evening light, maximize morning light, take 3.0mg melatonin 6.5h before bed.
- During travel: time light/melatonin to departure time zone, not arrival.

The article concludes that recommendations are based on latest circadian research but notes potential barriers to practical implementation and calls for field-based randomized controlled trials to assess efficacy in natural settings. Funding from Australian Research Council Discovery Project scheme (DP160104909).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Immediately after westward flight, the circadian system will be running ahead of the local time zone... To adjust to the new time zone, the circadian system has to delay, or shift backward, or move later. Conversely, immediately after eastward flight, the circadian system will be running behind the local time zone... To adjust to the new time zone, the circadian system has to advance, or shift forward, or move earlier."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: JCI Insight -
Circadian rhythm phase shifts caused by timed exercise vary with chronotype ---
URL: https://insight.jci.org/articles/view/134270

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in JCI Insight (2020;5(3):e134270) by researchers at the University of Kentucky, investigating how timed exercise affects circadian rhythm phase shifts depending on an individual's chronotype.

**Study Design & Methods:**
- 52 young, sedentary adults (16 men, 36 women; ages 18-45) were studied in free-living (non-laboratory) conditions
- Dim light melatonin onset (DLMO) was measured before and after 5 days of exercise
- Participants were randomized to morning exercise (10 hours after DLMO; n=26) or evening exercise (20 hours after DLMO; n=26)
- Exercise consisted of 30 minutes of supervised treadmill exercise at 70% VO2peak for 5 consecutive days
- Chronotype was assessed using the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ-SA) and Munich Chronotype Questionnaire (MCTQ)
- Data collected between July 2017 and March 2019 in Lexington, Kentucky

**Key Results:**
1. Morning exercise induced significant phase advances (0.62 ± 0.18 hours) compared to evening exercise (–0.02 ± 0.18 hours; P = 0.01)
2. Chronotype significantly influenced the effect of timed exercise:
   - Later chronotypes experienced phase advances from BOTH morning (0.54 ± 0.29 hours) and evening (0.46 ± 0.25 hours) exercise
   - Earlier chronotypes experienced phase advances from morning exercise (0.49 ± 0.25 hours) but phase delays from evening exercise (–0.41 ± 0.29 hours)
3. Sleep timing was earlier in the morning exercise group, but sleep quality and duration were similar between groups
4. No significant sex differences in phase shifts were observed

**Conclusions:**
- Morning exercise advances circadian phase and has the greatest potential to alleviate circadian misalignment in young adults (who typically have late chronotypes)
- Late chronotypes (who experience the most severe circadian misalignment) may benefit from exercise in either the morning or evening
- Evening exercise may exacerbate circadian misalignment in early chronotypes
- Personalized exercise timing prescription based on chronotype could alleviate circadian misalignment
- Chronotype questionnaires (e.g., preferred sleep timing) can serve as practical proxies for DLMO when prescribing exercise timing

**Trial Registration:** NCT04097886 (clinicaltrials.gov)
**Funding:** NIH grants UL1TR001998 and TL1TR001997, Barnstable Brown Diabetes and Obesity Center, and other University of Kentucky sources.

**Strengths noted:** Free-living conditions, standardized exercise intensity based on individual GXTmax, practical exercise regimen (30 min/day moderate exercise), and postexercise phase assessment performed the day after the final exercise session to avoid acute masking effects.

**Limitations noted:** Did not control for other phase-shifting stimuli (e.g., light exposure during travel), did not collect baseline sleep measures, only studied young healthy sedentary adults, and only investigated moderate cardiovascular exercise.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Morning exercise induced phase advance shifts (0.62 ± 0.18 hours) that were significantly greater than phase shifts from evening exercise (–0.02 ± 0.18 hours; P = 0.01)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: How To Travel the World Without Jet lag - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2829880

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article, published in Sleep Medicine Clinics (June 2009, doi: 10.1016/j.jsmc.2009.02.006, PMID: 20204161, PMCID: PMC2829880), was authored by Charmane I. Eastman (Professor and Director, Biological Rhythms Research Laboratory) and Helen J. Burgess (Associate Professor and Associate Director), both at Rush University Medical Center, Chicago. The article provides evidence-based strategies for preventing and minimizing jet lag using timed bright light exposure and melatonin supplementation.

KEY CONTENT:

1. JET LAG SYMPTOMS AND CONSEQUENCES: Jet lag causes difficulty sleeping, daytime sleepiness, impaired performance, fatigue, irritability, depressed mood, and gastrointestinal disturbance. It poses public safety risks (affecting diplomats and military), and frequent jet travel is associated with cognitive deficits, temporal lobe atrophy (per MRI), menstrual disturbances, increased cardiovascular disease and type II diabetes risk, and increased cancer risk in flight attendants. In 2007, over 31 million U.S. residents flew overseas (12 million to Europe, 7 million to Asia).

2. DIRECTIONAL ASYMMETRY: Jet lag is caused by temporary misalignment between the endogenous circadian clock (the SCN) and the destination time zone. Flying east requires a phase advance; flying west requires a phase delay. Because the average free-running period (tau) of the human circadian clock is slightly longer than 24h, humans naturally drift later, making phase advances more difficult. Real travelers phase delay ~92 min/day after westward flights but phase advance only ~57 min/day after eastward flights. With bright light, phase delays of ~2h/day and phase advances of ~1-1.5h/day are achievable. Antidromic (wrong-direction) re-entrainment is common after eastward travel crossing 8+ time zones—in one study, 7 of 8 subjects flying 11 time zones east re-entrained by phase delaying instead of phase advancing. Jet lag symptoms are worst when the temperature minimum (Tmin, the sleepiest circadian time) occurs during waking hours. The Tmin typically occurs 3-4.5h before wake time.

3. PHASE RESPONSE CURVES (PRCs): Bright light produces phase advances when applied late in the sleep episode/morning after the Tmin, and phase delays when applied early in sleep before the Tmin. Melatonin pills produce greatest phase advances when taken in the afternoon and greatest phase delays when taken in the morning. Melatonin is NOT FDA-approved for jet lag in the U.S. (classed as a dietary supplement), but research supports its efficacy. Optimal timing: 3.0 mg melatonin taken ~5h before DLMO (or 7.5h before sleep onset, or 12h before Tmin) for maximal phase advance; 0.5 mg taken ~2h before DLMO (4.5h before sleep, 9h before Tmin). Bright light at 3,500 lux (from light boxes) and 3.0 mg melatonin produce roughly equivalent phase advances. Outdoor sunlight is far more intense (10,000-100,000 lux). Both PRCs have "dead zones" of reduced sensitivity (midday for light, during endogenous melatonin secretion for melatonin).

4. RECOMMENDED STRATEGIES: The key principle is to reset the circadian clock at least partially toward the destination time zone BEFORE flying, while gradually shifting the sleep schedule to keep it aligned with the shifting clock (avoiding abrupt shifts that cause circadian misalignment). 
- For flying WEST: Use a bright light box in the 2h before bed for 2 nights before the flight, delay bedtime by ~2h/night, and avoid bright light after waking. After landing, ~1h/day phase delay is realistic.
- For flying EAST: Phase advance the sleep schedule by ~1h/day (or less for night owls), use intermittent bright light in the morning (~5,000 lux light box or outdoor light), take 0.5 mg melatonin in the afternoon (4.5h before bedtime, 1h earlier each day), and gradually shift meal times. A 1h/day advance schedule combined with bright light and melatonin did NOT produce jet lag symptoms in studies. Advancing more than 1h/day is not recommended.
- For flights crossing 8+ time zones east, some travelers (especially night owls) may prefer to phase delay instead of phase advance before the flight.
- Even just 1-2 days of preflight shifting helps reduce subsequent jet lag.

5. DRUGS AND LIMITATIONS: Caffeine, hypnotics, and large soporific doses of melatonin at bedtime only mask jet lag symptoms; they do not eliminate the underlying circadian misalignment, which persists until re-entrainment occurs. Hypnotics improve sleep quantity but sleepiness still occurs around the Tmin when it falls during waking hours.

6. PRACTICAL NOTES: Light boxes marketed for seasonal affective disorder (SAD) are useful for phase shifting. Larger illuminated-area boxes are recommended (easier to sit in front of). Blue-enriched light boxes are in vogue, but older cool-white fluorescent boxes produce equal phase shifts. Individual differences exist—early birds (shorter taus) have more trouble phase delaying; night owls (longer taus) have more trouble phase advancing. The authors suggest companies may one day keep light boxes on hand for traveling employees.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Jet travel across multiple time zones produces jet lag, which includes difficulty initiating or maintaining nighttime sleep, daytime sleepiness, decreased alertness, loss of concentration, impaired performance, fatigue, irritability, disorientation, depressed mood and gastrointestinal disturbance."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: What is jet lag? | Timeshifter® ---
URL: https://www.timeshifter.com/jet-lag/the-science-of-jet-lag

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from Timeshifter, a company that is a leader in circadian technology, offering apps and products that translate circadian science into solutions for improving human health, safety, and performance. The page is primarily an informational article titled "What is jet lag?" reviewed by Steven W. Lockley, Ph.D., Co-Founder & Chief Scientist of Timeshifter, who has over 30 years of research experience in circadian rhythms, sleep, and jet lag, and has advised NASA astronauts, Formula 1 teams, healthcare systems, and safety-critical industries.

Key content on the page includes:

**What is jet lag:** Jet lag is caused when the sleep-wake and light-dark cycle shifts too quickly for the brain's central circadian clock (located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus/SCN, a group of ~50,000 cells in the hypothalamus) to keep up.

**What causes jet lag:** The circadian clock regulates sleep, alertness, hormones, body temperature, digestion, immune function, and dozens of other systems, using light and darkness as main cues. When flying across time zones, the clock can only adjust by about an hour per day on its own. A flight from New York to Tokyo (13 time zones) takes roughly two weeks to fully catch up.

**East vs. west:** For most people, going east is harder than going west because the average human circadian clock runs slightly long (over 24 hours), making it easier to delay sleep than advance it. A minority of people with shorter-than-24-hour clocks find the opposite.

**Jet lag symptoms:** Difficulty sleeping, daytime sleepiness/fatigue, poor concentration and memory, reduced performance, mood changes, gastrointestinal problems, headache/malaise, weakened immune function, slower physical recovery, and reduced exercise capacity.

**How long jet lag lasts:** Approximately one day per time zone crossed without intervention (e.g., New York to London, 5 time zones east, typically causes ~5 days of jet lag). Factors affecting duration include direction of travel (eastward takes ~50% longer to recover), number of time zones crossed (linear scaling), chronotype (morning types recover faster westward, evening types faster eastward), age (older adults adjust slower), and whether you intervene correctly. With properly timed light exposure and light avoidance, the circadian clock can shift 3-4 hours per day rather than 1 hour.

**How to get over jet lag quickly:** The only effective way is individually-timed light exposure and light avoidance to reset the circadian clock, supported by correct type/dose/timing of melatonin. Popular advice (sleeping pills, hydration, diets, exercise) does not address underlying circadian misalignment. With a properly timed light and melatonin plan, adaptation can be 3-4 times faster. The page also contains extensive site navigation for other Timeshifter products (Jet lag app, Shift work app, Peak performance, My Circadian Day), resources on circadian rhythms, and links to related articles on jet lag myths, melatonin for jet lag, shift work, peak performance, and circadian medicine. Timeshifter states it is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease and is intended for healthy adults 18 years or older.
</summary>

URL: https://integrative-medicine.ca/jet-lag-recovery-how-to-keep-your-circadian-rhythm-in-sync-while-traveling-functional-hacks-to-adjust-to-new-time-zones

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a blog article by Dr. John Gannage of Markham Integrative Medicine titled "Jet Lag Recovery: How to Keep Your Circadian Rhythm in Sync While Traveling — Functional hacks to adjust to new time zones." The article provides science-backed, functional strategies to reset the body's circadian rhythm and minimize jet lag when crossing time zones.

Key content includes:
- Biology: Jet lag is a temporary misalignment between the internal clock (circadian rhythm, coordinated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus/SCN in the brain) and local time. Light is the dominant zeitgeber (cue), with meals, activity, caffeine, and melatonin signaling peripheral clocks.
- Three golden rules: (1) Control light exposure (strongest cue), (2) Time sleep and melatonin strategically, (3) Anchor peripheral clocks with meals, activity, and caffeine.
- Pre-travel tuning: Shift schedule 1–3 days before travel—go to bed 1–2 hours earlier each night for eastward travel; later for westward travel.
- Light strategy: Morning light advances the clock (eastward travel), evening light delays it (westward travel). Brief light-flash therapy during sleep can produce multi-hour phase shifts. Apps like Entrain recommend personalized light/dark timing.
- Melatonin: Low doses (0.5–3 mg) taken in the evening at destination time help shift circadian timing and improve sleep onset, especially for eastward travel. Prescription melatonin receptor agonists (e.g., tasimelteon) exist for severe cases. Timing is critical; avoid high doses without guidance.
- Meals and movement: Eat meals at local times, favor a substantial breakfast on day one, avoid large nighttime meals. Moderate exercise (especially morning) and outdoor walks reinforce phase shifts.
- Caffeine and naps: Caffeine improves alertness but doesn't reset the clock; avoid caffeine within 8 hours of target bedtime. Short naps (20–30 minutes) help alertness without sleep inertia; avoid long late-afternoon naps.
- Practical protocol: Example given for Toronto→London (eastward, 5 hours), including sleeping on plane if nighttime at destination, seeking bright morning light upon arrival, eating local-timed meals, taking 0.5–3 mg melatonin 30–60 minutes before local bedtime, scheduling morning workouts, and using caffeine early in the day only.
- Prescription options: Melatonin receptor agonists (tasimelteon) have clinical evidence for severe/prolonged jet lag or peak performers (athletes, pilots), supported by the 2020 JET study and 2020–2022 trials.

The article includes six peer-reviewed references (Cureus 2024; Sleep Medicine Clinics 2021; Scientific Reports 2023; Journal of Pineal Research 2022; Frontiers in Neurology 2020; Clocks & Sleep 2023). The author concludes that jet lag is solvable, predictable, and often preventable using the functional toolkit.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Jet lag isn't just annoying sleepiness. It's a temporary misalignment of your internal clock (the circadian rhythm) with local time, and it affects sleep, mood, digestion, cognition, and performance."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Resetting Time: The Role of Exercise Timing in Circadian Reprogramming for Metabolic Health ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4168/5/3/59

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a review article titled "Resetting Time: The Role of Exercise Timing in Circadian Reprogramming for Metabolic Health" by Stuart J. Hesketh from the School of Medicine, University of Central Lancashire, Preston, UK. Published in the MDPI journal *Obesities* (2025, volume 5, issue 3, article 59; DOI: 10.3390/obesities5030059), the paper was submitted 14 July 2025, revised 4 August 2025, accepted 6 August 2025, and published 7 August 2025. It is an open-access review with Academic Editor Carmine Finelli, having 6416 article views and 7 citations, and an Altmetric score of 71.

**Core Topic:** The review examines how skeletal muscle circadian clocks regulate metabolic health and how the timing of exercise can serve as a chronotherapeutic intervention to reset circadian rhythms and improve metabolic outcomes, particularly in obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).

**Key Findings:**

1. **Skeletal muscle as a central circadian regulator:** Skeletal muscle comprises ~40% of body mass, is a primary site for glucose disposal (~80% of postprandial glucose uptake), fatty acid oxidation, and thermogenesis. It exhibits robust circadian rhythms in gene expression, mitochondrial function, fuel utilisation, and insulin sensitivity. Approximately 2,300 genes in skeletal muscle cycle diurnally, including Ppargc1a, Glut4, and Cpt1b, with peaks coinciding with the active phase.

2. **Molecular clock mechanism:** The muscle clock involves a transcriptional–translational feedback loop with core genes BMAL1, CLOCK, PERs, and CRYs. Skeletal muscle-specific Bmal1 knockout in mice causes glucose intolerance, reduced insulin-stimulated glucose uptake, GLUT4 mislocalisation, defective mitochondrial respiration, and disrupted fuel partitioning.

3. **Circadian misalignment and metabolic disease:** Misalignment contributes to obesity and T2DM. A 3.5-day simulated night-shift protocol in 14 healthy men reduced insulin sensitivity by 23% (non-oxidative glucose disposal: 23.7 vs. 18.4 mg/kg/min, p=0.024). In obese individuals, mitochondrial fusion–fission cycles and respiratory oscillations are blunted. Lipid overload (palmitate exposure) alters BMAL1, PER3, CRY2, and DBP expression and reduces amplitude of lipid metabolite oscillations. High-fat diet during resting phases causes exaggerated weight gain in rodents. Clock and Per2 knockout mice are predisposed to obesity.

4. **Exercise as a non-photic zeitgeber:** Exercise can reset and amplify muscle circadian rhythms even in metabolically impaired states. Key molecular pathways include AMPK activation (promoting PER2 degradation and CRY1 nuclear translocation), SIRT1 activation via NAD+ (deacetylating BMAL1 and PGC-1α), and CaMKII activation via contraction-induced calcium flux (enhancing BMAL1 transcription and mitochondrial biogenesis).

5. **Time-of-day dependency:** Exercise effects are highly time-dependent, with late active-phase training producing superior outcomes in both rodents and humans. Per1/2 knockout mice lose the diurnal variation in exercise capacity, and the benefits of active-phase-aligned training are attenuated in Bmal1 knockout and Clock mutant mice. Exercise also induces chromatin-level modifications (increased chromatin accessibility at circadian and metabolic gene promoters in a BMAL1-dependent manner).

6. **Reversibility of clock disruption:** A longitudinal study showed Roux-en-Y gastric bypass partially restored clock gene expression (normalisation of BMAL1 and PER2 rhythms) in skeletal muscle biopsies from patients.

7. **Myokines and multi-omics:** Irisin, an exercise-induced myokine linked to PGC-1α activation, enhances thermogenesis and glucose homeostasis with potential circadian regulation. Multi-omic approaches are uncovering time-dependent molecular signatures and biomarkers that may inform personalised, temporally targeted interventions.

**Keywords:** circadian rhythm, skeletal muscle, obesity, metabolic disease, circadian misalignment, exercise timing, chronotherapy, type 2 diabetes.

**Conclusions:** The review positions skeletal muscle clocks as both regulators and therapeutic targets in metabolic disease, proposing a conceptual framework for chrono-exercise strategies and highlighting the promise of multi-omics in developing precision chrono-medicine approaches to restore circadian alignment and improve metabolic health.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Skeletal muscle accounts for ~40% of body mass and serves as a key site of glucose uptake, lipid oxidation, and thermogenesis, making it a pivotal tissue in metabolic homeostasis."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Effects of exercise on circadian rhythms in humans ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10598774

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive scientific review article published in Frontiers in Pharmacology (2023 Oct 11;14:1282357; doi: 10.3389/fphar.2023.1282357) by Bingyi Shen, Changxiao Ma, Guanlin Wu, Haibin Liu, Lihong Chen, and Guangrui Yang. The article examines the effects of exercise on circadian rhythms in humans.

KEY CONTENT:

1. **Biological Clock Background**: The central circadian pacemaker is located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus. At the molecular level, core clock genes (BMAL1, CLOCK, PER, CRY, ROR, REV-ERB) form transcriptional-translational feedback loops (TTFL). Light is the most potent zeitgeber, while exercise is an important non-photic zeitgeber that can entrain or reset circadian rhythms.

2. **Effects of Exercise on Circadian Rhythms**:
   - **Normal light/dark conditions**: Both morning and evening exercise advanced sleep-wake cycle and dim light melatonin onset (DLMO) in night owls, while evening exercise delayed DLMO phase in early birds. Morning exercise is recommended for the general population to improve sleep quality. Resistance exercise in morning/noon advanced core body temperature phase.
   - **Constant conditions**: Exercise timing affects melatonin phases differently—afternoon (CT8/CT17) and night (CT10/CT16) exercise delayed melatonin onset; high-intensity exercise increased melatonin peak levels without phase changes; morning exercise (CT3) delayed melatonin peak by ~1 hour.
   - **Disturbed light/dark conditions**: A single bout of exercise has minor effects on circadian rhythms compared to bright light. Regular exercise over prolonged periods significantly impacts circadian rhythms. Exercise can help adaptation to forced phase-shifted schedules (jet lag, shift work). A phase-response curve (PRC) of melatonin (aMT6s) to exercise was plotted, showing advances at 07:00, 13:00, 16:00 and delays at 19:00, 22:00—similar to the bright light PRC. Exercise at night usually delays circadian phase, making it harder to fall asleep.

3. **Exercise Timing and Circadian-Related Diseases**:
   - **Sleep disorders**: Aerobic exercise (e.g., 30 min morning running for 3 weeks) improves sleep quality, mood, and concentration. High-intensity interval exercise also improves sleep. Exercise influences SCN input/output and clock gene expression.
   - **Cardiovascular diseases**: Timed exercise can reset circadian system post-disruption. Evening exercise is better for lowering blood pressure and heart rate (45-min evening aerobic exercise reduced blood pressure in hypertensive individuals). A 12-week evening walking regimen produced better outcomes than morning walking in coronary artery disease patients. Midday-afternoon and evening exercise is more commonly recognized as beneficial for cardiovascular health.
   - **Cancer**: IARC classified shift work involving circadian disruption as "possibly carcinogenic to humans" (2019). Morning exercise was associated with lower risk of prostate and breast cancer. Daily exercise at a fixed time improved fatigue and quality of life in cancer survivors more than irregular exercise.
   - **Metabolic diseases**: Six-week moderate-intensity cycling before breakfast was three times more beneficial for lipid utilization than post-breakfast exercise, with greater benefits for insulin sensitivity. Exercise during the early active period may be more effective for metabolic disorders. Afternoon exercise showed advantages in some metabolic cases (type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes with HIIT, overweight/obese individuals).

4. **Methodology Notes**: The review highlights challenges in comparing studies due to varying exercise protocols (intensity, mode, duration), detection methods (DLMO in blood/saliva/urine, accelerometers, questionnaires), and individual differences. WHO recommends adults engage in at least 150–300 min of moderate-intensity or 75–150 min of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity per week.

The article concludes that exercise is a promising non-invasive, non-pharmaceutical intervention for regulating circadian rhythms, but optimal timing depends on multiple factors including exercise intensity, mode, duration, and frequency.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"External factors, such as the diurnal rhythm of light, have a significant impact on the body's internal clock. Additionally, as an important non-photic zeitgeber, exercise can regulate the body's internal rhythms to a certain extent, making it possible to become a non-drug intervention for preventing and treating circadian rhythm disorders."
</key_excerpts>
