<webpage_content>
1 pii: zsx118  http://dx.doi.org/10.1093/sleep/zsx118 SLEEP , Vol. 40, No. 9, 2017 Daytime naps briefly attenuate sleepiness—Saletin et al.
ORIGINAL ARTICLE Short Daytime Naps Briefly Attenuate Objectively Measured Sleepiness Under Chronic Sleep Restriction Jared M Saletin, PhD1,2; Cassie J Hilditch, PhD1,2,; William C Dement, PhD3; Mary A Carskadon, PhD1,2,4 1E.P . Bradley Hospital Sleep Research Laboratory, Providence, Rhode Island; 2Department of Psychiatry and Human Behavior, Alpert Medical School of Brown University, Providence, Rhode Island; 3Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Stanford Center for Sleep Sciences and Medicine, Palo Alto, California; 4Centre for Sleep Research, University of South Australia, Adelaide, South Australia, Australia Study Objectives: Napping is a useful countermeasure to the negative effects of acute sleep loss on alertness. The efficacy of naps to recover from chronic sleep loss is less well understood.
Methods: Following 2 baseline nights (10 hours' time-in-bed), participants were restricted to 7 nights of 5-hour sleep opportunity. Ten adults participated in the No-Nap condition, and a further 9 were assigned to a Nap condition with a daily 45-minute nap opportunity at 1300 h. Sleepiness was assessed using the multiple sleep latency test and a visual analogue scale at 2-hour intervals. Both objective and subjective indexes of sleepiness were normalized within subject as a difference from those at baseline prior to sleep restriction. Mixed-effects models examined how the daytime nap opportunity altered sleepiness across the day and across the protocol.
Results: Short daytime naps attenuated sleepiness due to chronic sleep restriction for up to 6–8 hours after the nap. Benefits of the nap did not extend late into evening. Subjective sleepiness demonstrated a similar short-lived benefit that emerged later in the day when objective sleepiness already returned to pre-nap levels. Neither measure showed a benefit of the nap the following morning after the subsequent restriction night.
Conclusions: These data indicate a short daytime nap may attenuate sleepiness in chronic sleep restriction, yet subjective and objective benefits emerge at different time scales. Because neither measure showed a benefit the next day, the current study underscores the need for careful consideration before naps are used as routine countermeasures to chronic sleep loss.
Keywords: countermeasure, MSLT, napping, sleepiness, sleep loss, sleep restriction.
INTRODUCTION Nearly 30% of the US population report obtaining 6 or fewer hours of sleep each night.1 This figure has increased over the past two decades, likely due to increased work and social pressures.2, 3 Apart from affecting alertness and performance, cumulative sleep loss is associated with several adverse health outcomes including cardiovascular, metabolic and mood disorders, obe-sity, and cancer.2 These issues raise a clear need for a coun-termeasure to the negative effects of chronic sleep restriction. While daytime naps may logically meet this need, little evidence exists as to whether, and for how long, daytime naps can atten-uate the negative consequences of cumulative reduced sleep.
A well-established consequence of chronic sleep restriction is a cumulative decline in alertness and performance.4–6 In fact, the impact of chronic sleep restriction can be as severe as acute total sleep deprivation. For example, participants restricted to 4 hours’ time-in-bed (TIB) for 6 days showed per-formance impairment equivalent to one night of total sleep loss.6 Similarly, Carskadon and Dement4 showed that follow-ing 7 days of 5 hours' TIB, sleep onset latency (SOL) was sig-nificantly reduced, with one-third of participants experiencing pathological levels of sleepiness (SOL <5 minutes).7 Moreover, while performance deficits coupled with increased physiolog-ical sleepiness is common, subjective awareness of sleepiness saturates at lower levels during chronic sleep restriction.6 Thus, chronic sleep restriction poses a unique hazard resulting from physiological sleepiness and performance impairment occur-ring with a simultaneous lack of subjective awareness.
In light of the consequences of chronic sleep restriction, naps have long been proposed as a potential countermeasure to the effects of cumulative sleep loss.8 The benefits of daytime naps following habitual sleep,9, 10 acute total sleep deprivation,11 and acute partial sleep restriction12-17 have been consistently demon-strated. Afternoon naps as short as 10 minutes have the poten-tial to restore alertness and performance to well-rested levels following sleep restriction;15–17 longer naps tend to provide a dose-dependent benefit.11, 18, 19 Following one night of sleep restriction (typically 4–5 hours' TIB), studies generally report improvements in self-rated sleep-iness for up to 1–2 hours post-nap,13–17 although one study claimed subjective benefits lasting up to 4 hours.12 Naps of at least 30 minutes duration have also shown increased sleep onset latency15–17 and reduced physiological markers of sleep-iness in the electroencephalogram12, 13 for 1–2 hours post-nap. These studies suggest that naps, at least in the short term, have the ability to “rescue” alertness in the face of acute sleep loss. Unclear, however, is how long the benefit from napping persists under conditions of chronic sleep loss, and the duration across multiple days of sleep restriction is yet to be investigated.
An initial report by Hayashi and colleagues10 studied the effects of a 20-minute nap at noon for 5 consecutive days of unrestricted sleep (on average about 7 hours). Naps taken later in the week were better able to suppress sleepiness in the afternoon, suggesting that under saturated sleep conditions, repetitive use of naps can have cumulative benefits. Napping was also effective at ameliorating the impact of sleep restriction following a week Statement of Significance This study shows that daytime naps provide short-term attenuation of sleepiness caused by chronic sleep restriction. The effects of these naps do not extend beyond 6–8 hours, and are undetectable the following day. Therefore, this study highlights the importance of recognizing both the benefits of naps to rescue alertness and the limits to these benefits. Investigations into different nap lengths may determine the amount of sleep needed to maintain alertness across successive days under chronic sleep restriction conditions.

Together, the literature to date suggests that daytime naps taken across consecutive days of sleep restriction may be able to allevi-ate the accumulation of sleepiness associated with chronic sleep loss. Indeed, a recent study of adolescents restricted to 5 nights of 5 hours’ TIB showed that a 1-hour afternoon nap opportunity was able to attenuate performance decline across the restriction period but did not restore performance to baseline levels.20 While the authors report that subjective sleepiness improved following a nap, this study did not include a physiological measure of sleepi-ness, such as the multiple sleep latency test (MSLT).21 Thus, the aim of this study is to explore the duration and pro-file of objective and subjective sleepiness following a 45-minute afternoon nap opportunity across successive days of sleep restric-tion in healthy young adults. We hypothesized that the nap would improve subsequent alertness on restriction days compared to not napping. Furthermore, we hypothesized that this effect would be strongest for measures taken shortly following the nap (e.g., within 6 hours), diminishing with further time awake.
METHODS Participants This study is an expansion of a prior investigation of the impact of chronic sleep restriction upon objective and subjective sleep-iness.4 The No Nap group is drawn from that prior report, while participants in the Nap group were recruited subsequent to this original study. In total, the sample consisted of 19 young adults participating in the in-laboratory Stanford Sleep Camp across three summers. Following informed consent, 10 partic-ipants (5 females; aged 17–24 [mean: 20] years) formed the No Nap group completing seven consecutive nights of chronic sleep restriction, while 9 participants (4 females; aged 18–26 [mean: 21] years) entered the Nap group, completing the same protocol with an additional 45-minute nap opportunity during the days of restricted sleep. No systematic differences were present between the two groups with respect of habitual sleep.
Study Design Participants completed an intensive 13-day in-laboratory proto-col involving nocturnal sleep recordings and daytime measure-ment of sleepiness. Figure 1 illustrates the portion of the study protocol germane to the current analysis.
Participants lived in the laboratory for the entirety of the study in a dormitory setting on the Stanford campus. Participants were continuously monitored in a light- and temperature-con-trolled laboratory environment during testing and sleep periods. Participants had access to regular meals, snacks, and free time when not testing although were restricted from caffeine while in the laboratory. Participants were not permitted to engage in strenuous physical exercise during the protocol. Participants were allowed to walk outside the laboratory in-between testing, monitored by research staff.
Following an initial adaptation night in the laboratory, partic-ipants completed two baseline days (three in the No Nap group) with a 10-hour sleep schedule (bedtime: 2200 h; rise time: 0800 h). During the day, the MSLT21 was completed 6 times at 2-hour intervals. In the evening of the final baseline day, the first night of sleep restriction extended bedtime to 0300 h, reducing the sleep opportunity to 5 hours. All participants slept on this reduced schedule for the next 6 nights. On the days following reduced sleep (Restriction Days 1–6), the same MSLT protocol was continued into extended wakefulness, with the final MSLT occurring at 0130 h. During sleep restriction, participants in the Nap group were given a 45-minute nap opportunity at 1300 h, supplanting the regularly scheduled 1330 h MSLT period. Those in the No Nap group continued the MSLT protocol as normal during these days. Bedtime on the seventh day of the sleep restriction protocol was restored to 2200 h, and partic-ipants were given two nights of recovery sleep before exiting the study.

A complete description of the sleep restriction results can be found in the earlier report of the No Nap group.4 The cur-rent study focuses on the first 6 days of testing following sleep restriction: consisting of nine MSLT tests across a 19-hour interval. The seventh restriction day only involved six MSLT tests, as bedtime was advanced to begin a recovery protocol; as such, this day is not examined in the current analysis.
As the Nap group was given two nights of unrestricted base-line sleep prior to the first day of wake extension while the No Nap group was given an additional third night, our analyses target the final night of unrestricted sleep, as the baseline con-dition (BSLN) for each group. Thus, it is sleep from this final unrestricted night and sleepiness metrics from the subsequent first day of wake extension that are taken as baseline measure-ments for each group for purposes of comparing to the 6 days of testing following restricted sleep.
Sleep Monitoring All nocturnal and daytime sleep (including MSLT testing) was monitored by polysomnography using Grass Model 7 poly-graphs. Electroencephalography included two central (C3; C4) and two occipital (O1; O2) derivations referenced to the contralateral mastoid. Electrooculography was placed at the right and left outer canthi, and electromyography was recorded from chin and submental electrodes. Recordings were con-ducted with a high-pass filter at 0.3 Hz, a low-pass filter at 35 Hz, and a paper speed of 10 mm/sec. All sleep was scored in 30-second epochs according to the standardized procedures of Rechtschaffen and Kales.22 Measures of Sleepiness Sleepiness throughout the protocol was assessed in two ways: (1) the objective MSLT21 and (2) a visual analogue scale (VAS) for sleepiness. The VAS is a 100-mm visual analogue scale where one pole corresponds to “very wide awake” and the other pole to “very sleepy.” Participants were instructed to view the line as a continuum between these two extremes and to place a mark at the point describing their current sleepiness. VAS data were scored by measuring the mark along the 100-mm line. Thus, a score of 0 indicates complete alertness and a score of 100 indicates complete sleepiness.
Each day, subjective assessments of sleepiness occurred immediately following morning awakening and at 30-minute intervals throughout the remainder of the day (see Figure 1 for timing relative to sleep episodes). Participants were not permit-ted to see previous scores at the time of each assessment.
The MSLT was conducted each day according to standard procedures,21 at 2-hour intervals throughout the day beginning at 0930 h (see Figure 1). On days where bedtime was 0300 h (during chronic sleep restriction), MSLTs continued until a ninth test at 0130 h. As in our prior studies, the MSLT involved participants lying quietly in their darkened bedroom where they were asked to “please close your eyes, lie quietly, and try to fall asleep.” The MSLT episode was measured using the same polysomnography techniques as with nocturnal sleep. The tests were terminated after three consecutive 30-second epochs of sleep (usually, but not always, Stage 1 non-rapid eye movement [NREM] sleep). Sleep latency formed the objective measure of sleepiness and was defined as the elapsed time from lights out to the first of the three consecutive scored epochs of sleep.
Statistical Methods Statistical analyses were completed in Stata SE 14 (StataCorp LP , College Station, Texas) using linear mixed-effects models. Each model utilized restricted maximum likelihood estimation. Statistical testing used Satterthwaite’s approximation of degrees of freedom to adjust inference for small sample sizes.
Sleepiness scores (both MSLT and subjective ratings) are presented as differences from baseline to account for any unex-pected variability in sleepiness at the start of the study between the two groups. A two-step analytical approach was followed for each data component. First, the entirety of the data was plot-ted (e.g., Figure 2). Based on clear clustering of effects to spe-cific times of day, subsequent analytical models divided the day into three equal segments with scores averaged to reduce the number of data points and improve our ability to systematically test time-of-day × group interactions in this small sample. Thus, this binning procedure increases our statistical power to detect within-subject effects, in contrast to treating each individual time point (particularly for subjective sleepiness separate). Nevertheless, post hoc between-subject t-tests are included for each original time point (displayed in figures) for the most com-plete description of the data possible.
RESULTS Nocturnal Sleep Sleep measures for each nocturnal sleep episode are reported in Table 1. Sleep on the baseline night prior to sleep restric-tion did not differ significantly between groups on any measure, with the exception more time spent in Stage 1 sleep in the No Nap group.
The same table presents nocturnal sleep architecture for both the Nap and the No Nap groups across sleep restriction. Examining total sleep time reveals the success of our protocol in limiting sleep to near 50% of baseline levels, in all partici-pants. While the effect of sleep restriction is clear across the six protocol days, no significant interaction of Day and Group was present in any sleep parameter (either in duration or in architec-ture; all p's ≥ .24). Therefore, there was no impact of the nap on nocturnal sleep.
Daytime Nap Opportunity Table 2 presents sleep architecture for the daytime nap oppor-tunity provided to those participants in the Nap group. Neither total sleep time nor the stage architecture of the nap varied across the protocol (all p's ≥ .30). Moreover, across the entirety of the protocol, nap sleep was predominately Stage 2 sleep, with limited slow-wave sleep, and negligible amounts of rapid eye movement sleep.
Objective Sleepiness (MSLT) The primary dependent variable in this report is sleepiness during chronic sleep restriction measured by the MSLT. DISCUSSION Our primary finding shows a short-lived amelioration of sleep-iness during chronic sleep restriction for objective and sub-jective sleepiness following an afternoon nap, with alertness levels returned to baseline levels within several hours of the nap. This return to baseline appeared at different rates for objec-tive and subjective measures, with objective sleepiness return-ing to baseline levels sooner. Furthermore, no benefit for either measure of sleepiness was observed the next morning following additional exposure to sleep restriction.
Previous reports have focused on napping as an effective coun-termeasure to sleepiness induced by sleep deprivation and acute sleep restriction.11–17 The current study adds to this literature by demonstrating that these benefits are present and consistent fol-lowing a daytime nap across 6 days of chronic sleep restriction. The daytime nap in this instance returned sleep onset latency to baseline levels for 6–8 hours after the nap and improved sub-jective sleepiness later in the evening. Importantly, however, neither objective nor subjective reductions in sleepiness were observed the next morning following a night of restricted sleep. Thus, while napping may temporarily “rescue” alertness, such recovery neither “pays forward” to later in the night or the next morning as long as sleep continues to be restricted.
Temporal Profile of Nap Benefits A fundamental aim of the current study was to assess how long lasting any gains from a 45-minute daytime nap may be for objective measures of sleepiness and subjective alertness. In keeping with prior discrepancies between subjective and objec-tive measures of alertness,6, 23 we observed different temporal profiles between the MSLT and the visual analogue scale of subjective sleepiness. Objective decreases in sleepiness, com-pared to the No Nap group, were observed 2 hours after the nap. Sleepiness returned to levels similar to those observed in the No Nap group after 6 hours.
Thus, by late in the evening Nap and No Nap patients were indistinguishable in physiological sleepiness. Subjective report of increased alertness following the nap, however, was only observable later in the evening, at a time when physiologically measured sleepiness was no longer different between the two groups. This disconnect between objective and subjective meas-ures of sleepiness has been demonstrated previously6, 20, 23 and highlights the need to measure both aspects of sleepiness when assessing the benefits of napping strategies.
In considering the benefit of the nap, it is critical to acknowl-edge that the physiological benefits of recovery were observed immediately, yet participants did not perceive an immediate benefit. Moreover, participants overestimated their benefits later in the night. Because Nap group participants failed to perceive an early benefit, and erroneously perceived rescue later in the day, this study highlights a distinct window for sleepiness-re-lated risk. Our findings speak to a potential danger in perceived recovery following a nap not matching actual alertness levels. Thus, the timing of safety-critical tasks to any prescribed nap in the context of short sleep schedules is of paramount impor-tance when examining the effectiveness of the nap. Subjective perceptions of sleepiness are important for decisions regarding behavior (e.g., whether to drive, continue work, and so on). Unfortunately, performance measures such as the psychomo-tor vigilance task24 were not available in the current data set. However, work by Dinges and colleagues25 identified overlap-ping time courses of impairment between the psychomotor vig-ilance test and the MSLT. Length of Nap Benefits Regardless of the sleepiness measure and the time frame in which a return to baseline was observed, no benefit to sleepiness was observed the morning following a successive night of restricted sleep. Moreover, no systematic differences in macro-architecture were observed in nocturnal sleep throughout the protocol in the Nap group. Thus, it appears that the afternoon nap in the current study was unable to provide any measurable relief to homeostatic sleep pressure accrual throughout chronic sleep restriction and, therefore, no long-lasting benefit to alertness. is the length of the nap opportunity itself. In this study, partici-pants slept for approximately 30 minutes each day in a 45-minute opportunity. This nap length appears to be too short to sustain long-term benefits or reduce overall sleepiness following a 5-hour restricted sleep opportunity. The nap in the current study was pre-dominantly composed of NREM Stage 2 sleep, perhaps lacking the depth of slow-wave sleep needed to alter the accrual of sleep pressure across the protocol. Our results echo those of Lo et al.,20 in which a 1-hour nap opportunity across chronic sleep restric-tion days (5 hours’ TIB) bestowed a benefit on the psychomotor vigilance task up to only 5 hours after the nap opportunity. In the report by Lo, some neurocognitive measures showed a significant improvement relative to the No Nap group in the second period of sleep restriction, yet this was not consistent across neurocognitive measures, nor were these benefits observed during the first period of sleep restriction. Additionally, when comparing our results to those reported by Lo and colleagues, a number of methodologi-cal considerations must be accounted for. First, while Lo utilized the discrete Karolinska Sleepiness Scale,26 we used a continu-ous visual analogue instrument. Second, our participants were assessed for subjective sleepiness every half-hour while awake, while whole KSS scores were taken 3 times each day during Lo. Third, our study restricted sleep by delaying bedtime while Lo advanced waketime in addition to delaying bedtime; thus, differ-ences in homeostatic load (time since waking) exist between the two protocols (exaggerated by the nap in Lo being scheduled for 1400 h, an hour later than in our protocol). Finally, the second period of restriction in Lo makes their design distinctly different from ours. Ultimately, while these factors make the two studies difficult to directly compare, they complement each other. When taken together they highlight the utility of a nap in combating sleep restriction the same day, while the same short (<1-hour) nap cannot reliably improve either performance or physiological sleepiness the following day.
A longer nap, perhaps more capable of sustained slow-wave sleep, or one placed later in the day, may be better able to sus-tain benefits the following morning. Our study’s nap opportu-nity occurred at 1300 h, 5 hours after rising, whereas Lo and colleagues20 provided a nap 6 hours after rising at 1400 h. A nap placed at 1500 h may be even more efficient in both its circa-dian timing and its extension of homeostatic load to adequately dissipate sleep pressure in a way that would persist to the fol-lowing morning. However, a potential consequence of such a nap may be unforeseen changes in nocturnal sleep. In the cur-rent study, our early nap, containing little slow-wave sleep, did not impact nocturnal sleep. An additional concern with a longer nap opportunity may be the increased risk of sleep inertia. Since the physiological impact on sleepiness in the current study was short lived, the potential for it to be masked by sleep inertia may occlude any gains in alertness. Taken together, while a nap has a short-term benefit, understanding the dose dependency and temporal dynamics of these benefits will ultimately require future research combining the physiological measurement of sleepiness with enriched performance testing.
No Cumulative Effect Across 6 Days As noted earlier, nocturnal sleep did not differ across the protocol in the Nap and No Nap groups, nor did we observe any changes across the protocol in the composition of the daytime nap itself, and the benefit of the nap for sleepiness did not change signifi-cantly across the protocol days. One might have expected a cumu-lative effect of nearly 30 minutes more sleep each day, just as deficits from short sleep accrue with time. While the formal test for an interaction between this group difference and time in the protocol was not significant, an intriguing trend, on inspection of the data, reveal that the groups begin to diverge on the sixth day following sleep restriction, with benefits of napping becoming more prominent. Whether this divergence results from a cumula-tive benefit beginning to manifest in the Nap group, or from the saturating impact of chronic sleep restriction in the No Nap group, is unclear. Longer chronic sleep restriction studies are needed to investigate the potential for daytime naps to provide a cumulative benefit under extended sleep restriction conditions. An alternative possibility is that the use of visual scoring techniques limit our ability to detect changes in sleep microstructure across the proto-col. For example, minor dissipation of sleep homeostatic pressure by the afternoon nap may alter slow wave dynamics during the subsequent nocturnal sleep episodes. Unfortunately, in contrast to more recent investigations27 of the impact of naps on oscillatory activity during sleep, our paper polygraph records preclude the use of modern signal-processing techniques such as spectral analysis.
In summary, in the context of repeated nights of restricted sleep, early afternoon naps “rescue” objectively measured sleepiness for about 4–6 hours but provide no benefit late in the evening and the subsequent morning. In contrast, such naps are perceived by participants to benefit alertness late in the evening, after objective gains have already diminished. The mismatch of objective and perceived benefits to alertness causes concern for operational safety in cases where such restricted schedules are introduced in the real world, yet a 45-minute afternoon nap may appear an attractive countermeasure.

args.summary:
This is a scientific research article (published in SLEEP journal, 2017) examining the efficacy of short daytime naps as a countermeasure to chronic sleep restriction. The study, conducted by researchers at Stanford University and Brown University, tested 19 healthy young adults (aged 17-26) who underwent an intensive 13-day in-laboratory protocol. After two baseline nights of 10-hour sleep opportunity, participants were restricted to 5-hour sleep opportunities for 7 nights. Ten participants were in a No-Nap control group, while nine received a daily 45-minute nap opportunity at 1300 h.

Key results: (1) Short daytime naps attenuated objectively measured sleepiness (via multiple sleep latency test/MSLT) from chronic sleep restriction for 6-8 hours after the nap, with sleep latency returning to baseline levels in the Nap group during the 1530-1930 h segment. (2) Subjective sleepiness (visual analogue scale) showed a delayed benefit that emerged later in the evening (approximately 8-13.5 hours after the nap), at a time when objective sleepiness had already returned to pre-nap levels. This mismatch between objective and subjective benefits highlights a potential safety concern. (3) No benefit was observed the following morning after subsequent restriction nights for either measure. (4) The nap did not affect nocturnal sleep architecture, and nap composition (predominantly Stage 2 NREM, with limited slow-wave sleep and negligible REM) remained consistent across the 6 restriction days. (5) No cumulative benefit of napping was detected across the 6 protocol days, though a non-significant trend of group divergence emerged on day 6.

The authors conclude that while a short afternoon nap can temporarily "rescue" alertness during chronic sleep restriction, such recovery neither extends late into the evening nor pays forward to the next morning. They caution that the mismatch between perceived and actual alertness following naps creates a potential safety risk in operational settings, and emphasize the need for careful consideration before naps are used as routine countermeasures to chronic sleep loss. The study notes that a longer nap (with more slow-wave sleep) or one placed later in the day might sustain benefits longer, but this requires future research. Funding sources included T32MH019927, K01MH109854, MH28461, NS13211, and MH05804.

## Abstract

### Objectives

Napping is a widely used countermeasure to [sleepiness](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/neuroscience/somnolence) and impaired performance caused by sleep loss and circadian pressure. Sleep inertia, the period of grogginess and impaired performance experienced after waking, is a potential side effect of napping. Many industry publications recommend naps of 30 min or less to avoid this side effect. However, the evidence to support this advice is yet to be thoroughly reviewed.

### Methods

Electronic databases were searched, and defined criteria were applied to select articles for review. The review covers literature on naps of 30 min or less regarding (a) sleep inertia, (b) slow-wave sleep (SWS) and (c) the relationship between sleep inertia and SWS.

### Results

The review found that although the literature on short afternoon naps is relatively comprehensive, there are very few studies on naps of 30 min or less at night. Studies have mixed results regarding the onset of SWS and the duration and severity of sleep inertia following short naps, making guidelines regarding their use unclear. The varying results are likely due to differing sleep/wake profiles before the nap of interest and the time of the day at waking.

### Conclusions

The review highlights the need to have more detailed guidelines about the implementation of short naps according to the time of the day and prior sleep/wake history. Without this context, such a recommendation is potentially misleading. Further research is required to better understand the interactions between these factors, especially at night, and to provide more specific recommendations.

## Introduction

Napping is a widely used countermeasure to sleepiness and impaired performance caused by sleep loss, extended wakefulness or staying awake during the night [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6]. Sleep inertia, the state of grogginess and impaired performance experience after waking, is often cited as a negative side effect of napping [2], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10], [11]. In fact, the effects of sleep inertia can be even more extreme than a night of sleep loss [12]. This period of impairment has been officially implicated in several real-world accidents and incidents [13], [14], [15], [16].

Sleep inertia has been observed after waking from a full habitual night of sleep under well-rested conditions and thus appears to be a ubiquitous step in the sleep–wake transition [12], [17], [18]. However, there are several key contributors to sleep inertia that have emerged from the literature. Conditions that tend to exacerbate sleep inertia include the following:
*   -waking during the circadian low in alertness (biological night) [19], [20], [21] 
*   -prior sleep loss or extended wakefulness before a sleep episode [19], [22] and 
*   -sleep depth [slow-wave sleep (SWS) in the prior sleep period or waking from deeper sleep stages] [19], [23], [24]. 

Napping is a recommended countermeasure to sleepiness in industry-focused journal articles [10], [25], [26], [27], [28] and industry best practice and government work safety publications [29], [30], [31]. The guidelines for the implementation of this countermeasure, however, are often vague. In general, a statement is made regarding the potential for impaired performance after waking, but rarely any specific details are provided concerning the severity or duration of sleep inertia following different napping situations. What is often cited, however, is that naps of 30 min or less (short naps) are generally considered to be effective in avoiding sleep inertia [32]. The National Sleep Foundation even recommends a short nap to avoid grogginess but does not mention the potential influence of the time of day [33]. Thus, it is broadly assumed that these nap lengths are ‘safe,’ with regard to the risk of sleep inertia. However, the recommendation to take a short nap to avoid sleep inertia is based on studies that have largely been conducted during the day, under conditions of limited wakefulness [9], [11], [34]. How these conditions translate to different scenarios common in the workplace (eg, naps on night shift) has not been comprehensively reviewed.

This leads to the overarching question: what is the evidence for recommending short naps to avoid sleep inertia? This review aims to address this question by investigating the three main assumptions of this recommendation as they relate to short naps: (a) the absence of sleep inertia, (b) the absence of SWS, and (c) the relationship between SWS and sleep inertia.

To investigate these assumptions, three structured narrative reviews (ie, narrative reviews of articles identified through a systematic search) were conducted. A structured narrative review approach was chosen to allow the comparison of findings from a broad range of literature including both laboratory and field studies [35]. The first assumption (absence of sleep inertia) was addressed by a systematic search to identify articles that investigated performance and/or alertness in the first 30 min after waking from short naps. The articles identified by these searches are summarised in Table 1 (daytime naps) and Table 2 (night-time naps). To address the second assumption (absence of SWS), articles identified in the first search were screened for SWS data, and an additional search for articles containing data on SWS in short naps (without sleep inertia data) was conducted. The articles identified by these searches are summarised in Table 3. To address the third assumption (relationship between SWS and sleep inertia), articles that met the combined inclusion criteria for the previous two searches were reviewed. These articles are identified in Table 1, Table 2 by an asterisk in the weight of evidence (WOE) classification column.

Show abstract Takeover performance in automated driving is subject to investigation in the context of a variety of driver states such as distraction or drowsiness. New driver states will emerge with increasing automation level with drivers potentially being allowed to sleep while driving a highly automated vehicle. Still at some point during a drive, drivers will be required to or voluntarily take back control of the vehicle. A simulator study was conducted to investigate drivers’ ability to take over the vehicle control after sleeping. In a within-subjects study design N = 25 test drivers completed a drive using a highly automated driving system a) during day time after a full night of sleep and b) early in the morning after a night of partial sleep deprivation. During the second drive, sleep was measured in drivers according to the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) standard using electroencephalography (EEG). In total, the participants had to handle four takeover requests (TORs) from the system, two while being awake (day drive) and two when being awakened from sleep stage N2 (morning drive). The objective criticality of the situations was assessed performing the Takeover Controllability rating (TOC-rating). The results indicate that the applied takeover time of 60 s was sufficient for drivers to reengage in driving after sleeping. Reaction times were extended by about 3 s after sleep compared to the wake condition. Takeover performance assessed with the TOC-rating however was clearly worse after sleep than after wakefulness which was also reflected in the drivers’ subjective perception of the criticality of the situation. This is a review article published in Sleep Medicine (Volume 32, April 2017, Pages 176-190) by Cassie J. Hilditch, Jillian Dorrian, and Siobhan Banks, titled "A review of short naps and sleep inertia: do naps of 30 min or less really avoid sleep inertia and slow-wave sleep?" (DOI: 10.1016/j.sleep.2016.12.016).

**Purpose/Objective:** The review investigates the widely-cited recommendation that naps of 30 minutes or less ("short naps") avoid sleep inertia (the period of grogginess and impaired performance after waking) and slow-wave sleep (SWS). The authors note that many industry publications recommend short naps as a countermeasure to sleepiness, but the evidence supporting this advice had not been thoroughly reviewed.

**Methodology:** Three structured narrative reviews were conducted using systematic searches of PubMed, Science Direct, and Scopus. The first search (24 July 2015) combined terms "sleep inertia" AND "nap," yielding 115 articles, of which 11 met inclusion criteria after filtering duplicates and non-qualifying studies. A second search (18 August 2015) using "slow wave sleep" AND "nap" yielded 139 articles. Additional articles were retrieved from reference lists, and the search was re-run on 27 June 2016 to capture recent literature. The review examined: (a) absence of sleep inertia, (b) absence of SWS, and (c) the relationship between SWS and sleep inertia in short naps.

**Key Findings:**
- Although the literature on short afternoon naps is relatively comprehensive, very few studies exist on naps of 30 minutes or less at night.
- Studies show mixed results regarding the onset of SWS and the duration/severity of sleep inertia following short naps.
- Naps shorter than 15 minutes during afternoon tend to avoid sleep inertia and SWS.
- Varying results are attributed to differing sleep/wake profiles before the nap and the time of day at waking.
- Sleep inertia can be more extreme than a night of sleep loss and has been implicated in real-world accidents and incidents (including aviation and marine incidents).
- Key contributors to exacerbated sleep inertia include: waking during the circadian low in alertness (biological night), prior sleep loss or extended wakefulness before a sleep episode, and sleep depth (SWS in the prior sleep period or waking from deeper sleep stages).

**Conclusions:** The review highlights that recommending a specific nap length without considering time of day and prior sleep/wake history is potentially misleading. The same length of nap can produce different sleep architecture and sleep inertia profiles under different conditions. More detailed guidelines are needed for implementing short naps, especially for shift workers, and further research is required to understand interactions between these factors, particularly at night. The purpose of the nap (e.g., sleepiness avoidance vs. performance enhancement) should also be considered.

**Article Metrics:** Cited by 83 articles, 136 Mendeley readers, 2 policy citations, and 1 news mention.
args.key_excerpts: "The review found that although the literature on short afternoon naps is relatively comprehensive, there are very few studies on naps of 30 min or less at night. Studies have mixed results regarding the onset of SWS and the duration and severity of sleep inertia following short naps, making guidelines regarding their use unclear."

This is a Semantic Scholar record for the research paper "Suppression of sleepiness in drivers: combination of caffeine with a short nap" by L.A. Reyner and James A. Horne, published in Psychophysiology on November 1, 1997 (DOI: 10.1111/J.1469-8986.1997.TB02148.X, PMID: 9401427).

The study found that caffeine and a <15-minute nap effectively and separately reduce sleepiness in drivers for 1 hour before a longer continuous monotonous afternoon drive in a car simulator. The mid-afternoon sleepiness peak was significantly reduced by caffeine and eliminated entirely by the combined treatment (caffeine + nap together).

The paper has 214 citations and cites 8 references. Key citing papers include:
- A 2020 pilot study by Centofanti et al. (Chronobiology International) finding the caffeine-nap may reduce sleep inertia in shift workers who nap on nightshift by improving vigilant attention and subjective fatigue in the 45 min post-nap opportunity.
- A 2001 study by De Valck and Cluydts (Journal of Sleep Research) on slow-release caffeine as a countermeasure to driver sleepiness induced by partial sleep deprivation, concluding caffeine can serve as a valuable countermeasure to performance decrements.
- A 2002 study by Reyner and Horne (Physiology & Behavior) on the efficacy of a 'functional energy drink' in counteracting driver sleepiness.
- A 2026 study by Filtness et al. (Scientific Reports) on optimising the caffeine nap for CPAP-treated obstructive sleep apnoea patients, finding two cans of coffee mitigated driver sleepiness more than one can (127.5 mg) and little benefit to a 30 min vs 15 min nap opportunity.
- A 2022 study by Soleimanloo et al. (Sleep Medicine) suggesting bright light could be a practical alternative to caffeine for sleepy drivers.

Key references cited by this paper include Horne & Reyner's earlier 1996 work on napping/caffeine/placebo effects on driver sleepiness, Bonnet & Arand's 1994 study showing a prophylactic nap + caffeine combination was more effective than nap alone in maintaining nocturnal alertness, Åkerstedt & Gillberg's 1990 work on subjective and objective sleepiness, and Horne & Reyner's 1995 BMJ study on sleep-related vehicle accidents.
args.key_excerpts: "Caffeine and a < 15-min nap effectively and separately reduce sleepiness in drivers for 1 hr before a longer continuous monotonous afternoon drive in a car simulator showed a mid-afternoon peak, significantly reduced by caffeine and eliminated by the combined treatment."

You are tasked with summarizing the raw content of a webpage retrieved from a web search. Your goal is to create a summary that preserves the most important information from the original web page. This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
1 CAFFNap: Self-administered caffeine-nap intervention for driver sleepiness: efficacy for obstructive sleep apnoea patients Appendix 1: Literature review Report authors: Professor Ashleigh Filtness Dr Sally Maynard December 2025 Project team: Professor Ashleigh Filtness, TSRC, Loughborough University Dr Sally Maynard, TSRC, Loughborough University Dr Karl Miller, TSRC, Loughborough University Dr Adam Asmal, TSRC, Loughborough University Prof Anna Anund, VTI Dr Andrew Hall, University Hospitals Leicester Mr Gary Spence, Leicester Sleep Apnoea Patient Association Mr David Graddon, Sleep Apnoea Trust Mr Chris Rogers, Sleep Apnoea Trust 2 Appendix 1: Literature review This research is concerned with attempting to evaluate the efficacy of a "caffeine-nap" as a countermeasure to driver sleepiness for obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) patients. The research is being undertaken because OSA patients are at increased risk of driver sleepiness and there is a gap in evidence for this speciﬁc demographic regarding what they should do if they experience sleepiness while driving. The project outcome will be an evidence-based recommendation for caffeine-nap best practice for tired OSA drivers. Caffeine nap A caffeine nap is the consumption of coffee immediately prior to a nap. It is a strategy for boosting alertness: consuming coffee prior to taking a short nap (less than 30 minutes), here referred to as a caffeine nap, has been proposed as a countermeasure for sleepiness which minimises sleep inertia, as the onset of the caffeine’s alerting effects coincides with waking from the nap, and the nap duration is purposely short to reduce the chance of waking from slow wave sleep. The efficacy of a caffeine nap has been recognised by the NHTSA (National Highway Traffic Safety Administration) of the USA, which recommends consuming caffeine prior to a 20-minute nap to increase alertness for a short period of time. The importance of napping in counteracting the negative consequences (short- and long-term) of sleep debt is generally recognised and it is widely agreed to be an effective countermeasure as an action against sleep deprivation (Faraut et al., 2017). The same can be claimed for caffeine in this context (see, for example, Alameddine et al., 2013). Some innovative research to investigate the effects of a caffeine nap is reported in the inﬂuential article by Horne & Reyner (1996) which studied the efficacy of feasible additional countermeasures that can be used during a break taken by sleepy drivers. The authors concluded that “caffeine and nap signiﬁcantly reduced driving impairments, subjective sleepiness and electroencephalographic (EEG) activity indicating drowsiness” (p309), making this countermeasure one which could avoid drivers falling asleep at the wheel. Apart from this research by Horne & Reyner (1996), there is limited research evidence investigating the effects of caffeine and napping on driving when fatigued or sleepy (Wundersitz & Baldock, 2008). However, there has been research carried out which compares the relative effects of each in terms of performance (p 10). See, for example, Horne et al. (2008). Another early study investigating caffeine naps was undertaken by Bonnet & Arand (1994.) The data from this study are consistent in showing that the combination of a 4 h prophylactic nap and the use of caffeine during a 24 h continuous operation results in 3 signiﬁcantly improved alertness, performance, and mood as compared to a 4 h prophylactic nap by itself. Taking into account periods of sleep of a longer length than caffeine nap is usually considered to be, the study was aiming to investigate the potential beneﬁcial effect of a combination of prophylactic sleep and caffeine in maintaining alertness and performance. It was thought this could mean it may be practical to decrease the length of the sleep and the amount of caffeine used during work periods. The participants were 24 young adult males who returned to bed from 16:00-20:00 prior to a 24 h period of sleep loss. Twelve subjects received caffeine at 01:30 and 07:30; the other 12 did not. Performance tests (correctly completed addition problems, vigilance sensitivity, and logical reasoning correct responses) all indicated maintenance of baseline performance levels in the caffeine group after administration of caffeine while performance declined in the placebo group. In addition, the group which was given the combination of nap and caffeine was able to maintain alertness and performance at very close to baseline levels throughout a 24 h period without sleep. This demonstrates the potential efficacy of a caffeine nap on performance. A study by Romdhani et al. (2021) has considered the idea of a caffeine nap in the context of athletics. The research aimed to compare the effect of a 20-minute nap, a ‘moderate’ dose of caffeine, or a moderate dose of caffeine taken before a 20-minute nap. Noting that it is customary for athletes to be in sleep debt, this study found that the “combination of caffeine ingestion and a short afternoon nap could improve repeated sprint performance and … reduce muscle damage” (p 717). Nine highly trained male judokas were the participants for the study; they were nonhabitual nappers, non-smokers and caffeine naïve. They were also regularly engaged in training approximately two hours per day, ﬁve days per week and had participated in competition for at least the previous ﬁve years. Participants performed ﬁve test sessions one week apart in a randomised and counterbalanced order and they were assigned to either: (1) baseline normal sleep night; (2) placebo; (3) 20-minute nap with PLA ingestion; (4) intake of caffeine without napping or (5) intake of caffeine before 20-minute nap. Each session involved attending the laboratory, eating a standard meal, 90 minutes of free activity time followed by bedtime (all lights and devices off). The following morning the eating and activities of the participants were controlled and monitored; at 1400 hours participants in the nap condition entered a room that was conducive to sleep (comfortably warm, fully dark and quiet). At this time, volunteers ingested either caffeine or a placebo depending on the condition they were experiencing. Participants then got into bed wearing earplugs and eye masks and had a 20-minute nap opportunity; those in the no-nap condition ingested caffeine or placebo at the same 4 time. Participants were awoken by an alarm and subjectively rated their sleep then undertook a running-based sprint test. Schweitzer et al. (2006) considered the use of caffeine naps as a means of improving the alertness and performance of shift workers during night-time working. They evaluated the effects of napping, caffeine, and napping plus caffeine; experiments were conducted in both laboratory and ﬁeld settings. The researchers concluded from their study that napping plus caffeine together (caffeine nap) helps improve the performance and alertness of night-shift workers. In the sleep laboratory setting the study employed a parallel-groups design which randomly assigned 68 healthy participants to one of four experimental conditions: a nap opportunity before the ﬁrst two of four consecutive simulated night shifts plus placebo taken prior to all four night shifts; caffeine taken 30 minutes prior to all four night shifts; a combination of the ﬁrst two conditions; and placebo before all four simulated night shifts with no naps on any evening. In the ﬁeld study a crossover design was utilised in which 53 shift workers who worked nights or rotating shifts experienced two conditions. The conditions were an evening nap on the ﬁrst two of four consecutive night shifts plus caffeine taken nightly compared with placebo taken nightly without naps. The study found that the caffeine and nap condition was the most effective for subjective sleepiness and performance and concluded that the effects of a short nap to counter mid-afternoon sleepiness could be enhanced by combining caffeine intake, exposure to bright light, or face washing. Another study which was concerned with shift work found that “Compared to placebo, the caffeine-nap resulted in improved vigilant attention and subjective fatigue in the 45 min post-nap opportunity” (Centofanti et al., 2020 p 1469). This ﬁnding led the authors to suggest that a caffeine nap might help to reduce sleep inertia in shift workers who nap whilst working a night shift. The study involved just six healthy adults who did not habitually work shifts; this low number of participants is recognised by the authors as being a limitation of the research. The method was a counter-balanced double-blind crossover study in which participants attended a laboratory twice for 36 h, with visits separated by one week. Participants’ sleep was measured using a sleep diary during the week prior to their attendance. They consumed either 200 mg of caffeine or decaffeinated coffee (placebo) immediately before a nap opportunity of 30 min at 03.30 h. Hayashi et al. (2003) took the idea of caffeine nap further; the objective of their study examined whether the combination of a short daytime nap with caffeine, bright light and face washing was effective against mid-afternoon sleepiness. There were ten young healthy adult participants who experienced ﬁve experimental conditions: nap only; taking a 20-minute nap; caffeine and nap (200mg of caffeine followed by a nap); nap and bright light; nap and face-washing; and no nap (taking a rest without sleep). The participants engaged in computer tasks for 15 minutes before napping and for one hour after napping. 5 As can be seen, caffeine nap has been shown to be effective in reducing sleepiness. However, only the study by Horne & Reyner (1996) considered caffeine nap in the context of driving. As noted by Bayne et al. (2020) in their literature review (and discussions with experts) of countermeasures to reduce drowsy driving, further “research is needed to explore the beneﬁts of combining caffeine and napping, including identifying the optimal length of naps and dosage of caffeine” (p.11). It is clear from the review, therefore, that the current study is original in its nature and will be able to add new knowledge to the ﬁeld. Napping behaviour Although recognised as an effective countermeasure to minimise sleepiness, there is a lack of research on the extent to which drivers generally use napping in this way; this includes a dearth of information relating to how they would practically achieve a nap. That is, potential answers relating to where inside the car they would nap, where they would park their vehicle and so on. Notably, a preliminary study has found that sleeping in a limited space is possible, but that the quality of sleep and comfort are signiﬁcantly lower (Smulders & Vink, 2021). The authors note that “tweaking the 2D dimensions of the reduced space can limit the negative impact on sleep quality” which is of relevance when considering the behaviour of drivers taking a nap in a vehicle. Vink et al. (2025) have also investigated sleeping postures in order to establish guidelines for the physical requirements for space and environment for sleeping in vehicles. Taking into account the lack of research on the napping behaviour of sleepy drivers, other research has concentrated on the effects of sleeping in a seat which is important when considering the potential of sleeping in a car. Roach et al. (2018) took into consideration how shift workers sleep in on-board rest facilities during duty periods and examined the impact of back angle on the quantity and quality of sleep obtained in a seat during a daytime nap. Under investigation were seats at 20° (upright), 40° (reclined), and 90° (ﬂat) and polysomnographic data were collected during all sleep episodes. In general, the quantity and quality of sleep obtained in the reclined and ﬂat seats were better than those obtained in the upright seat. When considering a car seat in particular, Hayashi and Abe’s (2008) study reinforces this ﬁnding. Their investigation involving 11 university students completing both a reaction time task and a vigilance task indicated that a 15-minute nap in a car seat “was effective in improving subjective sleepiness and fatigue as well as task performance and reducing nodding off during the task” (p 40). They also found that “… a seat angle closer to the horizontal produced added beneﬁts compared to a more perpendicular seat angle” (p 40). Importantly, sleep content was improved for the participants at a more horizontal angle. In a study involving 40 participants and carried out by Vink et al. (2023), discomfort was at the lowest level when the backrest angle was at an average of 125° (see also Vink et al., 2021). Ogata et al. (2022) explored the effect of seat angle when sleeping in a car in terms of an increasing need for resting in this way during disasters. They were in 6 agreement that a seat angle closer to the horizontal is more beneﬁcial than a more perpendicular seat angle. Zhao et al. (2010) investigated the effects of physical positions on sleep architectures and post-nap functions among habitual nappers in the situation of sleeping in a seat. Although this might not necessarily be a car seat it has relevance for considering the possibilities related to the beneﬁts which might be gained from napping as a countermeasure to driver sleepiness. The study aimed to investigate the subjective and physiological effects of a short-term midday nap in different physical positions. Thirty-six habitual nappers (18 men, 18 women) aged 18–23 years participated in the study and showed that taking a nap in a seat is a way to subjective restoration but taking a nap in a bed beneﬁts the habitual nappers subjectively and physiologically. Of additional note are two studies investigating nocturnal driving, both of which included a napping condition (Sagaspe et al., 2007 and Philip et al., 2006). In each case the study was taking into consideration caffeine and napping separately (rather than in the form of a caffeine nap); they are relevant here because both involved participants napping in a driver’s seat as part of the trial. For both studies, the method involved the driver’s seat being fully reclined and participants being covered with a blanket. A constant temperature was kept in the car (19° C) which was parked in a “quiet rest area” and guarded by the co-driver. A further indication of behaviour in private vehicles can be found in relatively recent studies which concentrate on autonomous vehicles (AVs). Since responsibility for the driving task will be largely removed from drivers of AVs, researchers have investigated non-driving related tasks; sleeping has been a focus, particularly for increasingly automated vehicles. Any ﬁndings in this context are necessarily different from those which might be taken from a stationery car, but they do provide insights into comfort and sleep quality. For example, Wilson et al. (2022) reviewed non-driving related tasks for future autonomous vehicle owners and found that sleep and relaxation were activities which they would be prepared to undertake in a car of the future. Furthermore, other studies have found that napping and sleeping are very popular non-driving related tasks (Becker et al., 2018; Kyriakidis, Happee & de Winter, 2015) and that this could be widespread with the wish to sleep during automated driving being related to an individual’s current mobility behaviour and their personal desire to enhance comfort during trips (Tomzig & Kremer, 2022). Bearing in mind that sleep is fundamental for human beings and one third of each day is spent sleeping, it might be expected that users of fully automated vehicles would choose to sleep while travelling (Caballero-Bruno et al., 2022). The act of sleeping in a moving AV might provide some insight into driver behaviour when napping in a parked vehicle. Caballero-Bruno et al. (2022) investigated the best 7 conditions to allow sleep and improve the quality of that sleep while travelling in AVs and focused on two seat positions: reclined (60° backrest decline) and ﬂat (87° backrest decline). Having undertaken two studies (a sleep study and a pressure distribution study) with 40 participants sleeping during a 90-minute drive, the authors concluded that the ﬂat seat position is the most comfortable and effective for sleeping. A similar study by Stanglmeier et al. (2020) aimed to predict the most favourable sleeping positions in car seats by evaluating the biomechanical quality of a variety of backrest and seat pan angle combinations. They involved 23 participants in assessing a total of nine (3x3) combinations of seat pan and backrest angles. Eight of the nine combinations were considered to be suitable for sleeping but their ﬁnal recommendation was for the speciﬁc mixture of a 40° seat pan angle and 155° backrest. A key ﬁnding was that people prefer a ﬂat-as-possible position for sleeping, which may have implications for where in a vehicle they might choose to nap. A study investigating environmental conditions and products to help with comfortable napping in vehicles focused on different seat backrest angles, but also considered other elements which support sleep quality. They found that the quality of a nap is not just inﬂuenced by physical aspects such as backrest, but that products such as blankets/sheets, pillows, blindfolds, socks and earplugs are required. Environmentally, participants noted they required it to be dark, warm, silent and/or cool (Vink et al., 2023). As noted above, there is a dearth of research investigating the real-world details of drivers’ napping behaviour, however advice is available on sleeping in a vehicle. This advice includes information relating to sleeping overnight, but this would be relevant to someone taking a nap. It should be noted that advice suggests that it is not illegal, but not necessarily advisable. Tips for staying safe include sleeping in the backseat – this is thought to be more comfortable and less likely to result in someone checking you are well. Other advice involves locking the doors; opening a window slightly to maximise fresh air; not leaving the engine running; setting an alarm to avoid oversleeping; and ﬁnding somewhere quiet to park, away from streetlights if possible (Compare the Market, undated). Managing daytime and driver sleepiness – OSA patients As noted above, the research is also concerned with OSA patients being at increased risk of driver sleepiness and the associated gap in evidence regarding what this speciﬁc demographic should do if they experience sleepiness while driving. The current situation with regard to OSA and permission to drive revolves around excessive sleepiness; that is, where excessive sleepiness is present and OSAS is suspected you must not drive until a diagnosis is conﬁrmed, and the excessive sleepiness symptoms are controlled. A diagnosis of mild, moderate or severe 8 Obstructive Sleep Apnoea (OSA) without excessive sleepiness means a person may continue to drive as normal and does not need to notify the DVLA (Sleep Apnoea Trust, 2022). The UK Government website defines excessive sleepiness as having had difficulty concentrating and finding yourself falling asleep whilst driving. The requirement is to inform the DVLA due to having confirmed “moderate or severe obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome (OSAS), with excessive sleepiness”. The rule is that individuals must not drive until they are free from excessive sleepiness or until their symptoms are under control and they are strictly following any necessary treatment (UK Government, 2023). The Sleep Apnoea Trust provides detailed support for those unsure about the position. Any Obstructive Sleep Apnoea diagnosis needs to be clear and precise so that a decision can be made on whether or not the DVLA should be informed. If Obstructive Sleep Apnoea without excessive sleepiness is diagnosed, no notiﬁcation is necessary. If the diagnosis is Obstructive Sleep Apnoea with excessive sleepiness, in other words, Obstructive Sleep Apnoea Syndrome (OSAS), notiﬁcation will be required. Professional drivers may adhere to different rules from those driving cars and motorcycles privately. The prevalence of OSA is estimated to be between three and ten per cent of the population (Young et al., 1993; Bearpark et al., 1995; Bixler et al., 2001), but this increases signiﬁcantly with age and with body mass gain (two cardinal demographic features of the UK population). OSA is an increasingly prevalent sleep disorder as improved diagnosis coincides with a population-level increase in obesity (Tregear et al., 2010) and has been shown to confer a 7-fold risk of car crash (Stradling, 2008). It is important to note the signiﬁcance of treatment in the driving context – when effectively treated by continuous positive air pressure (CPAP) therapy, patients with OSA have a level of driving performance that is comparable with that of controls (Filtness et al., 2011). Once treated many OSA patients are considered to be ﬁt to drive; post-treatment, the incidence of road traffic collisions for this group can be substantially reduced (Yamamoto et al., 2000; Hardinge, 2008) and is similar to that of healthy controls (George, 2001). However, our previous research has demonstrated that those with OSA have a greater vulnerability to sleep loss even with the appropriate treatment (Filtness et al., 2011); in addition, missing treatment can increase sleepiness (Filtness et al., 2012). Treated OSA patients are more vulnerable to sleep loss than are healthy controls7, and that missing treatment for just one night has catastrophic implications for driving14. This shows that treated OSA patients are still at risk of driver sleepiness and an awareness of this fact means that people with OSA may modify their driving behaviour (Hanning & Welsh, 1996). The prevalence amongst OSA patients of the use of countermeasures for staying alert (as compared to a control group without OSA) can be seen in a study by Dwarakanath et al. (2024). The authors recommend that future research should focus on the use of strategies within a journey and on which countermeasures are particularly appropriate for OSA patients. 9 it is clear that there are some medical interventions available for helping OSA patients with excessive daytime sleepiness, however, there is a dearth of literature considering how they manage it for themselves. There is a similar lack of research into how people with OSA manage driver sleepiness, although it is recognised that it is likely they will modify their driving behaviour (Hanning & Welsh, 1996). This may include increased knowledge and use of napping, but the evidence is not available. Furthermore, there is a suggestion that facilities to investigate and manage patients with OSA are inadequate in most countries throughout Europe (Krieger, 2007). At the time at which this article (Krieger, 2007) was written, OSA was a relatively recently recognised condition although of high prevalence. It is worth noting here that lack of diagnosis may also be an issue, for example, in a study involving truck drivers, Pylkkönen et al. (2015) had no participants with a diagnosed sleep disorder, although almost one fourth of the participating drivers reported symptoms indicative of sleep disorders. OSA being such a recent discovery might perhaps explain the general failure of administrators and those from other disciplines to recognise the importance of providing for the practice of sleep medicine. A further argument for effective management of OSA is the potential economic beneﬁt which exists in addition to the reduced risk of accidents. In relation to commercial motor vehicle drivers, Wada et al. (2019) have noted the importance of diagnosis of sleep disordered breathing (of which OSA is a common type). They highlight the signiﬁcance of CPAP therapy, suggesting that OSA drivers on CPAP therapy and drivers without OSA have been shown to demonstrate the same level of risk for traffic accidents. This therefore highlights the importance of adherence to the therapy, not just for general health purposes but also for safety when driving. The majority of research investigating the driving behaviour of those with OSA involves a simulated driving task. This is likely to be due to the idea that “… the multiple components of driving ability suggest that driving simulators may be better suited for the evaluation of driving ability” (Krieger 2007). For example, Boyle et al. (2008) used a driving simulator to ﬁnd that individuals with OSA who are at increased risk for drowsy driving demonstrate a greater level of impairments in driving performance in the moments during microsleep episodes compared to during periods of wakefulness. The degree of performance decrement correlated with microsleep episodes, suggesting that detecting microsleeps is relevant to the design and implementation of countermeasures. The participants had OSA that was diagnosed but not treated. Another study making use of a driving simulator found that adequate OSA management with either OA (oral appliance) or CPAP therapy (for two to three months) tended to result in substantial improvements in simulated driving (compared to no therapy) (Hoekema et al., 2007). However, they were not prepared use their data to draw conclusions beyond the fact that both treatments may improve simulated driving 10 performance; their ﬁndings therefore cannot necessarily be applied to driving on the road. In addition, Vakulin et al. (2014) used a driving simulator to demonstrate variations in the levels of daytime sleepiness in those with untreated OSA. They suggest that this rate of variation makes it difficult to identify patients at risk of impairment and therefore also hard to make decisions regarding an individual’s driving ability and accident risk. This document is a literature review (Appendix 1) for the CAFFNap project, a research study evaluating the efficacy of "caffeine-nap" (consuming coffee immediately prior to a short nap of less than 30 minutes) as a countermeasure to driver sleepiness specifically for obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) patients. The project is led by Professor Ashleigh Filtness and Dr Sally Maynard at Loughborough University's Transport Safety Research Centre (TSRC), with collaborators from VTI, University Hospitals Leicester, and patient organizations including the Leicester Sleep Apnoea Patient Association and the Sleep Apnoea Trust. The research aims to fill a gap in evidence regarding what tired OSA drivers should do when experiencing sleepiness while driving, ultimately producing an evidence-based recommendation for caffeine-nap best practice.

**Key findings on caffeine naps:**
- The NHTSA recommends consuming caffeine prior to a 20-minute nap to increase alertness.
- Horne & Reyner (1996) found that "caffeine and nap significantly reduced driving impairments, subjective sleepiness and electroencephalographic (EEG) activity indicating drowsiness" — the only study to date examining caffeine naps in a driving context.
- Bonnet & Arand (1994) demonstrated that a 4-hour prophylactic nap combined with caffeine maintained alertness, performance, and mood at near-baseline levels across a 24-hour sleep-loss period in 24 young adult males.
- Romdhani et al. (2021) found that caffeine combined with a 20-minute afternoon nap improved repeated sprint performance and reduced muscle damage in athletes.
- Schweitzer et al. (2006) concluded that napping plus caffeine improves performance and alertness in night-shift workers (68 participants in laboratory, 53 in field study).
- Centofanti et al. (2020) found caffeine-nap improved vigilant attention and subjective fatigue in the 45 minutes post-nap, suggesting reduced sleep inertia (though only 6 participants, acknowledged as a limitation).
- Bayne et al. (2020) noted further research is needed on optimal nap lengths and caffeine dosages for drowsy driving countermeasures.

**Key findings on napping behaviour:**
- Smulders & Vink (2021) found sleeping in limited space is possible but sleep quality and comfort are significantly lower.
- Hayashi & Abe (2008) showed a 15-minute nap in a car seat was effective in improving subjective sleepiness, fatigue, task performance, and reducing nodding off; a more horizontal seat angle produced added benefits.
- Vink et al. (2023) found discomfort was lowest at a backrest angle of approximately 125°.
- Roach et al. (2018) found reclined and flat seats yielded better sleep quantity/quality than upright seats.
- Caballero-Bruno et al. (2022) concluded flat seat position (87° backrest decline) is most comfortable and effective for sleeping in autonomous vehicles.
- Stanglmeier et al. (2020) recommended a 40° seat pan angle and 155° backrest for sleeping in car seats; people prefer flat-as-possible positions.
- Vink et al. (2023) found nap quality is influenced not just by backrest but by products like blankets, pillows, blindfolds, socks, and earplugs, and environments that are dark, warm, silent, and/or cool.
- Practical advice for sleeping in a car includes sleeping in the backseat, locking doors, opening a window slightly, not leaving the engine running, setting an alarm, and parking in quiet areas away from streetlights.

**Key findings on OSA and driving:**
- OSA prevalence is estimated at 3-10% of the population, increasing with age and body mass gain.
- OSA confers a 7-fold risk of car crash (Stradling, 2008).
- When effectively treated with CPAP therapy, OSA patients achieve driving performance comparable to controls (Filtness et al., 2011); post-treatment collision incidence is substantially reduced and similar to healthy controls (Yamamoto et al., 2000; Hardinge, 2008; George, 2001).
- However, treated OSA patients are more vulnerable to sleep loss than healthy controls, and missing CPAP treatment for just one night has "catastrophic implications for driving" (Filtness et al., 2012).
- UK driving regulations: individuals with confirmed moderate or severe OSAS with excessive sleepiness must not drive until symptoms are controlled and must notify the DVLA; OSA without excessive sleepiness requires no notification (UK Government, 2023; Sleep Apnoea Trust, 2022).
- There is a dearth of literature on how OSA patients self-manage driver sleepiness and daytime sleepiness, though they are likely to modify driving behaviour (Hanning & Welsh, 1996).
- Most OSA driving research uses driving simulators, with studies showing microsleep-related performance impairments (Boyle et al., 2008), improvements from OA or CPAP therapy (Hoekema et al., 2007), and individual variability in daytime sleepiness making risk identification difficult (Vakulin et al., 2014).
args.key_excerpts: "Caffeine and nap significantly reduced driving impairments, subjective sleepiness and electroencephalographic (EEG) activity indicating drowsiness" — Horne & Reyner (1996)
