# Caffeine and sleep: a useful guide to dose, timing, and half-life

The cup is gone in ten minutes. The caffeine is not. This guide separates what can be calculated from what has to be learned from your own sleep.

Checked against authoritative sources

Evidence reviewed 6 August 2026· 12minute read

General education, not individual medical advice.

The short answer

Caffeine can still matter hours after you drink it. EFSA describes an adult average half-life near four hours and a typical range of roughly two to eight hours, and even 100 mg close to bedtime can alter sleep in some adults.

Illustrative model

## One dose, three possible clearance curves

2-hour half-life4-hour half-life8-hour half-life

Percentage of the starting dose remaining. These are mathematical scenarios, not measured blood levels.

A practical sequence

## Dose first, timing second, sleep outcome last

1. 01

   Estimate the doseUse the product or café value where possible.
2. 02

   Count the hoursCompare faster, average, and slower clearance.
3. 03

   Watch the outcomeSleep onset, awakenings, and next-day function.

Explore this guide

[## Caffeine half-life, without the misleading countdown

Learn what caffeine half-life means, why four hours is only a population average, and how to read a decay estimate without treating it as a measurement.

Read the guide](/caffeine-and-sleep/caffeine-half-life)[## How long does caffeine last? A practical timeline

Follow a practical caffeine timeline from absorption to the long tail, with examples for common doses and guidance on interpreting lingering effects.

Read the guide](/caffeine-and-sleep/how-long-does-caffeine-last)[## Caffeine before bed: how to choose a cutoff

Use dose, half-life, and repeated sleep observations to choose a caffeine cutoff instead of copying a universal rule.

Read the guide](/caffeine-and-sleep/caffeine-before-bed)[## Caffeine during pregnancy: understanding the 200 mg guidance

Understand the widely used 200 mg pregnancy guidance, how to count all caffeine sources, and why your clinician's advice takes priority.

Read the guide](/caffeine-and-sleep/caffeine-during-pregnancy)[## How much caffeine is in coffee, tea, and energy drinks?

Compare caffeine sources, account for serving size, and learn how to record uncertain amounts when a measured value is unavailable.

Read the guide](/caffeine-and-sleep/caffeine-in-coffee-tea-and-energy-drinks)[Free tool

## Caffeine half-life calculator

Estimate how much caffeine may remain by bedtime, compare faster and slower clearance, and see every assumption behind the curve.

Open the tool](/tools/caffeine-half-life-calculator)

## Dose and timing are two different questions

Daily caffeine guidance and bedtime timing are often collapsed into one number. They answer different questions. A daily limit describes intake across a day for a broad population. Sleep timing asks how much of a particular dose may remain when you want to sleep.

For most healthy adults, the FDA cites 400 mg a day as an amount not generally associated with negative effects. That is not a promise that 400 mg will leave your sleep untouched. EFSA notes that a single 100 mg dose may affect sleep duration and patterns in some adults when consumed close to bedtime.

* Count caffeine from every source, not only coffee.
* Treat package or menu values as estimates unless the manufacturer gives a measured amount.
* Keep daily-intake guidance separate from your personal last-call time.

Sources for this section: [U.S. Food and Drug Administration](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/spilling-beans-how-much-caffeine-too-much), [European Food Safety Authority](https://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/topics/topic/caffeine).

## Half-life is a curve, not an expiry time

A four-hour half-life means an estimated half of a dose remains after four hours, one quarter after eight hours, and one eighth after twelve. The amount approaches zero gradually; it does not suddenly disappear at the eight-hour mark.

EFSA describes an average plasma half-life in healthy adults of about four hours, with a typical range from roughly two to eight hours. An older National Academies review reports a broader range. Genetics, pregnancy, smoking, medicines, liver health, and other factors can shift clearance. A calculator can show a range. It cannot identify your personal metabolism from a bedtime and a cup size.

Sources for this section: [European Food Safety Authority](https://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/topics/topic/caffeine), [National Academies Press via NCBI Bookshelf](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK223808/).

## What the sleep studies actually tell us

A frequently cited laboratory-and-home study tested a substantial 400 mg dose at bedtime and three or six hours before bedtime. Sleep was disrupted at all three timings. The result shows that a large late dose can reach farther into the night than people expect. It does not establish an identical six-hour rule for everyone.

A later systematic review and meta-analysis found caffeine reduced total sleep time, reduced deep sleep, and increased the time it took to fall asleep. Studies differed in dose, timing, participants, and measurement. That variation is exactly why a single universal cutoff is too neat.

Do not turn the six-hour finding into a guarantee. The study used 400 mg, far more than many ordinary servings, and individual responses vary.

Sources for this section: [Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine via PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24235903/), [Sleep Medicine Reviews via PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36870101/).

## Build a cutoff from observation, not bravado

Start with the sleep time you want to protect. Work backwards using a cautious half-life range, then run the same routine for a week: similar bedtime, similar caffeine dose, and no large weekend swing. Note how long it takes to fall asleep, night waking, and how you feel the next morning.

If sleep is poor, move the last dose earlier or make it smaller. Change one thing at a time. A 30-minute move is easier to learn from than a complete reset that also changes exercise, alcohol, screen use, and bedtime.

* Write down the actual milligrams when you can.
* Include chocolate, pre-workout products, energy drinks, tea, and medicines that contain caffeine.
* Keep the experiment boring enough that the result is interpretable.

## Pregnancy and medical context need different rules

Pregnancy changes both the recommended daily amount and how long caffeine may remain in the body. ACOG describes moderate consumption as less than 200 mg per day; EFSA says intake up to 200 mg per day from all sources does not raise safety concerns for the fetus. Your own clinician may advise a different limit for your circumstances.

Medicines and health conditions can also change sensitivity or clearance. If caffeine causes palpitations, marked anxiety, tremor, persistent insomnia, or other symptoms, a decay estimate is not the right tool for deciding what to do next. Speak with a qualified clinician.

Sources for this section: [American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2010/08/moderate-caffeine-consumption-during-pregnancy), [European Food Safety Authority](https://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/topics/topic/caffeine), [U.S. Food and Drug Administration](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/spilling-beans-how-much-caffeine-too-much).

## Use the calculation as a planning aid

The useful output is not a green or red verdict. It is a comparison: what changes if the drink is smaller, the bedtime is later, or your half-life sits at the slower end of a plausible range? Seeing those curves together makes timing less abstract.

Pair the estimate with your own sleep notes. The equation supplies consistency; your observations supply the missing personal context. If they disagree, trust the repeated real-world pattern rather than forcing your body to match the model.

Sources for this section: [National Academies Press via NCBI Bookshelf](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK223808/).

## Common questions

### How many hours before bed should I stop caffeine?

There is no universal cutoff. A 400 mg dose disrupted sleep even six hours before bed in one study, while dose and individual clearance vary widely. Start earlier than you think, then adjust from repeated sleep observations.

### Does caffeine leave the body after eight hours?

Not completely. With a four-hour half-life, about one quarter of the original dose remains after eight hours. Faster and slower metabolism change that estimate.

### Is 400 mg a sleep-safe amount?

No. The FDA figure is general daily guidance for most healthy adults, not a sleep guarantee. Smaller doses may disturb sleep in some people, especially near bedtime.

### Can I calculate my exact caffeine level?

Not from drink size and time alone. A calculator estimates a curve using an assumed half-life; it cannot measure blood levels or account for every personal factor.

## Sources and review notes

We favour public-health guidance, clinical bodies, official statistics, and original research. Source links are provided so you can inspect the wording and boundaries yourself.

1. 01[Spilling the Beans: How Much Caffeine is Too Much?](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/spilling-beans-how-much-caffeine-too-much)U.S. Food and Drug Administration
2. 02[Caffeine: safety guidance for adults and pregnancy](https://www.efsa.europa.eu/en/topics/topic/caffeine)European Food Safety Authority
3. 03[Pharmacology of Caffeine](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK223808/)National Academies Press via NCBI Bookshelf · 2001
4. 04[Caffeine effects on sleep taken 0, 3, or 6 hours before going to bed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24235903/)Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine via PubMed · 2013
5. 05[The effect of caffeine on subsequent sleep: a systematic review and meta-analysis](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36870101/)Sleep Medicine Reviews via PubMed · 2023
6. 06[Moderate Caffeine Consumption During Pregnancy](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2010/08/moderate-caffeine-consumption-during-pregnancy)American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists · 2010; reaffirmed 2026

# Caffeine and Sleep: Finding Your Personal Cutoff Time (It's Not 2PM for Everyone)

* Ryan - Kygo Health
* Jan 11
* 11 min read

Updated: Jul 28

**Last Updated: January 11, 2026**

You've probably heard the standard advice: stop drinking caffeine by 2 PM if you want good sleep. It's repeated so often in health circles that it's become gospel. There's just one problem with this rule—**research shows your personal caffeine cutoff time could be hours different from the generic recommendation.**

Some people can drink espresso at 8 PM and sleep like babies. Others find that even morning coffee affects their sleep quality that night. The difference isn't willpower or sleep hygiene—it's genetics, metabolism, and individual physiology. And the only way to discover your personal caffeine tolerance is by tracking how your body actually responds, not by following population averages that may not apply to you.

## The Research: Why Caffeine Wrecks Sleep (For Most People)

Before we dive into personal variation, let's understand what caffeine actually does to sleep. The research here is extensive and remarkably consistent.

### The Numbers Are Striking

A comprehensive meta-analysis examining 24 studies on caffeine and sleep revealed sobering results: consuming caffeine before bed leads to an average of **45 minutes less total sleep time** and approximately **7% lower sleep efficiency** (the percentage of time in bed actually spent asleep).

These aren't trivial effects. Losing 45 minutes of sleep consistently adds up to 5.25 hours per week—more than a full night's sleep lost weekly to an avoidable dietary choice. And the 7% reduction in sleep efficiency means more time lying awake, more fragmented rest, and less restorative sleep overall.

But here's where it gets interesting: these are averages across populations. The standard deviations in these studies show massive individual variation. Some participants experienced minimal sleep disruption from evening caffeine. Others showed dramatic effects, losing over 90 minutes of sleep.

### The 8.8-Hour Rule Nobody Talks About

Research on caffeine metabolism reveals why timing matters so much. Caffeine has a half-life of approximately 5-6 hours in most people, but the effects on sleep can persist much longer. Studies show that caffeine consumed even **8.8 hours before bedtime** significantly reduces total sleep time.

Think about what this means practically. If you go to bed at 11 PM, caffeine consumed as early as 2:10 PM could still be affecting your sleep. If you're a 10 PM sleeper, your cutoff moves to 1:10 PM. For night owls who sleep at midnight, you get until 3:10 PM.

The generic "no caffeine after 2 PM" advice? It's calibrated for an 11 PM bedtime. If you sleep earlier or later, that guideline doesn't match your physiology.

### How Caffeine Actually Works: The Adenosine Story

Understanding the mechanism helps explain why individual variation exists. Caffeine doesn't directly make you feel awake—it blocks the signals that make you feel sleepy.

Throughout the day, your brain accumulates a molecule called adenosine. As adenosine levels rise, it binds to receptors in your brain, creating "sleep pressure"—the growing feeling of tiredness that eventually compels you to sleep. This is your body's natural sleep-wake regulation system.

Caffeine is a molecular impostor. Its structure closely resembles adenosine, allowing it to occupy those same receptors without triggering the sleepiness signal. Adenosine keeps accumulating, but you don't feel it because caffeine is blocking the receptors.

Eventually, caffeine is metabolized and cleared from your system. When those receptors finally become available again, all the accumulated adenosine floods in at once. This is why caffeine "wears off" sometimes results in a crash—you suddenly feel all the tiredness that was masked for hours.

### The Vicious Cycle Problem

Here's where caffeine's sleep effects become truly problematic: yesterday's caffeine leads to today's sleep deficit, which leads to today's caffeine need, which leads to tonight's poor sleep, which leads to tomorrow's increased caffeine consumption.

Research demonstrates this clearly. People who consume caffeine regularly to combat tiredness caused by insufficient sleep create a feedback loop. The caffeine further impairs their sleep, increasing their need for caffeine the next day. Over time, baseline sleep quality deteriorates while caffeine consumption escalates.

Breaking this cycle requires identifying your personal caffeine cutoff time and respecting it—even when you're tired and tempted to grab that afternoon coffee.

## Why Your Caffeine Tolerance Is Unique

### Genetic Variation in Metabolism

Your liver processes caffeine using an enzyme called CYP1A2. The gene that produces this enzyme comes in different variants, and which variant you inherited determines how quickly you metabolize caffeine.

**Fast metabolizers** clear caffeine from their system in 3-4 hours. These are the people who can drink coffee late and still sleep well. Their bodies process and eliminate caffeine quickly enough that evening consumption doesn't significantly affect bedtime.

**Slow metabolizers** take 8-10 hours or longer to clear the same amount of caffeine. For these individuals, afternoon coffee can still be circulating in significant quantities at bedtime, dramatically affecting sleep quality.

You can't change which variant you inherited. But you can discover how your body actually responds by tracking caffeine intake against your sleep data.

### Age Changes Everything

Caffeine metabolism changes significantly across your lifespan. Adolescents and young adults typically metabolize caffeine faster than older adults. By age 60-70, caffeine clearance can slow by 30-50% compared to your twenties.

This means your caffeine cutoff time isn't static—it shifts as you age. The 4 PM coffee that was fine at age 25 might disrupt your sleep at 45. Your personal tolerance requires ongoing discovery, not a one-time assessment.

### Medication Interactions

Certain medications dramatically affect caffeine metabolism. Oral contraceptives can slow caffeine clearance by 40-60%. Antidepressants like fluvoxamine inhibit CYP1A2, extending caffeine's half-life significantly. Even some antibiotics alter how your body processes caffeine.

If you start or stop medications and suddenly find your sleep quality changing, caffeine timing might be the hidden variable.

### Pregnancy Amplifies Sensitivity

During pregnancy, caffeine metabolism slows dramatically. In the third trimester, caffeine's half-life can extend to 15-18 hours—triple the normal duration. This is why pregnant women are advised to limit caffeine, but it also explains why their personal cutoff time moves much earlier in the day.

## Finding Your Personal Caffeine Cutoff Time

Generic advice fails because your body's caffeine response is unique. The only reliable way to find your personal cutoff time is through systematic tracking and analysis.

### The Two-Week Discovery Protocol

Here's how to scientifically determine your personal caffeine tolerance:

**Week 1: Establish Your Baseline**

Track every source of caffeine you consume—coffee, tea, energy drinks, pre-workout supplements, even chocolate. Note the time and approximate caffeine content. Simultaneously track your sleep metrics: time to fall asleep (sleep latency), total sleep time, sleep quality ratings, and if you have a wearable device, deep sleep duration and HRV.

Don't change your habits yet. Just collect data on your current patterns. This baseline reveals your starting point and highlights correlations you might already notice.

**Week 2: The Systematic Test**

Start testing cutoff times systematically. For three days, stop all caffeine consumption by 2 PM. Track your sleep. Then for three days, extend the cutoff to 3 PM. Track sleep again. If you notice no difference, try 4 PM for three days.

The goal is to find the latest time you can consume caffeine without measurably affecting your sleep metrics. For most people, this falls somewhere between 12 PM and 4 PM, but your personal cutoff could be outside that range.

### What to Track (And Why Each Metric Matters)

**Sleep Latency (Time to Fall Asleep)**

This is often the first metric affected by late caffeine. If you normally fall asleep in 10-15 minutes but suddenly take 30-45 minutes, caffeine timing is the likely culprit. Research shows caffeine can increase sleep latency by 8-12 minutes on average, but some individuals experience much larger effects. Caffeine is one of [33 researched factors that affect sleep latency](https://www.kygo.app/tools/sleep-latency-factors).

**Deep Sleep Duration**

Caffeine can suppress deep sleep even when it doesn't affect sleep latency. You might fall asleep normally but spend less time in the restorative deep sleep stages. If you track sleep with an Oura Ring, Whoop, or similar device, watch how deep sleep percentage changes on days with different caffeine cutoff times. See what else raises or lowers [deep sleep](https://www.kygo.app/tools/deep-sleep-factors).

**Heart Rate Variability (HRV)**

Caffeine stimulates the sympathetic nervous system, which can suppress overnight HRV. Lower HRV indicates reduced parasympathetic (rest-and-digest) activity and poorer recovery. Some people show significant HRV suppression from late caffeine even when subjective sleep quality feels fine. Caffeine is one of [44 factors that move HRV](https://www.kygo.app/post/how-to-improve-hrv-factors-ranked-by-evidence).

**Sleep Quality Ratings**

Don't ignore subjective experience. How rested do you feel in the morning? Some objective metrics might show minimal change, but if you consistently feel groggier after late caffeine, that matters regardless of what the numbers say.

### The Surprising Patterns People Discover

When people systematically track their caffeine-sleep correlations, they often find unexpected patterns:

**The Delayed Effect**: Some individuals discover their sleep is affected not the same night, but the following night. This delayed pattern is less common but very real for slow metabolizers.

**The Dose-Response Relationship**: One cup of coffee at 3 PM might be fine, but two cups shows measurable effects. Your cutoff time may depend on quantity, not just timing.

**The Adaptation Myth**: Many people believe they've "adapted" to late caffeine because they can still fall asleep. But their sleep architecture data reveals suppressed deep sleep and elevated heart rate. Subjective adaptation doesn't mean physiological adaptation.

**The Compound Effect**: Late caffeine combined with other factors (alcohol, heavy meals, stress) shows amplified effects. You might tolerate 3 PM coffee normally, but not on days with evening wine or late dinners.

## The Science Behind Personal Correlation Analysis

Discovering your personal caffeine cutoff time manually is possible, but it's tedious and prone to errors. This is exactly where data-driven correlation analysis excels.

### Why Manual Tracking Falls Short

When you're manually comparing your caffeine intake to your sleep data, you're working with significant limitations:

You might remember that you had coffee at 2:30 PM, but did you account for the green tea at lunch? The chocolate after dinner? Each source adds caffeine that affects your total exposure.

You notice you slept poorly last night and try to remember what was different. Was it the afternoon espresso? The later dinner? The work stress? Without statistical analysis, you're guessing about causation.

Even if you keep meticulous records, calculating time-lagged correlations across weeks of data manually is impractical. You need statistical tools to identify patterns reliably.

### How Correlation Intelligence Works

At Kygo, we're building exactly this capability—not just data tracking, but intelligent pattern recognition that reveals your personal physiological responses.

Our approach combines comprehensive nutrition tracking with deep wearable integration, then applies statistical correlation analysis to discover relationships like:

**"Your sleep latency increases by 8 minutes when you consume caffeine after 3 PM."** The system examines dozens of nights, compares caffeine timing to sleep onset, accounts for confounding variables, and identifies your specific cutoff time with statistical confidence.

**"Your deep sleep decreases by 14% on nights following 200mg+ caffeine intake after 1 PM."** This correlation factors in both timing and dosage, revealing that your personal threshold is dose-dependent.

**"Your HRV drops by 12 points when you combine late caffeine with alcohol consumption."** The analysis identifies interaction effects—combinations of factors that show amplified impacts beyond individual effects.

This is the power of moving beyond manual tracking to automated correlation intelligence. The system does the statistical heavy lifting, identifying patterns you'd never spot manually, and delivers actionable insights: "Based on your data, avoid caffeine after 2:15 PM for optimal sleep quality."

### The Personalization Advantage

Generic research tells us that caffeine affects sleep. Statistical correlation analysis tells you *how* caffeine affects *your* sleep specifically.

Maybe you're a fast metabolizer who can drink coffee at 5 PM with minimal effects. Following the generic 2 PM rule unnecessarily restricts your enjoyment. Or maybe you're a slow metabolizer who needs to stop by noon—continuing with 2 PM coffee might be sabotaging your sleep without you realizing the connection.

The beauty of personalized correlation analysis is that it reveals your unique truth. No more following population averages that might not apply to your physiology. Just your data, showing your patterns, enabling informed decisions.

## Beyond Caffeine: The Broader Lesson About Personal Health Data

The caffeine-sleep relationship illustrates a fundamental truth about health optimization: **generic advice based on population averages often fails individual application.**

This same principle applies across nutrition and biometric correlations:

* Some people's HRV improves with high-fat diets; others do better with higher carbs
* Late meals disrupt sleep for many people, but some show no effect
* Certain supplements dramatically affect one person's recovery while doing nothing for another
* Exercise timing that optimizes one person's sleep might impair someone else's rest

The solution isn't better generic advice—it's personal data intelligence that reveals your unique patterns. This is why we built Kygo around correlation discovery rather than generic recommendations.

Just as [fragmented health data across multiple apps](https://www.kygo.app/post/centralize-health-data-multiple-devices) prevents you from seeing the full picture of your health, following generic health advice without personalization prevents you from optimizing your unique physiology. And just as people [quit food logging apps](https://www.kygo.app/post/why-80-of-people-quit-food-logging-apps-and-how-to-actually-stick-with-it) because they're tedious without delivering insights, generic health tracking without correlation analysis ultimately feels pointless.

## Practical Steps You Can Take Today

### Start Tracking, Even Without Special Tools

You don't need sophisticated technology to begin discovering your caffeine patterns. Start with a simple spreadsheet:

* Column 1: Date
* Column 2: All caffeine consumed (type, quantity, time)
* Column 3: Bedtime
* Column 4: Time to fall asleep
* Column 5: Sleep quality (1-10 scale)
* Column 6: How rested you feel in the morning

Track for two weeks. Look for patterns. On nights when you slept poorly or took longer to fall asleep, what was your caffeine timing?

This manual approach has limitations, but it's infinitely better than flying blind.

### Test Systematically, Not Randomly

Don't just change your habits randomly hoping for improvement. Test systematically. Pick a cutoff time, maintain it for 3-5 days, evaluate the results, then adjust.

This methodical approach isolates the variable you're testing and reveals cause-and-effect more clearly than random experimentation.

### Account for Caffeine Sources You're Overlooking

Coffee and energy drinks are obvious, but don't forget:

* **Tea** (20-60mg per cup depending on type and brewing)
* **Chocolate** (dark chocolate contains significant caffeine)
* **Pre-workout supplements** (often 200-300mg per serving)
* **Pain medications** (some contain 65-130mg of caffeine)
* **Soft drinks** (35-55mg in typical servings)

That innocent piece of dark chocolate at 7 PM might contain 25mg of caffeine—enough to affect sleep for sensitive individuals.

### Consider Your Complete Context

Caffeine doesn't exist in isolation. Your sleep is affected by:

* Meal timing and composition
* Alcohol consumption
* Exercise timing and intensity
* Stress levels
* Screen time before bed
* Room temperature and light exposure

When testing your caffeine cutoff time, try to keep other variables relatively consistent. Otherwise, you might attribute effects to caffeine when something else is actually responsible.

# Caffeine and Sleep Review Suggests Consumption Guidelines

Author(s)[_Justina Petrullo_](https://www.ajmc.com/authors/justina-petrullo)

A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effects of caffeine on sleep aimed to help determine clear guidelines.

Advertisement

To avoid [sleep](https://www.ajmc.com/compendium/sleep) time reductions, coffee (107 mg/250 mL) should be consumed at least 8.8 hours before bedtime and a standard serving of preworkout supplement (217.5 mg) should be consumed at least 13.2 hours before bedtime, according to a review published in _[Sleep Medicine Reviews](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1087079223000205?via%3Dihub)._

This study was conducted because the consumption of caffeine in response to inadequate sleep might weaken the onset and maintenance of ensuing sleep.

The researchers were trying to understand the effect of caffeine on the characteristics of night-time sleep, with the desire to recognize the time after which caffeine should not be consumed before bedtime in a systematic review and meta-analysis.

![Image 2: a cup of coffee with coffee beans](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/0vv8moc6/ajmc/6eee61c9d9d2f2fe2d50417f131178edeee09609-800x450.jpg/Image%20of%20cup%20of%20coffee.jpeg?w=800&max-h=450&fit=crop&auto=format)

a cup of coffee with coffee beans

![Image 3](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/0vv8moc6/ajmc/6eee61c9d9d2f2fe2d50417f131178edeee09609-800x450.jpg/Image%20of%20cup%20of%20coffee.jpeg?fit=crop&auto=format)

“The half-life of caffeine displays large variation across healthy adults (2 to 10 h), making it difficult to identify the appropriate time of day to discontinue caffeine intake to minimise disruptions to sleep,” explained the study authors.

The use of caffeine to stay awake might result in weakened onset and upholding of subsequent sleep and possibly creating a cycle of reduced sleep and ensuing caffeine dependance.

A systematic search of the literature was conducted with 24 studies included in the analysis.

Caffeine consumption diminished total sleep time by 45 minutes and sleep efficiency by 7%, with a rise in sleep onset latency of 9 minutes and wake after sleep onset of 12 minutes. Duration (+6.1 minutes) and proportion (+1.7%) of light sleep (N1) grew with caffeine intake and the duration (–11.4 minutes) and proportion (–1.4%) of deep sleep (N3 and N4) lowered with caffeine intake.

By quantifying the influence of the dose and timing of caffeine intake on subsequent sleep, the investigators highlighted, cutoff times for caffeine intake before bedtime can be initiated.

After evaluating sleep onset latency, the researchers found that there seemed to be a peak effect of caffeine on sleep onset latency that happens approximately 3 hours after consumption. The findings emphasized that the consumption of caffeine prolongs the onset of ensuing sleep. Caffeine consumption was linked with a 45-minute decrease in total sleep time over the subsequent evening.

Regarding the evaluation of REM onset latency, 10 studies explored the effects of caffeine on REM onset latency, and none showed significant effects.

Wake after sleep onset was examined in 13 studies, with 6 showing a significant increase when caffeine was consumed. In the current study, it could not be determined if the increase in wake after sleep onset was affected by the amount or timing of the final caffeine dose.

Upon review of sleep efficiency, 15 of 18 studies reported a significant decrease in sleep efficiency after caffeine consumption. Of the 3 studies finding no significant effect, 2 administered the caffeine dose over multiple days. Also, 1 study showed no effect after 1200 mg of caffeine given in 3 equal doses across the morning, afternoon, and evening.

When evaluating caffeine’s effect on sleep architecture, the effect of caffeine on absolute sleep architecture was examined in 12 studies. The findings suggested that no relationship exists between caffeine timing intake and alterations in sleep stage duration.

In terms of subjective sleep outcomes, 12 studies examined the effect of caffeine on the perceptions of sleep. Ultimately, it was determined that subjective sleep outcomes are an important metric and should be integrated alongside objective measures. Collective findings from the literature review for subjective sleep outcomes suggest that chronic caffeine exposure may increase tolerance.

Current study results give evidence-based guidance for the appropriate consumption of caffeine to alleviate the deleterious sleep effects.

The researchers recommend that consumers consider the cutoff times given as a starting point and adjust the amount and timing of when they consume caffeine in response to its effect on their subsequent sleep.

Some limitations of this study are that 3 studies employed activity monitors that may have underestimated wake duration, and so there might be variation in the calculation of some outcome measures. Secondly, caffeine was administered as a single daily dose or sustained dose across multiple days across studies, so there is potential for habituation.

“The results of the present study provide evidence-based guidance for the appropriate consumption of caffeine with respect to both dose and timing of consumption to mitigate the deleterious effects on sleep,” concluded the researchers.

**Reference**

Gardiner C, Weakley J, Burke LM, et al. The effect of caffeine on subsequent sleep: a systematic review and meta-analysis. _Sleep Med Rev._ 2023;69:101764. doi:10.1016/j.smrv.2023.101764

You've been told caffeine wears off in a few hours. The science tells a more complete story.

A study in the Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine found that caffeine consumed even 6 hours before bedtime significantly reduced total sleep time and sleep quality, without the participants being aware of the disruption.

Caffeine has a half-life of about 5 to 6 hours. That means if you have a 200 mg cup of coffee at 3 p.m., about 100 mg is still circulating at 9 p.m. And about 50 mg at 3 a.m.

It doesn't always prevent sleep onset. But it reduces deep sleep and REM sleep, leaving you tired the next day despite sleeping through the night.

The cruel loop: you drink more caffeine the next day to compensate. Which disrupts the next night. And on it goes.

In my practice, many patients discover they don't have a sleep problem. They have a caffeine timing problem.

Here's the fix. Stop all caffeine by noon, or at the very latest 2 p.m. Coffee, tea, chocolate, pre-workout powders, certain medications.

If you crave something warm in the afternoon, switch to herbal tea or decaf. Rooibos, chamomile, peppermint.

Give yourself 2 weeks with an early caffeine cutoff before judging the change.

Most people find their sleep improves dramatically.

This is a Facebook post by Dr. Laurie Marbas (dated April 24) discussing the impact of caffeine on sleep quality. Key points include:

- A study from the Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine found that caffeine consumed even 6 hours before bedtime significantly reduced total sleep time and sleep quality, often without participants being aware of the disruption.
- Caffeine has a half-life of approximately 5-6 hours. For example, a 200 mg cup of coffee at 3 p.m. leaves about 100 mg circulating at 9 p.m. and about 50 mg at 3 a.m.
- Caffeine may not always prevent falling asleep, but it reduces deep sleep and REM sleep, leading to daytime fatigue despite sleeping through the night.
- Dr. Marbas describes a "cruel loop" where people consume more caffeine the next day to compensate for poor sleep, which further disrupts the following night.
- In her clinical practice, many patients discover they don't have a sleep problem but rather a caffeine timing problem.

Recommendations provided:
- Stop all caffeine by noon, or at the very latest 2 p.m. This includes coffee, tea, chocolate, pre-workout powders, and certain medications.
- Switch to herbal tea (rooibos, chamomile, peppermint) or decaf for afternoon warm beverages.
- Allow 2 weeks with an early caffeine cutoff before judging results, with most patients finding their sleep improves dramatically.

The post received 792 reactions, 38 comments, and 167 shares. Comments include people sharing their personal caffeine cutoff practices (e.g., coffee by noon, cola/tea by 2 p.m.), questions about decaf, and a few individuals noting they don't experience sleep issues despite late caffeine consumption. One commenter, Melanie Hill, defended the post as sharing widely known information aimed at the majority, while acknowledging some may not have caffeine-related sleep problems.

# Caffeine & Sleep: How Long Does Caffeine Keep You Awake?

Instead of counting sheep you're counting hours of sleep. Specifically, the number of hours you're not getting. Or, maybe you're counting the number of hours you might get if you fell asleep right *now*. Nope, still not asleep.

Was it that latte you had after lunch??

You know caffeine can keep you awake, and there are the obvious times to avoid it. (Right before bed, for instance...just in case...)

But is an afternoon pick-me-up really a problem? At the time, it felt like you needed it just as much as the sleep you're not getting now.

“It’s very important to be sure you’re getting quality sleep,” says Dr. Rashad Ramkissoon, a primary-care physician at Houston Methodist. “Certain afternoon and evening habits can get in the way of that, and caffeinated beverages are one prominent example.”

So, when it comes to that gray area between late morning and early evening, how late is too late to drink that coffee you so desperately need — or even just a soda or iced tea with dinner — without it affecting your sleep?

## **How does caffeine work?**

Once consumed, caffeine is very quickly absorbed and distributed throughout your body, including to your brain. It's here that caffeine elicits its most classic effect — helping keep you alert and awake.

“Caffeine works by blocking sleep-promoting receptors in your brain called adenosine receptors,” says Dr. Ramkissoon. “It can do this because, structurally, caffeine looks very similar to adenosine, the molecule that usually binds to these receptors.”

Adenosine plays many roles, including helping to regulate your sleep/wake cycle. Its levels in your brain fluctuate — fairly low when you wake up and slowly building throughout the day. After several hours of being awake, adenosine levels increase to a point where they start the process of making you sleepy.

Unless its receptors are blocked by caffeine, that is. When this happens, the downstream sleep-promoting pathways aren’t activated, meaning you stay awake and alert in the meantime.

## **How long does caffeine last?**

“Fortunately, caffeine doesn’t hang around in your body forever,” says Dr. Ramkissoon. “It is important to understand how long it can, though, since the timing could overlap with a planned bedtime and affect sleep quality if you’re not careful.”

According to the FDA, the half-life of caffeine — the time it takes for the starting amount of the substance to reduce by half — is between four and six hours.

This means that up to six hours after drinking a caffeinated beverage, half of the caffeine you consumed is still present in your body — keeping you alert. And, if it's bedtime, potentially keeping you from falling or staying asleep.

“Getting enough sleep is important for waking up feeling well-rested, but it's also critical for our overall health," adds Dr. Ramkissoon. "A lack of quality sleep over time is linked to a wide range of health issues, from high blood pressure to obesity — so it's important to take steps to ensure you're getting a good night's rest."

## **How late is too late to drink caffeine?**

We know how it works. We know about how long it can last.

But what does all of this mean as far as when is too late to enjoy caffeine without it affecting your sleep? Unfortunately, it’s a question with somewhat of a murky answer.

“Caffeine tolerance can vary from person to person — some people are more sensitive to caffeine, others less sensitive,” says Dr. Ramkissoon. “And not everyone’s work schedules and bedtimes are the same.”

As a rule of thumb, though, the recommendation for someone who works a 9 to 5 and follows a standard evening bedtime is to cut off caffeine intake around 2 or 3 p.m.

“Research on the exact timing caffeine’s impact on sleep is limited, but there is one small study showing that having caffeine as early as six hours before bedtime can affect sleep, even if you don't notice the disruption,” says Dr. Ramkissoon. “When it comes to getting quality sleep, it’s better to be safe than sorry. So that’s a good timeline to work from no matter your usual bedtime.”

That said, the study’s participants were given the maximum daily dose of caffeine (which is 400 mg, by the way). This might not be a realistic representation of the average adult's afternoon consumption — though it may be a totally accurate representation of, say, a college student's.

Ultimately, there's probably no one-size-fits-all rule as to how late is too late when it comes to consuming caffeine.

And while your favorite drink may not have 400 mg of caffeine in it like the participants in the study mentioned above, you may be surprised just how much caffeine is in some common beverages.

# [Jet lag disorder](/diseases-conditions/jet-lag/symptoms-causes/syc-20374027)

## Diagnosis

To diagnose jet lag, your healthcare professional asks about your symptoms and your travel across time zones.

## Treatment

Jet lag is temporary and usually doesn't need treatment. Symptoms often improve within a few days, though they sometimes last longer.

If you're a frequent traveler bothered by jet lag, your healthcare professional may prescribe light therapy or medicines.

### Light therapy

Your body's internal clock is influenced by sunlight, among other factors. When you travel across time zones, your body must adjust to a new daylight schedule. This allows you to fall asleep and be awake at the right times.

One way to adjust to a new daylight schedule is through light therapy. This involves exposure to an artificial bright light or lamp that mimics sunlight. You use the light for a specific amount of time when you're meant to be awake. Light therapy comes in a variety of forms, including a light box that sits on a table, a desk lamp or a light visor that you wear on your head.

Light therapy may be useful if you're a business traveler and are often away from natural sunlight during the day in a new time zone.

### Medicines

You can take medicines — sometimes called sleeping pills — during your flight and for several nights afterward as you adjust to a new time zone. These medicines are usually only recommended for people who haven't been helped by other treatments.

Side effects of these medicine are not common but may include nausea, vomiting, amnesia, sleepwalking, confusion and morning sleepiness. Although these medicines appear to help you sleep better and longer, you may still feel jet lag symptoms during the day.

## Alternative medicine

The hormone melatonin and even exercise may help relieve jet lag symptoms.

### Melatonin

As a sleep aid, melatonin has been widely studied and is a common jet lag treatment. The latest research seems to show that melatonin aids sleep during times when you wouldn't typically be resting, making it beneficial for people with jet lag.

Your body treats melatonin as a darkness signal, so melatonin tends to have the opposite effect of bright light.

The time when you take melatonin is important. If you've flown east and need to reset your internal clock to an earlier schedule, take melatonin nightly in the new time zone. You can take it until you adjust to local time.

If you've flown west and need to reset your body's internal clock to a later schedule, take melatonin in the mornings in the new time zone until you adjust.

A dose as small as 0.5 milligram seems just as effective as a dose of 5 milligrams or higher, although some studies show that higher doses are better at making you sleep. Take melatonin 30 minutes before you plan to sleep. Or ask your healthcare professional about the proper timing.

It's not common to have side effects of melatonin, but it can cause dizziness, headaches, daytime sleepiness and loss of appetite. Melatonin also can cause nausea and disorientation. Don't drink alcohol when taking melatonin.

### Other possible remedies

Some people use morning exercise to try to ease the effects of jet lag.

If you want to try an alternative therapy, such as an herbal supplement, be sure to check with your healthcare professional first. Some alternative therapies may interact with medicines or cause side effects.

## Lifestyle and home remedies

### Sunlight

Being exposed to sunlight helps reset your internal clock. It's the most powerful natural tool for regulating the sleep-wake cycle.

Morning light exposure can help you adjust to an earlier time zone after traveling east. Evening light helps you adapt to a later time zone after traveling west.

Plan ahead to determine the best times for light exposure based on your departure and destination points and overall sleep habits:

**At your destination.** If you've traveled east and crossed 3 to 5 time zones, try avoiding bright daylight first thing in the morning. Try to get several hours of bright light exposure in mid-morning to late morning.

If you're crossing more time zones or traveling west, avoid bright light the morning of arrival but seek sunshine in the early afternoon. During the day, dark glasses can help block out light when you need to avoid exposure. At night, draw the window blinds or drapes, or use a sleep mask. For each day on your trip, gradually shift your light exposure earlier.

Combining light exposure with exercise such as walking or jogging may help you adapt to the new time even faster.

### Caffeine

Beverages with caffeine, such as coffee, espresso and soft drinks, may help offset daytime sleepiness. Choose drinks with caffeine wisely. Don't have caffeine after midday. It may make it even harder to fall asleep or sleep well.

## Preparing for your appointment

Jet lag symptoms usually resolve after your trip. You can reach out to your healthcare professional if you're looking for prevention strategies for future travel. Be sure to bring your travel itinerary to the appointment.

- **Sunlight:** The most powerful natural tool for regulating the sleep-wake cycle. Morning light exposure helps adjust to earlier time zones (after traveling east); evening light helps adapt to later time zones (after traveling west). Specific guidance: if traveling east across 3-5 time zones, avoid bright daylight first thing in the morning and seek several hours of mid-to-late morning light. For more time zones or west travel, avoid bright light the morning of arrival but seek early afternoon sunshine. Dark glasses, window blinds, and sleep masks can help control light exposure. Combining light exposure with exercise may speed adaptation.
- **Caffeine:** May help offset daytime sleepiness but avoid after midday as it can interfere with falling asleep.

**Appointment preparation:** Jet lag symptoms usually resolve after the trip. Patients seeking prevention strategies for future travel should bring their travel itinerary to the appointment.

# 8 Tips to Help Get Over Jet Lag

![](//i0.wp.com/post.healthline.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/Meir-Kryger-New-Headshot-500x500-Bio.png?w=105&h=105)

Medically reviewed by Meir Kryger, MD, FRCP(C) — Written by Natalie Silver — Updated on October 23, 2024

You may be able to reduce jet lag by adapting to your new time zone morecquickly. It may help to drink caffeine and get daylight exposure, among other practices.

[Share on Pinterest](https://www.pinterest.com/pin/create/button/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.healthline.com%2Fhealth%2Fhealthy-sleep%2Fhow-to-get-over-jet-lag&media=https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.post.rvohealth.io%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2F2020%2F04%2Fsilhouette-father-daughter-looking-out-window-airport-airplane-flying-1296x728-header.jpg&description=How%20to%20Get%20Over%20Jet%20Lag%3A%208%20Tips%20and%20Suggestions "Share on Pinterest")

d3sign/Getty Images

[Jet lag](https://www.healthline.com/health/jet-lag) occurs when you travel quickly across time zones and your body’s usual rhythm falls out of sync. Your body will eventually adjust to its new time zone, but there are ways you can reduce jet lag symptoms.

## Tips

Remember that your body will eventually adjust to the new time zone. However, if you’re on a quick trip or are required to be highly functional quickly after your flight, you may want to consider keeping these tips in mind.

### 1. Adapt quickly to your new time zone

When you arrive at your destination, update everything to your new time zone as soon as possible.

Your technology will likely update clocks automatically, but if you have a manually set watch or travel clock, set those to the new time as soon as you depart.

You’ll have trouble at your destination if you continue to eat and sleep according to the old time zone. Eat meals and go to bed [according to the time at your destination](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/page/jet-lag). This is especially important if your new time zone is more than 3 hours different than your old one.

### 2. Manage sleep time

Make sure you sleep when it’s most appropriate to your new schedule. Your flight may be in the air during your destination’s nighttime, so try to log some sleep while airborne. A few things that’ll help you rest include:

* noise-canceling headphones
* white noise
* eye masks
* earplugs
* comfortable travel pillows and blankets

You should also avoid the urge to [nap](https://www.healthline.com/health-news/afternoon-naps-can-boost-your-mental-agility-heres-why) when you arrive if it’s daytime. This can make it difficult to sleep later on. If you absolutely must nap, try to keep it to no more than [15 to 20 minutes](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/page/jet-lag) at a time.

### 3. Drink water

Long-distance travel [may cause dehydration](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/12/9/2574). Proper hydration [may help manage](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-46022-7_18) jet lag symptoms and travel fatigue, but more research is needed.

Regardless, [it is important](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/page/jet-lag) to stay hydrated. Carry an empty water bottle through airport security and fill it up once you’re in the terminal. You can also purchase water in the terminal or request it in-flight.

Alcohol is offered on many flights, but try to avoid it, as it can [disrupt sleep](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/page/jet-lag).

### 4. Eat smaller meals

The [CDC](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/page/jet-lag) recommends eating smaller meals to avoid stomach aches and other stomach problems, which can be symptoms of jet lag.

However, keep in mind that there have not been formal studies on meal size and jet lag symptoms.

### 5. Try light

Your exposure to light changes when you travel and change time zones, which can [interrupt your internal clock](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6001675/).

Getting outside in the sunshine at the right time can wake up your body and [reduce the release](https://academic.oup.com/edrv/article/39/6/990/5094958) of melatonin hormones that make you sleepy. If you are traveling east (e.g. JFK to Paris), after arriving try avoiding bright light until the time your body has been used to waking up. So if at home you wake up at 6 am add the number of time zones to this and you’ll get noon. Consider wearing dark glasses until then. Avoid napping that first day. After the first day, exposing yourself to morning light will help speed up adapting to the new time zone.

### 6. Drink a caffeinated beverage

Consuming [caffeine](https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/what-is-caffeine) won’t cure jet lag, but it may be a tool to help you stay alert and focused [during the daytime](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/page/jet-lag).

[One study](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6069654/) found that 300 mg of slow-release caffeine enhanced alertness in those traveling eastbound.

Some beverages that contain caffeine include [coffee](https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/top-evidence-based-health-benefits-of-coffee) and [tea](https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/top-10-evidence-based-health-benefits-of-green-tea). Try to avoid soda and energy drinks, as they are high in sugar.

Try to moderate or eliminate caffeine in the afternoon and evening. You [may have difficulty sleeping](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1087079223000205) from a combination of too much caffeine and jet lag.

### 7. Keep your sleeping space comfortable

Make sure that your sleeping arrangements while traveling are comfortable and facilitate proper sleep. Here are a few tips:

* Check the thermostat in your room to make sure you can set it for a comfortable, cool temperature overnight.
* Ensure that any phones or clocks in the room won’t ring or beep while you sleep.
* If you sleep with a white noise machine or fan, try to find something portable that can travel with you.
* Bring familiar items, such as a favorite throw blanket or a familiar scented lotion, to help you fall asleep.

### 8. Try melatonin

Your body naturally makes [melatonin](https://www.healthline.com/nutrition/melatonin-and-sleep) to trigger sleepiness, but it’s also available as a supplement. You may want to consider melatonin [to help your body get or stay sleepy while jet-lagged](https://www.healthline.com/health/melatonin-for-jet-lag).

You may consider using melatonin at night if your body isn’t ready for bed. You may even take it in the early morning hours to continue sleeping if you’ve traveled west. However, [more studies](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/yellowbook/2024/air-land-sea/jet-lag) on melatonin and jet lag are needed.

Be sure to talk to your doctor before you make the decision to try melatonin. Your doctor will let you know if it interacts with any of your current medications, or if you otherwise cannot take it.

## How long does it take to get over?

You’re likely to experience more extreme jet-lag symptoms if you’ve traveled across several time zones.

The rule of thumb is that for each time zone you cross, it’ll take a day to adjust. Therefore, if you change five time zones, you may experience jet lag symptoms for up to 5 days.

## Can you prevent it?

Travel comes with some inconveniences, such as jet lag.

Before your flight, you may consider going to bed at a time that aligns with your new destination. For example, if you are traveling east, you may go to bed 2 hours earlier. If traveling west, you may go to bed 2 hours later.

If you have an important event at your new destination, you may consider arriving 2 days prior to give yourself time to adjust before the event.

## The takeaway

Jet lag is a common condition that goes away after a few days or weeks. The symptoms of jet lag can be difficult to manage in your first few days of traveling to a different time zone.

Immediately adapting to your new schedule, drinking caffeine during the daytime, and managing your exposure to light are just a few of the interventions that may help reduce jet lag symptoms.

If you are considering trying melatonin or another sleep aid, talk to your doctor. They will be able to advise you on if it interacts with any of your current medications or is safe for you to take.

This webpage is a Semantic Scholar record for the scientific paper "Human circadian phase–response curves for exercise" by Shawn D. Youngstedt, Jeffrey A. Elliott, and Daniel F. Kripke, published in The Journal of Physiology on 18 March 2019 (DOI: 10.1113/JP276943, Volume 597, pages 2253-2268). The paper establishes phase–response curves (PRCs) for exercise's effect on the human circadian system, and importantly identifies a second phase-advance region in the afternoon in addition to known phase-shifting effects. The paper notes that along with known synergism with bright light, these PRCs could support both practical and clinical applications, being desired for adjustment to westward (afternoon phase advance) or eastward air travel.

The page documents 212 citations of this paper and lists 67 references. Key citing works include:
- A 2020 JCI Insight study (Thomas, Kern, Pendergast) showing circadian phase shifts from timed exercise vary with chronotype — late chronotypes may benefit from phase advances from morning or evening exercise, but evening exercise may exacerbate misalignment in early chronotypes.
- A 2020 bioRxiv study (Kemler, Wolff, Esser) demonstrating muscle contractions are sufficient to shift the skeletal muscle circadian clock phase, confirming exercise as a bona fide environmental time cue for skeletal muscle.
- A 2022 Frontiers in Endocrinology study (Youngstedt, Elliott, Parthasarathy) on circadian acclimatization using multiple phase-shifting stimuli (bright light + exercise + melatonin).
- A 2022 Comprehensive Physiology review (Brito et al.) on chronobiology of exercise and time-of-day effects on cardiovascular and metabolic benefits.
- A 2025 Journal of Pineal Research study (Post et al.) showing one-time exposure to moderate ambient hypoxia (~6.5h during early night) advances dim-light melatonin onset by 9 minutes.

Key foundational references cited by the paper include: Buxton et al. (2003) showing early evening high-intensity exercise may induce phase advances; van Reeth et al. (1994) demonstrating nocturnal exercise phase delays circadian rhythms of melatonin and thyrotropin; Barger et al. (2004) showing daily exercise facilitates phase delays of circadian melatonin rhythm in very dim light; Eastman et al. (1995) on exercise promoting circadian adaptation to night shift work; Miyazaki et al. (2001) showing daytime physical exercise accelerates phase-advance shifts of the human circadian pacemaker; and Baehr et al. (2003) finding phase-shifting effects of nocturnal exercise are preserved in older adults.

## Abstract

The biological clock system is an intrinsic timekeeping device that integrates internal physiology and external cues. Maintaining a healthy biological clock system is crucial for life. Disruptions to the body’s internal clock can lead to disturbances in the sleep-wake cycle and abnormalities in hormone regulation, blood pressure, heart rate, and other vital processes. Long-term disturbances have been linked to the development of various common major diseases, including cardiovascular diseases, metabolic disorders, tumors, neuropsychiatric conditions, and so on. External factors, such as the diurnal rhythm of light, have a significant impact on the body’s internal clock. Additionally, as an important non-photic zeitgeber, exercise can regulate the body’s internal rhythms to a certain extent, making it possible to become a non-drug intervention for preventing and treating circadian rhythm disorders. This comprehensive review encompasses behavioral, physiological, and molecular perspectives to provide a deeper understanding of how exercise influences circadian rhythms and its association with related diseases.

## 1 Introduction

Biological rhythms refer to repetitive processes that occur over specific periods of time, such as a day, a month, or a year. The circadian rhythm, which has a period of approximately 24 h, is particularly relevant to human health. Numerous behavioral, physiological, and biochemical activities demonstrate obvious circadian rhythms. For instance, the sleep-wake cycle, as well as daily changes in blood pressure, heart rate, and body temperature, are widely recognized to display discernible circadian patterns. When the internal biological clock becomes desynchronized with the external environment, it may lead to a mismatch between central and peripheral clocks, as well as between different tissues or organs, and even between different clock genes within the same organ (Reppert and Weaver, 2002). Long-term circadian disturbances are closely linked to the onset and progression of a variety of mental and physical diseases, including cardiovascular diseases, metabolic syndrome, neurodegenerative diseases, and tumors (Fatima and Rana, 2020; Meyer et al., 2022; Bolshette et al., 2023; Lane et al., 2023).

In mammals, the central pacemaker of circadian rhythms is located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN). SCN output is relayed through the nuclei of the hypothalamus thereby transmitting circadian signals to the brain regions that regulate the sleep-wake cycles and synchronizing the peripheral circadian rhythms of other tissues through neurohormonal mechanisms. At the molecular level, the core clock genes and proteins form a set of highly conserved transcriptional-translational feedback loops (TTFL) that have both positive and negative regulatory elements ([Figure 1](#F1)) (Chen and Yang, 2014; Fagiani et al., 2022). The transcription factors, BMAL1 and CLOCK form heterodimers, which bind to the E-box located in the promoter regions of the *per* and *cry* genes to promote the production of PER and CRY proteins. When they accumulate to a certain level in the cytosol, PER and CRY translocate to the nucleus to inhibit the activity of the BMAL1/CLOCK complex, thus repressing their own expressions. In addition, a second feedback pathway composed of nuclear receptors ROR and REV-ERB is involved in promoting and inhibiting the expression of BMAL1, respectively. These core clock components regulate hundreds of other genes, called clock-controlled genes (CCGs) in a circadian manner. Generally, core clockwork mechanisms exist in most tissues and cells of the body, but the expression of CCGs varies by cell type (Koike et al., 2012).

While the circadian rhythm continues to function under constant conditions, such as constant darkness (DD), it can be affected by environmental changes and spontaneous activities like light exposure, diet, and exercise. These daily changes are referred to as zeitgebers and can entrain or reset the circadian rhythms. Among them, light is the most potent zeitgeber (Fisk et al., 2018; Ruan et al., 2021). Non-photic factors including medication, temperature, diet, and exercise can also entrain circadian rhythms. For example, consuming food during specific time affects the transcription levels of clock genes ([Ulgherait et al., 2021](#B96); Deota et al., 2023), which can aid in maintaining normal circadian rhythms, mitigating metabolic disorders caused by a high-fat diet (HFD) (Hatori et al., 2012; Chaix et al., 2014; Li, 2022), improving the body’s ability to cope with circadian disruption (Ren et al., 2021; Ren et al., 2022), enhancing running endurance without prior exercise ([Xin et al., 2023](#B107)), and even prolonging lifespan (Acosta-Rodriguez et al., 2022).

Over the past few years, exercise has garnered increasing attention as a significant non-photic zeitgeber. Physical inactivity is recognized as a risk factor for numerous common illnesses, including cardiovascular diseases, metabolic disorders, neurodegenerative disorders, and tumors (Schloss et al., 2020; [Valenzuela et al., 2020](#B97)). At the molecular level, exercise has been shown to modulate the expression of clock genes (Martin et al., 2023; Sato and Yamanaka, 2023). Both aerobic and resistance exercise upregulate the expression of *BMAL1* and *PER2* in skeletal muscle ([Zambon et al., 2003](#B116); [Wolff and Esser, 2019](#B104)). Regular exercise is a healthy lifestyle, in part because it helps keep the biological clock running properly. Similar to light exposure, the timing of exercise affects the circadian rhythm ([Youngstedt et al., 2019](#B115)). Thus, exercise is expected to be a non-invasive, non-pharmaceutical intervention to facilitate the regulation of circadian rhythms. However, the best time of day for strength and endurance training to improve health remains unclear (Bruggisser et al., 2023). This review summarizes relevant literature and discusses two aspects: 1) the impact of exercise on circadian rhythms; and 2) the association between exercise and circadian disorders and related illnesses.

## 2 Effects of exercise on circadian rhythms

Establishing a correlation between exercise and circadian rhythms based on human studies is challenging due to the varying intensity, mode, and duration of exercise. Exercise can be classified as either aerobic or resistance training depending on the energy-producing systems and weight-bearing conditions, or continuous exercise and intermittent exercise based on the length of rest periods. In 2020, the *World Health Organization guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour* underscored the pivotal role of regular physical activity in preventing and treating non-communicable diseases, recommending that adults engage in at least 150–300 min of moderate-intensity or 75–150 min of vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity per week (Bull et al., 2020). Therefore, the majority of studies investigating the relationship between exercise and circadian rhythm have focused on moderate to high-intensity aerobic exercise lasting more than 30 min per day. This chapter reviews the associations of the timing of exercise with circadian rhythms under normal, constant, and disturbed light conditions ([Table 1](#T1)).

### 2.1 Normal light/dark (LD) condition

Chronotypes refer to different phenotypes that are produced by individuals entraining different exogenous and endogenous factors (Fischer et al., 2017), which play a crucial role in health and shift work tolerance (Reiter et al., 2021). Based on these variations, people can be classified into morning types (early birds), evening types (night owls), and those with no extreme bias (Honkalampi et al., 2021). Studies have investigated the effects of morning and evening exercise on circadian rhythms in individuals with different chronotypes. Both morning and evening exercise advanced the sleep-wake cycle and dim light melatonin onset (DLMO) in night owls, while evening exercise delayed the phase of DLMO in early birds ([Thomas et al., 2020](#B94)). A questionnaire survey on a large sample size (N = 909) found that evening exercise led to a delayed sleep onset time than morning exercise, and the night owls were more significantly affected (Glavin et al., 2021).

The timing of exercise is a crucial factor to consider. For instance, under a condition of 16-h light:8-h dark (LD16:8), resistance exercise in the morning or noon can advance the circadian phase of core body temperature, whereas long-term rest in bed can delay it (Mendt et al., 2021). Furthermore, research on the relationship between children’s physical activity and sleep found that exercise time is related to sleep duration and efficiency (Antczak et al., 2021). Proper exercise during normal photoperiods can effectively regulate circadian rhythms, and it is recommended that the general population chooses morning exercise to improve sleep quality and advance sleep onset time.

### 2.2 Constant condition

In a constant environment without time cues, Miyazaki et al. found that 2 hours of moderate-intensity intermittent exercise (using a bicycle ergometer) in the afternoon (CT8, the timepoint of wake-up was defined as CT0) or night (CT17) delayed the onset of melatonin, while the timing of melatonin peak remained unchanged in the morning exercise group (CT2), when subjects were exposed to a constant dim light (<10 lux, equivalent to the indoor light intensity at dusk) (Miyazaki et al., 2021). Similarly, moderate-intensity intermittent aerobic exercise using a bicycle ergometer in the afternoon (CT10) or night (CT16) also delayed the onset of melatonin. However, when the exercise was replaced with 1-h high-intensity aerobic exercise, the melatonin peak levels increased without any changes in phases (Buxton et al., 1997; [Yamanaka et al., 2015](#B110)). In the same study, the authors found that cycling for 2 h in the morning (CT3) delayed the phase of melatonin peak by 1 h ([Yamanaka et al., 2015](#B110)). Additionally, Buxton et al. found that high-intensity exercise in the afternoon (CT10.5) advanced the peak phase of melatonin, while exercise at CT1.5, CT5, and CT16.5 delayed the peak phase of melatonin (Buxton et al., 2003).

These findings suggest that the impact of exercise on the circadian rhythm is influenced not only by the timing of exercise but also by other factors, such as exercise duration, intensity, and volume. However, even when studies use the same exercise protocol with the same timing, type, and intensity, the results may not be entirely consistent, which could be attributed to variations in sleep-wake schedules, small sample sizes, or significant individual differences.

### 2.3 Disturbed light/dark condition

In daily life, shift work, smartphone overuse, and long-haul flights across time zones may cause acute circadian disruption, suppressed melatonin production, and sleep deprivation ([Wei et al., 2020](#B100); Roenneberg, 2023). To mitigate circadian disruption, people often attempt to synchronize their activities with natural time, adjust their sleep patterns and diet, or take melatonin supplements (Pfeffer et al., 2018). In recent years, more and more attention has been paid to the regulation of exercise on circadian rhythms. However, the impact of a single bout of exercise on circadian rhythms is relatively minor and much weaker than the effects of bright light exposure. Studies have shown that a single bout of exercise does not significantly influence the plasma melatonin (Minors et al., 1991; Buxton et al., 2003). In contrast, regular exercise over a prolonged period has a considerable impact on circadian rhythms, including the expression of core clock genes (Okamoto et al., 2013).

Studies investigating the impact of exercise on circadian disruption have employed various forced phase-shifted sleep-wake schedules. Under a forced schedule of 23.6-h sleep-wake cycle under dim light (<10 lux), Miyazaki et al. found that a 2-h cycling exercise at 3 and 7 h after waking advanced melatonin onset, which facilitate adaptation to the schedule, while the inactive group showed delayed phase of melatonin (Miyazaki et al., 2021). A study with an 8-h advanced phase shift has shown that cycling at 3-h and 7-h after waking for 4 consecutive days delayed the onset of melatonin and minimum core body temperature, which is opposite to the direction of phase shift ([Yamanaka et al., 2010](#B111)). In contrast, a few hours of intermittent bicycle exercise from CT7 for 3 consecutive days under a 9-hour-delayed sleep-wake schedule caused a delay in the phase of the minimum core body temperature. In addition, no difference was found between evening and morning types in the exercise groups, while the phase delay of the minimum core temperature was larger in the evening type in the control group.

Exercise during sleep time may negatively impact sleep quality due to increased body temperature and alertness (Baehr et al., 1999). Moderate or high-intensity aerobic cycling for 7 days was thought to synchronize melatonin rhythm with a 9-h delayed jet lag (Barger et al., 2004). Light intensity may also play a role in the effect of exercise on circadian rhythm. When subjects were exposed to bright light (>5,000 lux), cycling exercise was found to shift both melatonin and body temperature phases to the same direction as an 8-h advanced or 9-h delayed phase shift, while the control group showed desynchronization between melatonin and sleep-wake cycle (Baehr et al., 1999; [Yamanaka et al., 2014](#B109)). In the study simulating advanced jet lag, the time of exercise was set in the morning and the middle of the night, which may include both advance and delayed regions of the phase-response curves (PRC) ([Yamanaka et al., 2014](#B109)). As a result, the advanced shift of circadian rhythms in bright light may be due to exercise enhancing the entrainment of light to the circadian rhythm by regulating the 5-HT (5-hydroxytryptamine) system (Cymborowski, 1998; Mistlberger et al., 2010) or enhancing the light-sensing ability of the circadian system ([Yamanaka and Waterhouse, 2016](#B112)), which induced a larger advanced shift ([Figure 2](#F2)).

The entrainment of circadian rhythms by light and exercise. The central clock oscillator, which regulates rhythms of melatonin and body temperature, is located within the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), while oscillators governing the sleep-wake cycle may exist in brain regions beyond the SCN ([Yamanaka and Waterhouse, 2016](#B112); [Yamanaka, 2020](#B108)). Two potential pathways for entraining the central circadian rhythm through exercise are depicted: 1, exercise entrains the central clock directly; 2, exercise entrains oscillators in extra-SCN brain regions, which then transmit signals to the SCN. It is important to note that light serves as the most significant zeitgeber. The regulation of circadian rhythms by exercise can be influenced by the intensity of light, as exercise can impact the function of light perception or the entrainment process related to light.

In another interesting study, participants were subjected to a 90-min ultrashort sleep (60 min)-wake (30 min) cycle in a laboratory setting, with low light intensity during wakefulness (50 lux) and sleep (0.5 lux). Under such a condition, each individual conducted a 60-min moderate treadmill per day during one of eight periods of wakefulness (at 3-h intervals from 01:00) for three consecutive days. The PRC of aMT6s (6- sulphatoxymelatonin) onset to exercise was plotted ([Youngstedt et al., 2019](#B115)). It was found that aMT6 onset was advanced by exercise at 07:00, 13:00, and 16:00 and delayed by exercise at 19:00 and 22:00. Such pattern was similar to a PRC of bright light (Kripke et al., 2007). A study using hamster housed under DD showed that a 2-h wheel running during CT4-CT11 advanced the phase, while exercise during CT23−ΔΔCT3 and CT17−ΔΔCT20 delayed it (Reebs and Mrosovsky, 1989). Comparison of the results between humans and hamsters showed that exercise during the active period often led to opposite phase shifts, possibly due to differences in habitual activity timing (Challet, 2007). Although the study on ultrashort sleep-wake cycles cannot fully predict the circadian rhythm phase shifts after exercise during normal sleep-wake schedules, it provides guidance for shift workers, who may need to avoid afternoon exercise and strong light exposure.

Regular exercise has been shown to promote synchronization between the sleep-wake cycle and the circadian clock, regardless of the direction of phase shift. The closer the exercise time was to the previous melatonin onset, the larger the phase shift in post-exercise melatonin onset (Barger et al., 2004; [Yamanaka et al., 2010](#B111)). However, previous studies have been limited by the protocols of schedules and exercise, making it difficult to compare results directly and identify the optimal timing of exercise for preventing or treating circadian disorders. Furthermore, the phenomenon of internal desynchronization suggests that the circadian pacemakers regulating melatonin and body temperature may be independent of the sleep-wake cycle, and that other brain regions outside of the SCN may be involved in regulating the sleep-wake cycle ([Yamanaka, 2020](#B108)). Further research is needed to investigate the interaction between different circadian pacemakers and whether exercise directly regulates the rhythm of the SCN, or indirectly by influencing the sleep-wake cycle.

In general, exercise plays an important role in regulating circadian rhythms. Exercise at night usually delays the circadian phase, which means it can make it harder to fall asleep at night and wake up in the morning. However, the effect of daytime exercise on circadian rhythms is more controversial ([Figure 3](#F3)). It is important to note that the effects of exercise on circadian rhythms can vary depending on several factors such as exercise intensity, mode, duration, energy supply, and frequency. Therefore, it is essential to consider these variables when designing an exercise regimen that aims to regulate the body’s internal clock.
