--- SOURCE 12: Getting the Sleep You Need: Jet Lag and Shift Work ---
URL: https://sleep.hms.harvard.edu/education-training/public-education/sleep-and-health-education-program/sleep-health-education-81

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the Harvard Medical School Division of Sleep Medicine provides education on jet lag and shift work as part of its "Getting the Sleep You Need" series.

**Key takeaways:**
- Traveling across time zones disrupts regular sleep/wake patterns
- The internal circadian alerting system is strongest during daytime, making night shift work challenging
- Good sleep habits, a regular schedule, and simple workplace measures can help shift workers

**Jet Lag:**
- Jet lag occurs when the body's internal clock is out of sync with the current time zone, caused by the mismatch between the external environment and the internal biological clock (circadian misalignment)
- Symptoms include excessive daytime sleepiness, nighttime insomnia, headache, loss of appetite, gastrointestinal problems, and irritability or mild depression
- Jet lag is temporary because the internal clock adapts through "entrainment" — readjusting about one hour (or time zone) per day, though some body systems take longer
- Light is the most powerful synchronizer of the internal biological clock
- For eastward flights (e.g., North America to Europe), travelers should avoid bright light during their usual nighttime and seek light starting at about 5 a.m. internal time; light earlier than 5 a.m. internal time can shift the clock in the wrong direction
- Avoid long daytime naps in the new time zone to build sleep drive for nighttime sleep

**Shift Work:**
- Shift workers experience longer-term disruptions with both social and physiological implications, unlike travelers with temporary jet lag
- Night shift workers (e.g., 11 p.m. to 7 a.m.) must adapt to sleeping during daylight and being alert at night when the circadian alerting system is at its lowest point
- Social/family obligations make it difficult to maintain a consistent daytime sleep schedule, keeping the internal clock perpetually out of sync
- Rotating shifts (e.g., weekly changes among 7 a.m.–3 p.m., 3 p.m.–11 p.m., 11 p.m.–7 a.m.) cause continual desynchronization similar to jet lag

**Shift Work Disorder:**
- A chronic condition directly related to work schedules with two primary symptoms: insomnia when trying to sleep and excessive sleepiness when needing to be awake
- About half of all night shift workers report falling asleep at work
- Night shift workers average about 1.5 fewer hours of sleep per night than daytime workers
- Serious public health issue given shift workers include long-haul truck drivers, pilots, train operators, medical providers, and 24-hour infrastructure workers
- Chronic sleep loss may increase risk for obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease; increases work-related accidents at night and motor vehicle accidents after night shifts

**Workplace Measures to Help Shift Workers:**
- Enhance workplace lighting (increased intensity, blue-shifted wavelength to simulate daylight) improves adaptation to night work
- Strategic caffeine use: regular small doses better than fewer large doses; taper off halfway through shift if sleeping immediately after work
- 20- to 30-minute nap breaks improve performance
- If shifts must rotate, rotating day → evening → night is easier than reverse rotation
- Persistent problems warrant evaluation by a sleep specialist
- Protect sleep time and create a dark, comfortable, quiet sleep environment (turn off phone, disconnect doorbell, arrange childcare)

Content last reviewed October 1, 2021.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Traveling across time zones can disrupt regular patterns of sleep and wakefulness. Because the internal circadian alerting system is at its strongest during the daytime, night shift workers often find themselves struggling to sleep 'on the wrong side of the clock.'"
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 13: Caffeine for the prevention of injuries and errors in shift workers ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4160007

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Cochrane systematic review published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (2010, Issue 5, CD008508) titled "Caffeine for the prevention of injuries and errors in shift workers," authored by Katharine Ker, Philip James Edwards, Lambert M Felix, Karen Blackhall, and Ian Roberts (Cochrane Injuries Group and Department of Epidemiology and Population Health, London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, UK). The review was assessed as up-to-date on 1 April 2010 (PMCID: PMC4160007, PMID: 20464765).

BACKGROUND: Sleepiness deteriorates performance and attention and increases injury risk. Jet lag and shift work disorder (SWD) are circadian rhythm sleep disorders that elevate injury risk. Medical errors in the UK harm nearly 10% of NHS admissions (over 850,000 incidents/year, £2 billion in costs); in the USA, 44,000–98,000 deaths/year are caused by medical errors (eighth leading cause of death). Sleep deprivation of 24–30 hours reduces overall performance by one standard deviation. Caffeine is the most widely used psychoactive drug and promotes wakefulness, but its effects on injury and error were unclear.

OBJECTIVE: To assess the effects of caffeine for preventing injuries caused by impaired alertness in persons with jet lag or shift work disorder.

METHODS: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (parallel and cross-over). Databases searched included CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, TRANSPORT (to July 2008) and PubMed (to April 2010), plus internet and reference lists. Inclusion criteria: RCTs investigating caffeine effects on injury, error, or cognitive performance in people with jet lag or SWD (real or simulated). Data were extracted by two authors independently; risk of bias assessed using the Cochrane Collaboration tool. Treatment effects were pooled using fixed-effect models (odds ratios and standardized mean differences with 95% CIs). The combined search identified 3,616 records; after screening, 73 trials met inclusion criteria, of which 13 assessed caffeine.

RESULTS: Thirteen trials were included (4 parallel, 9 cross-over; 6–68 participants each; adults aged 18–65). None measured an injury outcome. Two trials measured errors (night-time driving and simulated flying). Caffeine significantly reduced errors compared to placebo: driving errors OR 0.14 (95% CI 0.05 to 0.41, P=0.0003); flight simulator altitude deviations SMD −1.30 (95% CI −1.93 to −0.68) and velocity deviations SMD −1.18 (95% CI −1.79 to −0.56). Pooled cognitive performance effects versus placebo: concept formation and reasoning (SMD −0.41; 95% CI −1.04 to 0.23), memory (SMD −1.08; 95% CI −2.07 to −0.09, P=0.03), orientation and attention (SMD −0.55; 95% CI −0.83 to −0.27), and perception (SMD −0.77; 95% CI −1.73 to 0.20); no beneficial effect on verbal functioning/language skills (SMD 0.18; 95% CI −0.50 to 0.87). One trial found significantly fewer errors with caffeine than with a nap; other comparisons with active interventions (nap, bright light, modafinil, chewing) showed no significant differences. Caffeine was administered as tablets/capsules, coffee, caffeinated food, and energy drinks (doses ranging from 80 mg to 300 mg, or 0.3–4 mg/kg). Risk of bias was high for allocation concealment adequacy and selective outcome reporting among the trials.

AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: Caffeine may be an effective intervention for improving performance in shift workers, but no trials assessed its effect on injuries. Results largely originate from studies of young participants under simulated conditions, so generalizability to older workers and real-world shift work is unclear. Based on current evidence, there is no reason for healthy individuals who already use caffeine within recommended levels to stop doing so. The assessment of caffeine's relative effects versus other countermeasures should be a focus of future research.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Caffeine may be an effective intervention for improving performance in shift workers however, there are no trials from which we can assess its effect on injuries."

--- SOURCE 14: Caffeine and jet lag | Dose & timing | Timeshifter® ---
URL: https://www.timeshifter.com/jet-lag/caffeine-and-travel

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the Timeshifter website's article "Caffeine and jet lag," written by Steven W. Lockley, Ph.D., Co-Founder & Chief Scientist at Timeshifter. The article explains the relationship between caffeine consumption and jet lag management.

Key points covered:
- Caffeine can help travelers stay alert when the circadian clock is out of sync with local time, but it does NOT reset the clock the way light and melatonin do—it masks fatigue rather than fixing the underlying misalignment.
- Used at the wrong time, caffeine can worsen jet lag by disrupting sleep at the destination.
- Recommended usage: a caffeinated drink (tea, coffee, or soda, ~50mg of caffeine) every two hours helps stay awake. Consuming more than that does not increase alertness and may reduce the ability to sleep later. Caffeine consumed 8 hours or less before bedtime negatively impacts sleep quality.
- Caffeine sources: tea, coffee, caffeinated sodas, chocolate, and some pain medications. Brewed 'drip' coffee and energy drinks have very high caffeine content—only half a cup every two hours is needed.
- How caffeine works: It is an adenosine-receptor antagonist that blocks adenosine from reaching its receptors, preventing the chemical buildup that causes sleepiness.
- Caffeine half-life is 3-5 hours. Example: 100mg at 10 a.m. leaves 50mg at 3 p.m., 25mg at 8 p.m., and ~12.5mg at 10 p.m.—enough to disrupt sleep.
- Best strategy: use caffeine "little and often," then stop as long as possible before bed.
- Caffeine should not be given to children due to their smaller size increasing relative dose.
- Timeshifter's app provides personalized advice on when to use and avoid caffeine during travel to support light-dark and sleep schedules.

The page also includes site navigation for Timeshifter's products (jet lag app, shift work app, peak performance, My Circadian Day), noting the jet lag app is trusted by 1.7 million+ travelers and is described as the most downloaded and highest-rated jet lag app in the world. Other related articles are linked (melatonin for jet lag, what is jet lag, jet lag myths debunked, caffeine and shift work, etc.). The site emphasizes that these statements have not been evaluated by the FDA and the product is intended for healthy adults 18+.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Caffeine can help you stay alert when your circadian clock is out of sync with local time, but it doesn't reset your clock the way light and melatonin do. Caffeine masks fatigue rather than fixing the underlying misalignment."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 15: Evidence summary on the non-pharmacological management of sleep disorders in shift workers ---
URL: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11325-023-02901-5

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents an open-access scientific article published in Sleep and Breathing (Volume 28, pages 909-918, 2024) titled "Evidence summary on the non-pharmacological management of sleep disorders in shift workers." Published on August 16, 2023, the study was conducted by Jin-yu Wu, Hui Li, Jun-kun Shuai, Yue He, and Peng-cheng Li to evaluate and integrate evidence on non-pharmacological interventions for sleep disorders among shift workers.

BACKGROUND: Approximately 15-30% of full-time workers worldwide engage in shift work (any schedule outside 7 a.m. to 6 p.m., including evening, night, early morning, and rotating shifts). About 25-30% of shift workers experience insomnia symptoms, and ~10% meet diagnostic criteria for shift work sleep disorder (SWSD). Shift work negatively affects health through circadian rhythm disruption, sleep deprivation, and suboptimal health behaviors, leading to traffic accidents, increased alcohol/drug use, and serious medical errors.

METHODS: Following the "6S" pyramid model of evidence, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of evidence-based databases (BMJ-Best Practice, UpToDate, DynaMed, Cochrane Library, JBI), clinical practice guideline websites, professional association websites, and literature databases (PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, CNKI, Wanfang, CBM) from inception to November 30, 2022. Two researchers independently evaluated literature quality using appropriate instruments (AGREE II for guidelines, JBI criteria for systematic reviews/consensuses, CASE checklist for clinical decisions). Evidence was graded using the JBI Evidence Recommendation Level System (Levels 1-5) and classified into grade A (strong) or B (weak) recommendations.

RESULTS: From 1,072 initially retrieved articles, 18 were ultimately included: 2 clinical decisions, 2 guidelines, 3 expert consensuses, and 11 systematic reviews. Twenty-five pieces of best evidence were summarized across six aspects: sleep assessment, sleep scheduling, sleep hygiene, light therapy, workplace intervention, and other managements.

KEY DISCUSSION POINTS: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine and National Sleep Foundation recommend adults aged 18-64 obtain 7-9 hours of sleep nightly. However, shift workers need at least 9-11 hours of sleep time between shifts to achieve the 7 hours needed for health maintenance and to reduce risks of impaired performance, errors, and injuries. Recommendations include choosing work schedules aligned with sleep preferences, prioritizing 3-4 hours of regular fixed sleep in the morning with adjustable second sleep periods, "banking sleep" before shifts, and providing workers control over working hours as a protective factor against work-life conflict.

CONCLUSION: The study provides best evidence for non-pharmacological management of sleep disorders in shift workers. Shift workers should reasonably arrange sleep time and develop good sleep hygiene, while work organizations should jointly promote sleep to improve sleep conditions and promote physical and mental health of shift workers.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Guideline Update October 2015 ---
URL: https://aasm.org/resources/practiceparameters/pp_circadianrhythm.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) Practice Parameters for the Clinical Evaluation and Treatment of Circadian Rhythm Sleep Disorders (CRSDs), published in SLEEP 2007;30(11):1445-1459, authored by Morgenthaler TI et al. (Standards of Practice Committee of the AASM). A subsequent 2015 clinical practice guideline update (Auger RR et al., J Clin Sleep Med 2015;11(10):1199-1236) updated these recommendations based on new evidence, particularly for elderly and children with/without comorbid psychiatric conditions.

The practice parameters address both exogenous CRSDs (shift work disorder [SWD] and jet lag disorder [JLD]) and endogenous CRSDs (advanced sleep phase disorder [ASPD], delayed sleep phase disorder [DSPD], free-running disorder [FRD], and irregular sleep-wake rhythm disorder [ISWR]). Recommendations are graded as Standard, Guideline, or Option based on evidence levels (Oxford System for Evidence-Based Medicine, adapted by Eddy).

KEY EVALUATION RECOMMENDATIONS:
- Sleep log/diary: Indicated for assessment of all suspected CRSDs (Guideline)
- Actigraphy: Indicated for diagnosis of ASPD, DSPD, SWD (Guideline); ISWR, FRD (Option); useful as outcome measure for treatment response in all CRSDs (Guideline)
- Polysomnography: Not routinely indicated for CRSD diagnosis, but indicated to rule out other primary sleep disorders (Standard)
- MEQ (Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire): Insufficient evidence for routine clinical use (Option)
- Circadian phase markers: Useful to confirm FRD diagnosis in sighted and unsighted patients (Option); insufficient evidence for SWD, JLD, ASPD, DSPD, ISWR

TREATMENT RECOMMENDATIONS BY DISORDER:
- SWD: Planned napping before/during night shift (Standard); timed light exposure in work environment with morning light restriction (Guideline); melatonin before daytime sleep (Guideline); hypnotics for daytime sleep (Guideline); modafinil (Guideline) and caffeine (Option) for alertness; MEQ and circadian markers of unproved usefulness (Option)
- JLD: Melatonin at appropriate time to reduce symptoms and improve sleep (Standard); home-based sleep hours for brief stays ≤2 days (Option); morning bright light + shifting sleep schedule pre-eastward travel (Option); benzodiazepine receptor agonist hypnotics short-term for insomnia (Option); caffeine for sleepiness but may disrupt nighttime sleep (Option); insufficient evidence for actigraphy, PSG, or circadian markers (Option)
- ASPD: Prescribed sleep/wake scheduling, timed light, or timed melatonin (all Option); PSG not routinely indicated (Standard); MEQ and circadian markers insufficient evidence (Option)
- DSPD: Morning light exposure (Guideline); properly timed melatonin (Guideline); chronotherapy (Option); Vitamin B12 NOT indicated (Guideline); PSG not routinely indicated (Standard); insufficient evidence for hypnotics/stimulants (Option)
- FRD: Sleep logs useful (Option); circadian phase markers confirm diagnosis in sighted and unsighted (Option); prescribed sleep/wake scheduling in sighted (Option); timed light in sighted (Option); timed melatonin in sighted (Option); timed melatonin indicated for blind individuals (Guideline)
- ISWR: Mixed modality therapy may be effective in elderly-demented/nursing home patients (Guideline) or those with moderate to severe mental retardation (Option); timed melatonin may be effective in moderate-severe mental retardation but not recommended for elderly-demented/nursing home patients (Option)

The literature review retrieved 2,084 articles; all evidence grading was performed by independent review by at least two experts (one evidence review professional, one content expert). All authors completed conflict-of-interest statements; the paper was not industry supported. ~20% of U.S. workers are involved in some form of shift work.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Use of a sleep log or diary is indicated in the assessment of patients with a suspected circadian rhythm sleep disorder (Guideline)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Guidelines in Development | American Academy of Sleep Medicine ---
URL: https://aasm.org/clinical-resources/practice-standards/guidelines-in-development

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) details clinical practice guidelines currently in development. The AASM develops guidelines that provide physicians with recommendations for evaluation, diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up of patients with sleep disorders. The process involves the AASM Guidelines Advisory Panel reviewing and prioritizing topics, the Board of Directors approving topics, and expert task forces performing systematic reviews of published evidence using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) methodology. Drafts undergo a 4-week public comment period before Board approval for publication.

Four guidelines are in development:

1. **Medications for Residual Sleepiness in Adults Treated for Obstructive Sleep Apnea** — Provides practice recommendations for treating residual sleepiness in effectively treated adults with OSA. Task Force Chair: Chitra Lal, MD. BOD Liaison: Alexandre Rocha Abreu, MD; GAP Liaison: James Rowley, MD. Target population: adults with OSA (age ≥18, AHI ≥5/hr) adequately treated with primary therapy who still have residual sleepiness.

2. **Diagnostic Testing for Adult OSA (Focused Update)** — Prioritizes a focused update of the existing clinical practice guideline for adult OSA diagnostic testing, with an updated literature search to capture evidence for newer devices. Task Force Chair: Indu Ayappa, PhD. BOD and GAP Liaison: Vishesh Kapur, MD, MPH. Staff: Gerard Carandang, MS. Target population: uncomplicated adults with signs/symptoms indicating increased OSA risk.

3. **Use of a Home Sleep Apnea Test (HSAT) for the Diagnosis of OSA in Children (Update)** — Provides recommendations for HSAT use in diagnosing OSA in children, updating and replacing the 2017 position paper. Task Force Chair: Lynn D'Andrea, MD. BOD Liaison: Anuja Bandyopadhyay, MD; GAP Liaison: Carol Rosen, MD. Staff: Taylor Shaffer, MS. Target population: children with suspected OSA (<18 years old).

4. **Treatment of Jet Lag Disorder (Update)** — Provides recommendations for treating jet lag disorder in adults, updating and replacing existing practice parameters. Task Force Chair: Sabra Abbott, MD, PhD. BOD and GAP Liaison: Lynn Marie Trotti, MD, MSc. Target population: adults with jet lag disorder.

The page also highlights AASM resources including the AASM Link (AI-powered access to clinical practice guidelines and standards, free monthly for members), the Patient-reported Longitudinal Assessment Tool for OSA (PLATO), the AASM Scoring Manual Version 3 eBook, the ICSD-3-TR (International Classification of Sleep Disorders, Third Edition, Text Revision), and on-demand CME/CEC courses. Contact information: 2510 North Frontage Road, Darien, IL 60561; Phone: (630) 737-9700; Fax: (630) 737-9790.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) website, announcing that practice parameters published in the November 1 issue of the journal SLEEP provide recommendations for the evaluation and treatment of Circadian Rhythm Sleep Disorders (CRSDs). The standards, developed by the AASM Standards of Practice Committee, are intended to positively impact professional behavior, patient outcomes, and potentially healthcare costs. The committee commissioned content experts in CRSDs to review and grade evidence from peer-reviewed scientific literature. The recommendations are categorized into three levels: Standards (generally accepted patient-care strategies reflecting high clinical certainty), Guidelines (strategies reflecting moderate clinical certainty), and Options (strategies reflecting uncertain clinical use). Committee member Timothy I. Morgenthaler, MD of the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, MN noted that the expanding science of circadian rhythm biology prompted the AASM to convene a task force of experts. The article is titled "Practice Parameters for the Clinical Evaluation and Treatment of Circadian Rhythm Sleep Disorders." Contact for interviews is Jim Arcuri, public relations coordinator, at (708) 492-0930 ext. 9317 or jarcuri@aasm.org. The page also includes navigation links to AASM resources (coding & reimbursement, telemedicine, accreditation, membership, education, and clinical practice standards), as well as related posts about sleep medicine topics such as business of sleep medicine, JCSM reviewers, ASTEP access, and various sleep health news items.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a comprehensive guide on caffeine and sleep, covering dose, timing, and half-life considerations. The key messages include:

**Core Findings:**
- Caffeine's effects can last hours after consumption. EFSA describes an average adult half-life of about four hours, with a typical range of roughly two to eight hours.
- Even 100 mg of caffeine close to bedtime can alter sleep in some adults.
- A four-hour half-life means half of a dose remains after four hours, one quarter after eight hours, and one eighth after twelve hours; caffeine does not suddenly disappear at the eight-hour mark.

**Dose vs. Timing:**
- Daily caffeine guidance and bedtime timing answer different questions. A daily limit (e.g., FDA's 400 mg/day for most healthy adults) describes intake across a day for a broad population, while sleep timing asks how much of a particular dose may remain at bedtime.
- EFSA notes a single 100 mg dose may affect sleep duration and patterns in some adults when consumed close to bedtime.

**Sleep Research:**
- A 2013 laboratory-and-home study (Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine) tested a 400 mg dose at bedtime and three or six hours before bedtime, finding sleep disrupted at all three timings. This does not establish a universal six-hour rule.
- A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis (Sleep Medicine Reviews) found caffeine reduced total sleep time, reduced deep sleep, and increased time to fall asleep, though studies varied widely in dose, timing, and participants.

**Practical Approach:**
- Build a caffeine cutoff from observation, not a universal rule: estimate the dose, count the hours using a cautious half-life range, and watch sleep outcomes (onset, awakenings, next-day function) over a week with consistent bedtime and dose.
- Change one variable at a time; a 30-minute move is easier to learn from than a complete reset.

**Pregnancy and Medical Context:**
- ACOG describes moderate consumption as less than 200 mg/day during pregnancy; EFSA says intake up to 200 mg/day from all sources does not raise safety concerns for the fetus. Individual clinician advice takes priority.
- If caffeine causes palpitations, marked anxiety, tremor, persistent insomnia, or other symptoms, a decay estimate is not the right tool—consult a clinician.

**Key Takeaways:**
- There is no universal cutoff for caffeine before bed. Caffeine is not completely gone from the body after eight hours. The FDA's 400 mg figure is general daily guidance, not a sleep guarantee. A calculator estimates a curve using an assumed half-life but cannot measure blood levels or identify personal metabolism.

- Sources cited include the FDA, EFSA, National Academies Press, Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine (2013), Sleep Medicine Reviews (2023), and ACOG (2010, reaffirmed 2026).

2. DIRECTIONAL ASYMMETRY: Jet lag is caused by temporary misalignment between the endogenous circadian clock (the SCN) and the destination time zone. Flying east requires a phase advance; flying west requires a phase delay. Because the average free-running period (tau) of the human circadian clock is slightly longer than 24h, humans naturally drift later, making phase advances more difficult. Real travelers phase delay ~92 min/day after westward flights but phase advance only ~57 min/day after eastward flights. With bright light, phase delays of ~2h/day and phase advances of ~1-1.5h/day are achievable. Antidromic (wrong-direction) re-entrainment is common after eastward travel crossing 8+ time zones—in one study, 7 of 8 subjects flying 11 time zones east re-entrained by phase delaying instead of phase advancing. Jet lag symptoms are worst when the temperature minimum (Tmin, the sleepiest circadian time) occurs during waking hours. The Tmin typically occurs 3-4.5h before wake time.

3. PHASE RESPONSE CURVES (PRCs): Bright light produces phase advances when applied late in the sleep episode/morning after the Tmin, and phase delays when applied early in sleep before the Tmin. Melatonin pills produce greatest phase advances when taken in the afternoon and greatest phase delays when taken in the morning. Melatonin is NOT FDA-approved for jet lag in the U.S. (classed as a dietary supplement), but research supports its efficacy. 4. RECOMMENDED STRATEGIES: The key principle is to reset the circadian clock at least partially toward the destination time zone BEFORE flying, while gradually shifting the sleep schedule to keep it aligned with the shifting clock (avoiding abrupt shifts that cause circadian misalignment).

- For flying EAST: Phase advance the sleep schedule by ~1h/day (or less for night owls), use intermittent bright light in the morning (~5,000 lux light box or outdoor light), take 0.5 mg melatonin in the afternoon (4.5h before bedtime, 1h earlier each day), and gradually shift meal times. Melatonin tablets are not recommended on the NHS for jet lag due to insufficient evidence of effectiveness. The main symptoms include difficulty sleeping at bedtime and waking up, tiredness and exhaustion, difficulty staying awake during the day, poor sleep quality, and concentration and memory problems. Jet lag can also cause indigestion, nausea, constipation, changes in appetite, and mild anxiety. The page was last reviewed on May 31, 2023, with the next review due May 31, 2026.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Jet lag is when your normal sleep pattern is disturbed after a long flight. It usually improves within a few days as your body adjusts to the new time zone."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 14: Jet lag disorder - Diagnosis and treatment - Mayo Clinic ---
URL: https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/jet-lag/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20374031

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Mayo Clinic webpage about Jet Lag Disorder, covering diagnosis, treatment, and management strategies. Key points include:

**Diagnosis:** A healthcare professional diagnoses jet lag by asking about symptoms and travel across time zones.

**Treatment:** Jet lag is temporary and usually doesn't require treatment; symptoms typically improve within a few days. For frequent travelers, healthcare professionals may prescribe light therapy or medicines:
- **Light therapy:** Involves exposure to artificial bright light (light box, desk lamp, or light visor) that mimics sunlight, used for specific amounts of time when meant to be awake. Useful for business travelers often away from natural sunlight in new time zones.
- **Medicines (sleeping pills):** Taken during flights and for several nights afterward; usually only recommended when other treatments haven't helped. Side effects (uncommon) may include nausea, vomiting, amnesia, sleepwalking, confusion, and morning sleepiness.

**Alternative medicine:**
- **Melatonin:** Widely studied and common jet lag treatment; the body treats it as a darkness signal (opposite effect of bright light). Timing matters: when flying east, take it nightly in the new time zone; when flying west, take it in the mornings. A dose as small as 0.5 milligram is as effective as 5 milligrams or higher (though higher doses may be better for sleeping). Take 30 minutes before sleep. Side effects may include dizziness, headaches, daytime sleepiness, loss of appetite, nausea, and disorientation. Don't drink alcohol when taking melatonin.
- **Other remedies:** Some use morning exercise; herbal supplements should be checked with a healthcare professional first due to potential interactions.

**Lifestyle and home remedies:**
- **Sunlight:** The most powerful natural tool for regulating the sleep-wake cycle. Morning light exposure helps adjust to earlier time zones (after traveling east); evening light helps adapt to later time zones (after traveling west). Specific guidance: if traveling east across 3-5 time zones, avoid bright daylight first thing in the morning and seek several hours of mid-to-late morning light. For more time zones or west travel, avoid bright light the morning of arrival but seek early afternoon sunshine. Dark glasses, window blinds, and sleep masks can help control light exposure. Combining light exposure with exercise may speed adaptation.
- **Caffeine:** May help offset daytime sleepiness but avoid after midday as it can interfere with falling asleep.

**Appointment preparation:** Jet lag symptoms usually resolve after the trip. Patients seeking prevention strategies for future travel should bring their travel itinerary to the appointment.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Your body's internal clock is influenced by sunlight, among other factors. When you travel across time zones, your body must adjust to a new daylight schedule."
</key_excerpts>



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


--- SOURCE 15: How to Get Over Jet Lag: 8 Tips and Suggestions - Healthline ---
URL: https://www.healthline.com/health/healthy-sleep/how-to-get-over-jet-lag

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Healthline provides 8 tips to help get over jet lag, medically reviewed by Meir Kryger, MD, FRCP(C) and written by Natalie Silver, updated on October 23, 2024. The article explains that jet lag occurs when traveling quickly across time zones causes the body's usual rhythm to fall out of sync, and while the body eventually adjusts, there are ways to reduce symptoms.

The 8 tips are:
1. **Adapt quickly to your new time zone** - Set watches to new time upon departure and eat/sleep according to destination time, especially if the time difference exceeds 3 hours.
2. **Manage sleep time** - Sleep while airborne using noise-canceling headphones, eye masks, earplugs, and travel pillows; avoid daytime napping, but if necessary keep naps to 15-20 minutes.
3. **Drink water** - Long-distance travel may cause dehydration; carry an empty water bottle through security and fill up in the terminal; avoid alcohol as it disrupts sleep.
4. **Eat smaller meals** - The CDC recommends smaller meals to avoid stomach aches and problems, though no formal studies exist on meal size and jet lag.
5. **Try light** - Getting outside in sunshine at the right time can wake the body and reduce melatonin release; when traveling east, avoid bright light until the body's accustomed waking time and consider wearing dark glasses; after the first day, morning light helps speed adaptation.
6. **Drink a caffeinated beverage** - One study found 300 mg of slow-release caffeine enhanced alertness in eastbound travelers; coffee and tea are good sources, but avoid sugary sodas and energy drinks; moderate caffeine in the afternoon and evening to avoid sleep difficulties.
7. **Keep your sleeping space comfortable** - Check thermostat for cool temperature, silence phones/clocks, bring portable white noise machines, and bring familiar items like throw blankets or scented lotion.
8. **Try melatonin** - Consider melatonin supplements to help get or stay sleepy; consult a doctor first to check for medication interactions.

**Recovery timeline:** The rule of thumb is one day to adjust for each time zone crossed (e.g., five time zones = up to 5 days of symptoms).

**Prevention:** Before the flight, go to bed at a time aligned with the destination (2 hours earlier for eastbound, 2 hours later for westbound). Consider arriving 2 days before important events to allow adjustment time.

**Key takeaway:** Jet lag is common and resolves in a few days or weeks. Immediately adapting to the new schedule, drinking daytime caffeine, and managing light exposure are key interventions. Consult a doctor before trying melatonin or other sleep aids.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Jet lag occurs when you travel quickly across time zones and your body's usual rhythm falls out of sync." "The rule of thumb is that for each time zone you cross, it'll take a day to adjust. Therefore, if you change five time zones, you may experience jet lag symptoms for up to 5 days." "One study found that 300 mg of slow-release caffeine enhanced alertness in those traveling eastbound." "Getting outside in the sunshine at the right time can wake up your body and reduce the release of melatonin hormones that make you sleepy." "Immediately adapting to your new schedule, drinking caffeine during the daytime, and managing your exposure to light are just a few of the interventions that may help reduce jet lag symptoms."
</key_excerpts>

10.1177/0748730403258422 ARTICLE JOURNALOF BIOLOGICALRHYTHMS / December 2003 Crowley et al. / ENTRAINMENT TO NIGHT SHIFT WORK Combinations of Bright Light, Scheduled Dark, Sunglasses, and Melatonin to Facilitate Circadian Entrainment to Night Shift Work Stephanie J. Crowley, Clara Lee, Christine Y. Tseng, Louis F. Fogg, and Charmane I. Eastman1 Biological Rhythms Research Laboratory, Rush University Medical Center, Chicago, IL 60612, USA Abstract Various combinations of interventions were used to phase-delay circa-dian rhythms to correct their misalignment with night work and day sleep.
Young participants (median age = 22, n = 67) participated in 5 consecutive simu-lated night shifts (2300 to 0700) and then slept at home (0830 to 1530) in darkened bedrooms. Participants wore sunglasses with normal or dark lenses (transmis-sion 15% or 2%) when outside during the day. Participants took placebo or melatonin (1.8 mg sustained release) before daytime sleep. During the night shifts, participants were exposed to a moving (delaying) pattern of intermittent bright light (~5000 lux, 20 min on, 40 min off, 4-5 light pulses/night) or remained in dim light (~150 lux). There were 6 intervention groups ranging from the least complex (normal sunglasses) to the most complex (dark sunglasses + bright light + melatonin). The dim light melatonin onset (DLMO) was assessed before and after the night shifts (baseline and final), and 7 h was added to estimate the tem-perature minimum (Tmin). Participants were categorized by their amount of re-entrainment based on their final Tmin: not re-entrained (Tmin before the day-time dark/sleep period), partially re-entrained (Tmin during the first half of dark/sleep), or completely re-entrained (Tmin during the second half of dark/ sleep). The sample was split into earlier participants (baseline Tmin ≤0700, sun-light during the commute home fell after the Tmin) and later participants (base-line Tmin > 0700). The later participants were completely re-entrained regardless of intervention group, whereas the degree of re-entrainment for the earlier par-ticipants depended on the interventions. With bright light during the night shift, almost all of the earlier participants achieved complete re-entrainment, and the phase delay shift was so large that darker sunglasses and melatonin could not increase its magnitude. With only room light during the night shift, darker sun-glasses helped earlier participants phase-delay more than normal sunglasses, butmelatonin did notincrease thephase delay. Theauthors recommendthecom-bination of intermittent bright light during the night shift, sunglasses (as dark as possible) during the commute home, and a regular, early daytime dark/sleep period if the goal is complete circadian adaptation to night-shift work.
Key words circadian rhythms, human, shift work, melatonin, bright light, sleep, phase shifts 513 1. To whom all correspondence should be addressed: Charmane I. Eastman, Biological Rhythms Research Laboratory, 1645 W.
Jackson, Suite 425, Chicago, IL 60612; e-mail: ceastman@rush.edu.
JOURNAL OF BIOLOGICAL RHYTHMS, Vol. 18 No. 6, December 2003 513-523 DOI: 10.1177/0748730403258422 © 2003 Sage Publications at COLUMBIA UNIV on April 11, 2014 jbr.sagepub.com Downloaded from Millions of night-shift workers maintain our 24-h society, but not without negative consequences. The most common complaint of shift workers is not get-ting enough sleep (e.g., Kecklund and Akerstedt, 1995). Other problems include fatigue, gastrointesti-nal disturbances, impaired performance, and dimin-ished job and public safety (e.g., Folkard and Monk, 1985). These serious problems are caused by circadian misalignment. Night-shift workers are required to work during the “wrong” phase of their circadian cycle, when they are the most inefficient and sleepy, often fall asleep, and are most prone to accidents (e.g., Akerstedt, 1988; Mitler et al., 1988). Subsequently, they try to sleep during the day, again during the “wrong” phase of their circadian cycle, which results in disrupted and shortened sleep (e.g., Akerstedt, 1995). Phase-shifting circadian rhythms to align with night work and day sleep schedules (re-entrainment) can alleviate the physiological symptoms of night work because the period of sleepiness occurs during the new daytime dark period and the period of alertness occurs during the night shift.
The circadian clocks of real-shift workers do not usually phase shift (e.g., Akerstedt, 1995; Dumont et al., 2001) because they are exposed to the natural light-dark (LD) cycle and other possible 24-h zeitgebers (Eastman et al., 1995). Sunlight in the morning during the commute home after each night shift usually coin-cides with the phase-advance portion of the light phase response curve (PRC), which is after the tem-perature minimum (Tmin), and thus inhibits circadian rhythms from phase-delaying. Wearing dark goggles during the commute home can help attenuate advanc-ing sunlight in the morning and facilitate re-entrain-ment to night work and day sleep (Eastman et al., 1994). Ensuring a dark environment for sleep as soon as possible after the night shift will further block out advancing light and will also form the basis of a delayed LD cycle that can delay the circadian clock.
Phase shifting circadian rhythms to completely re-entrain to the night work and day sleep schedule has been reliably produced in many field studies of simu-lated night work (see Eastman and Martin, 1999; Bur-gess et al., 2002 for reviews) and in a real night-shift work setting (Boivin and James, 2002) by using artifi-cial bright light (BL) at night and constructing periods of darkness during the day. Our laboratory has fre-quently taken advantage of a gradually moving pat-tern of BL to phase-shift circadian rhythms (Eastman, 1992; Mitchell et al., 1997; Martin and Eastman, 1998; Burgess et al., 2003). Theoretically, the BLmoves along with the circadian clock and its PRC so that the BL always occurs at a more optimal time for the desired phase shift. A moving pattern of BL is also a way to facilitate a phase shift in participants with varying ini-tial circadian phases. The BL acts like a broom, “sweeping” the participants with early and late circa-dian phases together and in the desired phase-shifting direction. For example, to facilitate a phase delay, BL timed to occur early in the night will be closer to the Tmin of the participants with earlier phases and phase delay these participants more than those with later phases. Then, as the BL moves later and later each night, it will fall closer to the Tmins of the participants with later phases and have more of a phase-shifting effect on those participants.
In a real night-work setting, it may be difficult for workers to remain exposed to a light source for an extended amount of time. Intermittent exposure would be more likely to occur and more practical to implement. In one of our simulated night shift studies, 40-min light pulses (~5000 lux) alternating with 20 min of room light (< 500 lux) during the first 6 h of the night shift was used to help phase-delay circadian rhythms and produce re-entrainment to the daytime sleep schedule (Baehr et al., 1999). Asubsequent labo-ratory study showed that 46 min of BL (~9500 lux) alternating with 44 min of dark over 5 h (timed with the majority of the light pulses after the Tmin to facili-tate a phase advance) produced similar phase shifts as a 5 h, continuous light pulse (Rimmer et al., 2000).
Similarly, a recent study in our lab showed that 3.5 h of intermittent BL (30 min of BL ≥3000 lux alternating with 30 min of room light < 60 lux) produced similar phase advances as 3.5 h of continuous light (≥3000 lux) (Burgess et al., 2003).
The pineal hormone melatonin (M) can also phase shift the circadian clock. The M PRC of Lewy et al.
(1998) suggests that a small dose of M (0.5 mg) admin-istered approximately 10 h after the dim light melatonin onset (DLMO) (in most cases, in the early morning hours) will produce the largest phase delay of circadian rhythms. See the simplified M PRC, Fig-ure 1 in Burgess et al. (2002). We found that M helped phase-advance circadian rhythms to adapt to the night shift when sleep was taken in the afternoon/ evening (an advance of sleep) (Sharkey and Eastman, 2002), but few studies have tested M to facilitate a phase delay and thus circadian adaptation to night work when sleep is taken in the morning/afternoon (a delay of sleep).
514 JOURNAL OF BIOLOGICAL RHYTHMS / December 2003 at COLUMBIA UNIV on April 11, 2014 jbr.sagepub.com Downloaded from The purpose of the current study was to test the rel-ative contribution and the combined effectiveness of various interventions, namely, BL, sunglasses (SG), and M to phase-delay circadian rhythms and realign them with sleep in the morning after the night shift.
Intermittent BL was used in a moving pattern during the night shift. From previous studies in our lab, we estimated that the Tmin, and thus the crossover point in the light PRC, would be, on average, around 0500 (Baehr et al., 2000). Therefore, we ended the BLduring the first night shift at 0500 and moved it 1 h later on each subsequent night shift. We used 5 consecutive simulated night shifts from 2300 to 0700, as this is a common pattern in real shift-work settings. We required participants to remain in bed and in the dark from 0830 to 1530 after each night shift because we think that this is a reasonable daytime sleep schedule for a real night-shift worker. SG with normal or very dark lenses were used to attenuate sunlight during the commute home, which we expected to coincide with the phase-advance portion of the light PRC. M (1.8 mg, sustained release) was taken immediately before each daytime sleep (0830), a time expected to facilitate phase delays. The study included six intervention groups (six combinations of the interventions men-tioned above), which differed in the type and number of interventions and therefore in the amount of effort that would be required if adopted by real night-shift workers and their employers.
MATERIALS AND METHOD Participants A total of 67 participants (35 females and 32 males) between the ages of 18 and 43 (mean age ± SD = 23.9 ± 6.2 years) completed the study. Participants did not have any obvious medical, psychiatric, or sleep disor-ders as assessed by interviews, the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory-2, a sleep ques-tionnaire, and a health questionnaire. Participants were not taking prescription medications, except for oral contraceptives. To ensure the dose (mg/kg) of M was not too low, individuals who weighed more than 105 kg were excluded. Participants had not worked night shifts or traveled across more than 3 time zones within the month before starting the study. Most par-ticipants had never worked night shifts. The protocol was approved by the Rush-Presbyterian–St. Luke’s Medical Center Institutional Review Board. All partic-ipants gave written informed consent and were paid for their participation.
Design There was a baseline week with no set sleep sched-ule. Figure 1 displays days 8-14 of the protocol. We made participants’ bedrooms completely dark by cov-Crowley et al. / ENTRAINMENT TO NIGHT SHIFT WORK 515 16 18 20 22 0 2 4 6 8 10 12 14 16 14 13 12 11 10 9 8 Dark/ Sleep Baseline Phase Assessment Final Phase Assessment L L L L L L L L L L L L L L L L L L L L L L L Night Shifts Day of Study Time of Day Figure 1. Participants were required to wear SG whenever they were outside during the day. The study took place during 3 summers (July-September). During the baseline week, participants wore N SG (15% transmis-sion, standard gray lens, Uvex Safety Inc, Smithfield, RI). During the 2nd week, groups 1 and 4 continued to wear N SG, and the rest were given D SG (2% trans-mission, shade 5.0 welding lens, Uvex Safety Inc.).
Both SG had the same black frames with top and side shields (Flashback frames, Uvex Safety Inc.).
Participants in groups 3 and 6 took M (1.8 mg sus-tained release, Ecological Formulas, Concord, CA), whereas the remaining groups took a matching pla-cebo just before bedtime at 0830. Circadian phase variables were analyzed using a one-way multivariate analysis of variance and Tukey HSD post hoc tests. Dependent variables were base-line DLMO, final DLMO, and phase shift. Chi-square analyses were performed using the 3 re-entrainment categories.

DISCUSSION We found that the circadian phase of participants before starting night work was the most important factor for determining whether their circadian rhythms would delay enough to align with the day-time sleep schedule and thus produce circadian adap-tation to night work. During the baseline week, partic-ipants were free to sleep almost anytime because we wanted them to start the night shift with a wide range of circadian phases, to simulate what we would expect in real night-shift workers. The participants who had Tmins before the start of the commute time home at 0700 (the earlier participants) benefited the most from our interventions, whereas the later participants achieved complete re-entrainment regardless of inter-vention group. For the earlier participants, 1) intermit-tent BL during the night shift consistently produced large phase delays; 2) very dark SG used to attenuate sunlight during the commute home after the night shift helped delay circadian rhythms more than nor-mal SG; 3) however, we could not demonstrate a benefit from the administration of M before daytime sleep.
We converted the DLMOs obtained in this study to estimated Tmins (by adding the constant of 7 h) for 2 reasons of convenience. First, the Tmin is an estimate for the sleepiest part of the circadian cycle and the time of greatest performance decrements, although for some measures and protocols the “circadian dip” is actually slightly later (e.g., Johnson et al., 1992). A second reason for referring to the Tmin instead of the DLMO is that the Tmin is an estimate for the light PRC cross-over point from delays to advances (Czeisler et al., 1989; Eastman and Martin, 1999), although in some studies it appears to be slightly later (e.g., Minors et al., 1991).
Sunglasses for the Commute Time Home For the earlier participants, sunlight during the commute home probably coincided with the phase advance portion of their light PRC. This can explain why so many participants did not re-entrain when they wore normal SG and why significantly more par-ticipants were re-entrained when they wore darker SG (group 2 vs. group 1). However, the darker welders lenses were not designed for driving, whereas the nor-mal lenses do meet color traffic signal recognition requirements. Therefore, the mode of transportation is an essential detail to consider when recommending welders glasses. Our participants were tested in the summer and were exposed to relatively intense light during the commute. Light intensity would be lower in winter, especially at more extreme latitudes, or dur-ing earlier commute times. In those circumstances, we would expect more participants to re-entrain with just normal SG. In conclusion, we recommend wearing SG during the commute home (as dark as possible), com-bined with an early, regular dark period for sleep after the night shift as a simple, inexpensive, and effective way to produce at least some degree of circadian adaptation in workers who start the night shift with earlier circadian phases.
Bright Light during the Night Shift When our participants were exposed to intermit-tent BL during the night shift, 96% of them (26/27) achieved complete re-entrainment. Given BL, darker SG and M conferred no additional benefit. BLand nor-mal SG (and of course the D/S period) produced com-plete re-entrainment, even in participants with earlier baseline phases.
We used a moving pattern of BL pulses to phase-delay the rhythms as far as possible. However, most of the Tmins clustered near the end of dark/sleep. It would have been better to have the Tmins delay no further than about 2-3 h before wake, for a more nor-mal phase relative to sleep (cf. Baehr et al., 2000). Thus, the BLpattern we used was too powerful. The ideal BL pattern should delay the rhythms to realign with sleep as fast as possible, but then not delay them much fur-ther in subsequent days. Modifications that could be tested include a stationary pattern of light pulses, lower intensities of BL, durations shorter than 20 min, fewer pulses of BL per night, and fewer nights with BL.
There are circumstances in which partial rather than complete re-entrainment might be preferable, such as for night shift workers who would not be able to cope with the symptoms caused by misalignment of their circadian rhythms on their days off. Therefore, we have designed compromise schedules (Eastman and Martin, 1999; Burgess et al., 2002) in which circa-dian phase is delayed so that the worker is partially entrained to a night work and day sleep schedule and partially entrained to sleeping at night and enjoying leisure time during their days off. The worker is instructed to adopt as late a sleep schedule as possible during days off, and we would use a BL pattern that produces partial re-entrainment. These schedules are intended for permanent night work systems, and the goal is to achieve partial re-entrainment during all night shifts, starting with the 2nd block of night shifts.
Future studies are planned to test such compromise schedules. However, older workers are less phase tol-erant and may need complete re-entrainment to achieve substantial benefits (Campbell, 1995; Dijk et al., 1999). Obviously, the ideal degree of entrainment to day sleep and night work depends on many factors, including the hazard potential of the job. Another solution to completeadaptation to the night shift, such as after extended periods of night work on offshore oil rigs or during space shuttle missions, is to use light boxes to help workers adjust back to day life (Stewart et al., 1995; Bjorvatn et al., 1999).
A recent study (Boivin and James, 2002) tested BL on night nurses by setting up light boxes in the nurs-ing station. Circadian rhythms were measured before and after an average of 12 8-h night shifts, with some days off in between. The treatment group was given a combination of interventions similar to our group 4 (D/S, N SG (15% transmission, Uvex) + BL). They were exposed to about 3000 lux of intermittent BLdur-ing the first 6 h of every night shift and were instructed to go to bed for 8 h starting 2 h after the end of the night shift. The control group had D/S, clear glasses, and 520 JOURNAL OF BIOLOGICAL RHYTHMS / December 2003 at COLUMBIA UNIV on April 11, 2014 jbr.sagepub.com Downloaded from their usual lighting during the night shift (~100 lux).
Both groups were permitted to sleep freely on days off. All the participants in the treatment group achieved partial or complete re-entrainment, whereas the participants in the control group showed a wide range of final circadian phases, from none to complete re-entrainment. This study demonstrates that inter-ventions similar to our group 4 can be implemented in a real shift work setting and are effective in producing circadian adaptation, despite intervening days off.
As in all of our previous simulated night shift stud-ies, we used a fixed daytime D/S period to create a strong, shifted LD cycle. The utility of this technique was corroborated by a recent study (Horowitz et al., 2001). Circadian phase was measured before and after 3 consecutive simulated night shifts (2300 to 0700 h).
During the night shifts, participants were exposed to either room light (~150 lux) for the entire night shift or BL (~2500 lux, continuous) for the first 6 h of each night shift. After each night shift, they either slept from 0800 to 1600 h (fixed sleep) or chose when they slept, which was often later (free sleep). There were 4 groups: Room Free, Bright Free, Room Fixed, and Bright Fixed. The Bright Fixed group phase-delayed the most, and about half of these participants achieved re-entrainment by our definition. Almost none of the participants in the other groups phase delayed enough for re-entrainment. The results from the Bright Free group show that despite BL during the night shift, when participants were free to choose their own daytime sleep schedules, circadian adaptation was unlikely to occur. These results confirm our rec-ommendation that night shift workers adopt an early fixed D/S period after night work.
Melatonin Administration When we compared groups 2 versus 3 and groups 5 versus 6 (placebo vs. M), there were no statistically significant differences by any of our analyses. There-fore, there was no benefit in taking this particular dose of M (1.8 mg sustained release) at this particular time (0830 h or about 9 h after the baseline DLMO). All of the participants in BL groups 5 and 6 achieved com-plete re-entrainment. M could not increase the phase delay because they were already phase-shifted as far as possible, creating a ceiling effect (Fig. 2). However, when groups 2 and 3 are considered, there was room for many participants to phase-delay later. Perhaps a nonoptimal timing or dose of M was the reason that the circadian rhythms of some of the participants in group 3 did not delay further.
Many studies have shown M’s phase-advancing effects (e.g., Krauchi et al., 1997; Sharkey and East-man, 2002). However, the current study was one of the few in which M was tested to delay circadian rhythms in humans and in which circadian phase was mea-sured. One simulated night shift study (Dawson et al., 1995) tested M administered at 0800 (2 mg), 1100 (1 mg), and 1400 h (1 mg) versus placebo. There was no difference between the phase-delay shifts attained by those who took M or those who took placebo (4.7 h vs.
4.2 h) probably because the times of M administration coincided with both the phase-delay and phase-advance portions of the M PRC. In another study (summarized in Sack and Lewy, 1997), 24 night shift workers (nurses and hospital clerical staff) alternated between 7 consecutive 10-h night shifts (2130 to 0730 h) and 7 consecutive days off. M (0.5 mg immediate release) or placebo was administered at bedtime after the night shifts and at bedtime during their week off.
This was a double-blind crossover design, and M was taken during one 2-week block and placebo was taken during the other. The DLMO was assessed weekly.
Only 7 out of the 24 participants responded to M dur-ing the night shift week, meaning that their final DLMO was shifted at least 3 h later with M in compari-son to placebo. Some delayed and some advanced equally as far with placebo or M, and others did not shift with either treatment. These variable results could be due to different light exposure patterns cre-ated by the participants’ sleep schedules and whether or not they wore SG. The timing of M administration varied because the workers chose when they went to sleep and took the M before going to sleep. In conclu-sion, neither these studies nor our current study pro-vides much evidence that M can help phase-delay circadian rhythms in a night shift work situation.
CONCLUSIONS This study has many practical applications for nightshift workers and their employers. Simple habits like wearing SG during the commute home (the darker the lenses the better), creating a dark bedroom, and adhering to a regular daytime sleep schedule starting soon after the night shift can reduce circadian misalignment. Future studies should focus on determining the ideal degree of re-entrainment for various circumstances (e.g., age of worker, hazard potential of job) and the optimal light pattern to produce the desired amount of realignment.

args.summary:
This scientific article (Crowley et al., 2003, Journal of Biological Rhythms) investigates combinations of bright light, scheduled dark, sunglasses, and melatonin to facilitate circadian entrainment to night shift work. The study was conducted at Rush University Medical Center, Chicago, IL.

**Study Design:** 67 young participants (median age 22, ages 18-43, mean 23.9 ± 6.2 years; 35 females, 32 males) completed 5 consecutive simulated night shifts (2300-0700) followed by daytime dark/sleep at home (0830-1530 in darkened bedrooms). Six intervention groups were tested, ranging from least to most complex: (1) D/S + normal sunglasses (15% transmission), (2) D/S + dark sunglasses (2% transmission), (3) D/S + dark sunglasses + melatonin (1.8 mg sustained release), (4) D/S + normal sunglasses + bright light, (5) D/S + dark sunglasses + bright light, and (6) D/S + dark sunglasses + melatonin + bright light. Bright light was intermittent (~5000 lux, 20 min on/40 min off, 4-5 pulses/night in a moving/delaying pattern); control groups had ~150 lux room light. Circadian phase was assessed via dim light melatonin onset (DLMO) before and after the shifts; Tmin was estimated as DLMO + 7 hours.

**Key Results:**
- Participants were split by baseline circadian phase: "earlier" participants (baseline Tmin ≤0700) and "later" participants (baseline Tmin >0700).
- All "later" participants achieved complete re-entrainment regardless of intervention group.
- For "earlier" participants, intervention complexity mattered significantly. With bright light during night shifts, ~96% (26/27) achieved complete re-entrainment; the phase delay was so large that darker sunglasses and melatonin could not increase it (ceiling effect).
- Darker sunglasses helped earlier participants phase-delay more than normal sunglasses (significant benefit).
- Melatonin (1.8 mg sustained release taken at 0830) showed no significant benefit for phase delay in any comparison (groups 2 vs. 3, and 5 vs. 6).
- Group 1 (normal sunglasses only) had 70% of earlier participants fail to re-entrain; adding dark sunglasses, melatonin, or bright light significantly improved outcomes.

**Conclusions/Recommendations:** The authors recommend combining intermittent bright light during night shifts, sunglasses (as dark as possible) during the commute home, and a regular early daytime dark/sleep period for complete circadian adaptation. Simple habits (dark sunglasses, dark bedroom, regular early daytime sleep) can reduce circadian misalignment. The bright light pattern used was noted to be "too powerful," over-delaying Tmins to near the end of the dark/sleep period; ideal patterns should delay to about 2-3 hours before wake. Future studies should determine optimal re-entrainment degree for different circumstances (age, job hazard potential) and optimal light patterns. Partial re-entrainment compromise schedules may be preferable for some workers. The study was supported by NIOSH grant R01 OH003954.
args.key_excerpts: "The authors recommend the combination of intermittent bright light during the night shift, sunglasses (as dark as possible) during the commute home, and a regular, early daytime dark/sleep period if the goal is complete circadian adaptation to night-shift work."

# Beating Jet Lag: A Guide to Strategic Light Exposure

While many strategies exist to combat jet lag — from adjusting meal times to taking melatonin to tweaking sleep schedules — exposure to light is one of the most powerful natural remedies (1, 2, 3). In conversation with Dr. Jamie Zeitzer, we explore how to harness light in your favor to achieve optimal performance in different time zones.

By Kristy Hamilton and Jamie Zeitzer

May 8, 2024

![](https://humanperformancealliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/thumbnail_IMG_20190117_112853020_HDR-Copy-3-225x300.jpg)

### Jamie Zeitzer, PhD

[Dr. Jamie Zeitzer](https://profiles.stanford.edu/jamie-zeitzer) is a Professor (Research) of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences – Sleep Medicine at Stanford University. Specifically, he is circadian physiologist specializing in the understanding of the impact of light on circadian rhythms and other aspects of non-image forming light perception.

You’ve just landed at your destination. It’s the middle of the day, but you go straight to the hotel for a long nap. The culprit? Jet lag, a familiar foe for millions of globetrotters crossing time zones each year. 

Whether you’re a sprinter flying across the continent for a championship race or a traveler on vacation, jet lag is a common hurdle. But in sports, where milliseconds can separate athletes at the finish line, every detail matters. The last thing athletes want is to be fatigued and disoriented on game day.

As Dr. Jamie Zeitzer and colleagues explain, “Having to respond to mental challenges when their brains are prepared to sleep puts them at reduced cognitive capacity and can result in impaired reaction time and decision-making.”[1](#citations)

### **Why Do We Experience Jet Lag?**

Jet lag is no surprise, really. Human evolution did not equip us with the ability to cruise through numerous time zones in just a few hours. Air travel exposes our bodies to a phenomenon we never would have encountered naturally. Jet lag may seem simple, but it’s actually a sophisticated interplay between our internal biological clocks and the external environment. 

![](https://humanperformancealliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/Copy-of-Playbook-Instagram-Post-with-Tip-1024x683.png)

*Canva Pro Images*

Deep inside the brain in a region called the suprachiasmatic nucleus, there’s an internal ticking clock. Roughly every 24 hours, 20,000 pacemaker cells synchronize and signal to the rest of the body whether it is day or night. The primary cue for the pacemaker cells is light. These signals influence various physiological processes, including the release of hormones like melatonin and cortisol, which, in turn, regulate [sleep-wake cycles](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/sleep/sleep-wake-cycle) and other bodily functions. 

“You have a central circadian clock in the brain, but you also have molecular clocks in every tissue in your body,” said Dr. Zeitzer. “They are in your lungs, your liver, your skin, your immune cells — all these tissues have their own clocks. These clocks work in coordination, much like the conductor of an orchestra.” [2,4,5](#citations)

When we rapidly cross time zones, we disrupt the routine of pacemaker cells and they struggle to synchronize to a new day-night rhythm. As a result, we experience the infamous brain fog and insomnia of jet lag (scientifically termed desynchronosis).[6](#citations)

### **Jet Lag’s Influence on Performance**

A review of airline travel and physical performance noted that prospective and retrospective studies seem to show support for a deterioration in athletic performance after travel across multiple time zones. Furthermore, crossing more time zones seems to have an additive effect on performance deterioration.[7](#citations)

A few studies have attempted to tackle the question of jet lag outcomes for sports teams using many years of data. For example, one study analyzed 10 years’ worth of National Football League team performance data, while another examined 20 years’ worth of Major League Baseball team data.[8,9](#citations) Both studies found that negative effects of jet lag are more evident after eastward, rather than westward, journeys.

![](https://humanperformancealliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/Baseball-Jet-Lag-1024x681.jpg)

*Canva Pro Images*

However, there are issues with evaluating jet lag study outcomes.[7](#citations) For one, it’s difficult to disentangle jet lag from other factors such as habitual training times, time-of-day, and individual chronotypes. For example, a study analyzing Olympic swim times over a 12-year period found that time-of-day is a significant influence on performance.[10](#citations)

Second, some of the research is based on performance measures such as grip strength that provide a limited window into a person’s overall athletic performance.  Additionally, past studies on this topic often only include a small number of participants. It is unclear how these can be generalized to overall athletic performance.[7](#citations)

![](https://humanperformancealliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/3-1-150x150.png)

### Why is studying jet lag so complex?

There are many factors at play when trying to study circadian phase delay and jet lag. The phrase “correlation does not equal causation” is especially relevant here. It means that just because two things are related statistically (e.g., they are both trending upwards), it doesn’t mean one causes the other. There could be other factors at play (e.g., the time of day an athlete typically trains or general fatigue due to travel).

### **How Long Will My Jet Lag Last?**

The more time zones you travel, the more your circadian clock falls out of sync with its rhythm. According to Dr. Zeitzer, a general guideline is to allow for about one day for adjustment per time zone traveled.[1,2](#citations) The qualification of “about” one day is necessary; even though we all share a 24-hour daily cycle, our personal circadian clocks are not universally standardized. 

![](https://humanperformancealliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/light-1024x683.jpg)

*Scott Thompson/Adobe Free Photos*

“If you were kept in total darkness, your internal clock would run on average around 24 hours and 12 minutes,” said Dr. Zeitzer. “But for some people, it’s longer. For others, it’s shorter. Some people are night owls. Some people prefer morning hours.” [2](#citations)

![](https://humanperformancealliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/Playbook-Icons-Lightbulb-150x150.png)

### Did You Know?

On average, it takes about one day to adjust to each time zone crossed during travel. If you cross six time zones, it could take six days for your body to fully adapt to the new schedule.

### **Bright Ideas for Beating Jet Lag**

Let’s be straightforward – there is no cure for jet lag. There are only strategies to reduce its severity. Light plays a crucial role in overcoming jet lag.[1,2,3,6](#citations) A common misunderstanding, however, is that all light is equal. 

“Understanding light intensity levels in different environments is key,” said Dr. Zeitzer. A person can adjust their circadian rhythms by approximately one hour each day if they expose themselves to the right amounts of light at the right times.[1,11](#citations) Avoiding light at the correct times is also crucial for rapid adaptation to jet lag.

“The body does not look at light as an absolute quantity but rather as a relative quantity,” said Dr. Zeitzer.

When dealing with time zone changes of 12 hours or less, follow these general guidelines: When traveling Eastward, you want to get light in the morning and avoid light in the evening. When traveling Westward, avoid light in the morning and get light in the evening.

![](https://humanperformancealliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/Playbook-Icons-Lightbulb-150x150.png)

### Did You Know?

Eastward travel across time zones is often harder to adjust to than Westward. It’s generally more challenging to fall asleep earlier when traveling East than stay awake later when traveling West.[1,6](#citations) Our internal clocks naturally run a bit longer than 24 hours, and when there’s a lack of consistent light cues – such as when traveling across time zones – the pacemaker cells in our bodies tend to favor a longer day.[12](#citations)

How much light do you need, though? While common room light is between 50 and 250 lux (brighter in offices and bathrooms), outdoor light on a typical day in California can range from 50,000 to 100,000 lux.[3](#citations) Even on cloudy or foggy days in California it’s around 10,000 lux.

![](https://humanperformancealliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/Walking-Jet-Lag-1024x681.jpg)

*Canva Pro Images*

“If you are getting light after a night of sleep, even regular room light will impact your clock, so avoid this when going Westward,” said Dr. Zeitzer. “Going outside will be an even more potent stimulus.” 

Light in the evening, however, is a little different because you’ve been exposed to light already during the day. “You’ll need brighter light to change your clock, especially if you have been outside during the daytime,” added Dr. Zeitzer. “So if you’ve traveled Eastward and are trying to avoid light in the evening, you don’t need to worry too much about the light you get in normal hotels if you have been outside during the daytime.[13,14](#citations)

![](https://humanperformancealliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/3-1-150x150.png)

### How much light does a person need to adjust to non-jetlagged performance?

We don’t know the specific answer to this as the physiological drivers behind performance (muscle, neuromuscular, endocrine, metabolic, neural, etc.) are likely sport specific. Other variables like the timing of eating and exercise are capable of acting as secondary circadian cues and may alter the amount of light needed.

You can also start to synchronize your circadian rhythm before traveling. Consider the scenario of an athletic team moving eastward from Mountain Standard Time (MST) Zone to Eastern Standard Time (EST) Zone, where players “lose” two hours (e.g., from 8pm MST to 10pm EST). To acclimate to the new time zone prior to departure, athletes should aim to shift their circadian system by 2 hours. In the 2-3 days preceding travel, they should move their bedtime and wake time 30-60 minutes earlier than usual. Upon waking, they should expose themselves to bright light, getting outside being ideal. In the evening, they should try to dim the lights (e.g., turn off overhead lights and use a book light if needed) for 2 hours before going to sleep.[1,6](#citations)

For those with limited access to sunshine, you can also try a light therapy box. Ideally, the light box should be rated to emit 10,000 lux of light and minimize as much UV light as possible.[3](#citations)

![](https://humanperformancealliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/Playbook-Icons-Designed-150x150.png)

### Is a light box right for me?

It’s advisable to consult with your healthcare provider when selecting a light box. The [Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/seasonal-affective-disorder/in-depth/seasonal-affective-disorder-treatment/art-20048298) warns that increasing exposure too fast or for too long can induce manic symptoms in people with bipolar disorder. Individuals with a history of eye issues like glaucoma, cataracts, or diabetes-related eye damage should also seek guidance from their eye specialist before starting light therapy.

Planning the optimal timing of light exposure across different time zones can be tricky, so consider exploring apps that specialize in planning light exposure before travel. These apps help create a personalized schedule based on factors like time zone differences, departure and arrival times, and more. 

Additional behaviors like the timing of food intake, sleep, exercise, and melatonin can all help with jet lag.[1,2,6](#citations) Look out for more on these influences in future Playbook articles.

![](https://humanperformancealliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/2-1-150x150.png)

### Training Tip

To combat jet lag, strategic planning is essential. Adjusting natural light exposure based on the direction of travel—more light in the morning and less in the evening if you’re traveling eastward, more light in evening and less in the morning if you’re traveling westward—can aid in faster synchronization.

# [Jet lag disorder](/diseases-conditions/jet-lag/symptoms-causes/syc-20374027)

## Overview

Jet lag is a temporary sleep condition that can affect anyone who quickly travels across several time zones.

Your body has its own internal clock, called circadian rhythms. They signal to your body when to stay awake and when to sleep.

Jet lag occurs because your body's internal clock is synced to your original time zone. It hasn't changed to the time zone you've traveled to. The more time zones you cross, the more likely you are to experience jet lag.

Jet lag can cause daytime fatigue, a feeling of not being well, trouble staying alert and stomach problems. Although symptoms are temporary, they can affect your comfort while on vacation or during a business trip. But you can take steps to help prevent or lessen the effects of jet lag.

### Products & Services

## Symptoms

Symptoms of jet lag can vary. You may experience only one symptom or you may have many. Jet lag symptoms may include:

### Symptoms are worse the farther you travel

Jet lag symptoms usually occur within a day or two after traveling across at least two time zones. Symptoms are likely to be worse or last longer the farther you travel. This is especially true if you fly east. It usually takes about a day to recover for each time zone crossed.

### When to see a doctor

Jet lag is temporary. But if you travel often and experience jet lag, you may benefit from seeing a sleep specialist.

## Causes

### A disruption to your circadian rhythms

Jet lag can occur anytime you cross two or more time zones. Crossing multiple time zones puts your internal clock out of sync with the time in your new locale. Your internal clock, also called circadian rhythms, regulates your sleep-wake cycle.

For example, if you leave New York on a flight at 4 p.m. on Tuesday and arrive in Paris at 7 a.m. Wednesday, your internal clock still thinks it's 1 a.m. That means you're ready for bed just as Parisians are waking up.

It takes a few days for your body to adjust. In the meantime, your sleep-wake cycle and other body functions such as hunger and bowel habits remain out of step with the rest of Paris.

### The effect of sunlight

A key influence on circadian rhythms is sunlight. Light affects the regulation of melatonin, a hormone that helps cells throughout the body work together.

Cells in the tissue at the back of the eye transmit light signals to an area of the brain called the hypothalamus. When the light is low at night, the hypothalamus signals to a small organ in the brain called the pineal gland to release melatonin. During daylight hours, the opposite occurs. The pineal gland releases very little melatonin.

Because light is so crucial to your internal clock, you may be able to ease your adjustment to a new time zone by exposing yourself to daylight. However, the timing of light needs to be done properly.

### Airline cabin pressure and atmosphere

Some research shows that changes in cabin pressure and high altitudes associated with air travel may contribute to some symptoms of jet lag, regardless of travel across time zones.

In addition, humidity levels are low in planes. If you don't drink enough water during your flight, you can get slightly dehydrated. Dehydration also may contribute to some symptoms of jet lag.

## Complications

Auto accidents caused by drowsy driving may be more likely in people who are jet-lagged.

## Prevention

A few basic steps may help prevent jet lag or reduce its effects:

**Properly time bright light exposure.** Light exposure has a big influence on your body's circadian rhythms. After traveling west, expose yourself to light in the evening to help you adjust to a later than usual time zone. After traveling east, expose yourself to morning light.

The one exception is if you've traveled across more than eight time zones. Your body might mistake early-morning light with evening dusk or vice versa. If you've traveled more than eight time zones to the east, wear sunglasses and avoid bright light in the morning. Then expose yourself to as much sunlight as possible in the late afternoon for the first few days. If you've traveled west by more than eight time zones, avoid sunlight a few hours before dark for the first few days.

It occurs because the body's internal clock (circadian rhythms) remains synced to the original time zone rather than adjusting to the destination. Exception: if traveling across more than eight time zones, adjust accordingly (wear sunglasses in the morning if traveling east by more than eight zones and seek light in the late afternoon; avoid sunlight a few hours before dark if traveling west by more than eight zones).
- **When to see a doctor**: Jet lag is temporary, but frequent travelers experiencing it may benefit from seeing a sleep specialist.
