DENVER – With the right combination of morning bright light exposure, low-dose melatonin, and gradually advancing bedtimes in the days prior to flying eastward, travelers can avoid the hassles of jet lag, Victoria L. Revell, Ph.D., said at the annual meeting of the Associated Professional Sleep Societies.

“With a little bit of preparation you can arrive with no jet lag, and not waste any days, and be more productive at your meeting, and enjoy your trip,” added her coinvestigator, Charmane I. Eastman, Ph.D., professor of psychology and director of the Biological Rhythms Research Laboratory at Rush University Medical Center, Chicago.

The investigators explained that jet lag is the result of misalignment between circadian rhythms and the destination time zone. It is worse after flights eastward because people find it more difficult to phase advance than phase delay. The purpose of pretrip re-entrainment is to help travelers, once they arrive at their destination, keep their circadian temperature drop where it belongs: during the night, when they're sleeping.

DENVER – With the right combination of morning bright light exposure, low-dose melatonin, and gradually advancing bedtimes in the days prior to flying eastward, travelers can avoid the hassles of jet lag, Victoria L. Revell, Ph.D., said at the annual meeting of the Associated Professional Sleep Societies.

“With a little bit of preparation you can arrive with no jet lag, and not waste any days, and be more productive at your meeting, and enjoy your trip,” added her coinvestigator, Charmane I. Eastman, Ph.D., professor of psychology and director of the Biological Rhythms Research Laboratory at Rush University Medical Center, Chicago.

The investigators explained that jet lag is the result of misalignment between circadian rhythms and the destination time zone. It is worse after flights eastward because people find it more difficult to phase advance than phase delay. The purpose of pretrip re-entrainment is to help travelers, once they arrive at their destination, keep their circadian temperature drop where it belongs: during the night, when they're sleeping.

“People think, 'Oh, if only I could sleep at night; I'll just take a sleeping pill.' But that only solves half the problem because if you do that to sleep, you'll still feel bad during the day walking around out of phase with your temperature minimum,” Dr. Eastman added.

The program developed by the Chicago investigators involves four 30-minute light-box sessions in the morning, alternating with 30 minutes of ordinary room light. The first session begins upon awakening. The single light box emits about 5,000 lux using cool white fluorescent lamps. A light box is used because it's convenient; bright morning sunlight isn't available every day. The alternating 30-minute bright-light/room-light sessions are, once again, a matter of convenience.

It's possible, for example, to fit in one light box session while reading the morning paper, then go take a shower, then return to the light box while eating breakfast, then go get dressed before having another light session while working at the computer.

Bedtime is moved 1 hour earlier each evening for the same number of days as time zones to be crossed. Melatonin at a dose of 0.5 mg is taken roughly 5 hours before bedtime, which prior sleep lab work has established as the optimal time to take the hormone in order to induce phase advances. The melatonin enhances the size of the daily phase advance, thereby cutting down on the number of days a traveler needs to follow the program.

The investigators reported on 44 healthy volunteers who participated in a blinded three-night sleep lab study that established 0.5 mg as the optimal melatonin dose. Each morning the participants received four intermittent 30-minute sessions of bright light. Each night they went to bed 1 hour earlier than the night before. And each afternoon they took 0.5 or 3.0 mg of melatonin or placebo.

The mean phase advance was determined by dim-light melatonin onset measured via saliva samples. (See box.)

To ensure that the phase advancement wasn't causing jet lag-type symptoms, participants completed the Columbia Jet Lag Scale daily and the Stanford Sleepiness Scale five times per day.

The results were reassuring except that subjects on 3.0 mg/day of melatonin reported a slight increase in daytime sleepiness. It wasn't enough to pose a safety hazard, but since the efficacy wasn't significantly greater than with 0.5 mg/day, the investigators decided low-dose therapy was the way to go, Dr. Revell explained.

Outside of the controlled laboratory setting, Dr. Eastman said she and numerous friends and colleagues have employed the phase-shift travel preparation method with great success.

The study was supported by the National Institutes of Health. Melatonin and matching placebos were provided by Ecological Formulas.

# How to Use Melatonin for Jet Lag – A Complete Guide to Recovery and Conquering Time Zones

![man yawning due to jet lag with melatonin tablets and clock on the table](https://www.quadrawellness.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/sleep-jet-lag-and-melatonin-1024x683.webp)

Taking melatonin for jet lag has been researched for quite some time now. If you’ve ever stepped off a long-haul flight feeling like your body and brain are operating in completely different time zones, you’re familiar with the misery of jet lag. This common travel companion affects millions of flyers annually, leaving them fatigued, disoriented, and unable to fully enjoy the first days of their trip or function effectively upon return.

While jet lag is an inevitable consequence of crossing multiple time zones, scientific research has revealed several evidence-based strategies to minimize its impact, with melatonin supplementation often leading the conversation. But is this naturally occurring hormone truly effective for mitigating jet lag? What about timing, dosage, and potential alternatives?

This comprehensive guide examines the science behind melatonin for jet lag, offering practical recommendations based on current research while exploring complementary approaches to help you recover your circadian rhythm more quickly after long-distance travel.

## Understanding Jet Lag: A Circadian Rhythm Disorder

Jet lag occurs when your body’s internal clock—regulated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in your brain’s hypothalamus—remains synchronized to your departure time zone while you’ve physically moved to a new one. This mismatch creates a temporary circadian rhythm disorder with symptoms that can include:

* Disturbed sleep (insomnia or excessive sleepiness)
* Daytime fatigue
* Difficulty concentrating
* Digestive problems
* Mood disturbances
* Reduced physical performance

The severity of jet lag typically correlates with the number of time zones crossed and the direction of travel. Eastward travel (such as flying from North America to Europe) generally produces more severe symptoms than westward travel because it’s easier for our bodies to adapt to a later bedtime than an earlier one.

## The Melatonin Connection: How It Works for Jet Lag

Melatonin is often called the “sleep hormone” or “darkness hormone” because your pineal gland naturally produces it in response to darkness, signaling to your body that it’s time to prepare for sleep. According to a systematic review published in the Cochrane Database, melatonin’s effectiveness for jet lag stems from its ability to reset your body’s internal clock when taken at strategic times [PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8958662/).

When you travel across multiple time zones, your natural melatonin production remains synchronized to your departure location, contributing to jet lag symptoms. Supplemental melatonin can help realign your circadian rhythm to your new location by providing time cues to your body’s master clock.

### Does Melatonin Actually Work for Jet Lag?

The research on melatonin for jet lag is quite promising. A comprehensive review of ten clinical trials found that melatonin, when taken close to the target bedtime at the destination (10pm to midnight), significantly decreased jet lag symptoms for travelers crossing five or more time zones [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12076414/).

In fact, the study concluded that melatonin is “remarkably effective in preventing or reducing jet lag” with an estimated number needed to treat (NNT) of just 2, meaning you need to treat only two people with melatonin for one person to experience significant relief from jet lag symptoms.

---

**Ready to take the first step toward better sleep? [Book a free discovery call](https://quadrawellness.practicebetter.io/#/5d2e9653627d141b34b1bf6f/bookings?step=services) to explore how our approach might help with your unique sleep challenges.**

---

## Melatonin Dosage for Jet Lag: Finding the Sweet Spot

When it comes to melatonin supplementation, more isn’t necessarily better. Research has investigated various dosages to determine the optimal amount for jet lag relief.

### Recommended Dosages

According to [a research on PubMed – Melatonin for the prevention and treatment of jet lag](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12076414/) – doses between 0.5 mg and 5 mg are similarly effective for addressing jet lag symptoms, though people may fall asleep faster and sleep better with the 5 mg dose compared to 0.5 mg. Doses exceeding 5 mg appear to offer no additional benefits.

The [Sleep Foundation](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/melatonin/melatonin-dosage-how-much-should-you-take) recommends:

* For jet lag specifically: 0.5-5 mg (with 3 mg being sufficient for most people)
* Take 30 minutes before your intended bedtime at your destination

It’s worth noting that the [NHS in the UK recommends a standard dose of 3 mg for jet lag](https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/melatonin/common-questions-about-melatonin/), potentially increasing to 6 mg if needed, but not exceeding this higher dose.

### Immediate vs. Slow-Release Formulations

Research indicates that immediate-release (fast-acting) melatonin is more effective for jet lag than slow-release formulations. According to the same [Cochrane review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8958662/), the “relative ineffectiveness of 2 mg slow-release melatonin suggests that a short-lived higher peak concentration of melatonin works better”.

[The Timeshifter jet lag app also recommends “a low-dose (1-3mg) fast release preparation](https://www.timeshifter.com/jet-lag/melatonin-for-jet-lag-type-dose-timing) when indicated to help reset the clock” since “slow release formulations and higher doses are available but they may stay in the system too long and confuse the circadian clock.”

## The Critical Timing Factor: When to Take Melatonin for Jet Lag

Unlike most medications where timing isn’t critical, melatonin’s effectiveness for jet lag relies heavily on when you take it. The timing of administration determines whether melatonin will advance (shift earlier) or delay (shift later) your internal clock.

### Basic Timing Principles

* **Eastward travel** (e.g., North America to Europe): Take melatonin at your destination’s local bedtime to advance your body clock
* **Westward travel** (e.g., Europe to North America): Melatonin may be less useful since your body naturally adjusts more easily to a later bedtime

[The NHS also provides this specific melatonin and jet lag guidance](https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/melatonin/common-questions-about-melatonin/): “When you arrive at your destination, take melatonin at your normal bedtime (but not earlier than 8pm and not later than 4am). You can use melatonin for up to 5 nights in a row”.

### Advanced Timing Strategies

For those wanting to maximize melatonin’s effectiveness, more sophisticated timing strategies exist based on the concept of the Phase Response Curve (PRC) for melatonin:

* Taking melatonin during your biological late afternoon/early evening (approximately 6-8 hours before your usual bedtime) produces the strongest phase-advancing effect (helping with eastward travel)
* Taking melatonin during your biological morning produces a phase-delaying effect (helpful for westward travel)

Some travelers begin taking melatonin several days before departure to pre-adjust their circadian rhythm, though this approach requires careful planning and understanding of your internal clock’s timing.

## Safety Considerations and Side Effects

Melatonin is generally considered safe for short-term use, though it’s important to remember that in many countries (including the United States), melatonin is sold as a dietary supplement rather than a regulated medication, meaning quality and actual content can vary between brands.

### Potential Side Effects

Most people tolerate melatonin well, but possible side effects may include:

* Daytime drowsiness
* Headaches
* Dizziness
* Nausea
* Vivid dreams or nightmares

### Contraindications and Precautions

Exercise caution with melatonin if you:

* Are pregnant or breastfeeding (insufficient safety data)
* Have autoimmune disorders
* Take blood thinners (possible interaction with warfarin)
* Have epilepsy (case reports suggest possible concerns)
* Take certain medications, including some antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and immunosuppressants

Always consult with a healthcare provider before starting melatonin, especially if you have chronic health conditions or take other medications.

### Avoid These Combinations

* **Alcohol**: When combined with melatonin, alcohol can cause excessive drowsiness and reduce melatonin’s effectiveness for jet lag
* **Caffeine**: Counteracts melatonin’s effects
* **Sedative medications**: May cause additive effects and excessive sedation

## Light Exposure: The Powerful Complement to Melatonin

While melatonin can help reset your internal clock, strategic light exposure is equally—if not more—important for circadian rhythm adjustment. Light is the most powerful zeitgeber (time cue) for your biological clock.

### Basic Light Principles for Jet Lag

* **Morning light exposure** helps advance your clock (useful after eastward travel)
* **Evening light exposure** helps delay your clock (useful after westward travel)
* **Avoiding light** at certain times is equally important to prevent sending contradictory signals to your body clock

[The Timeshifter app emphasizes that “light is the most important time cue for resetting your circadian clock”](https://www.timeshifter.com/jet-lag/melatonin-for-jet-lag-type-dose-timing) and that “if you take melatonin, but your light exposure isn’t timed correctly, melatonin may not help you adapt to your new time zone any faster.”

### Practical Light Strategies

* Get outside for natural daylight exposure in the morning after eastward travel
* Use sunglasses to avoid evening light after eastward travel
* For westward travel, seek evening light exposure and avoid morning light when possible
* Consider using a small, portable light therapy device when traveling if natural light timing is impractical

## Beyond Melatonin: Alternative Approaches to Jet Lag

While [melatonin is the most researched supplement for jet lag](https://www.quadrawellness.com/blog/jet-lag-and-melatonin-for-sleep-issue/), several other approaches may help reduce symptoms or complement melatonin use.

### Prescription Medications

Several prescription medications have been investigated for jet lag:

* **Short-acting sleep medications**: Zolpidem (Ambien), zopiclone, and similar drugs can help with short-term sleep adjustment but don’t reset the circadian rhythm
* **Melatonin receptor agonists**: Ramelteon (Rozerem) and tasimelteon (Hetlioz) are prescription medications that act on melatonin receptors and may help with jet lag, though more research is needed
* **Chronobiotics**: Armodafinil and modafinil are wakefulness-promoting medications sometimes used to combat daytime sleepiness from jet lag

According to the CDC’s Yellow Book, “Ramelteon, a melatonin-receptor agonist, is an FDA-approved treatment for insomnia. One milligram taken just before bedtime can decrease sleep onset latency after eastward travel across 5 time zones” [CDC](https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/yellowbook/2024/air-land-sea/jet-lag).

### Other Natural Approaches

* **Caffeine**: Strategically timed caffeine consumption can help maintain alertness during the adjustment period
* **Hydrocortisone**: Some research suggests that hydrocortisone (20 mg) taken upon awakening may function as a chronobiotic, though this approach isn’t widely established [PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8527561/)
* **B vitamins**: Some travelers report benefits from B-complex vitamins for energy during the adjustment period
* **Adaptogens**: Herbs like ashwagandha and rhodiola may help with stress management during travel and adjustment

### Behavioral Strategies

Non-pharmacological approaches can significantly reduce jet lag severity:

* **Pre-adjustment**: Gradually shift your sleep schedule before departure (1 hour per day for 3-4 days) in the direction of your destination’s time zone
* **In-flight hydration**: Dehydration can exacerbate jet lag symptoms
* **Strategic napping**: Short (20-30 minute) naps can help manage fatigue without disrupting nighttime sleep
* **Exercise**: Moderate exercise during daylight hours at your destination can help reset your body clock
* **Meal timing**: Adjust your meal schedule to match local mealtimes immediately upon arrival

## Putting It All Together: A Comprehensive Jet Lag Protocol

For those seeking maximum protection against jet lag, a comprehensive approach combining multiple strategies may be most effective.

### For Eastward Travel (e.g., North America to Europe)

**Before Departure:**

* Begin shifting your sleep schedule earlier by 1 hour per day for 2-3 days prior
* Ensure you’re well-rested before travel

**During Flight:**

* Stay hydrated
* Minimize alcohol and caffeine
* Set your watch to your destination time zone
* Try to sleep if it’s nighttime at your destination

**Upon Arrival:**

* Take melatonin (0.5-5 mg) 30 minutes before local bedtime
* Get morning light exposure (ideally outdoors) for at least 30 minutes
* Avoid bright light in the evening
* Follow local meal times
* Stay active during daylight hours, but avoid strenuous exercise close to bedtime
* Continue melatonin for 2-4 nights as needed

### For Westward Travel (e.g., Europe to North America)

**Before Departure:**

* Shift your sleep schedule later by 1 hour per day for 2-3 days prior
* Ensure you’re well-rested before travel

**During Flight:**

* Stay hydrated
* Minimize alcohol
* Set your watch to your destination time zone
* Try to stay awake if it’s daytime at your destination

**Upon Arrival:**

* Seek evening light exposure
* Avoid bright morning light if possible (sunglasses can help)
* Follow local meal times
* Stay active during daylight hours
* Consider melatonin only if you have difficulty falling asleep at the later local bedtime

---

## Technology-Assisted Jet Lag Management

Several technological solutions have emerged to help travelers manage jet lag more effectively:

### Jet Lag Apps

* **Timeshifter**: Developed with input from circadian rhythm researchers, this app provides personalized recommendations for light exposure, melatonin timing, caffeine, and sleep based on your itinerary and personal preferences
* **Jet Lag Rooster**: Offers free basic advice for jet lag management
* **Entrain**: Created by researchers at the University of Michigan to help travelers adjust their circadian rhythms

### Light Therapy Devices

* **Portable light boxes**: Compact light therapy devices can provide bright light exposure when natural light isn’t available
* **Light therapy glasses**: Wearable devices that deliver light directly to the eyes while allowing mobility
* **Smart light bulbs**: Can be programmed to provide appropriate light intensity and spectrum at different times

## Jet Lag Considerations for Special Populations

### Older Adults

Older adults may experience more severe jet lag and slower adaptation to new time zones. For those over 65:

* Consider starting with a lower melatonin dose (0.5-1 mg)
* Allow more recovery time after travel
* Pay particular attention to light exposure strategies
* Consider extending melatonin use for a few extra days if needed

### Frequent Travelers

Those who travel across time zones frequently face unique challenges:

* For trips lasting less than 2-3 days, consider maintaining your home time zone schedule if possible
* For longer trips, use the strategies outlined above to adapt quickly
* Allow recovery time between long-haul trips when possible
* Consider regular sleep hygiene practices at home to build resilience

### Athletes and Business Travelers

Performance-focused travelers have additional considerations:

* Schedule important competitions or meetings at least 3-4 days after arrival if possible
* Use melatonin and light therapy more aggressively for faster adaptation
* Consider consulting with a sleep or sports medicine specialist for personalized protocols
* Monitor hydration status carefully, as dehydration can worsen performance and jet lag

## Conclusion: Finding Your Optimal Jet Lag Strategy

Jet lag affects travelers differently based on age, direction of travel, individual circadian patterns, and even genetic factors. While melatonin has proven effective for many travelers, the optimal approach often involves personalization and experimentation.

When using melatonin for jet lag, remember these key principles:

1. Use appropriate dosage (0.5-5 mg, with 3 mg sufficient for most people)
2. Choose immediate-release formulations rather than slow-release
3. Time administration carefully based on direction of travel and destination bedtime
4. Combine with strategic light exposure for maximum effectiveness
5. Consider complementary approaches like pre-adjustment and behavioral strategies
6. Consult healthcare providers if you have underlying health conditions or take medications

By taking a science-based, comprehensive approach to jet lag management, you can minimize its impact on your travel experience and arrive at your destination ready to explore, work, or compete at your best.

Safe travels and better sleep!

### Ask the doctor

**Q.** *My wife and I are planning a trip to Europe and we are dreading the jet lag, which hits both of us hard. Is there any evidence that melatonin really helps? Are there any prescription drugs we could ask our doctor about?*

**A**. Jet lag refers to fatigue or a disturbed sleep pattern after travel across multiple time zones. Some small studies have suggested that melatonin is helpful for jet lag if taken a few days before and after travel. Melatonin is a natural substance released by our brain to help with our circadian (day/night) rhythm. This rhythm is disturbed with travel across three or more time zones.

When traveling eastward to Europe, daytime sleepiness and insomnia could be a big challenge. After the westward return leg, early morning awakening would be more typical. Melatonin has been more effective at treating eastward jet lag, and so might be more helpful to you on the outbound trip—when taken close to the target bedtime. Typical dosages in melatonin dietary supplements are 3 to 5 mg.

Other possible ways to combat jet lag include exposure to a special bright-light source in the early morning, starting earlier each day for several days before travel, to mimic the change in time zones. Once again, this would be useful after the eastbound flight, when the destination wake-up time will be earlier than your usual time.

Long-distance flyers commonly use prescription sleep aids, such as zolpidem (Ambien), to get more sleep during the uncomfortable travel period, but they don't treat the circadian rhythm disturbance. In addition, some individuals experience hangover effects from these medications. It is a good idea to take a trial run with these medications at home before travel to make sure you can tolerate them.

The article addresses whether melatonin supplements and prescription drugs can help with jet lag when traveling across multiple time zones (specifically a trip from the US to Europe).

Key content includes:
- Jet lag is defined as fatigue or disturbed sleep patterns after travel across multiple time zones, caused by disruption of the body's circadian (day/night) rhythm when crossing three or more time zones.
- Small studies suggest melatonin can be helpful for jet lag if taken a few days before and after travel. Melatonin is a natural substance released by the brain to regulate circadian rhythm.
- Melatonin is more effective for eastward jet lag (traveling to Europe), and is best taken close to the target bedtime. Typical dosages in dietary supplements range from 3 to 5 mg.
- Traveling eastward causes daytime sleepiness and insomnia, while returning westward typically causes early morning awakening.
- Alternative strategies include exposure to special bright-light sources in the early morning, starting earlier each day for several days before travel to mimic time zone changes.
- Prescription sleep aids such as zolpidem (Ambien) are commonly used by long-distance flyers, but they do not treat the underlying circadian rhythm disturbance and can cause hangover effects in some individuals. A trial run at home before travel is recommended to test tolerance.
- The article includes a disclaimer that content should not be used as a substitute for direct medical advice from a doctor.

# It Depends: Flying East or West? How to Use Blue Light-Blocking Glasses to Beat Jet Lag

 Ana Martins, PhD 

If you've ever landed in a distant city only to feel like your body is still somewhere over the Atlantic, you've experienced one of biology's most stubborn challenges. Jet lag isn't just fatigue - it's a biological mismatch between your circadian clock and the external world around you.[[1]](#ref1)

But here's the empowering part: you have more control over this process than you might think. One of your most powerful tools? Blue light-blocking glasses, worn with strategic foresight.

## Inside Your Body's Timekeeping System

Deep in your brain, nestled within a region called the hypothalamus, sits a tiny cluster of neurons known as the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) - your body's master clock.[[1]](#ref1) This remarkable structure orchestrates a 24-hour rhythm that governs everything from your hormone release to your body temperature, from your alertness to your hunger.

When you fly across time zones, something fascinating and frustrating happens: your internal clock keeps ticking to the rhythm of your departure city, while the sun, the meal times, and the social schedules around you operate on an entirely different schedule. Your body doesn't simply flip a switch. Instead, it adjusts slowly - roughly half a day for each time zone when you travel westward, but a full day per time zone when you head eastward.[[1]](#ref1)

That transatlantic flight from New York to London? Without intervention, your body may take five to six days to fully synchronize with local time.

## How Light Writes the Rules of Your Internal Clock

Light is the most powerful signal your body uses to set its circadian rhythm.[[1]](#ref1) But not all light affects you equally.

Inside your eyes, you have specialized cells called intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs). These cells contain a light-sensitive protein called melanopsin, which responds most strongly to light in the blue-green range - specifically, wavelengths around 464 nanometers.[[2]](#ref2) When melanopsin detects this blue-enriched light, it sends a direct signal to your SCN, essentially announcing: "It's daytime. Stay alert. Suppress melatonin."

This system evolved to keep us synchronized with the sun. But in our modern world, artificial light - from your phone screen, your laptop, cabin lighting on overnight flights - floods your eyes with these same blue wavelengths long after the sun has set. The result? Your brain receives conflicting messages, and your circadian phase shifts later, making it harder to fall asleep when you need to.

Blue light blocking glasses filter out wavelengths in the 400-550 nanometer range, effectively creating an artificial sunset for your brain. Even when you're surrounded by bright artificial light, your melanopsin system registers darkness.

A systematic review examining 29 studies with 453 patients found that wearing these glasses in the evening substantially reduces the time it takes to fall asleep and helps melatonin production begin earlier.[[2]](#ref2)

You're manually overriding the environmental light signals that would otherwise keep you awake.

## Strategic Timing: Direction Matters

The key to using blue light blocking glasses effectively lies in understanding which direction you're traveling, and what your circadian system needs to do to adapt biologically.

### When You Fly East: Advancing Your Clock

Eastward travel - say, from Los Angeles to London - requires your body to shift forward in time. You need to sleep earlier and wake earlier than your body currently wants to. This is particularly challenging because your natural circadian rhythm tends to run slightly longer than 24 hours, making it easier to stay up late than to go to bed early.

Your approach:

* During overnight flights: Wear blue blockers during the latter portion of the flight to help facilitate sleep
* Morning at destination: Do NOT wear blue blockers. Instead, seek bright morning light—this is what advances your clock forward
* Evening at destination: Wear your glasses 2-3 hours before your destination bedtime.[[2]](#ref2) Evening light would otherwise delay your already-late circadian phase.

Duration: Continue wearing them nightly until you've adapted—roughly one day per time zone crossed.

### When You Fly West: Delaying Your Clock

Westward travel - from London to Los Angeles, for instance - requires the opposite adjustment. Your body needs to delay its rhythm, staying awake and sleeping later than it naturally wants to.

Your approach:

* Early morning at destination: If you arrive very early in the morning, wear blue blockers to prevent morning light from advancing your clock when you actually need it to delay.
* Afternoon and evening: Stay awake and seek light exposure - this helps delay your circadian phase.
* During flight: Generally, avoid wearing blue blockers so you can align more naturally with the later schedule at your destination.

Remember: Blue light is everywhere: not just your phone or laptop, but also your TV, overhead lights, even the glow from your refrigerator. For maximum effect, wear your glasses throughout the evening until sleep, not just during screen time.

## Combining Strategies: The Power of Multiple Signals

Your circadian system responds to more than just light. When you combine multiple interventions, the synergy becomes powerful:[[1]](#ref1)

Strategic light exposure remains your primary tool. Morning light advances your circadian clock, helping you sleep and wake earlier. Evening light delays it, helping you sleep and wake later. Natural sunlight is the most effective synchronizer, so get outside at your destination.

Meal timing matters more than you might expect. Your peripheral clocks - the ones in your liver, gut, and other organs - respond strongly to when you eat. Align your meals with destination time zones, even if you're not particularly hungry at first.

Exercise timing provides another lever for adjustment. Physical activity resets both your central clock and your peripheral clocks throughout your body. Early evening exercise tends to advance your phase, helping you sleep earlier. Late-night exercise delays it, helping you sleep later. Morning chronotypes may benefit especially from light to moderate morning exercise.

These signals work together, each reinforcing the others, creating a coherent message to your body about what time it is.

## What This Means for You

When used strategically, blue light blocking glasses are a scientifically validated tool for recalibrating your circadian rhythm. The research is robust: blue light blocking glasses are particularly effective at reducing sleep onset latency (the time it takes to fall asleep) in patients with sleep disorders, jet lag, or variable shift work schedules.[[2]](#ref2)

This isn't about fighting your biology - it's about working with it. Your circadian system is remarkably adaptive when you send it the right signals at the right times. Blue light blocking glasses give you that control, transforming artificial light from a disruptor into something you can manage.

Travel well, sleep deeply, and let your body find its rhythm again.

**The Science of Jet Lag and Light:**

- The body adjusts roughly half a day per time zone when traveling westward, but a full day per time zone when heading eastward. A New York-to-London flight can take 5-6 days to fully synchronize without intervention.

# Effect of evening blue light blocking glasses on subjective and objective sleep in healthy adults: A randomized control trial

Author links open overlay panel Jeremy A.Bigalke MS a b, Ian M.Greenlund MS a b, Jennifer R.Nicevski BS a, [Jason R.Carter PhD a b](https://www.sciencedirect.com/author/7403988857/goncalo-figueiredo-augusto)

[https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sleh.2021.02.004](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sleh.2021.02.004 "Persistent link using digital object identifier")[Get rights and content](https://s100.copyright.com/AppDispatchServlet?publisherName=ELS&contentID=S2352721821000127&orderBeanReset=true)

## Abstract

### Objectives

Evening blue light has been shown to suppress [melatonin](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/melatonin), which can negatively impact sleep quality. The impact of evening blue light blocking (BLB) interventions on sleep remains ambiguous due to lack of [randomized control trials](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/randomized-controlled-trial). The present study tests the hypothesis that BLB glasses improve subjective and objective sleep in a population of healthy adults.

### Design

Two-week, randomized, controlled, crossover design.

### Setting

At-home testing of individuals in Michigan and Montana.

### Participants

Twenty healthy adults (11 men, 9 women, age: 32 ± 12, [body mass index](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/body-mass-index): 28 ± 4 kg/m 2).

### Intervention

Following a 1-week run-in baseline (ie, no glasses), participants were randomized to 1-week of BLB or control (ie, clear lens) glasses. Upon finishing the 1-week intervention, participants crossed over to the opposite condition. In both conditions, glasses were worn for 7 consecutive days from 6 PM until bedtime.

### Measurements

Objective sleep parameters were obtained using wrist [actigraphy](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/actigraphy). Subjective sleep measures were assessed using sleep diaries. Karolinska Sleep Diaries were used to assess perceived sleep quality.

### Results

BLB reduced subjective sleep onset (21 ± 28 vs 24 ± 21 minute, _P_ = .033) and awakenings (1.6 ± 1.0 vs 2.2 ± 1.0 awakenings, _P_=.019) compared to the control condition. In contrast, objective measures of sleep were not significantly impacted. In fact, our primary outcome variable of total [sleep time](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/nursing-and-health-professions/sleep-time) (TST) tended to be paradoxically shorter in the BLB condition for both subjective (468 ± 45 vs 480 ± 48 minute, _P_=.066) and objective (433 ± 40 vs 449 ± 39 minute, _P_=.075) TST.

### Conclusions

Blue light blocking glasses did not improve objective measures of [sleep time](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/neuroscience/sleep-time) or quality in healthy adults.

## Introduction

Pervasive light exposure has gained notoriety for its role in circadian rhythm regulation, and subsequent impact on sleep.1 Specifically, blue light exposure has an established role in the reduction of melatonin secretion through activation of melanopsin-containing intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells, which directly regulate circadian rhythm regularity.2,3 Additionally, blue light exposure has been shown to suppress melatonin release in humans.2,4 Most commercially available electronic devices utilize light-emitting diodes (LED) that primarily emit blue spectrum wavelengths.5 Presentation of evening LED light via backlit computer screens, or even electronic eReaders, have been reported to significantly inhibit melatonin release and decrease sleep quality.6,7 Blocking low-wavelength light in the evening has offered promise as a low-cost, convenient intervention to mitigate melatonin suppression,8,9 and has been suggested as a means to help alleviate sleep disturbance.[9], [10], [11], [12], [13]

A study of bilateral cataract surgery patients reported that those who received blue light blocking (BLB) surgical lens implants experienced improvements in 2-month postoperative subjective sleep quality utilizing the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI).12 Similarly, Feng et al 13 reported that BLB cataract lens replacement improved subjective sleep quality over a 12-month postoperative period, again using the PSQI. However, there were no differences in subjective sleep quality improvements at the 12-month period compared to traditional ultraviolet blocking intraocular lens implants.13

A recent assessment of blue light in adolescents showed that BLB glasses reduced the LED-screen induced melatonin suppression and increased subjective evening sleepiness, but did not change polysomnography measured sleep parameters.9 Utilizing a randomized study design, Burkhart and Phelps 10 demonstrated that wearing BLB glasses three hours prior to bedtime for 2 weeks resulted in significantly improved subjective ratings of sleep quality using a 10-point Likert scale in participants with self-report insomnia. In addition to the self-report nature of the insomnia, the baseline sleep quality between the 2 experimental groups differed, offering potential confounders.10 More recently, 2 randomized controlled trials performed in individuals with insomnia reported that BLB improved subjective measures of sleep quality both alone 11 and in conjunction with cognitive behavioral therapy.14 However, despite use of actigraphy measurement in both studies, only one of these showed improvement in objectively measured total sleep time.11 To our knowledge, only one pseudo-randomized control trial has assessed sleep quality following BLB in a healthy population using a 5-point Likert scale of subjective sleep quality,15 and ultimately reporting no improvements.

Despite the evidence implicating blue light exposure in melatonin suppression and decreased sleep quality, the results of BLB interventions on sleep quality remain equivocal. Similarly, the divergent findings in the subjective and limited number of objective measures make it difficult to ascertain the true impact of BLB treatment. Further, the randomized controlled trials that have been conducted thus far have been limited to primarily participants with self-report or clinical insomnia 10,11,14 or healthy adults with no objective assessment of sleep.15 The widespread notion that BLB glasses improve sleep, in addition to the contradictory lack of research to support it, outlines the importance of further exploration in both clinical and nonclinical populations. This is particularly important as other healthy populations, such as athletes, are beginning to acknowledge the importance of sleep in human performance and healthy living.16 Accordingly, the present study aims to assess the effect of evening BLB glasses utilizing a randomized, controlled, crossover design in a population of healthy individuals. We hypothesized that both subjective (self-report surveys) and objective (wrist actigraphy) measures of sleep quality would increase with BLB glasses when compared to the control condition.

args.summary:
This is a scientific research article published in the journal Sleep Health (Volume 7, Issue 4, August 2021, Pages 485-490) titled "Effect of evening blue light blocking glasses on subjective and objective sleep in healthy adults: A randomized control trial" by Jeremy A. Bigalke, Ian M. Greenlund, Jennifer R. Nicevski, and Jason R. Carter.

STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: The study used a two-week, randomized, controlled, crossover design with at-home testing of individuals in Michigan and Montana. Twenty healthy adults (11 men, 9 women, mean age 32 ± 12 years, BMI 28 ± 4 kg/m²) participated. Following a 1-week run-in baseline (no glasses), participants were randomized to 1 week of blue light blocking (BLB) glasses or control (clear lens) glasses, then crossed over to the opposite condition. Glasses were worn for 7 consecutive days from 6 PM until bedtime. Objective sleep parameters were measured using wrist actigraphy; subjective measures used sleep diaries and Karolinska Sleep Diaries.

KEY RESULTS: BLB glasses reduced subjective sleep onset (21 ± 28 vs 24 ± 21 minutes, P=.033) and awakenings (1.6 ± 1.0 vs 2.2 ± 1.0, P=.019) compared to control. However, objective measures of sleep were not significantly impacted. Paradoxically, total sleep time (TST) tended to be shorter in the BLB condition for both subjective (468 ± 45 vs 480 ± 48 min, P=.066) and objective (433 ± 40 vs 449 ± 39 min, P=.075) measures.

BACKGROUND CONTEXT: The study was motivated by evidence that evening blue light suppresses melatonin through melanopsin-containing intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells, and that most electronic devices use LED screens emitting blue spectrum wavelengths. Prior research showed BLB interventions helped insomnia patients but results in healthy populations were equivocal, with limited objective assessments.

CONCLUSION: Blue light blocking glasses did not improve objective measures of sleep time or quality in healthy adults, contrary to the study hypothesis. The authors describe this as the first randomized control trial reporting both subjective and objective sleep outcomes of BLB glasses in healthy adults. While BLB was associated with significant improvements in subjective awakenings and sleep onset latency (and objective awakenings in self-report poor sleepers), these results should be interpreted cautiously given the trends toward reduced subjective and objective TST.

ARTICLE METRICS: The article has been cited by 23 other works, has 1 policy citation, and 102 Mendeley readers. No conflicts of interest were declared, and no funding was received.

# Can Blue Light Glasses Really Improve Your Sleep Quality?

## The Modern Dilemma: Screens, Blue Light, and Your Sleep

Many of us have been there. After a long day, you unwind by scrolling through your phone or watching a series on your tablet, only to find yourself staring at the ceiling hours later, unable to fall asleep. It’s a common frustration, and a growing body of evidence points to a specific culprit: the blue light emitted from our digital screens. This has led to a surge in popularity for blue light blocking glasses, but can they truly improve your sleep quality?

The short answer is yes, but with important caveats. While these glasses are a powerful tool for managing your body's internal clock, they are not a cure for all sleep problems or the solution for digital eye strain many believe them to be.

This article delves into the science of how blue light impacts your sleep cycle, examines the clinical evidence for and against blue light glasses, and provides a practical guide to using them effectively as part of a healthy evening routine.

### TL;DR: Quick Takeaways

* **For Sleep? Yes.** Strong evidence shows that wearing blue light blocking glasses in the evening can help you fall asleep faster.
* **For Eye Strain? No.** The consensus among ophthalmologists is that digital eye strain is caused by reduced blinking and focusing issues, not blue light itself.
* **Timing is Everything.** These glasses are most effective when worn for 1-3 hours *before* your intended bedtime. Wearing them during the day can be counterproductive.
* **Not All Lenses Are Equal.** Amber or orange-tinted lenses designed for evening use are far more effective for sleep than the clear, "computer glasses" style coatings.

## The Science: How Blue Light Controls Your Internal Clock

To understand how these glasses work, we first need to understand our biology. Every person operates on a circadian rhythm, an internal 24-hour clock that regulates our sleep-wake cycle, hormone release, and other bodily functions. This clock's primary environmental cue is light.

For millennia, the rising and setting of the sun kept this rhythm in sync. Bright, blue-rich sunlight in the morning signals our brain to be awake and alert. As the sun sets, the absence of this blue light triggers the pineal gland to produce melatonin, the hormone that makes us feel sleepy.

The problem is that our modern, screen-filled environment disrupts this natural process. As [Harvard Health Publishing explains](https://www.health.harvard.edu/blog/can-blue-light-blocking-glasses-improve-your-sleep-202110262625), the specific wavelengths of blue light (around 450-480 nm) emitted by LEDs in our phones, laptops, and TVs are particularly effective at suppressing melatonin. When you're exposed to this light after dusk, your brain gets a mixed signal. It thinks it's still daytime, delaying the onset of sleepiness and shifting your entire circadian rhythm.

A comprehensive review in the journal *Chronobiology International* reinforces this, noting that blue light is not an inherent "toxin" but a powerful biological signal. The issue isn't the light itself, but its timing. By filtering out these specific wavelengths, blue light glasses prevent this "it's daytime" signal from reaching your brain, allowing melatonin production to proceed naturally.

## The Evidence: What Clinical Studies Say About Sleep

The claim that blue light glasses can aid sleep isn't just theoretical; it's backed by significant clinical research. A [systematic review published in PubMed Central](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34030534/) analyzed 16 randomized controlled trials and found "substantial evidence" that wearing blue-blocking glasses in the evening reduces sleep onset latency—the time it takes to fall asleep—for people with insomnia, jet lag, or variable sleep schedules.

Some studies have even quantified the benefit. Research highlighted by Harvard suggests improvements can be modest but meaningful, potentially shortening the time to fall asleep by 8-15 minutes and increasing total sleep time by about 25 minutes.

Interestingly, one study uncovered a fascinating paradox between subjective feeling and objective data. Researchers found that while participants *felt* they fell asleep faster and slept better, actigraphy data (from sleep-tracking devices) showed little objective change. This suggests the glasses have a powerful effect on our perceived sleep quality, which is a crucial part of feeling rested.

### Expert Warning: Blue Light Glasses Are Not a Cure for Digital Eye Strain

Here we must address the single most common misconception about blue light glasses. Despite widespread marketing claims, there is no strong evidence that they prevent or reduce digital eye strain.

A rigorous [double-blind, randomized controlled trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32007978/) had participants perform a reading task and found no significant difference in eye strain symptoms between those wearing blue-blocking lenses and those wearing placebo lenses.

According to ophthalmologist Dr. Nicole Bajic in a [Cleveland Clinic article](https://health.clevelandclinic.org/do-blue-light-blocking-glasses-actually-work), digital eye strain isn't caused by blue light. Instead, it's a result of two things:

1. **Reduced Blink Rate:** When we stare at screens, we tend to blink less frequently, leading to dry, irritated eyes.
2. **Accommodation Issues:** The constant effort of focusing on a close-up screen fatigues the small muscles inside our eyes.

The most effective, expert-recommended solution for digital eye strain is the "20-20-20 rule": every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for at least 20 seconds. This relaxes your eye muscles and helps reset your blink rate. Using preservative-free artificial tears can also provide significant relief for dryness.

## A Practical Guide to Choosing and Using Blue Light Glasses

To get the real sleep benefits from blue light glasses, you need to use the right type at the right time. Not all lenses are created equal, and their effectiveness depends entirely on how and when you wear them.

### When to Wear Them: Timing is Key

The number one rule is to use them exclusively in the evening. As a clinical heuristic, start wearing them **1 to 3 hours before you plan to go to sleep.**

Wearing them during the day is not recommended. Exposure to natural blue light in the morning and afternoon is essential for setting your circadian rhythm, promoting alertness, and boosting mood. Blocking it can be counterproductive. Think of them as "sunglasses for artificial light" that you put on after the sun has gone down.

### What to Look For: Daytime Filters vs. Nighttime Lenses

The difference between a cheap "computer coating" and a lens designed for sleep is significant. An analysis in the journal *PMC* explains that high-quality filters work selectively. They aim to reduce the most disruptive blue light (400–455nm) while allowing some of the less disruptive turquoise light (455–500nm) to pass through, which helps maintain better color perception.

Here’s a breakdown of the common types:

| Lens Type | Primary Purpose | Blue Light Reduction | Best For |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Clear / "Computer" Lens** | Reducing glare, minimal filtering | Low (10-25%) | Daytime screen use for those sensitive to glare. Not effective for sleep. |
| **Amber / Orange Lens** | Melatonin preservation, sleep cycle regulation | High (70-99%) | Evening use (1-3 hours before bed) to prepare the body for sleep. |
| **Red Lens** | Maximum light blocking | Very High (>99%) | Advanced use for shift workers or individuals with severe circadian disruption. |

For most people seeking better sleep, an **amber or orange-tinted lens** is the ideal choice. While the color shift is noticeable, it's a sign that the lens is effectively filtering the wavelengths that suppress melatonin.

### A Note on Fit and Quality

Even the best lenses won't work if the frames don't fit well. A poor fit can allow unfiltered light to leak in from the top and sides, defeating the purpose. When choosing a pair, ensure they provide good coverage. If you wear prescription glasses, you can find options for fit-overs or custom lenses. For more guidance on ensuring your glasses are made correctly, see our [checklist for buying prescription glasses online safely](https://www.lensmartonline.com/blogs/lensmartonline/buying-prescription-glasses-online-safe-checklist).

## Wrapping Up: A Powerful Tool, Not a Magic Bullet

Blue light blocking glasses can be a highly effective and non-pharmacological tool to improve your sleep, particularly if you have a habit of using screens before bed. By filtering the specific light wavelengths that suppress melatonin, they help your body's natural sleep processes function as they should.

However, it's crucial to use them correctly: wear amber or orange lenses for 1-3 hours before bed, and don't expect them to solve digital eye strain. They are one component of good sleep hygiene, which also includes maintaining a consistent sleep schedule, creating a dark and quiet bedroom, and avoiding caffeine late in the day. When used as intended, they can be a game-changer for reclaiming a healthy sleep cycle in our modern, brightly-lit world.

## Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

### Can I wear blue light glasses all day?

It is not recommended. Your body needs exposure to natural blue light during the day to maintain a healthy circadian rhythm and stay alert. Reserve blue light glasses for evening use, 1-3 hours before bed.

### Will blue light glasses help with my screen-induced headaches?

While some people report fewer headaches, this is likely due to a reduction in glare or correcting an underlying vision issue with a prescription. For headaches caused by eye strain, the 20-20-20 rule and ensuring your prescription is correct are more direct solutions.

### What's the difference between cheap and expensive blue light glasses?

The primary difference lies in the quality and technology of the lens filter. More advanced lenses, often found in mid-range to higher-priced glasses, use selective filtering technology to block the most harmful blue light wavelengths while minimizing color distortion. Cheaper glasses may use a simple surface coating that filters less effectively or blocks a broader spectrum, leading to poor color perception.

### Are blue light blocking glasses safe for children?

This is an area that requires caution. Some research, like a theoretical model from the [Mayo Clinic](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12009466/), suggests that altering the spectrum of light reaching a child's developing eyes could potentially interfere with normal eye growth (a process called emmetropization). For this reason, it's best to consult with an optometrist or ophthalmologist before having a child use blue light glasses regularly. Prioritizing non-screen activities before bed is the safest approach.

# Who Should Not Take Melatonin?

 by [Dave Kimbell](/pages/author-dave-kimbell)

📅 **Last Updated:** April 14, 2026

# Who Should Not Take Melatonin?

Melatonin is widely promoted as a natural sleep aid, and [short-term use appears safe for most adults](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/melatonin-what-you-need-to-know). But melatonin is a hormone—not a simple vitamin—and it's not appropriate for everyone. [Between 2012 and 2021, pediatric melatonin ingestions increased 530%](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/71/wr/mm7122a1.htm), and certain medical conditions and medications create significant safety concerns. This guide identifies who should avoid melatonin and why, based on research and clinical evidence.

## Key Takeaways

* [People with dementia, epilepsy, autoimmune diseases, and those taking warfarin should not use melatonin](https://www.merckmanuals.com/home/special-subjects/dietary-supplements-and-vitamins/melatonin) without explicit medical clearance.
* [Children under age 2 should avoid melatonin entirely, and use requires pediatrician consultation](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/71/wr/mm7122a1.htm) for all children.
* [Melatonin reduces blood clotting factors by 15–21%, increasing bleeding risk in those on anticoagulants](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18289163/).
* [People with certain genetic variants (MTNR1B) experience 11.7% worsening of glucose tolerance when taking melatonin](https://academic.oup.com/sleep/article/47/Supplement_1/A381/7655307).
* [Melatonin supplement content varies from less than one-half to more than 4 times the labeled amount, creating overdose risk](https://aasm.org/advocacy/position-statements/melatonin-use-in-children-and-adolescents-health-advisory/).

## Table of Contents

1. [Medical Conditions That Contraindicate Melatonin](#medical-contraindications)
2. [Major Drug Interactions to Know](#drug-interactions)
3. [Age and Demographic Restrictions](#demographic-restrictions)
4. [Circadian and Sleep-Related Nuances](#circadian-conditions)
5. [Product Quality and Accidental Overdose Risk](#quality-safety)
6. [Long-Term Safety Concerns and Emerging Evidence](#long-term-concerns)
7. [BioAbsorb Melatonin — Premium Quality Assurance](#bioabsorb-quality)
8. [Frequently Asked Questions](#faq)
9. [Conclusion](#conclusion)

## 1. Medical Conditions That Contraindicate Melatonin

Certain medical conditions are incompatible with melatonin supplementation due to how the hormone interacts with disease pathology or immune function. [The Merck Manual explicitly recommends against melatonin use in people with dementia, epilepsy, autoimmune diseases](https://www.merckmanuals.com/home/special-subjects/dietary-supplements-and-vitamins/melatonin), and those trying to conceive. The reason is mechanistic, not precautionary.

**Dementia:** While melatonin is studied for evening restlessness in Alzheimer's, [the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends against melatonin in dementia](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/melatonin-what-you-need-to-know). Older adults metabolize melatonin slowly, causing daytime drowsiness, confusion, and falls—particularly dangerous in dementia.

**Epilepsy and Seizure Disorders:** [Melatonin may increase seizure frequency in people with epilepsy](https://www.merckmanuals.com/home/special-subjects/dietary-supplements-and-vitamins/melatonin), particularly in children with neurological disorders. The mechanism isn't fully understood, but case reports and mechanistic studies suggest melatonin can lower the seizure threshold. Anyone with a seizure disorder must avoid melatonin without neurologist approval.

**Autoimmune Diseases:** [Melatonin stimulates immune pathways and may exacerbate autoimmune diseases like lupus and rheumatoid arthritis](https://www.merckmanuals.com/home/special-subjects/dietary-supplements-and-vitamins/melatonin). Avoidance is the cautious approach without specialist guidance.

## 2. Major Drug Interactions to Know

Melatonin interacts with multiple medication classes, sometimes dangerously. [Mayo Clinic documents interactions with blood pressure medications, CNS depressants, diabetes medications, contraceptive drugs, and medications metabolized by the CYP1A2 and CPY2C19 liver enzymes](https://www.mayoclinic.org/drugs-supplements-melatonin/art-20363071). The most critical are blood thinners.

**Anticoagulants and Blood Thinners (Warfarin):** This is the most serious interaction. [Melatonin can increase the effects of warfarin, raising bleeding risk](https://www.mayoclinic.org/drugs-supplements-melatonin/art-20363071). The mechanism involves reduced clotting factors: [a controlled study found that a single 3mg melatonin dose decreased plasma clotting factor VIII by 21% and fibrinogen by 15% compared to placebo](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18289163/). [A case series of 10 patients on concurrent melatonin-warfarin therapy showed elevated INR (International Normalized Ratio) in all patients, with 6 classified as "possible" and 2 as "probable" drug interactions](https://www.lifesciencesite.com/lsj/life130616/06_30694lsj130616_46_51.pdf). For safety, anyone on warfarin should avoid melatonin unless their doctor approves and monitors INR levels closely.

**Blood Pressure Medications:** [Melatonin may worsen blood pressure control in people taking antihypertensive medications](https://www.mayoclinic.org/drugs-supplements-melatonin/art-20363071). Additionally, melatonin may interfere with calcium-channel blockers like nifedipine, reducing their effectiveness. People on blood pressure medications should discuss melatonin with their doctor before use.

**CNS Depressants and Sleep Medications:** [Combining melatonin with sedatives, tranquilizers, benzodiazepines, or other sleep medications can cause additive drowsiness](https://www.mayoclinic.org/drugs-supplements-melatonin/art-20363071). This raises the risk of daytime impairment, falls, and accidents. Combining should only occur under medical direction.

**Diabetes Medications:** [Melatonin may affect blood sugar levels and interfere with glucose-lowering medications](https://www.mayoclinic.org/drugs-supplements-melatonin/art-20363071). The interaction is complex and timing-dependent. Some research suggests melatonin impairs glucose tolerance when taken with food, while other evidence suggests benefits. Anyone with diabetes or prediabetes should consult their doctor before melatonin use.

## 3. Age and Demographic Restrictions

Age dramatically affects melatonin safety. The most vulnerable populations are infants, young children, and women of reproductive age.

**Infants and Young Children:** [The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends against melatonin in children under 2 years](https://aasm.org/advocacy/position-statements/melatonin-use-in-children-and-adolescents-health-advisory/), where sleep issues are behavioral, not biological. [For older children, melatonin should address only insomnia or circadian rhythm disorders under medical supervision](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1389945725000474), with thorough evaluation to rule out other causes first.

**Accidental Ingestion Risk:** [From 2012 to 2021, melatonin ingestions in children increased 530%, totaling 260,435 reported cases, with 4,000+ requiring hospitalization and 2 deaths](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/71/wr/mm7122a1.htm). Most ingestions were unintentional, involving children under age 5 who mistook gummies for candy. [The AASM advises storing melatonin in child-resistant packaging and locked cabinets, treating it like any prescription medication](https://aasm.org/advocacy/position-statements/melatonin-use-in-children-and-adolescents-health-advisory/).

**Pregnant and Breastfeeding Women:** [Safety of melatonin during pregnancy and breastfeeding is unknown, and melatonin may affect fertility in women trying to conceive](https://www.merckmanuals.com/home/special-subjects/dietary-supplements-and-vitamins/melatonin). Because melatonin crosses the placenta and passes into breast milk, avoidance is the cautious approach unless a doctor approves supplementation.

## 4. Circadian and Sleep-Related Nuances

Surprisingly, melatonin isn't appropriate for all sleep problems, even in healthy adults. Efficacy varies dramatically by sleep issue type.

**Insomnia Without Circadian Dysfunction:** [The American Academy of Sleep Medicine notes insufficient evidence for melatonin in chronic insomnia](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/melatonin-what-you-need-to-know). Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT-I) is preferred first-line treatment.

**Timing Sensitivity:** [Melatonin's effects on glucose depend on timing relative to food—elevated melatonin during meals decreases glucose tolerance and insulin secretion](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7349733/). Shift workers and late-night eaters are at higher metabolic risk.

**Genetic Susceptibility:** [People carrying the G-allele of the MTNR1B melatonin receptor gene show 11.7% worsening of glucose tolerance when given melatonin, a 25.2% decrease in early insulin secretion, and 40% reduction in first-phase insulin response](https://academic.oup.com/sleep/article/47/Supplement_1/A381/7655307). These individuals may have increased type 2 diabetes risk from melatonin supplementation. Genetic testing isn't routine, but people with a strong family history of diabetes should discuss melatonin risk with their doctor.

## 5. Product Quality and Accidental Overdose Risk

One of the largest hidden risks with melatonin is product quality variability. Because melatonin is unregulated as a dietary supplement in the United States, contents vary wildly and dangerously.

**Labeling Accuracy Crisis:** [A study of 31 melatonin supplements found content ranging from −83% to +478% of labeled amount](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9842516/). [88% of melatonin gummies were inaccurately labeled](https://aasm.org/advocacy/position-statements/melatonin-use-in-children-and-adolescents-health-advisory/), meaning you cannot reliably know the true dose.

**Contaminant Risk:** [Some melatonin supplements contain unlabeled serotonin and other pharmaceutically active contaminants](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9842516/). These can interact with medications and cause adverse effects independent of melatonin itself.

**Why Quality Matters for Safety:** If you take an "overdose" of an unlabeled supplement—a person who unknowingly consumes 4 mg when the label says 1 mg—side effects escalate. Symptoms can include severe headaches, nausea, dizziness, and extreme next-day drowsiness. [Quality manufacturers like BioAbsorb use third-party testing and GMP certification to verify exact melatonin content and absence of contaminants](https://www.bioabsorbnutraceuticals.com), reducing overdose and adverse effect risk significantly.

## 6. Long-Term Safety Concerns and Emerging Evidence

While short-term melatonin use (up to 3 months) is generally considered safe, long-term effects remain poorly understood—and emerging data raises concerns.

**Cardiovascular Safety Questions:** [A preliminary American Heart Association analysis of 130,828 adults on melatonin ≥1 year found associations with increased heart failure risk and mortality](https://newsroom.heart.org/news/long-term-use-of-melatonin-supplements-to-support-sleep-may-have-negative-health-effects), though causation cannot be proven. This warrants caution for long-term use.

**Unknown Long-Term Effects in Children:** Pediatricians express concern that [long-term melatonin effects on growth, puberty, and hormonal development are unknown, and regular use in children should be avoided pending further research](https://aasm.org/advocacy/position-statements/melatonin-use-in-children-and-adolescents-health-advisory/). Melatonin influences reproductive hormones; chronic supplementation might affect fertility or pubertal timing, but we lack long-term data.

**Tolerance and Dependency:** Some users report melatonin effectiveness decreases with nightly use. Whether stopping leads to worse insomnia isn't well-studied. Use melatonin only for short-term acute sleep issues, not chronic daily use.

## 7. BioAbsorb Melatonin — Premium Quality Assurance

For people for whom melatonin is appropriate, product quality is the first safety barrier. [BioAbsorb Nutraceuticals manufactures premium melatonin with third-party testing, GMP certification, and rigorous quality control—verifying exact content and absence of contaminants](https://www.bioabsorbnutraceuticals.com). This precision reduces the need for high doses and improves consistency. [Available in 1mg, 3mg, and 5mg formulations with precise graduated droppers, BioAbsorb allows fine-tuned dosing—critical for safe supplementation](https://www.bioabsorbnutraceuticals.com/products/liposomal-liquid-melatonin).

Even with a quality product, remember: melatonin is a hormone, not a sleeping pill. It should never replace medical evaluation for sleep problems. If you're considering melatonin, work with a healthcare provider to ensure it's appropriate for your health status, medications, and condition.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can I take melatonin if I'm on antidepressants?

It depends on the specific antidepressant. [Melatonin can interact with SSRIs and other CNS-active medications, increasing drowsiness and potentially affecting serotonin levels](https://www.mayoclinic.org/drugs-supplements-melatonin/art-20363071). Discuss melatonin with your prescribing doctor before starting, especially if you're on fluvoxamine or other serotonergic drugs.

### Is melatonin safe for people with bipolar disorder?

[Melatonin may trigger mood episodes or interact with mood stabilizer medications](https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/melatonin-what-you-need-to-know). Anyone with bipolar disorder should not use melatonin without explicit psychiatric guidance.

### What if my child accidentally swallows a handful of melatonin gummies?

Most pediatric melatonin overdoses are asymptomatic or cause mild drowsiness. However, [some children require hospitalization for overdose symptoms including severe headache, dizziness, nausea, and extreme lethargy](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/71/wr/mm7122a1.htm). Call Poison Control immediately: 1-800-222-1222. Keep melatonin in locked storage, never accessible to children.

### I have a family history of diabetes. Should I avoid melatonin?

[If you carry the MTNR1B G-allele genetic variant, melatonin worsens glucose tolerance and impairs insulin secretion](https://academic.oup.com/sleep/article/47/Supplement_1/A381/7655307). Talk to your doctor about whether melatonin is appropriate given your diabetes risk. Genetic testing is not routine, but your family history should prompt caution.

### Can I use melatonin long-term for chronic insomnia?

[Emerging evidence linking long-term melatonin use to increased cardiovascular risk warrants caution](https://newsroom.heart.org/news/long-term-use-of-melatonin-supplements-to-support-sleep-may-have-negative-health-effects). Melatonin is best used for short-term, acute sleep issues. Chronic insomnia should be addressed with CBT-I, good sleep hygiene, and medical evaluation for underlying causes.

## Conclusion

Melatonin is not the "natural, risk-free" sleep solution marketing often portrays. People with epilepsy, dementia, autoimmune diseases, those taking blood thinners or certain other medications, infants, young children, and pregnant women should avoid melatonin entirely. Even healthy adults should use melatonin only for short-term sleep issues after medical evaluation, preferably with a quality, third-party tested product. [If melatonin is appropriate for you, BioAbsorb's third-party tested liposomal formulation removes quality and contamination concerns, allowing you to use melatonin safely with confidence in your dose](https://www.bioabsorbnutraceuticals.com/products/liposomal-liquid-melatonin). # From Birth Control to Blood Thinners: 9 Melatonin Interactions to Be Aware of

![Emilie White, PharmD](https://www.grxstatic.com/4f3rgqwzdznj/2iEZjTaNMWTxKKhgsSEoes/c4cabcdf9c4121d07ec2cb5705443747/Emilie-White.webp?w=96&q=85&fm=webp)
