From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Graph of phase response

A **phase response curve** (**PRC**) illustrates the transient change ([phase response](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_response "Phase response")) in the cycle period of an [oscillation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_harmonic_motion "Simple harmonic motion") induced by a perturbation as a function of the [phase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_(waves) "Phase (waves)") at which it is received. PRCs are used in various fields; examples of biological oscillations are the heartbeat, [circadian rhythms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circadian_rhythm "Circadian rhythm"), and the regular, repetitive firing observed in some neurons in the absence of noise.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[*[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")*]

## In circadian rhythms

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phase_response_curve&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: In circadian rhythms")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/PRC-Light%2BMel.png/250px-PRC-Light%2BMel.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PRC-Light+Mel.png)

Phase response curves for light and for melatonin administration

In humans and animals, there is a regulatory system that governs the phase relationship of an organism's internal [circadian clock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circadian_clock "Circadian clock") to a regular periodicity in the external environment (usually governed by the solar day). In most organisms, a stable phase relationship is desired, though in some cases the desired phase will vary by season, especially among mammals with seasonal mating habits.

In [circadian rhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circadian_rhythm "Circadian rhythm") research, a PRC illustrates the relationship between a [chronobiotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chronobiotic "Chronobiotic")'s time of administration (relative to the internal circadian clock) and the magnitude of the treatment's effect on circadian phase. Specifically, a PRC is a graph showing, by convention, time of the subject's endogenous day along the *x*-axis and the amount of the phase shift (in hours) along the *y*-axis. Each curve has one peak and one trough in each 24-hour cycle. Relative circadian time is plotted against phase-shift magnitude. The treatment is usually narrowly specified as a set intensity and colour and duration of light exposure to the retina and skin, or a set dose and formulation of melatonin.

These curves are often consulted in the therapeutic setting. Normally, the body's various physiological rhythms will be synchronized within an individual organism (human or animal), usually with respect to a master biological clock. Of particular importance is the sleep–wake cycle. Various sleep disorders and externals stresses (such as [jet lag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_lag "Jet lag")) can interfere with this. Humans with [non-24-hour sleep–wake disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-24-hour_sleep–wake_disorder "Non-24-hour sleep–wake disorder") often experience an inability to maintain a consistent internal clock. Extreme [chronotypes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chronotype "Chronotype") usually maintain a consistent clock, but find that their natural clock does not align with the expectations of their social environment. PRC curves provide a starting point for therapeutic intervention. The two common treatments used to shift the timing of sleep are [light therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_therapy "Light therapy"), directed at the eyes, and administration of the hormone [melatonin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melatonin "Melatonin"), usually taken orally. Either or both can be used daily. The phase adjustment is generally cumulative with consecutive daily administrations, and — at least partially — additive with concurrent administrations of distinct treatments. If the underlying disturbance is stable in nature, ongoing daily intervention is usually required. For jet lag, the intervention serves mainly to accelerate natural alignment, and ceases once desired alignment is achieved.

Note that phase response curves from the experimental setting are usually aggregates of the test population, that there can be mild or significant variation within the test population, that individuals with sleep disorders often respond atypically, and that the formulation of the chronobiotic might be specific to the experimental setting and not generally available in clinical practice (e.g. for melatonin, one sustained-release formulation might differ in its release rate as compared to another); also, while the magnitude is dose-dependent,[[2]](#cite_note-2) not all PRC graphs cover a range of doses. The discussions below are restricted to the PRCs for the light and melatonin in humans.

### Light

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phase_response_curve&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Light")]

[![A typical Human Light PRC](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/d/dc/Human_PRC.png/500px-Human_PRC.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Human_PRC.png)

The time shown on the *x* axis is vague: dawn –  mid-day –  dusk –  night –  dawn. These times do not refer to actual sun-up etc. nor to specific clock times. Each individual has their own circadian "clock" and chronotype, and dawn in the illustration refers to an individual's time of spontaneous awakening when well-rested and sleeping regularly. The PRC shows when a stimulus, in this case light to the eyes, will effect a change, an advance or a delay. The curve's highest point coincides with the subject's lowest body temperature.

Starting about two hours before an individual's regular bedtime, exposure of the eyes to light will delay the circadian phase, causing later wake-up time and later [sleep onset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleep_onset "Sleep onset"). The delaying effect gets stronger as evening progresses; it is also dependent on the wavelength and [illuminance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illuminance "Illuminance") ("brightness") of the light. The effect is small if indoor lighting is dim (< 3 lux).

About five hours after usual bedtime, coinciding with the body temperature trough (the lowest point of the core body temperature during sleep) the PRC peaks and the effect changes abruptly from phase delay to phase advance. Immediately after this peak, light exposure has its greatest phase-advancing effect, causing earlier wake-up and sleep onset. Again, illuminance greatly affects results; indoor light may be less than 500 lux, while [light therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_therapy "Light therapy") uses up to 10,000 lux. The effect diminishes until about two hours after spontaneous wake-up time, when it reaches approximately zero.

During the period between two hours after usual wake-up time and two hours before usual bedtime, light exposure has little or no effect on circadian phase (slight effects generally cancelling each other out).

Another image of the PRC for light is here (Figure 1).[[3]](#cite_note-3) Within that image, the explanatory text is

* *Delay region: evening light shifts sleepiness later* and
* *Advance region: morning light shifts sleepiness earlier*.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Light therapy, typically with a light box producing 10,000 lux at a prescribed distance, can be used in the evening to delay or in the morning to advance an individual's sleep timing. Because losing sleep to obtain bright light exposure is considered undesirable by most people, and because it is very difficult to estimate exactly when the greatest effect (the PRC peak) will occur in an individual, the treatment is usually applied daily just prior to bedtime (to achieve phase delay), or just after spontaneous awakening (to achieve phase advance).

In addition to its use in the adjustment of circadian rhythms, light therapy is used as treatment for several [affective disorders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mood_disorder "Mood disorder") including [seasonal affective disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seasonal_affective_disorder "Seasonal affective disorder") (SAD).[[5]](#cite_note-5)

In 2002 [Brown University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_University "Brown University") researchers led by David Berson announced the discovery of special cells in the [human eye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_eye "Human eye"), ipRGCs ([intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intrinsically_photosensitive_retinal_ganglion_cells "Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells")),[[6]](#cite_note-6) which, many researchers now believe, control the light entrainment effect of the phase response curve. In the human eye, the ipRGCs have the greatest response to light in the 460–480 nm (blue) range. In one experiment, 400 lux of blue light produced the same effects as 10,000 lux of white light from a fluorescent source.[[7]](#cite_note-7) A theory of spectral opponency, in which the addition of other spectral colors renders blue light less effective for circadian phototransduction, was supported by research reported in 2005.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

### Melatonin

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phase_response_curve&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Melatonin")]

The phase response curve for melatonin is roughly twelve hours out of phase with the phase response curve for light.[[9]](#cite_note-9) At spontaneous wake-up time, [exogenous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exogenous "Exogenous") (externally administered) melatonin has a slight phase-delaying effect. The amount of phase-delay increases until about eight hours after wake-up time, when the effect swings abruptly from strong phase delay to strong phase advance. The phase-advance effect diminishes as the day goes on until it reaches zero about bedtime. From usual bedtime until wake-up time, exogenous melatonin has no effect on circadian phase.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11)

The human body produces its own ([endogenous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endogenous "Endogenous")) melatonin starting about two hours before bedtime, provided the lighting is dim. This is known as *dim-light melatonin onset*, DLMO.[[12]](#cite_note-12) This stimulates the phase-advance portion of the PRC and helps keep the body on a regular sleep-wake schedule. It also helps prepare the body for sleep.

Administration of melatonin at any time may have a mild [hypnotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypnotic "Hypnotic") (sleep-inducing) effect. The expected effect on sleep phase timing, if any, is predicted by the PRC.

### Additive effects

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phase_response_curve&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Additive effects")]

In a 2006 study Victoria L. Revell *et al.* showed that a combination of morning bright light and afternoon melatonin, both timed to phase advance according to the respective PRCs, produce a larger phase advance shift than bright light alone, for a total of up to 21⁄2 hours over the course of 3 days. All times are approximate and vary from one individual to another. In particular, there is no convenient way to accurately determine the times of the peaks and zero-crossings of these curves in an individual. Administration of light or melatonin close to the time at which the effect is expected to change sense abruptly may, if the changeover time is not accurately known, produce an opposite effect to that desired.[[13]](#cite_note-13)

### Exercise

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phase_response_curve&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Exercise")]

In a 2019 study Shawn D. Youngstedt *et al.*, showed that in humans "Exercise elicits circadian phase‐shifting effects, but additional information is needed. [...] Significant phase–response curves were established for [aMT6(melatonin derivative)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6-Hydroxymelatonin "6-Hydroxymelatonin") onset and acrophase with large phase delays from 7:00 pm to 10:00 pm and large phase advances at both 7:00 am and from 1:00 pm to 4:00 pm"[[14]](#cite_note-14)

### Origin

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phase_response_curve&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Origin")]

The first published usage of the term "phase response curve" was in 1960 by [Patricia DeCoursey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patricia_DeCoursey "Patricia DeCoursey"). The "daily" activity rhythms of her [flying squirrels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_squirrel "Flying squirrel"), kept in constant darkness, responded to pulses of light exposure. The response varied according to the time of day – that is, the animals' subjective "day" – when light was administered. When DeCoursey plotted all her data relating the quantity and direction (advance or delay) of phase-shift on a single curve, she created the PRC. It has since been a standard tool in the study of biological rhythms.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

## In neurons

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Phase_response_curve&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: In neurons")]

Further information: [Phase precession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phase_precession "Phase precession")

Phase response curve analysis can be used to understand the intrinsic properties and oscillatory behavior of regular-[spiking neurons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiking_neuron "Spiking neuron").[[16]](#cite_note-16) The neuronal PRCs can be classified as being purely positive (PRC type I) or as having negative parts (PRC type II). Importantly, the PRC type exhibited by a neuron is indicative of its input–output function (excitability) as well as synchronization behavior: networks of PRC type II neurons can synchronize their activity via mutual excitatory connections, but those of PRC type I can not.[[17]](#cite_note-17)

Experimental estimation of PRC in living, regular-spiking neurons involves measuring the changes in inter-spike interval in response to a small perturbation, such as a transient pulse of current. Notably, the PRC of a neuron is not fixed but may change when firing frequency[[18]](#cite_note-18) or [neuromodulatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuromodulation_(biology) "Neuromodulation (biology)") state of the neuron[[19]](#cite_note-19) is changed.

This Wikipedia article explains the Phase Response Curve (PRC), a graph illustrating the transient change in the cycle period of an oscillation induced by a perturbation, plotted as a function of the phase at which it is received. PRCs are used across various fields, with biological examples including the heartbeat, circadian rhythms, and repetitive neuronal firing.

KEY DETAILS ON CIRCADIAN RHYTHMS:
- A PRC shows the relationship between a chronobiotic's time of administration (relative to the internal circadian clock) and the magnitude of its effect on circadian phase. The x-axis represents time of the subject's endogenous day, and the y-axis represents the phase shift (in hours). Each curve has one peak and one trough per 24-hour cycle.
- PRCs are used therapeutically for sleep disorders, jet lag, and non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder. Common treatments include light therapy (directed at the eyes) and oral melatonin administration.

LIGHT PRC (Human):
- Starting ~2 hours before regular bedtime, light exposure delays the circadian phase (later wake-up and sleep onset). The delaying effect strengthens as evening progresses and depends on wavelength and illuminance; effects are small below 3 lux.
- About 5 hours after usual bedtime (coinciding with the body temperature trough), the PRC peaks and switches from phase delay to phase advance. Immediately after the peak, light has its greatest phase-advancing effect. Light therapy can use up to 10,000 lux.
- Between 2 hours after wake-up and 2 hours before bedtime, light has little or no effect on phase.
- In 2002, Brown University researchers (led by David Berson) discovered ipRGCs (intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells) which control the light entrainment effect. These cells respond most to 460-480 nm (blue) light; 400 lux of blue light produced effects equivalent to 10,000 lux of white fluorescent light.

MELATONIN PRC:
- The melatonin PRC is roughly 12 hours out of phase with the light PRC. At wake-up time, exogenous melatonin has a slight phase-delaying effect, increasing until ~8 hours after wake-up, then abruptly switching to strong phase advance, diminishing to zero by bedtime.
- The body's endogenous melatonin (dim-light melatonin onset, DLMO) begins ~2 hours before bedtime in dim lighting, stimulating the phase-advance portion of the PRC.

ADDITIVE EFFECTS:
- A 2006 study (Revell et al.) showed that combining morning bright light and afternoon melatonin (both timed to phase advance) produced up to 2.5 hours of phase advance over 3 days, greater than bright light alone. Caution is noted because inaccurate timing near phase-switch points can produce opposite effects.

EXERCISE:
- A 2019 study (Youngstedt et al.) found exercise elicits circadian phase-shifting effects, with large phase delays from 7:00-10:00 pm and large phase advances at 7:00 am and 1:00-4:00 pm.

ORIGIN:
- The term "phase response curve" was first used in 1960 by Patricia DeCoursey, based on her flying squirrel experiments in constant darkness where light pulses shifted activity rhythms depending on the time of day. The PRC has since become a standard tool in biological rhythm research.

IN NEURONS:
- PRC analysis helps understand regular-spiking neuron oscillatory behavior. Neuronal PRCs are classified as Type I (purely positive) or Type II (having negative parts). Networks of Type II neurons can synchronize via mutual excitatory connections; Type I networks cannot. A neuron's PRC can change with firing frequency or neuromodulatory state. PRCs are experimentally estimated by measuring changes in inter-spike intervals in response to small perturbations (e.g., transient current pulses).

The curve's highest point coincides with the subject's lowest body temperature.", "In the human eye, the ipRGCs have the greatest response to light in the 460–480 nm (blue) range. In one experiment, 400 lux of blue light produced the same effects as 10,000 lux of white light from a fluorescent source.", "The phase response curve for melatonin is roughly twelve hours out of phase with the phase response curve for light.", "[The PRC is] the single most important methodological tool in the study of all biological rhythms."

# How to Get Over Jet Lag

![Eric Suni](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Eric-Suni-Headshot-150x150.jpg)

Eric Suni

Contributing Writer

Eric Suni has over a decade of experience as a science writer and was previously an information specialist for the National Cancer Institute.

Want to read more about all our experts in the field?

![Abhinav Singh, MD, MPH, FAASM](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Dr.-Abhinav-Singh-SF-150x150.jpg)

Abhinav Singh, MD, MPH, FAASM

Board-Certified Sleep Medicine Physician

Dr. Abhinav Singh, board certified in Sleep Medicine and Internal Medicine, is the Medical Director of the Indiana Sleep Center, which is accredited by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. He is also a Clinical Assistant Professor at Marian University College of Medicine in Indianapolis, where he developed and teaches a Sleep Medicine rotation.

Want to read more about all our experts in the field?

Whether you’re traveling for business, vacation, or an athletic competition, a big trip is usually cause for excitement. Unfortunately, problems can arise from the process of traveling. When long airplane flights are involved, jet lag is frequently encountered.

[Jet lag](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/travel-and-sleep/jet-lag) is commonly associated with international plane travel, but it can arise on any flight that goes east or west across three or more time zones. Jet lag frequently causes sleep disruptions, which can throw your body’s internal clock out of sync with the day-night cycle at your destination.

Knowing how to prevent and recover from jet lag can help you maintain your sleep schedule and overall wellness during your travels, so you can make the most of your trip.

### Looking to improve your sleep? Try upgrading your mattress.

![Helix Midnight Luxe Mattress](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/SF_HelixMidnightLuxe_1-1-768x406.jpg)

## What Is Jet Lag?

Jet lag is a disruption of the body’s [circadian rhythm](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/circadian-rhythm) that occurs with plane travel across three or more time zones[Trusted Source](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/about-us/editorial-policy)Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)As the nation’s health protection agency, CDC saves lives and protects people from health threats.[View Source](#references-83211). Symptoms frequently include sleeping problems, daytime drowsiness, impaired mental or physical performance, general malaise, and gastrointestinal issues.

Jet lag can last from a few days to a few weeks[Trusted Source](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/about-us/editorial-policy)American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM)AASM sets standards and promotes excellence in sleep medicine health care, education, and research.[View Source](#references-78259). Although some people prefer to travel east, jet lag tends to be worse when traveling east[Trusted Source](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/about-us/editorial-policy)National Library of Medicine, Biotech InformationThe National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information.[View Source](#references-78562) and when a greater number of time zones are crossed.

Not everyone is affected by jet lag to the same degree. Trip itinerary and individual factors can affect the severity and duration of jet lag.

Is Your Troubled Sleep a Health Risk?

A variety of issues can cause problems sleeping. Answer three questions to understand if it’s a concern you should worry about.

## What’s the Best Way To Reduce or Resolve Jet Lag?

The key to getting over jet lag is to get your body’s circadian clock aligned with the sunrise and sunset schedule at your destination. Many steps can also be taken to minimize symptoms caused by jet lag.

### Realigning Your Circadian Rhythm

Overcoming jet lag depends on getting your body’s 24-hour internal clock synchronized with the 24-hour day at your destination. However, the best way the achieve this varies, depending on factors specific to your trip:

Because of these variables, there’s no single remedy for jet lag and generic advice does not work. Instead, quickly overcoming jet lag typically requires a plan that involves appropriately-timed light exposure and melatonin. Both are power influencers of the circadian rhythm and can help retrain your internal clock[Trusted Source](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/about-us/editorial-policy)National Library of Medicine, Biotech InformationThe National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information.[View Source](#references-80639).

Proper timing[Trusted Source](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/about-us/editorial-policy)National Library of Medicine, Biotech InformationThe National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information.[View Source](#references-81763) is key to adjusting your circadian rhythm. In fact, light exposure and melatonin intake at the wrong time of the day can further desynchronize your circadian rhythm and exacerbate jet lag.

Even with a well-developed plan, you may still experience symptoms of jet lag. Every individual adjusts differently to a rapid time zone change, but working to reorient your circadian rhythm can reduce the chances[Trusted Source](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/about-us/editorial-policy)Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)As the nation’s health protection agency, CDC saves lives and protects people from health threats.[View Source](#references-83211) that jet lag will negatively impact your trip.

#### Light Exposure

[Light](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/bedroom-environment/light-and-sleep), especially natural light, has the biggest influence on circadian rhythm. Light from the sun, even on a cloudy day, is a critical signal interpreted by the brain to regulate our internal clock.

Exposure to natural light at your destination speeds up the process of acclimating to the new time zone; however, you may not want to immediately rush outside. Depending on how far you’ve traveled and the time you land, it may be better to avoid light when you first arrive and then have extended light exposure earlier the next day.

Man-made light, including electronic devices, also affects circadian rhythm. For this reason, try to avoid electric light during planned periods of darkness and sleep.

When natural light exposure isn’t an option, bright indoor lights, phones and laptops, or light therapy lamps can provide higher illuminance with a greater circadian effect.

Light avoidance[Trusted Source](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/about-us/editorial-policy)National Library of Medicine, Biotech InformationThe National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information.[View Source](#references-236342), avoiding light exposure at the wrong time, is also important to prevent your clock from shifting in the wrong direction and making jet lag worse. When indicated, avoiding light can mean dimming indoor lights, avoiding use of electronic devices, or wearing sunglasses. The circadian system measures changes in light, so light avoidance does not mean darkness — just less light exposure than when advised to see light.

## Get Better Sleep on the Road

Sign up to receive emails about how to improve your sleep, as well as our comprehensive Better Sleep Guidebook.

![Person stretching their arms](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/Email-Capture-Icon.svg)

#### Melatonin

The hormone [melatonin](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/melatonin) is naturally made by the body and is the biochemical signal of darkness. Melatonin production usually starts at night two to three hours before your normal bedtime. Two key functions of melatonin are helping sleep initiation and regulating your circadian rhythm.

When your circadian rhythm is disrupted by jet lag, the timing of melatonin production can be thrown off. A number of studies have found that taking low-dose (1-3mg) melatonin supplements[Trusted Source](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/about-us/editorial-policy)National Library of Medicine, Biotech InformationThe National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information.[View Source](#references-83318) at the right time may help realign your internal clock. Like light, melatonin can shift the clock either earlier or later and so timing is crucial.

Melatonin is sold as an over-the-counter dietary supplement available without a prescription in the U.S. In most countries, it is a prescription medication. Some prescription drugs also boost melatonin levels.

Most people can take melatonin without significant side effects, but in some people, it can cause grogginess or stomach problems and may have interactions with other medications. Some people should not take melatonin, so make sure to check the safety advice or ask your doctor. Do not take melatonin for the first time on the plane in case of unexpected reactions. As with any drug or supplement, it’s best to consult with your doctor before taking melatonin.

#### Pre-Trip Adjustments to Your Sleep Schedule

For many travelers, the best way to get over jet lag is to take steps to prevent it.

You can begin avoiding jet lag by gradually shifting your circadian rhythm in the one to two days leading up to the flight. Then, you’ll be more adjusted to the time zone at your destination when you arrive.

A revamped sleep schedule along with strategically timed light exposure and melatonin supplements can help adjust your circadian rhythm. These changes require careful coordination and may pose logistical challenges for many travelers. However, for people who prioritize optimal physical and mental performance after travel, such as athletes and business executives, the effort may be worth it.

#### Tools to Plan a Trip and Avoid Jet Lag

With so many factors to account for, planning to avoid jet lag can feel overwhelming. The timing of events is not intuitive, however, and it’s easy to get it wrong. Plan ahead or try an app to help create an adjusted sleep schedule.

You can also consult with your doctor, a sleep specialist, or a travel clinic for specific advice about overcoming jet lag given your travel plans and personal health history.

### Minimizing Symptoms of Jet Lag

Although you can’t fully recover from jet lag until your circadian rhythm adjusts to the new time zone, you can take practical steps[Trusted Source](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/about-us/editorial-policy)Medline PlusMedlinePlus is an online health information resource for patients and their families and friends.[View Source](#references-83295) to minimize symptoms[Trusted Source](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/about-us/editorial-policy)Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)As the nation’s health protection agency, CDC saves lives and protects people from health threats.[View Source](#references-83603). Many of these tips also cut down on travel fatigue or the dehydration and exhaustion that can occur during long trips.

#### Can Naps Help With Jet Lag?

A quick nap may help you overcome excess daytime sleepiness related to jet lag, but it’s important to be careful with naps. If you nap for too long or too late in the day, it may throw off your sleep schedule even more. Try to keep naps less than 30 minutes and nap at least eight or more hours before your planned bedtime.

#### Can Sleep Aids Help With Jet Lag?

[Sleep aids](https://www.sleepfoundation.org/sleep-aids/over-the-counter-sleep-aids) other than melatonin, including both prescription sleeping pills and over-the-counter drugs, do not cure jet lag because they don’t realign your circadian rhythm and therefore will not address the underlying cause of jet lag. That said, if jet lag is causing sleep deprivation, a sleep aid may help address that symptom.

Most sleeping pills have a powerful effect that can make you feel out-of-sorts and groggy for longer than expected, including after you wake up. The risk of falls or accidents is often higher after taking sleep medications. Frequent use of sleep aids may also make it harder to recognize an ongoing case of jet lag.

Before taking any sleep aid, it’s best to consult your doctor. They can review the potential benefits and side effects and offer advice on how to safely take them, based on your specific travel plans.

This webpage from SleepFoundation.org is an educational article titled "How to Get Over Jet Lag" written by Eric Suni (Contributing Writer) and medically reviewed by Dr. Abhinav Singh, MD, MPH, FAASM (Board-Certified Sleep Medicine Physician, Medical Director of the Indiana Sleep Center).

**What Is Jet Lag?** Jet lag is a disruption of the body's circadian rhythm that occurs with plane travel across three or more time zones. Symptoms include sleeping problems, daytime drowsiness, impaired mental or physical performance, general malaise, and gastrointestinal issues. Jet lag can last from a few days to a few weeks. It tends to be worse when traveling east and when a greater number of time zones are crossed.

**Best Ways to Reduce/Resolve Jet Lag:** The key is getting your circadian clock aligned with the sunrise/sunset schedule at your destination. The most effective approaches include:
1. **Light Exposure**: Natural light has the biggest influence on circadian rhythm. Timing is critical—light exposure at the wrong time can worsen jet lag. Man-made light (electronic devices, phones, laptops, light therapy lamps) also affects circadian rhythm. Light avoidance (dimming indoor lights, avoiding devices, wearing sunglasses) at the wrong times is also important.
2. **Melatonin**: Low-dose (1-3mg) melatonin supplements taken at the right time may help realign the internal clock. Melatonin is the biochemical signal of darkness. It's available over-the-counter in the U.S. but is prescription in most countries. Some people should not take it; consult a doctor first. Do not take melatonin for the first time on a plane.
3. **Pre-Trip Adjustments**: Gradually shift your circadian rhythm in the 1-2 days leading up to the flight. A revamped sleep schedule with strategically timed light exposure and melatonin can help, especially for athletes and business executives.
4. **Planning Tools**: Use apps or consult a doctor, sleep specialist, or travel clinic to create an adjusted sleep schedule.

**Minimizing Symptoms:**
- **Naps**: Keep naps under 30 minutes and nap at least 8+ hours before planned bedtime. Long or late naps can worsen sleep schedule disruption.
- **Sleep Aids**: Prescription or OTC sleep aids do NOT cure jet lag because they don't realign the circadian rhythm. They may help address sleep deprivation symptoms but can cause grogginess, increased fall/accident risk, and may mask ongoing jet lag. Consult a doctor before use.

**Key Facts:** The article cites 12 sources including the CDC, American Academy of Sleep Medicine, National Library of Medicine, and Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. Jet lag can occur on any flight crossing three or more time zones east or west. Light exposure and melatonin are both "power influencers" of circadian rhythm, and proper timing is essential—doing either at the wrong time can further desynchronize the clock.

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: Interventions to Minimize Jet Lag After Westward and ... ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physiology/articles/10.3389/fphys.2019.00927/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed opinion article published in Frontiers in Physiology (July 31, 2019, Volume 10, DOI: 10.3389/fphys.2019.00927) by Gregory D. Roach and Charli Sargent of the Appleton Institute for Behavioural Science, Central Queensland University, Adelaide, Australia. The paper provides practical recommendations for minimizing jet lag after transmeridian flight, specifically aimed at athletes traveling to the Tokyo 2020 Olympic Games, though applicable to all travelers.

**Key Concepts:**
- Distinguishes between travel fatigue (symptoms during/immediately after flight: fatigue, disorientation, headache, caused by sleep loss, dehydration, hypoxia, discomfort of aircraft cabins) and jet lag (symptoms in days after flight across 3+ time zones: headache, irritability, daytime sleepiness, poor sleep, poor mental/physical performance, GI dysfunction, caused by mismatch between the circadian system aligned to departure time zone and desired sleep/wake timing at destination).
- Human circadian rhythms (~24h) are generated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus with a period of ~24.2h, entrained by zeitgebers; sunlight is the most powerful zeitgeber.

**Phase Response Curves (PRCs):**
- Light: Exposure in ~12h prior to CBTmin causes phase delay; ~12h after CBTmin causes phase advance; largest shifts in the 3–6h either side of CBTmin. Larger shifts with longer duration, higher intensity, and shorter (blue) wavelengths.
- Melatonin: Late afternoon/early evening ingestion causes phase advance; morning ingestion causes phase delay. A 3.0mg (pharmacological) dose produces more reliable phase shifts than 0.5mg (physiological) dose, though similar in size.
- Exercise: 1h moderate-intensity bout shifts circadian system (delay ~9h before CBTmin, advance ~9h after), but PRC established under 50 lux light so effects independent of light not yet confirmed.
- Light and melatonin effects are additive (especially for advances); light and exercise are not additive, so exercise excluded from guides.

**Direction of Travel:**
- Westward flight: circadian system runs ahead of local time; must delay (shift later). Example: London to Los Angeles (8h west), CBTmin at 20:00 in LA initially; person feels sleepy in evening, difficulty staying asleep.
- Eastward flight: circadian system runs behind local time; must advance (shift earlier). Example: LA to London (8h east), CBTmin at midday; sleepy late morning/early afternoon, difficulty falling asleep at night.
- Indiscriminate sunlight exposure helps adaptation after westward travel but can be counterproductive after eastward travel (provides contradictory signals). After eastward travel, avoid sunlight before midday and maximize exposure 3–6h after midday.

**Adaptation Schedules (based on assumed sleep 23:00–07:00, CBTmin ~04:00, arrival at 13:00 local):**
Westward:
- 3h west (e.g., Wellington NZ to Tokyo): delay 3h; partial adaptation day 1, complete day 4
- 6h west (e.g., Anchorage to Tokyo): delay 6h; partial day 2, complete day 6
- 9h west (e.g., Minneapolis to Tokyo): delay 9h; partial day 3, complete day 7
- 12h west (e.g., Buenos Aires to Tokyo): partial day 6, complete day 10 (using delay, which is favored given ~24.2h natural period)
Eastward:
- 3h east (e.g., Dhaka to Tokyo): advance 3h; partial day 1, complete day 4
- 6h east (e.g., Doha to Tokyo): advance 6h; partial day 3, complete day 6
- 9h east (e.g., London to Tokyo): advance 9h; partial day 5, complete day 8
- 12h east: advance schedule partial day 7, complete day 10

**Practical Implementation Notes:**
- Light exposure during daytime: be outside in sunlight without sunglasses; after sunset: bright indoor light, light box, or light-emitting glasses.
- Light avoidance: inside with lights off/dim; naps limited to 1h; wrap-around sunglasses with minimal light transmission if outside unavoidable.
- Complete adaptation = CBTmin occurs at same time as pre-travel (04:00); partial adaptation = CBTmin occurs during night-time sleep (practical goal, greatly reduces jet lag symptoms).
- If athletes use melatonin, ensure it's not a prohibited substance under relevant drug code and sourced from reputable supplier.

**Evidence of Efficacy:**
- Computer simulations with validated mathematical models support light schedule effectiveness; laboratory trials show light and melatonin independently shift circadian timing and are additive in combination.
- Field studies on light-based jet lag interventions are equivocal; meta-analysis of 10 field studies shows melatonin-based interventions effective at shifting body clock and reducing jet lag (Herxheimer and Petrie, 2002). Combined light/melatonin efficacy in field settings not yet assessed—identified as critical next step.

**Pre-shifting (Before/During Travel):**
- Advantages: reduces adaptation time, less pronounced jet lag. Disadvantages: may interfere with sleep, be socially disruptive, complicate estimating CBTmin timing upon arrival.
- To delay (westward) 3–4 days before: move bedtime/get-up later (30–60 min/day), maximize evening light, minimize morning light, take 3.0mg melatonin 1h after rising.
- To advance (eastward) 3–4 days before: move bedtime/get-up earlier, minimize evening light, maximize morning light, take 3.0mg melatonin 6.5h before bed.
- During travel: time light/melatonin to departure time zone, not arrival.

The article concludes that recommendations are based on latest circadian research but notes potential barriers to practical implementation and calls for field-based randomized controlled trials to assess efficacy in natural settings. Funding from Australian Research Council Discovery Project scheme (DP160104909).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Immediately after westward flight, the circadian system will be running ahead of the local time zone... To adjust to the new time zone, the circadian system has to delay, or shift backward, or move later. Conversely, immediately after eastward flight, the circadian system will be running behind the local time zone... To adjust to the new time zone, the circadian system has to advance, or shift forward, or move earlier."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: JCI Insight -
Circadian rhythm phase shifts caused by timed exercise vary with chronotype ---
URL: https://insight.jci.org/articles/view/134270

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in JCI Insight (2020;5(3):e134270) by researchers at the University of Kentucky, investigating how timed exercise affects circadian rhythm phase shifts depending on an individual's chronotype.

**Study Design & Methods:**
- 52 young, sedentary adults (16 men, 36 women; ages 18-45) were studied in free-living (non-laboratory) conditions
- Dim light melatonin onset (DLMO) was measured before and after 5 days of exercise
- Participants were randomized to morning exercise (10 hours after DLMO; n=26) or evening exercise (20 hours after DLMO; n=26)
- Exercise consisted of 30 minutes of supervised treadmill exercise at 70% VO2peak for 5 consecutive days
- Chronotype was assessed using the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ-SA) and Munich Chronotype Questionnaire (MCTQ)
- Data collected between July 2017 and March 2019 in Lexington, Kentucky

**Key Results:**
1. Morning exercise induced significant phase advances (0.62 ± 0.18 hours) compared to evening exercise (–0.02 ± 0.18 hours; P = 0.01)
2. Chronotype significantly influenced the effect of timed exercise:
   - Later chronotypes experienced phase advances from BOTH morning (0.54 ± 0.29 hours) and evening (0.46 ± 0.25 hours) exercise
   - Earlier chronotypes experienced phase advances from morning exercise (0.49 ± 0.25 hours) but phase delays from evening exercise (–0.41 ± 0.29 hours)
3. Sleep timing was earlier in the morning exercise group, but sleep quality and duration were similar between groups
4. No significant sex differences in phase shifts were observed

**Conclusions:**
- Morning exercise advances circadian phase and has the greatest potential to alleviate circadian misalignment in young adults (who typically have late chronotypes)
- Late chronotypes (who experience the most severe circadian misalignment) may benefit from exercise in either the morning or evening
- Evening exercise may exacerbate circadian misalignment in early chronotypes
- Personalized exercise timing prescription based on chronotype could alleviate circadian misalignment
- Chronotype questionnaires (e.g., preferred sleep timing) can serve as practical proxies for DLMO when prescribing exercise timing

**Trial Registration:** NCT04097886 (clinicaltrials.gov)
**Funding:** NIH grants UL1TR001998 and TL1TR001997, Barnstable Brown Diabetes and Obesity Center, and other University of Kentucky sources.

**Strengths noted:** Free-living conditions, standardized exercise intensity based on individual GXTmax, practical exercise regimen (30 min/day moderate exercise), and postexercise phase assessment performed the day after the final exercise session to avoid acute masking effects.

**Limitations noted:** Did not control for other phase-shifting stimuli (e.g., light exposure during travel), did not collect baseline sleep measures, only studied young healthy sedentary adults, and only investigated moderate cardiovascular exercise.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Morning exercise induced phase advance shifts (0.62 ± 0.18 hours) that were significantly greater than phase shifts from evening exercise (–0.02 ± 0.18 hours; P = 0.01)."
</key_excerpts>



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


--- SOURCE 3: How To Travel the World Without Jet lag - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2829880

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scientific article, published in Sleep Medicine Clinics (June 2009, doi: 10.1016/j.jsmc.2009.02.006, PMID: 20204161, PMCID: PMC2829880), was authored by Charmane I. Eastman (Professor and Director, Biological Rhythms Research Laboratory) and Helen J. Burgess (Associate Professor and Associate Director), both at Rush University Medical Center, Chicago. The article provides evidence-based strategies for preventing and minimizing jet lag using timed bright light exposure and melatonin supplementation.

KEY CONTENT:

1. JET LAG SYMPTOMS AND CONSEQUENCES: Jet lag causes difficulty sleeping, daytime sleepiness, impaired performance, fatigue, irritability, depressed mood, and gastrointestinal disturbance. It poses public safety risks (affecting diplomats and military), and frequent jet travel is associated with cognitive deficits, temporal lobe atrophy (per MRI), menstrual disturbances, increased cardiovascular disease and type II diabetes risk, and increased cancer risk in flight attendants. In 2007, over 31 million U.S. residents flew overseas (12 million to Europe, 7 million to Asia).

2. DIRECTIONAL ASYMMETRY: Jet lag is caused by temporary misalignment between the endogenous circadian clock (the SCN) and the destination time zone. Flying east requires a phase advance; flying west requires a phase delay. Because the average free-running period (tau) of the human circadian clock is slightly longer than 24h, humans naturally drift later, making phase advances more difficult. Real travelers phase delay ~92 min/day after westward flights but phase advance only ~57 min/day after eastward flights. With bright light, phase delays of ~2h/day and phase advances of ~1-1.5h/day are achievable. Antidromic (wrong-direction) re-entrainment is common after eastward travel crossing 8+ time zones—in one study, 7 of 8 subjects flying 11 time zones east re-entrained by phase delaying instead of phase advancing. Jet lag symptoms are worst when the temperature minimum (Tmin, the sleepiest circadian time) occurs during waking hours. The Tmin typically occurs 3-4.5h before wake time.

3. PHASE RESPONSE CURVES (PRCs): Bright light produces phase advances when applied late in the sleep episode/morning after the Tmin, and phase delays when applied early in sleep before the Tmin. Melatonin pills produce greatest phase advances when taken in the afternoon and greatest phase delays when taken in the morning. Melatonin is NOT FDA-approved for jet lag in the U.S. (classed as a dietary supplement), but research supports its efficacy. Optimal timing: 3.0 mg melatonin taken ~5h before DLMO (or 7.5h before sleep onset, or 12h before Tmin) for maximal phase advance; 0.5 mg taken ~2h before DLMO (4.5h before sleep, 9h before Tmin). Bright light at 3,500 lux (from light boxes) and 3.0 mg melatonin produce roughly equivalent phase advances. Outdoor sunlight is far more intense (10,000-100,000 lux). Both PRCs have "dead zones" of reduced sensitivity (midday for light, during endogenous melatonin secretion for melatonin).

4. RECOMMENDED STRATEGIES: The key principle is to reset the circadian clock at least partially toward the destination time zone BEFORE flying, while gradually shifting the sleep schedule to keep it aligned with the shifting clock (avoiding abrupt shifts that cause circadian misalignment). 
- For flying WEST: Use a bright light box in the 2h before bed for 2 nights before the flight, delay bedtime by ~2h/night, and avoid bright light after waking. After landing, ~1h/day phase delay is realistic.
- For flying EAST: Phase advance the sleep schedule by ~1h/day (or less for night owls), use intermittent bright light in the morning (~5,000 lux light box or outdoor light), take 0.5 mg melatonin in the afternoon (4.5h before bedtime, 1h earlier each day), and gradually shift meal times. A 1h/day advance schedule combined with bright light and melatonin did NOT produce jet lag symptoms in studies. Advancing more than 1h/day is not recommended.
- For flights crossing 8+ time zones east, some travelers (especially night owls) may prefer to phase delay instead of phase advance before the flight.
- Even just 1-2 days of preflight shifting helps reduce subsequent jet lag.

5. DRUGS AND LIMITATIONS: Caffeine, hypnotics, and large soporific doses of melatonin at bedtime only mask jet lag symptoms; they do not eliminate the underlying circadian misalignment, which persists until re-entrainment occurs. Hypnotics improve sleep quantity but sleepiness still occurs around the Tmin when it falls during waking hours.

6. PRACTICAL NOTES: Light boxes marketed for seasonal affective disorder (SAD) are useful for phase shifting. Larger illuminated-area boxes are recommended (easier to sit in front of). Blue-enriched light boxes are in vogue, but older cool-white fluorescent boxes produce equal phase shifts. Individual differences exist—early birds (shorter taus) have more trouble phase delaying; night owls (longer taus) have more trouble phase advancing. The authors suggest companies may one day keep light boxes on hand for traveling employees.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Jet travel across multiple time zones produces jet lag, which includes difficulty initiating or maintaining nighttime sleep, daytime sleepiness, decreased alertness, loss of concentration, impaired performance, fatigue, irritability, disorientation, depressed mood and gastrointestinal disturbance."
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://www.timeshifter.com/jet-lag/the-science-of-jet-lag

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from Timeshifter, a company that is a leader in circadian technology, offering apps and products that translate circadian science into solutions for improving human health, safety, and performance. The page is primarily an informational article titled "What is jet lag?" reviewed by Steven W. Lockley, Ph.D., Co-Founder & Chief Scientist of Timeshifter, who has over 30 years of research experience in circadian rhythms, sleep, and jet lag, and has advised NASA astronauts, Formula 1 teams, healthcare systems, and safety-critical industries.

Key content on the page includes:

**What is jet lag:** Jet lag is caused when the sleep-wake and light-dark cycle shifts too quickly for the brain's central circadian clock (located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus/SCN, a group of ~50,000 cells in the hypothalamus) to keep up.

**What causes jet lag:** The circadian clock regulates sleep, alertness, hormones, body temperature, digestion, immune function, and dozens of other systems, using light and darkness as main cues. When flying across time zones, the clock can only adjust by about an hour per day on its own. A flight from New York to Tokyo (13 time zones) takes roughly two weeks to fully catch up.

**East vs. west:** For most people, going east is harder than going west because the average human circadian clock runs slightly long (over 24 hours), making it easier to delay sleep than advance it. A minority of people with shorter-than-24-hour clocks find the opposite.

**Jet lag symptoms:** Difficulty sleeping, daytime sleepiness/fatigue, poor concentration and memory, reduced performance, mood changes, gastrointestinal problems, headache/malaise, weakened immune function, slower physical recovery, and reduced exercise capacity.

**How long jet lag lasts:** Approximately one day per time zone crossed without intervention (e.g., New York to London, 5 time zones east, typically causes ~5 days of jet lag). Factors affecting duration include direction of travel (eastward takes ~50% longer to recover), number of time zones crossed (linear scaling), chronotype (morning types recover faster westward, evening types faster eastward), age (older adults adjust slower), and whether you intervene correctly. With properly timed light exposure and light avoidance, the circadian clock can shift 3-4 hours per day rather than 1 hour.

**How to get over jet lag quickly:** The only effective way is individually-timed light exposure and light avoidance to reset the circadian clock, supported by correct type/dose/timing of melatonin. Popular advice (sleeping pills, hydration, diets, exercise) does not address underlying circadian misalignment. The Timeshifter jet lag app creates personalized plans based on sleep pattern, chronotype, itinerary, and personal preferences.

**Melatonin:** The right type, dose, and timing of melatonin can help shift faster and sleep better, but without correct light timing, it is not effective.

**Examples/stats:** A San Francisco to London trip (8 time zones each way) without intervention results in 16 days of jet lag for a one-week vacation. With a properly timed light and melatonin plan, adaptation can be 3-4 times faster. The app is trusted by more than 1.7 million travelers and is described as the most downloaded and highest-rated jet lag app in the world.

The page also contains extensive site navigation for other Timeshifter products (Jet lag app, Shift work app, Peak performance, My Circadian Day), resources on circadian rhythms, and links to related articles on jet lag myths, melatonin for jet lag, shift work, peak performance, and circadian medicine. Timeshifter states it is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease and is intended for healthy adults 18 years or older.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In your brain, you have a central circadian clock located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) — a group of around 50,000 cells in the hypothalamus. Jet lag is caused when the sleep-wake and light-dark cycle shift too quickly for this circadian clock to keep up."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Resetting Time: The Role of Exercise Timing in Circadian Reprogramming for Metabolic Health ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2673-4168/5/3/59

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a review article titled "Resetting Time: The Role of Exercise Timing in Circadian Reprogramming for Metabolic Health" by Stuart J. Hesketh from the School of Medicine, University of Central Lancashire, Preston, UK. Published in the MDPI journal *Obesities* (2025, volume 5, issue 3, article 59; DOI: 10.3390/obesities5030059), the paper was submitted 14 July 2025, revised 4 August 2025, accepted 6 August 2025, and published 7 August 2025. It is an open-access review with Academic Editor Carmine Finelli, having 6416 article views and 7 citations, and an Altmetric score of 71.

**Core Topic:** The review examines how skeletal muscle circadian clocks regulate metabolic health and how the timing of exercise can serve as a chronotherapeutic intervention to reset circadian rhythms and improve metabolic outcomes, particularly in obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).

**Key Findings:**

1. **Skeletal muscle as a central circadian regulator:** Skeletal muscle comprises ~40% of body mass, is a primary site for glucose disposal (~80% of postprandial glucose uptake), fatty acid oxidation, and thermogenesis. It exhibits robust circadian rhythms in gene expression, mitochondrial function, fuel utilisation, and insulin sensitivity. Approximately 2,300 genes in skeletal muscle cycle diurnally, including Ppargc1a, Glut4, and Cpt1b, with peaks coinciding with the active phase.

2. **Molecular clock mechanism:** The muscle clock involves a transcriptional–translational feedback loop with core genes BMAL1, CLOCK, PERs, and CRYs. Skeletal muscle-specific Bmal1 knockout in mice causes glucose intolerance, reduced insulin-stimulated glucose uptake, GLUT4 mislocalisation, defective mitochondrial respiration, and disrupted fuel partitioning.

3. **Circadian misalignment and metabolic disease:** Misalignment contributes to obesity and T2DM. A 3.5-day simulated night-shift protocol in 14 healthy men reduced insulin sensitivity by 23% (non-oxidative glucose disposal: 23.7 vs. 18.4 mg/kg/min, p=0.024). In obese individuals, mitochondrial fusion–fission cycles and respiratory oscillations are blunted. Lipid overload (palmitate exposure) alters BMAL1, PER3, CRY2, and DBP expression and reduces amplitude of lipid metabolite oscillations. High-fat diet during resting phases causes exaggerated weight gain in rodents. Clock and Per2 knockout mice are predisposed to obesity.

4. **Exercise as a non-photic zeitgeber:** Exercise can reset and amplify muscle circadian rhythms even in metabolically impaired states. Key molecular pathways include AMPK activation (promoting PER2 degradation and CRY1 nuclear translocation), SIRT1 activation via NAD+ (deacetylating BMAL1 and PGC-1α), and CaMKII activation via contraction-induced calcium flux (enhancing BMAL1 transcription and mitochondrial biogenesis).

5. **Time-of-day dependency:** Exercise effects are highly time-dependent, with late active-phase training producing superior outcomes in both rodents and humans. Per1/2 knockout mice lose the diurnal variation in exercise capacity, and the benefits of active-phase-aligned training are attenuated in Bmal1 knockout and Clock mutant mice. Exercise also induces chromatin-level modifications (increased chromatin accessibility at circadian and metabolic gene promoters in a BMAL1-dependent manner).

6. **Reversibility of clock disruption:** A longitudinal study showed Roux-en-Y gastric bypass partially restored clock gene expression (normalisation of BMAL1 and PER2 rhythms) in skeletal muscle biopsies from patients.

7. **Myokines and multi-omics:** Irisin, an exercise-induced myokine linked to PGC-1α activation, enhances thermogenesis and glucose homeostasis with potential circadian regulation. Multi-omic approaches are uncovering time-dependent molecular signatures and biomarkers that may inform personalised, temporally targeted interventions.

**Keywords:** circadian rhythm, skeletal muscle, obesity, metabolic disease, circadian misalignment, exercise timing, chronotherapy, type 2 diabetes.

**Conclusions:** The review positions skeletal muscle clocks as both regulators and therapeutic targets in metabolic disease, proposing a conceptual framework for chrono-exercise strategies and highlighting the promise of multi-omics in developing precision chrono-medicine approaches to restore circadian alignment and improve metabolic health.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Skeletal muscle accounts for ~40% of body mass and serves as a key site of glucose uptake, lipid oxidation, and thermogenesis, making it a pivotal tissue in metabolic homeostasis."

--- SOURCE 7: Effects of exercise on circadian rhythms in humans ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10598774

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive scientific review article published in Frontiers in Pharmacology (2023 Oct 11;14:1282357; doi: 10.3389/fphar.2023.1282357) by Bingyi Shen, Changxiao Ma, Guanlin Wu, Haibin Liu, Lihong Chen, and Guangrui Yang. The article examines the effects of exercise on circadian rhythms in humans.

KEY CONTENT:

1. **Biological Clock Background**: The central circadian pacemaker is located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus. At the molecular level, core clock genes (BMAL1, CLOCK, PER, CRY, ROR, REV-ERB) form transcriptional-translational feedback loops (TTFL). Light is the most potent zeitgeber, while exercise is an important non-photic zeitgeber that can entrain or reset circadian rhythms.

2. **Effects of Exercise on Circadian Rhythms**:
   - **Normal light/dark conditions**: Both morning and evening exercise advanced sleep-wake cycle and dim light melatonin onset (DLMO) in night owls, while evening exercise delayed DLMO phase in early birds. Morning exercise is recommended for the general population to improve sleep quality. Resistance exercise in morning/noon advanced core body temperature phase.
   - **Constant conditions**: Exercise timing affects melatonin phases differently—afternoon (CT8/CT17) and night (CT10/CT16) exercise delayed melatonin onset; high-intensity exercise increased melatonin peak levels without phase changes; morning exercise (CT3) delayed melatonin peak by ~1 hour.
   - **Disturbed light/dark conditions**: A single bout of exercise has minor effects on circadian rhythms compared to bright light. Regular exercise over prolonged periods significantly impacts circadian rhythms. Exercise can help adaptation to forced phase-shifted schedules (jet lag, shift work). A phase-response curve (PRC) of melatonin (aMT6s) to exercise was plotted, showing advances at 07:00, 13:00, 16:00 and delays at 19:00, 22:00—similar to the bright light PRC. Exercise at night usually delays circadian phase, making it harder to fall asleep.

3. **Exercise Timing and Circadian-Related Diseases**:
   - **Sleep disorders**: Aerobic exercise (e.g., 30 min morning running for 3 weeks) improves sleep quality, mood, and concentration. High-intensity interval exercise also improves sleep. Exercise influences SCN input/output and clock gene expression.
   - **Cardiovascular diseases**: Timed exercise can reset circadian system post-disruption. Evening exercise is better for lowering blood pressure and heart rate (45-min evening aerobic exercise reduced blood pressure in hypertensive individuals). A 12-week evening walking regimen produced better outcomes than morning walking in coronary artery disease patients. Midday-afternoon and evening exercise is more commonly recognized as beneficial for cardiovascular health.
   - **Cancer**: IARC classified shift work involving circadian disruption as "possibly carcinogenic to humans" (2019). Morning exercise was associated with lower risk of prostate and breast cancer. Daily exercise at a fixed time improved fatigue and quality of life in cancer survivors more than irregular exercise.
   - **Metabolic diseases**: Six-week moderate-intensity cycling before breakfast was three times more beneficial for lipid utilization than post-breakfast exercise, with greater benefits for insulin sensitivity. Exercise during the early active period may be more effective for metabolic disorders. Afternoon exercise showed advantages in some metabolic cases (type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes with HIIT, overweight/obese individuals).

4. **Methodology Notes**: The review highlights challenges in comparing studies due to varying exercise protocols (intensity, mode, duration), detection methods (DLMO in blood/saliva/urine, accelerometers, questionnaires), and individual differences. WHO recommends adults engage in at least 150–300 min of moderate-intensity or 75–150 min of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity per week.

The article concludes that exercise is a promising non-invasive, non-pharmaceutical intervention for regulating circadian rhythms, but optimal timing depends on multiple factors including exercise intensity, mode, duration, and frequency.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"External factors, such as the diurnal rhythm of light, have a significant impact on the body's internal clock. Additionally, as an important non-photic zeitgeber, exercise can regulate the body's internal rhythms to a certain extent, making it possible to become a non-drug intervention for preventing and treating circadian rhythm disorders."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 1: Getting the Sleep You Need: Jet Lag and Shift Work ---
URL: https://sleep.hms.harvard.edu/education-training/public-education/sleep-and-health-education-program/sleep-health-education-81

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the Harvard Medical School Division of Sleep Medicine provides education on jet lag and shift work as part of its "Getting the Sleep You Need" series.

**Key takeaways:**
- Traveling across time zones disrupts regular sleep/wake patterns
- The internal circadian alerting system is strongest during daytime, making night shift work challenging
- Good sleep habits, a regular schedule, and simple workplace measures can help shift workers

**Jet Lag:**
- Jet lag occurs when the body's internal clock is out of sync with the current time zone, caused by the mismatch between the external environment and the internal biological clock (circadian misalignment)
- Symptoms include excessive daytime sleepiness, nighttime insomnia, headache, loss of appetite, gastrointestinal problems, and irritability or mild depression
- Jet lag is temporary because the internal clock adapts through "entrainment" — readjusting about one hour (or time zone) per day, though some body systems take longer
- Light is the most powerful synchronizer of the internal biological clock
- For eastward flights (e.g., North America to Europe), travelers should avoid bright light during their usual nighttime and seek light starting at about 5 a.m. internal time; light earlier than 5 a.m. internal time can shift the clock in the wrong direction
- Avoid long daytime naps in the new time zone to build sleep drive for nighttime sleep

**Shift Work:**
- Shift workers experience longer-term disruptions with both social and physiological implications, unlike travelers with temporary jet lag
- Night shift workers (e.g., 11 p.m. to 7 a.m.) must adapt to sleeping during daylight and being alert at night when the circadian alerting system is at its lowest point
- Social/family obligations make it difficult to maintain a consistent daytime sleep schedule, keeping the internal clock perpetually out of sync
- Rotating shifts (e.g., weekly changes among 7 a.m.–3 p.m., 3 p.m.–11 p.m., 11 p.m.–7 a.m.) cause continual desynchronization similar to jet lag

**Shift Work Disorder:**
- A chronic condition directly related to work schedules with two primary symptoms: insomnia when trying to sleep and excessive sleepiness when needing to be awake
- About half of all night shift workers report falling asleep at work
- Night shift workers average about 1.5 fewer hours of sleep per night than daytime workers
- Serious public health issue given shift workers include long-haul truck drivers, pilots, train operators, medical providers, and 24-hour infrastructure workers
- Chronic sleep loss may increase risk for obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease; increases work-related accidents at night and motor vehicle accidents after night shifts

**Workplace Measures to Help Shift Workers:**
- Enhance workplace lighting (increased intensity, blue-shifted wavelength to simulate daylight) improves adaptation to night work
- Strategic caffeine use: regular small doses better than fewer large doses; taper off halfway through shift if sleeping immediately after work
- 20- to 30-minute nap breaks improve performance
- If shifts must rotate, rotating day → evening → night is easier than reverse rotation
- Persistent problems warrant evaluation by a sleep specialist
- Protect sleep time and create a dark, comfortable, quiet sleep environment (turn off phone, disconnect doorbell, arrange childcare)

Content last reviewed October 1, 2021.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Traveling across time zones can disrupt regular patterns of sleep and wakefulness. Because the internal circadian alerting system is at its strongest during the daytime, night shift workers often find themselves struggling to sleep 'on the wrong side of the clock.'"
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Jet Lag: Current and Potential Therapies - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3086113

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in Pharmacy and Therapeutics (P&T) by Mary Choy, PharmD, and Rebecca L. Salbu, PharmD, CGP (Touro College of Pharmacy), provides a comprehensive review of jet lag (circadian desynchrony) and its current and potential therapies. 

**Overview of Jet Lag:** Jet lag is a sleep disorder caused by rapid travel across multiple time zones, creating a mismatch between the body's natural circadian rhythm and the external environment. It affects all age groups but has more pronounced effects on the elderly. Symptoms typically appear after crossing at least two time zones and include disturbed sleep, daytime fatigue, decreased mental/physical performance, reduced alertness, and headaches. Eastward travel produces longer-lasting jet lag than westward travel. Potential long-term sequelae include cognitive deficits, GI disturbances, and increased risk of cancer, infertility, and heart disease.

**Circadian Clock Mechanism:** The central circadian clock is located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus, which receives light signals from the retina. Zeitgebers (time-givers) are rhythmic environmental cues that synchronize the internal body clock, with light being the strongest. Other non-photic zeitgebers include temperature, social interaction, exercise, and meal timing.

**Treatments Reviewed:**
1. **Light Therapy:** Natural sunlight is the ideal mechanism for counteracting jet lag; artificial bright light therapy (light box, lamp, visor) is an alternative for frequent travelers.
2. **Melatonin:** A nutraceutical synthesized from serotonin in the pineal gland that helps shift circadian rhythms. Taken in afternoon/evening promotes phase advance; taken in morning promotes phase delay. Doses of 0.5-5 mg are used; studies show little difference in efficacy across this range. The first double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Arendt et al.) used 5 mg/day starting 3 days before an eastbound flight, with significantly fewer severe symptoms (P=0.009).
3. **Melatonin Plus Light Therapy:** Combining both treatments at appropriate times can mitigate jet lag symptoms; timing must be tailored to the individual's body clock.
4. **Melatonin Receptor Analogues:** Ramelteon (Rozerem) - FDA-approved for insomnia; a study of 110 patients showed only the 1 mg dose produced statistically significant reduction in latency to persistent sleep (10.64 minutes faster than placebo, P=0.030). Tasimelteon - investigational; phase 3 study (n=411) showed improved sleep latency, quality, and maintenance at 20/50/100 mg doses; received FDA orphan drug designation for non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder in blind individuals in January 2010.
5. **Non-benzodiazepine Hypnotics (Zolpidem/Ambien):** A study by Jamieson et al. (n=130 experienced travelers) found zolpidem 10 mg/day improved total sleep time, reduced awakenings, and improved sleep quality. Not FDA-approved for jet lag.
6. **Caffeine:** A systematic review of 13 trials found caffeine improved cognition vs. placebo. Slow-release caffeine 300 mg allowed quicker resynchronization of hormonal rhythms.
7. **Diphenhydramine (Benadryl):** No studies exist for jet lag use; should be avoided in elderly due to anticholinergic sensitivity.
8. **Armodafinil (Nuvigil):** A CNS stimulant; phase 3 study showed 150 mg/day significantly improved sleep latency (11.7 vs 4.8 min, P<0.001). Cephalon withdrew its FDA approval application in December 2010 after receiving a second complete response letter.

**Table 1** details agents, availability, classes, doses, and costs, including melatonin (OTC, $7.99/bottle), ramelteon ($66.99/10 days), zolpidem ($14.99/10 days), caffeine ($6.99/box), diphenhydramine ($3.49/box), and armodafinil ($72.99/10 days).

**Conclusion:** The pharmacist plays a key role in helping travelers select appropriate jet lag treatments, considering flight schedule, purpose of travel, physical condition, and cost. Non-drug therapy should be promoted, and medication history reviewed before recommending specific pharmacotherapy.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Jet lag, also known as circadian desynchrony, is a sleep disorder in which there is a mismatch with the body's natural circadian rhythm and the external environment as a result of rapid travel across multiple time zones."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Jet Lag Disorder | CDC Yellow Book™ ---
URL: https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/travel-air-sea/jet-lag-disorder.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This CDC Yellow Book™ webpage provides comprehensive clinical guidance on Jet Lag Disorder for healthcare professionals providing care to international travelers. Jet lag is a sleep disorder caused by rapid travel across time zones, resulting in temporary desynchronization between the internal biological clock and local time. It manifests as sleep disturbances, cognitive impairment, daytime sleepiness, general malaise, and gastrointestinal disturbances. A recent survey reported 68% of international business travelers experienced negative symptoms regularly. Risk factors include number of time zones traveled, exposure to time cues, genetic differences, and medication use.

**Diagnostic criteria (ICSD-3)**: Insomnia or excessive daytime sleepiness with reduced total sleep time associated with trans-meridian travel across at least two time zones, plus impairment of daytime function/malaise/somatic symptoms within 1-2 days after travel, not better explained by another disorder.

**Key physiology**: "Advancing" the circadian rhythm moves the biological clock earlier; "delaying" moves it later. Eastward travel requires advancing (harder); westward requires delaying (easier). Westward adaptation averages 1.5 hrs/day; eastward averages 1 hr/day.

**Management strategies** are divided into pre-travel, during travel, and at destination phases:
- Strategic sleep shifting: shift sleep 1 hour later (westward) or earlier (eastward) per day 2-3 days prior; minimize alcohol and caffeine (both cause dehydration and worsen jet lag); short 20-30 min naps help, longer naps interfere with nighttime sleep.
- Timed light exposure: bright light in morning promotes phase advances (helps eastward travel); evening exposure promotes phase delays (helps westward travel); timing based on direction and time zones crossed.
- Timed melatonin: 0.5-1 mg is often sufficient; high-dose (>5mg) not recommended; timing depends on travel direction (taken when internal clock thinks it's morning = phase delay for westward; early evening = phase advance for eastward); melatonin is not FDA-regulated so labeled amounts may vary.
- Hypnotics/stimulants: caffeine (half-life ~5 hrs) and modafinil (~12 hrs) promote wakefulness; zolpidem and eszopiclone are AASM-recommended hypnotic options; avoid antihistamines, long-acting benzodiazepines, and long-acting BZRAs due to cognitive impairment and other risks.

**WRAIR practical tips**: Time activities to destination time zone; for trips under 2 days, avoid adapting and keep home time zone schedule. Westward travel tips include avoiding bright light in early morning, avoiding caffeine in early morning, napping in early morning. Eastward tips include getting bright light in early morning, taking caffeine, avoiding evening light. Upon arrival: get daylight, take 200 mg caffeine every 4 hours (stop 6 hours before bed), use ~20 min naps. Jet lag calculators provide individualized recommendations based on phase-response curves for sleep, light, caffeine, and melatonin timing.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"For most people, it is easier to delay than advance the circadian rhythm since the average period of the intrinsic circadian rhythm is slightly longer than 24 hours... westward travel is easier to adapt to than eastward travel, with an average rate of adaptation of 1.5 hrs/day for westward travel and 1 hr/day for eastward travel."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Caffeine and jet lag | The correct dose & timing | Timeshifter® ---
URL: https://www.timeshifter.com/jet-lag/caffeine-and-travel

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the Timeshifter website's article "Caffeine and jet lag," written by Steven W. Lockley, Ph.D., Co-Founder & Chief Scientist at Timeshifter. The article explains the relationship between caffeine consumption and jet lag management.

Key points covered:
- Caffeine can help travelers stay alert when the circadian clock is out of sync with local time, but it does NOT reset the clock the way light and melatonin do—it masks fatigue rather than fixing the underlying misalignment.
- Used at the wrong time, caffeine can worsen jet lag by disrupting sleep at the destination.
- Recommended usage: a caffeinated drink (tea, coffee, or soda, ~50mg of caffeine) every two hours helps stay awake. Consuming more than that does not increase alertness and may reduce the ability to sleep later. Caffeine consumed 8 hours or less before bedtime negatively impacts sleep quality.
- Caffeine sources: tea, coffee, caffeinated sodas, chocolate, and some pain medications. Brewed 'drip' coffee and energy drinks have very high caffeine content—only half a cup every two hours is needed.
- How caffeine works: It is an adenosine-receptor antagonist that blocks adenosine from reaching its receptors, preventing the chemical buildup that causes sleepiness.
- Caffeine half-life is 3-5 hours. Example: 100mg at 10 a.m. leaves 50mg at 3 p.m., 25mg at 8 p.m., and ~12.5mg at 10 p.m.—enough to disrupt sleep.
- Best strategy: use caffeine "little and often," then stop as long as possible before bed.
- Caffeine should not be given to children due to their smaller size increasing relative dose.
- Timeshifter's app provides personalized advice on when to use and avoid caffeine during travel to support light-dark and sleep schedules.

The page also includes site navigation for Timeshifter's products (jet lag app, shift work app, peak performance, My Circadian Day), noting the jet lag app is trusted by 1.7 million+ travelers and is described as the most downloaded and highest-rated jet lag app in the world. Other related articles are linked (melatonin for jet lag, what is jet lag, jet lag myths debunked, caffeine and shift work, etc.). The site emphasizes that these statements have not been evaluated by the FDA and the product is intended for healthy adults 18+.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Caffeine can help you stay alert when your circadian clock is out of sync with local time, but it doesn't reset your clock the way light and melatonin do. Caffeine masks fatigue rather than fixing the underlying misalignment."
</key_excerpts>
