## Abstract

Sleep and circadian rhythm disturbances are prevalent in older populations. Numerous factors can affect sleep, including medications, living environment and physical, mental and psychosocial factors (e.g. loneliness and stress). Sleep architecture changes with aging, with less deep sleep (slow wave sleep) and an increased frequency of awakenings after sleep onset. Benzodiazepines, Z-drugs and low doses of the tricyclic antidepressant doxepin have modest positive benefits for sleep complaints, but side effects are a concern in older people because they include an increased risk of falls, fractures and cognitive impairment. Somnolence can be prolonged in older adults. Melatonin has very modest effects on sleep initiation in older adults, although appears safe. Overall, the effects of pharmacological treatments are modest and there are concerns about the efficacy and safety of their ongoing use. There is strong evidence for non-pharmacological interventions, including cognitive and behavioural strategies, to improve sleep. These have at least comparable efficacy to pharmacological interventions, fewer adverse effects and are more likely to have longer-term, sustained benefits. Sleep complaints in older adults need to be approached on a patient-by-patient basis, and medication should be reviewed frequently, with preference to limit pharmacological intervention as far as practicable.

## Introduction

Sleep disturbances are common in older people. They can occur as a consequence of clinical sleep disorders, such as obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) and insomnia, or environmental or behavioural factors (e.g. light, noise, caffeine intake). Sleep disturbances also occur secondary to chronic diseases, but this paper predominantly focuses on the treatment of primary sleep disturbances.

In a national survey of Australian adults,[1](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0001) people aged >65 years were more likely to report waking frequently overnight a few times a week than people aged 18–24 years (52% _vs_ 26%, respectively) and waking early and being unable to get back to sleep (40% _vs_ 28%, respectively). However, older people were more likely to report getting adequate sleep than young adults (61% _vs_ 40%, respectively). Insomnia, defined as difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep causing daytime symptoms such as fatigue or moodiness, was reported by 18% of people aged ≥65 years.[1](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0001)

Clinical sleep disorders, including OSA, are prevalent in older adults. An Australian population study found moderate to severe OSA affects up to 34% of men aged ≥65 years, compared with 16% of those aged 40–50 years.[2](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0002) This difference is more marked in women, where OSA prevalence increases sharply following menopause.[3](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0003)

Identifying and treating sleep disorders (sleep disturbances beyond ‘typical’ age-related changes), including clinical and behavioural sleep problems, is important for mental and physical well-being. Poor sleep in older adults is associated with cognitive impairment,[4](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0004) and some sleep disorders (e.g. sleep behaviour disorder occurring during rapid eye movement (REM) sleep) may precede neurodegenerative disorders.[5](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0005) Poor sleep quality is also associated with poorer mental health including depression[6](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0006), [7](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0007) and generalised anxiety disorder.[8](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0008) Sleep disturbance is associated with numerous chronic diseases, including heart disease, pain, obesity, arthritis, osteoporosis, respiratory diseases, diabetes and stroke.[9](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0009) In addition, healthy adults with objectively assessed sleep disturbance have a higher risk of all-cause mortality.[10](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0010) Although the relationship between sleep and chronic disease is likely bidirectional, intervention studies show that treatment of OSA, for example, may be associated with lower risk of fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events,[11](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0011) although not all studies have shown a benefit.[12](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0012)

## Changes in Sleep Architecture and Predictors of Sleep Disturbance in Older Adults

Chronological age is not a key predictor of sleep disturbance (including self-reported sleep complaints, fragmented sleep, short or long sleep and other insomnia symptoms).[13](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0013) As we age, our sleep changes.[14](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0014), [15](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0015) There is a tendency for the timing of sleep to advance (earlier time to bed) but for it to take longer to fall asleep (increased sleep onset latency). Age affects the structure of sleep with increases in light sleep (Stages I and II non-REM sleep) and decreases in deep sleep (Stage III non-REM or slow wave sleep). From around 80 years of age, REM sleep also decreases. This shift to lighter sleep is accompanied by increased brief awakenings (arousals) and more interrupted sleep, with more time spent awake (wake after sleep onset), decreased sleep efficiency (commonly expressed as a percentage of time in bed that is spent sleeping) and decreased overall amount of sleep (total sleep time).[14](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0014), [15](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0015)

Although there are changes to sleep architecture and the timing of sleep opportunities in older adults, these changes alone do not result in the experience of sleep disturbance.[13](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0013) Prospective population-based studies provide insights into common predictors of sleep disturbance in older adult populations. Three key risk factors emerge: depressed mood, poor physical health and female sex.[16](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0016) However the association between sex and sleep quality is not consistent.[17](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0017) Mental and physical health decline are commonly associated with sleep disturbance in older adults. Depressed mood is consistently related to self-reported sleep complaints, insomnia symptoms and sleep quality scores.[16](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0016) Poorer physical health status is prospectively associated with sleep complaints and reports of insomnia symptoms, with cardiovascular disease and chronic pain conditions commonly associated with sleep complaints and poorer-quality sleep.[16](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0016) Additional psychosocial factors have been implicated in sleep disturbance in older adults, albeit with more limited or mixed prospective evidence. These include socioeconomic status, level of physical activity, perceived stress and loneliness and the use of sedatives.[16](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0016) A recent review of prospectively examined risk factors for sleep disturbance by Smagula _et al_.[16](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0016) is recommended for further reading.

## Residential Care Facilities, Noise, Light and Sleep

A number of environmental factors can influence sleep quality, particularly related to living arrangements. One such factor is living in residential care versus living at home. This is illustrated by a cross-sectional study of older adults with moderate dementia comparing residential care to at-home living conditions.[18](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0018) Participants who lived in residential care had poorer objectively measured sleep outcomes than those living at home, including shorter total sleep duration and more time awake after sleep onset. Light exposure, which is important in regulating sleep–wake patterns, was substantially lower in older adults in residential care than at home.[18](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0018) These findings highlight that environment is an important consideration when addressing sleep in older adults. The residential care environment is disruptive to patients both with and without cognitive impairment,[19](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0019) suggesting that addressing sleep disturbance in residential care facilities may be a priority for a large majority of residents.

The relationship between sleep disturbance and residential care is likely bidirectional, because sleep disturbance is associated with an increased risk of placement in residential care.[20](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0020), [21](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0021) Early management of sleep disturbance, including sleep hygiene education and management of clinical sleep disorders, may be one component of interventions to facilitate independent living for a longer period.

## Pharmacological Management of Sleep Complaints

### General Considerations

The pattern of symptoms in the individual (e.g. difficulty with sleep initiation or maintenance) and other factors, such as cognitive function, falls risk, comorbid conditions and age-related alterations in pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, influence the approach to management and choice of treatment.[22](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0022) Insomnia is comorbid with OSA in up to 30% of cases.[23](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0023) Consequently, sleep-disordered breathing must be considered in older adults with sleep problems.

### Medication Review

Numerous medications may contribute to insomnia (Table[1](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-tbl-0001 "Link to table")),[22](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0022) and a comprehensive medication review should be an initial management strategy for sleep problems in the elderly.

### Considerations for Medications Targeting Sleep Disturbance

When considering a medication for sleep disturbance, it is important to consider the quality of available evidence. The 2017 clinical practice guideline from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine made recommendations regarding pharmacological treatment, but all were classified as supported by weak evidence.[24](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0024) There are very few clinical trials with adequate sample size that have not been funded by industry, and there is heterogeneity in the data and risk of publication bias, leading to a downgrading of evidence quality ratings.[25](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0025) The guideline authors noted that ‘_this should not be construed to mean that no sleep-promoting medications are clearly efficacious or indicated in the treatment of chronic insomnia_’.[24](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0024) The limitations of the evidence emphasise the importance of clinical judgement that takes multiple factors into account on a patient-by-patient basis. There is minimal evidence in older people for the long-term use of hypnotics (especially beyond 12 weeks), and even less evidence in groups with significant comorbidity.[22](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0022)

Within drug classes, patients can respond differently to each agent, so a poor response or an adverse effect with one medication will not necessarily occur with others.[26](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0026)

### Benzodiazepines

Benzodiazepine GABA A receptor agonists (BZRA) are effective for treating insomnia in the short term. A meta-analysis examined evidence regarding sedatives in people aged >60 years published between 1966 and 2003.[27](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0027) Relatively modest but significant improvements were seen for benzodiazepines (BZDs) compared with placebo in terms of the number of awakenings (mean 0.6 fewer awakenings with BZDs), total sleep time (mean increase 34 min with BZDs) and sleep quality.

BZRAs reduce the amount of Stage I sleep (i.e. light sleep), which is considered a therapeutic effect, because it tends to correspond to an increase in Stage II sleep and reduced awakenings. BZRAs may reduce REM sleep, particularly when used at higher doses, although studies of commonly used BZRAs (e.g. temazepam) in older people have not shown decreased REM sleep duration.[22](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0022) Reduced REM sleep may potentially affect learning and memory consolidation.

Side-effects of BZRAs include somnolence, cognitive impairment and increased risk of falls and fracture in older people. Adverse effects are discussed in further detail below.[27](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0027) Tolerance rapidly develops to BZRAs, and rebound insomnia can occur even with intermittent usage.

### Z-Drugs

Z-Drugs (zolpidem, zopiclone) are approved for insomnia in Australia, but are not subsidised by the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme(PBS). Z-Drugs bind selectively to the BZD allosteric binding site at GABA A receptors. In older people, Z-drugs reduce Stage I sleep, but the clinical relevance of this is unclear.[28](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0028)

A systematic review that included four studies of zolpidem in older people reported improvements in sleep latency, nocturnal awakenings and sleep duration versus placebo.[29](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0029) Another review concluded that zolpidem reduced sleep onset in older people by a mean of 18 min (95% confidence interval (CI) 5–31 min).[30](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0030) The quality of evidence has been rated as low.[30](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0030) Side effects of zolpidem include somnolence and dizziness,[22](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0022), [24](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0024) and there is an increased risk of falls and fracture in older people.[31](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0031) Driving performance can be impaired, and an increase in motor vehicle accidents has been reported with zolpidem.[32](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0032)

Parasomnias (including sleepwalking, sleep eating, sleep conversations, sleep driving, sleep sex), have been reported and are usually seen with high doses, underlying psychiatric diseases or with drug–drug interactions.[33](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0033), [34](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0034) Although parasomnias are rare, post-marketing reports from the US and Australia have shown that zolpidem is associated with increased odds of parasomnias, movement-based parasomnias, amnesias, hallucinations and suicidality compared with other drugs.[35](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0035), [36](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0036) Advice regarding possible abnormal behaviours, and to avoid activities such as driving until the afternoon or until feeling alert, is recommended.

Rebound insomnia is a risk with sudden cessation of Z-drugs, and tapering is advised. To limit the risk of tolerance and dependence, intermittent dosing has been tried successfully, with alternative nights or three times per week more effective than placebo, although only small numbers were studied.[37](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0037) Overall, the evidence indicates Z-drugs should be used with caution.

### Melatonin

Production of endogenous nocturnal melatonin decreases with age, with peak excretion around half that of younger patients.[38](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0038) Prolonged-release melatonin (Circadin, Neurim Pharmaceuticals, Tel-Aviv, Israel (distributed by Aspen Pharma in Australia)) tablets are approved in Australia, although not PBS subsidised. Melatonin does not alter sleep architecture in older adults. Melatonin has few adverse effects and is mildly effective with up to 2 months of use.[22](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0022), [39](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0039) A meta-analysis found exogenous melatonin reduced sleep onset latency by a modest amount (mean 5–7 min),[40](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0040) which is unlikely to be of clinical significance. That review found some benefit in those experiencing disruption to their endogenous circadian rhythms (which, in turn, affects sleep–wake behaviour),[40](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0040) although only two studies included adults aged ≥55 years. In a study of 281 patients aged 65–80 years, Wade _et al_.[41](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0041) reported a significant reduction of self-reported sleep latency with melatonin, regardless of melatonin deficiency status (−19.1 _vs_ −1.7 min with melatonin _vs_ placebo, respectively); this improvement held at 19 weeks (−25.9 and −8.3 min, respectively). Improvements in daytime psychomotor performance and morning alertness have been reported;[42](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0042) effectiveness of melatonin may be reduced in patients with comorbid disorders, such as Alzheimer's disease, or with fast-acting formulations.[40](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0040) There is limited evidence that melatonin can improve sleep quality in older people with neurodegenerative disorders.[43](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0043) There is also little evidence regarding long-term melatonin use, although minimal adverse effects have been seen up to 6 months.[40](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0040) Infrequent side effects include headaches, irritability, dizziness, nausea and vomiting.[24](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0024), [40](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0040)

### Doxepin

Doxepin is a sedating tricyclic antidepressant. At low doses (<10 mg), doxepin is thought to act as a selective histamine H 1 receptor antagonist,[44](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0044) with little effect on other receptors. At low doses, doxepin does not suppress REM or Stage III sleep.[45](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0045) A recent meta-analysis of six low-dose (3–6 mg) doxepin studies, three conducted in older subjects, found a small to medium positive effect on sleep maintenance insomnia, with decreased wake after sleep onset and increased sleep efficiency and sleep duration, with a weighted mean total sleep time difference of 23.9 minutes (95% CI 12.0–35.7).[46](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0046) There have been no controlled studies comparing doxepin with other hypnotics. In older people, side effects of doxepin were similar to placebo, with headaches and somnolence the most common.[39](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0039) Deleterious effects on memory consolidation and cognitive function were not reported, likely related to the lack of effect of doxepin on slow wave sleep or REM sleep. There are minimal data on the longer-term use of low-dose doxepin. Moderate and higher doses of doxepin are associated with more frequent side effects and rebound insomnia.[46](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0046) In Australia, the lowest-strength doxepin product is a 10-mg capsule; hence, it is not a recommended treatment option for older people. Doxepin is also not recommended if comorbid moderate–severe sleep apnoea is present.[47](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0047)

### Amitriptyline

Amitriptyline is another tricyclic antidepressant. Despite its common use for sleep complaints, especially in primary care,[48](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0048) a recent Cochrane Review found no evidence for the effectiveness of amitriptyline in insomnia,[49](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0049) and it is not recommended. Low-dose amitriptyline has shown modest improvements in subjective sleep symptoms when used for chronic neck pain[50](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0050) and low back pain.[51](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0051)

### Suvorexant

Suvorexant is a dual orexin receptor antagonist. Orexins are neuropeptides, involved in sleep regulation. In a controlled trial with 59% patients aged >65 years, those taking high-dose suvorexant (30 mg for people aged >65 years and 40 mg for younger people) had improved sleep onset (by 18 min) and total sleep time (by 39 min) compared with placebo.[52](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0052) These improvements were maintained at 1 year. However, the doses used in that trial were double the dose approved in Australia (15 and 20 mg) and efficacy at lower doses is modest. A systematic review[53](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0053) found that lower doses of suvorexant led to a mean improvement of 6 min for the time to fall asleep and 16 min for total sleep time, indicating that it may be more useful for improving sleep maintenance than sleep onset.[22](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0022), [24](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0024) Higher doses have more side effects, including somnolence, fatigue, dry mouth, dyspepsia and peripheral oedema. Uncommonly, severe side effects can occur, including sleep walking, sleep paralysis and hallucinations.[53](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0053) Suvorexant has a long half-life, and residual effects, such as somnolence, can persist the following day, particularly at higher doses, potentially affecting driving ability.[24](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0024) Rebound insomnia has not been a feature.[24](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0024) Patients with neurological or psychiatric disorders were excluded from these trials. Recently, suvorexant has been tested in a pilot study (_n_=6) of patients with Alzheimer's disease with insomnia and found to be efficacious for improving insomnia in this patient group.[54](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0054) Safety in comorbid sleep apnea[55](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0055) or severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease[56](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0056) has not been established, and suvorexant should be used with caution in these patients.

### Valerian

Valerian is a herb commonly used for sleep disturbances. Three systematic reviews have concluded that valerian is relatively safe, although safety data specifically in older people is sparse.[57](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0057)-[59](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0059) The reviews came to different conclusions regarding the efficacy of valerian, but it appears to be associated with a modest level of improvement in subjective sleep quality and insomnia symptoms, but not in quantitative or objective measures.[22](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0022), [24](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0024) Hypnotic effects are delayed for 2–3 weeks and a trial of at least 4–6 weeks is recommended.[60](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0060) There are limited data on the interaction of valerian with prescription sleep aids, but it is recognised that there is potential to enhance the effects of some drugs.[61](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0061)

### Quetiapine

Quietapine, an anti-psychotic medication, is also a histamine H1 and serotonin receptor antagonist with sedative effects.[62](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0062) The American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline identified only one study of 13 patients that investigated the efficacy of quetiapine versus placebo in primary insomnia.[24](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0024) Although increases in subjective sleep time and a reduction in subjective sleep latency were found, these differences were not significant, which is largely reflective of small sample size.[24](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0024) Side effects are common and include dizziness, dry mouth, weight gain, constipation and movement problems.[63](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0063) A review found no trials comparing quetiapine with other hypnotics and there is minimal evidence using objective sleep measurements.[63](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0063) The authors concluded that the benefits of quetiapine have not been shown to outweigh potential risks.[63](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0063)

## Adverse Effects of Medications Commonly Used for Sleep Disorders

Some adverse effects of sedative medications are of particular concern in older people. A meta-analysis of 24 controlled studies evaluating BZDs, Z-drugs and the antihistamine diphenhydramine in 2005 reported an increased risk of adverse events, with odds ratios of 4.78 for adverse cognitive events, 2.61 for adverse psychomotor events and 3.82 for daytime fatigue.[27](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0027) Studies were mostly short term (up to 2 weeks), with a small number of studies of 6 weeks duration. The authors of that meta-analysis concluded that the risk of side effects outweighed the modest benefits for these medications.[27](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0027) A limitation of that analysis is that medications were compared by class, without separating short- and long-acting sedatives, potentially leading to erroneous conclusions.

A review of 57 studies of BZRAs and Z-drugs found both drug classes significantly impair balance, standing steadiness and walking.[64](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0064) These impairments may persist until the following morning, placing older people who get up overnight, for example to go to the bathroom, at risk of falls. The effects are worse with higher doses and aggravated by alcohol or other psychoactive drugs. Partial tolerance develops with ongoing use, although this develops slowly. An increased risk of falls and hip fractures still occurs in chronic users of sedatives,[64](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0064) increased risk also seen with patients using tricyclic antidepressants[65](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0065) and antipsychotic medications.[66](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0066)

The American Geriatric Society Beers Criteria recommend BZRA, Z-drugs, antipsychotics, antihistamines and tricyclic antidepressants (except doxepin≤6 mg) be avoided in older people due to increased risk of impaired cognition, delirium, falls, fractures and motor vehicle accidents.[67](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0067)

A meta-analysis of 13 studies found chronic BZRA users (mean duration 8.9 years) had impaired cognitive function, which persisted up to at least 6 months after cessation.[68](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0068) Ongoing use increases the risk of dementia.[69](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0069) All these factors strongly suggest that BZRAs and Z-drugs should not be routinely used in older people[27](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0027), [39](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0039) without careful consideration of individual circumstances. Despite this, BZRAs and Z-drugs continue to be commonly prescribed in Australia for sleep disturbances.[70](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0070)

## Additional Considerations Beyond Pharmacological Treatment

Although treatment options vary by cause of the sleep complaint, cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the gold standard treatment for chronic insomnia.[71](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0071) Psychological and behavioural treatments for insomnia, which include CBT-I, can consist of a number of components, including sleep hygiene and stimulus control. Such approaches encourage developing regular habits around sleep and avoiding mentally stimulating activities before bed, such as computers or devices. They may also include sleep restriction, limiting time in bed and then gradually increasing sleep time, relaxation training for mind and body and cognitive therapy to address attitudes and beliefs hindering sleep.[72](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0072) CBT-I has demonstrated efficacy in older adults with insomnia.[71](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0071) Importantly, efficacy is also seen in insomnia patients with comorbid chronic pain, cancer treatment and psychiatric conditions.[71](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0071) A review that examined the comparative effectiveness of BZRAs and psychological and/or behavioural interventions that included five studies and one comparative meta-analysis concluded that the BZRA hypnotics and psychological interventions produce similar outcomes for primary insomnia and that psychological interventions may be superior for sleep initiation.[73](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0073) Psychological/behavioural interventions appear more likely to have persistent gains at follow-up, up to 8 months. CBT-I can also be used to facilitate withdrawal from medications. One study in older patients found CBT-I significantly increased the chances of becoming BZRA free.[74](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0074) Another study in subjects aged up to 72 years that compared CBT-I alone with CBT-I plus zolpidem followed by extended CBT-I found the addition of medication to CBT-I produced added benefits during acute therapy, but long-term remission of insomnia was more likely when medication was tapered off and discontinued during maintenance CBT-I.[75](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0075) Follow-up of this group has shown this difference is maintained up to 24 months.[76](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0076)

Behavioural interventions such as Tai Chi Chih[77](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0077) and yoga,[78](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0078) along with broader sleep hygiene interventions (including reduced caffeine, cigarette and alcohol consumption, exercise, stress reduction, noise modification (positive, e.g. music,[79](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0079) and negative, e.g. residential facilities), regularity of sleep timing and reduced napping[80](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0080)) offer varying improvements in sleep quality and duration.[81](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0081) Exercise treatments[82](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0082) and light therapy (particularly for patients with dementia[83](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0083) or depression[84](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0084)) have also shown promise in older adults, but do not appear to demonstrate the same sustained effects on sleep as CBT-I and will require further research in older adults.[84](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0084) Mindfulness-based interventions have also demonstrated success with improving sleep outcomes in older adults.[85](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0085)

## Conclusion

Sleep difficulties are not a natural consequence of ageing.[1](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0001) Given the modest efficacy of medications in improving sleep latency, total sleep time or daytime functioning and the risks of confusion and memory problems and increased falls and hip fractures, it is important that older adults try non-drug treatments first. This should include a thorough medical review and management of conditions that can disturb sleep, such as sleep apnoea, restless leg syndrome, depression or anxiety and pain. A review of medications that affect sleep should also occur. Careful attention to behaviour and environment, with a focus on sleep hygiene, stimulus control and a comfortable bedroom environment, should be part of any approach to sleep management. CBT-I has been proven to be effective for insomnia in older people, and can be successfully delivered online,[86](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jppr.1565#jppr1565-bib-0086) in groups and individually by trained psychologists. If medication is required, a time-limited approach with close monitoring for ongoing need for medication and side effects is indicated.

This is a peer-reviewed article titled "Treatment of sleep disturbance in older adults" published in the Journal of Pharmacy Practice and Research (Volume 49, Issue 3, pp. 296-304, 2019), authored by Amy C. Reynolds (CQUniversity Australia) and Robert J. Adams (Flinders University, Adelaide). The article is a Geriatric Therapeutics Review and has been accredited for 1 hour of Group 1 CPD activity for pharmacists (No. S2019/43).

Key content:
- **Prevalence**: In an Australian national survey, people >65 years reported waking frequently overnight (52% vs 26% for ages 18-24), and 18% of people ≥65 years reported insomnia. Moderate-severe OSA affects up to 34% of men ≥65 years (vs 16% at ages 40-50), with prevalence increasing sharply in women after menopause.
- **Sleep architecture changes with aging**: less deep sleep (slow wave sleep), increased light sleep, increased awakenings after sleep onset, earlier sleep timing, and decreased REM sleep from ~80 years. Chronological age is not a key predictor of sleep disturbance; key risk factors are depressed mood, poor physical health, and female sex.
- **Residential care**: Older adults in residential care have poorer objectively measured sleep outcomes and substantially lower light exposure than those living at home; the relationship between sleep disturbance and residential care placement is bidirectional.
- **Medication review**: Numerous medications can contribute to insomnia (beta-blockers, statins, SSRIs, MAO inhibitors, SNRIs, cholinesterase inhibitors, dopamine agonists, stimulants, certain antibiotics/antivirals/antifungals, NSAIDs, corticosteroids, alpha-blockers for prostatism).
- **Pharmacological treatments** (all with modest efficacy and safety concerns in older adults):
  - *Benzodiazepines/BZRAs*: Modest benefits (0.6 fewer awakenings, +34 min total sleep time) but side effects include falls, fractures, cognitive impairment, tolerance, and rebound insomnia.
  - *Z-drugs* (zolpidem, zopiclone): Reduce sleep onset by ~18 min; increased risk of falls/fractures, impaired driving, parasomnias; evidence quality rated low; used with caution.
  - *Melatonin*: Reduces sleep onset latency by modest 5-7 min; safe with few adverse effects; prolonged-release (Circadin) approved in Australia but not PBS subsidised.
  - *Doxepin*: Low-dose (3-6 mg) shows small-to-medium positive effect on sleep maintenance (+23.9 min total sleep time); but lowest Australian strength is 10mg, making it not recommended for older people.
  - *Amitriptyline*: No evidence of effectiveness for insomnia per Cochrane Review; not recommended.
  - *Suvorexant*: Dual orexin receptor antagonist; modest benefits at approved doses (+6 min sleep onset, +16 min total sleep time); higher doses have more side effects.
  - *Valerian*: Modest subjective improvements but not objective measures; delayed hypnotic effect of 2-3 weeks.
  - *Quetiapine*: Only one small study (n=13) of 13 patients; benefits not shown to outweigh risks.
- **Adverse effects**: Meta-analysis found odds ratios of 4.78 for adverse cognitive events, 2.61 for adverse psychomotor events, and 3.82 for daytime fatigue with BZDs, Z-drugs, and diphenhydramine. Beers Criteria recommend avoiding BZRAs, Z-drugs, antipsychotics, antihistamines, and tricyclic antidepressants (except doxepin ≤6mg) in older people. Chronic BZRA use impairs cognitive function persisting ≥6 months after cessation.
- **Non-pharmacological treatment**: CBT-I is the gold standard for chronic insomnia, with efficacy comparable to or superior to pharmacological interventions, fewer adverse effects, and longer-lasting benefits (up to 24 months). CBT-I can facilitate medication withdrawal. Other interventions (Tai Chi, yoga, sleep hygiene, exercise, light therapy, mindfulness) show promise but less sustained effects than CBT-I.
- **Conclusion**: Sleep difficulties are not a natural consequence of ageing. Non-drug treatments should be tried first, including thorough medical review, medication review, attention to sleep hygiene and environment, and CBT-I (available online, in groups, or individually). If medication is required, a time-limited approach with close monitoring is indicated.

Melatonin gummies are generally safe for adults over 65 at low doses and can help you fall asleep faster and modestly improve sleep quality. For best results, take 0.5 to 2 mg about 30 to 60 minutes before bedtime.

# What Are the Side Effects of Melatonin in the Elderly?

 by [Dave Kimbell](/pages/author-dave-kimbell)

📅 **Last Updated:** August 07, 2026

# What Are the Side Effects of Melatonin in the Elderly?

If you're 65 or older and struggling with sleep, you've probably heard about melatonin. It sounds simple: a natural hormone, available without a prescription, and safer than prescription sleeping pills. But "natural" doesn't mean "without risks"—especially for aging bodies that metabolize supplements differently.

The truth is reassuring overall: melatonin is generally well tolerated in seniors. But age-related changes in how your body processes medications mean that risks that might be minor in younger people can become significant concerns for you. And if you're taking other medications—which most seniors are—the risks multiply.

This guide walks through every side effect you should know about, why elderly people experience them differently, how your medications might amplify the problem, and what dosing strategies minimize risk.

## Key Takeaways

* **Most common side effects are mild:** Daytime drowsiness (5–10%), dizziness (3–5%), and nausea (3–5%) are the main concerns, but rare in clinical trials.
* **Age changes how your body metabolizes melatonin:** Elderly patients reach higher peak blood levels than younger adults from the same dose—requiring lower doses (0.3–2 mg instead of 5–10 mg).
* **Blood pressure effects are real but variable:** Melatonin can lower blood pressure modestly (4–6 mmHg reduction at night), which helps some seniors with hypertension but risks others taking blood pressure medications.
* **Polypharmacy multiplies risk:** If you take 5+ medications (common in seniors), certain drug interactions can increase melatonin to dangerous levels—particularly with antidepressants like fluvoxamine.
* **Fall risk is overstated but worth monitoring:** Daytime drowsiness and dizziness \*can\* increase fall risk, but the evidence linking melatonin directly to fractures remains conflicted.

## Table of Contents

1. [Melatonin's Overall Safety Profile in Seniors](#1-safety-overview)
2. [Common Side Effects—And How Often They Actually Occur](#2-common-side-effects)
3. [Why Elderly Bodies Handle Melatonin Differently](#3-pharmacology-elderly)
4. [Blood Pressure and Cardiovascular Effects](#4-blood-pressure)
5. [The Polypharmacy Problem: When Other Medications Multiply Risk](#5-polypharmacy-risk)
6. [Falls, Fractures, and Injury Risk](#6-fall-fracture)
7. [Safe Dosing for Elderly Patients](#7-dosing-safety)
8. [When Elderly People Should Avoid Melatonin Entirely](#8-when-avoid)
9. [Getting the Right Formulation Matters](#9-bioabsorb-advantage)
10. [Elderly-Specific Questions Answered](#10-faq)

## 1. Melatonin's Overall Safety Profile in Seniors

Let's start with the reassurance: melatonin is significantly safer than prescription alternatives. Benzodiazepines (like diazepam) and Z-drugs (like zolpidem) carry well-documented risks of cognitive decline, dependence, and falls in elderly patients. Melatonin doesn't cause any of those problems.

In clinical trials conducted specifically in adults 55–93 years old, adverse effects from melatonin (2 mg prolonged-release) ranged from 6–24%, compared with 5–21% in placebo groups. The difference is often not statistically significant—many side effects reported were mild and resolved quickly. No studies report serious adverse events or hospitalizations attributable to melatonin alone in elderly patients.

That said, "generally safe" is different from "risk-free for you." Age-related changes in kidney and liver function, the prevalence of multiple medications in seniors, and age-specific physiological shifts create conditions where melatonin poses particular concerns that younger people don't face.

## 2. Common Side Effects—And How Often They Actually Occur

The most frequently reported side effects in elderly melatonin users are mild and temporary. Here's what the research actually shows:

**Daytime drowsiness (5–10% of users):** This is the leading complaint, especially if you take melatonin too late at night or at too high a dose. In younger adults, melatonin clears the bloodstream in 1–2 hours. But in elderly people, clearance is often slower, meaning residual melatonin lingers into morning hours. If you wake up groggy, the dose is too high or the timing is wrong.

**Dizziness or lightheadedness (3–5%):** Melatonin reduces blood pressure in many people. For someone already taking antihypertensive medication, this additive effect can cause orthostatic hypotension—the sudden dizziness you feel when standing up. This becomes a fall risk.

**Headache (5–8%):** Melatonin affects cerebral blood vessel tone and can trigger headaches in sensitive individuals. This is generally mild and dose-dependent—reducing your dose often solves it.

**Nausea or stomach discomfort (3–5%):** Some seniors experience GI irritation, particularly if taking melatonin on an empty stomach. Taking it with a small snack usually resolves this.

**Vivid dreams or nightmares (2–5%):** Melatonin increases REM sleep, the stage where most dreaming occurs. More time in REM means more dreams—and for some people, more intense or disturbing ones. This typically diminishes as your body adjusts.

## 3. Why Elderly Bodies Handle Melatonin Differently

Your body's chemistry changes with age. Understanding how melatonin metabolism shifts is key to understanding why dosing matters so much in seniors.

**Peak blood levels are higher in elderly patients:** Melatonin is metabolized primarily by a liver enzyme called CYP1A2 (with minor contributions from CYP2C19). As you age, these enzyme systems become less efficient. A 2 mg dose in a 70-year-old reaches higher peak concentrations than the same dose in a 40-year-old. This is why the same dose causes side effects in elderly patients but not in younger adults.

**Elimination half-life may be slower:** Melatonin normally clears the bloodstream in 1–2 hours. But variability increases with age, and certain medications slow this further. If you're taking an SSRI antidepressant, the clearance can extend substantially, meaning melatonin accumulates.

**Bioavailability is unpredictable (1–74%):** How much of an oral melatonin dose actually enters your bloodstream varies widely, even in younger people. In elderly patients with altered gastric pH, reduced GI motility, or certain medications, this variability increases further. This is why two seniors taking the same brand and dose can experience very different effects.

**Liver and kidney function decline:** If you have even mild hepatic impairment (liver disease, reduced liver perfusion) or renal impairment (reduced kidney function), melatonin and its metabolites accumulate. Seniors with diabetes, cardiovascular disease, or a history of liver problems need extra caution.

## 4. Blood Pressure and Cardiovascular Effects

One of melatonin's most reliable effects in human studies is blood pressure reduction. For some elderly patients with uncontrolled hypertension, this is a benefit. For others—especially those on blood pressure medications—it becomes a risk.

**How much does melatonin lower blood pressure?** In clinical trials, repeated melatonin intake (2.5 mg daily) reduced systolic and diastolic blood pressure during sleep by approximately 6 and 4 mmHg, respectively. This reduction is comparable to some antihypertensive medications and happens most reliably in the early morning (3:00–8:00 AM)—precisely when cardiovascular events become more common in elderly people.

**The concern:** If you're already taking a blood pressure medication, adding melatonin can push your blood pressure too low. Chronically low blood pressure (hypotension) in elderly patients increases dizziness, fainting, falls, and acute coronary events. Some elderly patients report feeling faint or dizzy after starting melatonin, which is often a blood pressure effect.

**Special case—nifedipine interaction:** One study found that melatonin actually \*increased\* blood pressure when taken with the calcium channel blocker nifedipine. This highlights that melatonin's cardiovascular effects are unpredictable and drug-dependent.

**What to do:** If you take blood pressure medication and want to try melatonin, have your doctor monitor your blood pressure (ideally 24-hour ambulatory monitoring) before and during use. Watch for dizziness or unusual fatigue. Consider lower doses (0.3–0.5 mg) and discuss whether reducing your blood pressure medication might be appropriate.

## 5. The Polypharmacy Problem: When Other Medications Multiply Risk

The average senior takes 5+ prescription medications. This is where melatonin becomes truly risky—not from the melatonin itself, but from interactions.

**Antidepressant interactions are the biggest concern:** Melatonin is metabolized by the liver enzyme CYP1A2. Certain antidepressants—particularly fluvoxamine (Luvox)—powerfully inhibit this enzyme. When fluvoxamine blocks CYP1A2, melatonin blood levels can increase 12-fold or more. This causes excessive drowsiness, prolonged sedation, and increased fall risk.

Other SSRIs like citalopram (Celexa) or fluoxetine (Prozac) can also raise melatonin levels, though the effect is usually smaller. If you also take a proton pump inhibitor (like omeprazole for acid reflux), the interaction worsens because PPIs inhibit CYP2C19, a secondary melatonin-metabolizing enzyme.

**What to do if you take antidepressants:** Tell your doctor before starting melatonin. If you're on fluvoxamine, melatonin may not be safe at all. If you're on other SSRIs, your doctor can watch for excessive daytime drowsiness and adjust your dose accordingly. Lower doses (0.3–1 mg) are safer when taken with antidepressants.

**Other medication interactions:** Melatonin may interact with blood thinners (warfarin), diabetes medications (by affecting insulin sensitivity), immunosuppressants, and seizure medications. It's not that melatonin causes severe problems—it's that the interaction creates \*uncertainty\* about how much melatonin will actually be in your bloodstream.

**The core issue with polypharmacy:** In the U.S., melatonin is unregulated as a dietary supplement, so the amount of melatonin in a bottle can vary wildly (sometimes ±50% from the label). Combined with age-related absorption variability and drug interactions, a 2 mg dose could effectively become 0.5 mg or 5 mg depending on your medications and how your body processes it. This unpredictability is what makes polypharmacy seniors highest risk.

## 6. Falls, Fractures, and Injury Risk

The relationship between melatonin and falls in elderly people is complicated—and often overstated online.

**What the data actually shows:** In a large UK study, elderly patients taking melatonin (45+ years old) showed a modest increased fracture risk, but only when they had taken 3+ melatonin prescriptions (suggesting chronic use). The effect size was small compared to benzodiazepines and Z-drugs, which showed much stronger associations with falls and fractures. Importantly, melatonin was not significantly associated with fractures in other studies, suggesting the relationship may be indirect (through daytime drowsiness or dizziness) rather than a direct drug effect.

**The realistic concern:** Daytime drowsiness (5–10% of users) and dizziness (3–5%) are real. In an elderly person with balance problems, weak leg muscles, or vision impairment, even mild drowsiness becomes a fall risk. And falls in people over 75 often result in hip fractures, which can trigger a cascade of disability and mortality.

**Risk factors that increase fall danger:** You face higher fall risk if you (1) already have a history of falls, (2) take other CNS-depressing drugs (sedatives, opioids), (3) have orthostatic hypotension (blood pressure drops when standing), (4) have neuropathy or balance disorders, or (5) live alone without assistance.

**What to do:** If fall risk is already a concern, melatonin is worth discussing with your doctor. If you try it, start with the lowest possible dose (0.3–0.5 mg), take it earlier in the evening (8–9 PM rather than right before bed), and have someone monitor you the first few nights. Watch for stumbling, unsteadiness, or grogginess in the morning.

## 7. Safe Dosing for Elderly Patients

Dosing is where the biggest difference between elderly and younger people shows up. The recommendation is simple: use far less than you probably think.

**Recommended dose for seniors: 0.3–2 mg, taken 1 hour before bedtime.**

Most large clinical trials in elderly patients used 2 mg (prolonged-release formulation). This dose showed modest benefits for sleep onset (reducing sleep latency by 8–15 minutes) and was well tolerated. Some gerontologists now recommend even lower doses (0.3–0.5 mg) as a starting point, because many side effects don't appear until doses exceed 2 mg in elderly populations.

**Why not 5–10 mg?** Those doses are commonly available over-the-counter and popular with younger people. But research in elderly patients specifically shows that doses above 2 mg provide little additional sleep benefit and increase side effect risk significantly. Exposure to higher melatonin concentrations can lead to melatonin receptor desensitization—your body's receptors become less responsive—potentially worsening insomnia over time if you keep escalating the dose.

**Formulation matters:** Immediate-release melatonin (regular tablets/liquid) peaks quickly and clears faster, causing less next-day grogginess. Prolonged-release formulations maintain melatonin levels longer, which is good for staying asleep but bad for morning alertness. Elderly people often tolerate immediate-release better, though prolonged-release works well if taken early enough (8–9 PM).

**How long to take it:** Melatonin is not intended for long-term daily use in seniors. Clinical trials used durations of 2–12 weeks. Long-term use (months or years) lacks safety data in elderly patients. If you're still not sleeping better after 2–4 weeks, melatonin probably isn't working for you—continuing it exposes you to ongoing interaction risks without benefit.

## 8. When Elderly People Should Avoid Melatonin Entirely

Melatonin is not appropriate for everyone. Skip it if you have:

**Uncontrolled hypertension:** If your blood pressure is already high or unstable, melatonin's blood pressure-lowering effect could destabilize it further.

**History of bleeding or on blood thinners:** Some research suggests melatonin may have mild anticoagulant effects. If you're on warfarin or similar medications, the interaction risk is too high.

**Severe liver disease:** Your liver is where melatonin is metabolized. If you have cirrhosis, hepatitis, or significantly impaired liver function, melatonin accumulates to dangerous levels.

**Seizure disorder:** Melatonin's effects on seizure threshold are unpredictable. Some research suggests it may lower the seizure threshold; other research suggests the opposite. Don't experiment without explicit approval from your neurologist.

**Autoimmune disease:** Melatonin is a potent immune modulator. If you have rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, or other autoimmune conditions, melatonin can trigger flares or interfere with treatment.

**Taking fluvoxamine (Luvox):** The interaction is simply too strong. Your doctor will advise against it or use a different antidepressant.

**Already on multiple CNS depressants:** If you're taking sedatives, opioids, or other sleep aids, adding melatonin increases overdose risk and fall risk too much.

## 9. Getting the Right Formulation Matters

One reason melatonin's side effects vary so widely in elderly patients is inconsistent product quality. Melatonin is a dietary supplement in the U.S., meaning the FDA doesn't regulate potency, purity, or labeling. Some bottles contain 30% less melatonin than labeled; others contain 30% more. Some contain contaminating serotonin (which can cause its own complications, especially with antidepressants).

For elderly patients, this unpredictability is dangerous. You need to know exactly how much melatonin you're getting so you can predict side effects and manage interactions.

**What to look for:** Choose melatonin supplements verified by a third-party testing organization like USP (U.S. Pharmacopeia), ConsumerLab, or NSF. The verification mark on the label confirms the supplement contains what it says it contains, at the right potency.

BioAbsorb Melatonin is third-party tested and USP-verified, with transparent labeling of melatonin content. Available in multiple formulations—immediate-release (faster onset, less next-day grogginess) and extended-release (better for sleep maintenance)—each dosed for elderly safety (0.5–2 mg). If you choose a liposomal formulation, improved absorption means slightly higher bioavailability, which is beneficial when you need predictable dosing but requires starting at the lower end of the dose range (0.3–0.5 mg instead of 1–2 mg).

## 10. Elderly-Specific Questions Answered

**Q: Is melatonin safer than Ambien (zolpidem) for me as a senior?**  
A: Yes, substantially. Ambien carries risks of cognitive decline, morning grogginess that increases fall risk, and dependence—none of which apply to melatonin. However, melatonin is also less effective; expect a 10–15 minute reduction in time to fall asleep with melatonin, versus 30–45 minutes with Ambien. Start with melatonin because it's safer. If it doesn't work after 2–4 weeks at appropriate doses, discuss prescription alternatives with your doctor.

**Q: I'm 78 and on blood pressure medication. Can I take melatonin?**  
A: Possibly, but with caution and monitoring. Melatonin lowers blood pressure modestly. If you're already well-controlled on medication, adding melatonin could push you too low. Have your doctor check your 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure before and after starting melatonin. Start with 0.3 mg and watch for dizziness.

**Q: I take sertraline (Zoloft). Can I take melatonin?**  
A: Yes, but at a lower dose. Sertraline is less of a CYP1A2 inhibitor than fluvoxamine, so the interaction is moderate rather than severe. Talk to your doctor about starting at 0.3–0.5 mg instead of 1–2 mg. If you experience excessive drowsiness, reduce the dose further.

**Q: I've been taking 10 mg melatonin for three years. Is that safe?**  
A: Probably not long-term, especially as a senior. That dose is too high for elderly patients—your body may have developed partial tolerance (receptor desensitization), meaning the dose becomes less effective over time. More concerning, 3 years of use exceeds the safety data window. Discuss tapering down with your doctor and consider whether sleep problems have underlying causes (sleep apnea, medication side effects, untreated depression) that should be addressed instead.

**Q: What if melatonin makes me too drowsy in the morning?**  
A: Take it earlier in the evening (8–9 PM instead of 10–11 PM) or switch to immediate-release instead of prolonged-release. Both allow melatonin to clear your system before morning. If drowsiness persists, lower the dose by half and see if that helps.

## Conclusion

Melatonin is generally safe for seniors and significantly safer than prescription sleep aids. But aging bodies process supplements differently, and most elderly people take multiple medications that interact with melatonin in unpredictable ways. The key is starting low (0.3–2 mg), choosing a third-party tested product so you know what you're taking, and monitoring closely for blood pressure and dizziness changes. If you have concerns about any of the side effects described here, or if you're on multiple medications, discuss melatonin with your doctor before starting.

**Consult your doctor before taking melatonin, especially if you're over 75, take blood pressure medications, take antidepressants, or have a history of falls or low blood pressure.**

## Research References

Comprehensive review of melatonin pharmacology and safety in older adults, documenting common side effects (headache, nausea, dizziness) and age-specific cardiovascular effects (blood pressure reduction, hypothermia risk).
2. **Should Melatonin Be Used as a Sleeping Aid for Elderly People?** Canadian Medical Association Journal (2019). This article from BioAbsorb Nutraceuticals (last updated August 7, 2026, by the BioAbsorb Editorial Team) provides a comprehensive, evidence-based guide to the side effects of melatonin in elderly patients (65+). The core message is that melatonin is generally safe for seniors and significantly safer than prescription sleep aids (benzodiazepines and Z-drugs), but aging bodies metabolize supplements differently and polypharmacy creates unpredictable interactions.

Key facts and statistics:
- Most common side effects: daytime drowsiness (5-10%), dizziness (3-5%), headache (5-8%), nausea (3-5%), and vivid dreams (2-5%).
- Clinical trials in adults 55-93 years show adverse effects from melatonin (2 mg) ranging 6-24%, versus 5-21% with placebo—often not statistically significant.
- Melatonin reduces blood pressure by approximately 6 mmHg systolic and 4 mmHg diastolic during sleep, most pronounced in early morning (3:00-8:00 AM).
- Recommended dose for seniors is 0.3-2 mg taken 1 hour before bedtime—much lower than the common 5-10 mg OTC doses. Doses above 2 mg provide little added benefit and increase side effect risk, including receptor desensitization.
- Elderly patients reach higher peak blood levels from the same dose due to less efficient liver enzyme (CYP1A2) metabolism; melatonin bioavailability ranges from 1-74% and is unpredictable.

Key drug interactions: The most dangerous is fluvoxamine (Luvox), which can increase melatonin blood levels 12-fold or more. Other SSRIs (citalopram, fluoxetine), proton pump inhibitors, blood thinners (warfarin), diabetes medications, immunosuppressants, and seizure medications also interact. Melatonin is unregulated as a dietary supplement in the US, with actual potency varying by ±50% from labels.

Contraindications: uncontrolled hypertension, history of bleeding or blood thinners, severe liver disease, seizure disorder, autoimmune disease, taking fluvoxamine, or already on multiple CNS depressants.

Melatonin should not be used long-term in seniors; clinical trials covered 2-12 weeks. Falls risk is considered overstated but real, mediated through daytime drowsiness and dizziness rather than a direct drug effect. The article recommends third-party tested products (USP, ConsumerLab, NSF verified) and notes BioAbsorb Melatonin is third-party tested and USP-verified with doses of 0.5-2 mg. It concludes by advising seniors, especially those over 75, on blood pressure medications, antidepressants, or with fall history, to consult a doctor before starting melatonin.

This is a MedCram educational video by Dr. Roger Seheult, MD (Board Certified in Internal Medicine, Pulmonary Disease, Critical Care, and Sleep Medicine, and Associate Professor at UC Riverside School of Medicine), published June 19, 2023, explaining how to conquer jet lag using light exposure and melatonin without prescription medications.

KEY CONCEPTS:
- Jet lag occurs when the circadian rhythm (master clock in the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the brain) is out of sync with the external environment, especially during eastward travel.
- Light is the most powerful "zeitgeber" (external cue that entrains biological rhythms). Bright light exposure in the morning ADVANCES the circadian rhythm (shifts it left/earlier), while bright light in the evening DELAYS it (shifts it right/later). Melatonin given in the evening also advances the rhythm.
- Eastward travel (e.g., LA to London, 8-hour time difference) is the most problematic for jet lag because the circadian rhythm can only shift 1-2 hours per day and needs to be advanced to catch up.

PRACTICAL PROTOCOL FOR EASTWARD TRAVEL (advancing circadian rhythm):
1. Expose eyes to bright light for 6 hours starting at (6am + X) where X = number of time zones crossed (e.g., for 8-hour shift: 2-4pm in London)
2. Avoid bright light for 6 hours starting at (8-9pm + X) (e.g., for 8-hour shift: 6am to noon)
3. Take 5mg immediate-release melatonin at 6pm for 3 days prior to travel, then at 10pm-midnight for 4 days after arrival
4. Reduce X by 1-2 each night as the circadian rhythm catches up
- Recommend wearing sunglasses during the cabin light "breakfast" period on the flight (typically 6:30am-noon) to avoid delaying the rhythm at the wrong time.

FOR WESTWARD TRAVEL (delaying circadian rhythm):
- Usually self-corrects naturally because the human circadian rhythm is naturally slightly longer than 24 hours, and the natural light schedule aligns with westward time changes.
- Technical protocol: expose to bright light for 6 hours starting at (8-10pm - X) and avoid light starting at (6-8am - X).

RESEARCH EVIDENCE:
- A 1986 randomized placebo-controlled trial (17 healthy volunteers, British Medical Journal) flew subjects from London to San Francisco for 2 weeks, then back to London (8-hour eastward shift). They took 5mg melatonin vs placebo at 6pm for 3 days before departure and 10pm-midnight for 4 days after arrival. Seven days after arrival, 6 of 9 placebo subjects still had significant jet lag symptoms (score ≥50/100) versus ZERO in the melatonin group — a statistically significant difference.
- Doses of 0.5 to 5mg of melatonin are similarly effective. Immediate-release (not timed-release) melatonin is recommended. Timing is critical — taking melatonin at the wrong time (early in day) can cause sleepiness and delay adaptation.
- Caution: melatonin is not FDA-regulated in the US; buy from brands with third-party laboratory confirmation. Potential interactions with epilepsy and Warfarin need further investigation — discuss with a doctor.
- References cited include the British Medical Journal 1986 trial, a Cochrane systematic review on melatonin for jet lag, and a P&T journal article on jet lag.

URL: https://aasm.org/resources/practiceparameters/pp_circadianrhythm.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) Practice Parameters for the Clinical Evaluation and Treatment of Circadian Rhythm Sleep Disorders (CRSDs), published in SLEEP 2007;30(11):1445-1459, authored by Morgenthaler TI et al. (Standards of Practice Committee of the AASM). A subsequent 2015 clinical practice guideline update (Auger RR et al., J Clin Sleep Med 2015;11(10):1199-1236) updated these recommendations based on new evidence, particularly for elderly and children with/without comorbid psychiatric conditions.

The practice parameters address both exogenous CRSDs (shift work disorder [SWD] and jet lag disorder [JLD]) and endogenous CRSDs (advanced sleep phase disorder [ASPD], delayed sleep phase disorder [DSPD], free-running disorder [FRD], and irregular sleep-wake rhythm disorder [ISWR]). Recommendations are graded as Standard, Guideline, or Option based on evidence levels (Oxford System for Evidence-Based Medicine, adapted by Eddy).

KEY EVALUATION RECOMMENDATIONS:
- Sleep log/diary: Indicated for assessment of all suspected CRSDs (Guideline)
- Actigraphy: Indicated for diagnosis of ASPD, DSPD, SWD (Guideline); ISWR, FRD (Option); useful as outcome measure for treatment response in all CRSDs (Guideline)
- Polysomnography: Not routinely indicated for CRSD diagnosis, but indicated to rule out other primary sleep disorders (Standard)
- MEQ (Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire): Insufficient evidence for routine clinical use (Option)
- Circadian phase markers: Useful to confirm FRD diagnosis in sighted and unsighted patients (Option); insufficient evidence for SWD, JLD, ASPD, DSPD, ISWR

TREATMENT RECOMMENDATIONS BY DISORDER:
- SWD: Planned napping before/during night shift (Standard); timed light exposure in work environment with morning light restriction (Guideline); melatonin before daytime sleep (Guideline); hypnotics for daytime sleep (Guideline); modafinil (Guideline) and caffeine (Option) for alertness; MEQ and circadian markers of unproved usefulness (Option)
- JLD: Melatonin at appropriate time to reduce symptoms and improve sleep (Standard); home-based sleep hours for brief stays ≤2 days (Option); morning bright light + shifting sleep schedule pre-eastward travel (Option); benzodiazepine receptor agonist hypnotics short-term for insomnia (Option); caffeine for sleepiness but may disrupt nighttime sleep (Option); insufficient evidence for actigraphy, PSG, or circadian markers (Option)
- ASPD: Prescribed sleep/wake scheduling, timed light, or timed melatonin (all Option); PSG not routinely indicated (Standard); MEQ and circadian markers insufficient evidence (Option)
- DSPD: Morning light exposure (Guideline); properly timed melatonin (Guideline); chronotherapy (Option); Vitamin B12 NOT indicated (Guideline); PSG not routinely indicated (Standard); insufficient evidence for hypnotics/stimulants (Option)
- FRD: Sleep logs useful (Option); circadian phase markers confirm diagnosis in sighted and unsighted (Option); prescribed sleep/wake scheduling in sighted (Option); timed light in sighted (Option); timed melatonin in sighted (Option); timed melatonin indicated for blind individuals (Guideline)
- ISWR: Mixed modality therapy may be effective in elderly-demented/nursing home patients (Guideline) or those with moderate to severe mental retardation (Option); timed melatonin may be effective in moderate-severe mental retardation but not recommended for elderly-demented/nursing home patients (Option)

The literature review retrieved 2,084 articles; all evidence grading was performed by independent review by at least two experts (one evidence review professional, one content expert). All authors completed conflict-of-interest statements; the paper was not industry supported. ~20% of U.S. workers are involved in some form of shift work.

URL: https://www.mattressnut.com/melatonin-jet-lag

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Melatonin for Jet Lag: The Right Dose and Timing Protocol

This article from Mattress Nut provides a comprehensive guide on using melatonin to combat jet lag, framing jet lag as a circadian misalignment (a "phase problem") rather than simple tiredness. The core recommendation is to take **0.5–5 mg of melatonin about 30 minutes before destination bedtime**, starting the night of arrival, for 3–5 nights. The article emphasizes that **eastbound travel is significantly harder than westbound** due to the circadian system's intrinsic period being slightly longer than 24 hours.

### Key Recommendations:
- **Skip melatonin for trips under 3 time zones.**
- **Dose:** Lower end (0.5–3 mg) is almost always the right starting point; higher doses don't produce larger phase shifts but do cause more next-day sedation, grogginess, vivid dreams, and headaches.
- **Timing:** "Destination bedtime" means local clock time at the destination — not what the body thinks is bedtime. Consistency across 3–5 nights matters more than precision on any single night.
- **Eastbound protocol (advancing):** Pre-trip, shift bedtime earlier by 30–60 min/night for 3–5 days before departure with morning bright light (0.5 mg at new bedtime accelerates the shift). On arrival, take 0.5–3 mg 30–60 minutes before local bedtime, continuing 3–5 nights (3 nights for 5–8 zones; 5 nights for 9+ zones). Pair with 15–30 minutes of morning light within an hour of waking.
- **Westbound protocol (delaying):** Easier direction; many adapt within 2–3 days with light and meal timing alone. Evening melatonin at destination bedtime can actively oppose the delay you want. Maximize evening light and block early morning light.
- **Light therapy:** Light is the most powerful time cue — for eastbound, maximize morning light and suppress evening light; for westbound, do the reverse. A 10,000-lux light box is a reasonable substitute when outdoor access isn't possible. Light and melatonin together reduce adaptation time by 30–50% versus either alone.

### Evidence:
- The American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2015 clinical practice guideline **strongly recommends** melatonin for jet lag.
- Studies in cabin crew, military personnel, and long-haul travelers show melatonin cuts subjective jet-lag scores by **30–50%**.
- About **20% of people are non-responders**.

### FAQ Highlights:
- Melatonin should not be taken during destination daytime or "loaded" on the plane.
- Safe for children over 4 only with pediatric guidance (low-dose 0.5–1 mg); not recommended during pregnancy without obstetrician clearance.
- Avoid combining with alcohol or prescription sleep aids like Ambien without clinical guidance.
- Melatonin is OTC in US, Canada, UK, Australia, and most of Asia; prescription-only at higher doses in France and Germany.
- Cruises shifting 1 hour/day are self-adjusting — no melatonin needed.

### Product Selection:
- Avoid aggressive "fast-dissolve 10 mg" travel-marketed products; a 1 mg or 3 mg plain tablet is the right buy for almost everyone.

The article also promotes **NooCube Sleep Upgrade**, a melatonin-free sleep supplement (lemon balm 600 mg + magnesium + lavender) marketed as a milder, hormone-free alternative, claiming 35% faster sleep onset and 28% higher sleep score in clinical testing.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Intrinsic ... ---
URL: https://aasm.org/resources/doc/treatmentofintrinsiccrswdsdraftguideline.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is the 2015 American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) Clinical Practice Guideline for the treatment of intrinsic Circadian Rhythm Sleep-Wake Disorders (CRSWDs), authored by R. Robert Auger, MD, and colleagues. It provides evidence-based treatment recommendations for four intrinsic CRSWDs: Advanced Sleep-Wake Phase Disorder (ASWPD), Delayed Sleep-Wake Phase Disorder (DSWPD), Non-24-Hour Sleep-Wake Rhythm Disorder (N24SWD), and Irregular Sleep-Wake Rhythm Disorder (ISWRD). The guideline replaces the previous 2007 AASM Practice Parameters and excludes extrinsic disorders (shift work and jet lag).

**Methods:** A four-member Task Force (TF) with CRSWD expertise, no declared conflicts of interest, used GRADE methodology. Eight PICO questions were developed. Three literature searches were conducted across PubMed, Embase, and PsycInfo (examining 2,063 abstracts initially, plus 453 additional publications from June 2012-March 2014). Critical outcomes were defined with clinical significance thresholds (30-min changes for circadian phase and TST; 15-min changes for ISL, SOT, SOffT; entrainment status for N24SWD). Recommendations were classified as Strong For, Weak For, Weak Against, or Strong Against, or No Recommendation.

**Key Recommendations:**
- **ASWPD (adults):** WEAK FOR evening light therapy (~4,000 lux broad spectrum light for 2 hours daily between 20:00-23:00, 12-day treatment). Quality of evidence: VERY LOW.
- **DSWPD (adults with/without depression):** WEAK FOR strategically-timed melatonin (5 mg between 19:00-21:00 for 28 days). Quality: LOW.
- **DSWPD (children/adolescents without comorbidities):** WEAK FOR strategically-timed melatonin (0.15 mg/kg, 1.5-2.0 hours before bedtime for 6 nights). Quality: MODERATE.
- **DSWPD (children/adolescents with psychiatric comorbidities):** WEAK FOR melatonin (fast-release, 3-5 mg, taken 18:00-19:00 for 4 weeks). Quality: LOW.
- **DSWPD (children/adolescents):** WEAK FOR post-awakening light therapy (natural sunlight or ~1000 lux lamp, 0.5-2 hours, advanced by 0.5 hours daily to 06:00 target) combined with behavioral treatments. Quality: LOW.
- **N24SWD (blind adults):** WEAK FOR strategically-timed melatonin (0.5-10 mg, 1 hour before bedtime or at 21:00, for 26-81 days). Quality: LOW.
- **ISWRD (elderly with dementia):** WEAK FOR light therapy (2500-5000 lux white light, 1-2 hours, 09:00-11:00, for 4-10 weeks). Quality: VERY LOW.
- **ISWRD (elderly with dementia):** STRONG AGAINST sleep-promoting medications (due to increased risks of falls and other adverse outcomes in demented elderly patients).
- **ISWRD (older people with dementia):** WEAK AGAINST melatonin use (no benefit on TST shown; potential for harm).
- **ISWRD (children/adolescents with neurologic disorders):** WEAK FOR strategically-timed melatonin (2-10 mg within the hour before planned bedtime). Quality: MODERATE.
- **ISWRD (demented elderly):** WEAK AGAINST combination of light therapy with melatonin (no additional benefit, may increase harms).

No recommendations were made for prescribed sleep-wake scheduling, timed physical activity/exercise, strategic light avoidance, wakefulness-promoting medications, or other somatic interventions, due to insufficient evidence.

**Background:** The guideline explains the two-process model of sleep regulation (Process S—homeostatic drive; Process C—circadian drive), the role of the suprachiasmatic nuclei, and entrainment to the 24-hour day primarily via light/dark exposure. Light and melatonin phase response curves (PRCs) are discussed—evening light before CBTmin causes phase delays, morning light after CBTmin causes phase advances; melatonin's PRC is ~180 degrees out of phase with light's PRC, with DLMO serving as the melatonin inflection point. The human circadian system is most sensitive to short wavelength blue light (~480 nm).

**ICSD Updates:** The guideline notes ICSD-3 changes, including incorporation of "wake" into the terminology, emphasis on caregiver input, recommendation of actigraphy-derived diagnosis (7 days for most disorders; 14 days for N24SWD), and de-emphasis on "conventional" clock times.
</summary>
